articles.title: From Document Classification to Scholar Shortlists: An Audit of Shortlist Sensitivity to OpenAlex's Topic-Classifier Update
articles.authors: Yuan Gao
articles.abstract: Open databases assign topics to works; their case rests on work-level agreement, institutional mix and citation-impact ranking. A list of people adds an ordering rule and a cutoff; none of the three checks covers an author profile or a fixed-length list. In October 2026 OpenAlex replaced its topic assignment. We scored a frozen set under both assignments, holding works, authors, pool and cutoff fixed and re-estimating weights per label world. At work level, 47.0% of 429,985 works changed their primary topic. In top-50 lists we build for six keyword-defined query domains, 80 of 300 seats changed hands (26.7%), 18% to 42% by domain. Across the two specifications built from the archived label tables (B, C) the pooled figure stays between 23.7% and 26.7%; a crossed bracket (D) gives 24.7%, a counting variant (E) 23.3%, and a separate endpoint bracket (A), read on 16 October, 29.3%; three to eight of each top ten kept their seats. Pooled, 42 of the 80 dropped seats fall outside the narrow band, so enrichment at the cut is partial; shorter lists turn over faster. Labels, text and weights moved together, so this is an association between two versions of one database, not an isolated classifier effect. For research evaluation, the question is whether the list, at its length, still names the same people. A shortlist is a reading of one label version at one length; its stability is separate from label accuracy. We state what it should report: the label version, the date it was scored, the length, and the width of the cutoff band.

articles.title: Gate the claim, not the tool: verification for AI-accelerated research in nutrition
articles.authors: Tauseef Ahmad Khan; Paraskevi Massara
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and agentic workflows can accelerate nutrition science across living systematic reviews, dietary assessment and cohort analyses, yet they have also fuelled a surge of formulaic papers mined from open datasets. Journals and funders have responded largely by restricting how AI may be used, especially in writing. Because AI use leaves no reliable trace in a single paper, such rules cannot be enforced; they drive use out of sight, penalize honest authors who disclose it, and fall out of date within months as models improve. A gate works only when what it checks is visible at submission. When three publishers stopped accepting unvalidated papers built on the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), their NHANES publications fell by 72% in the first nine months of 2026, showing that visible gates work, though a rule that blunt can also turn away sound epidemiology. Rather than policing the tool, nutrition science should use AI openly under human scientific judgement and hold every result to four verification gates scaled to its consequence: depositing data, code and agent logs so others can rerun the work; naming an accountable investigator who understands the study design and answers for each claim made; independently verifying findings that could change clinical practice or dietary policy; and disclosing what AI and humans did without penalty. As output grows, papers will likely become concise accounts for human readers resting on machine-auditable records, shifting prestige from the journal name to whether a claim matters when verified.

articles_hidden.title: Paper I: A Funder-Driven Registered Report Initiative Compared with Standard Applications: A Study on Research Quality
articles_hidden.authors: Sigrid Hegna Ingvaldsen; Ida Svege; Jan-Ole Hesselberg
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background and aim: A registered report (RR) commits researchers to a peer-reviewed protocol before results are known, reducing reporting bias and promoting open science. Foundation Dam, a health research funder, launched a two-year initiative incentivising RR applications. This study describes projects choosing RR versus standard applications (SA) and assesses differences in reviewer scores.

Method: The sample comprises all research grant applicants at Foundation Dam, 2023 to 2025 (N=1194). Using a multilevel linear regression model, we compared Excellence and Implementation scores between RR and SA applications across the 2023 research call (SA n=358) with those from the 2024/2025 calls (RR n=142, SA n=694). Intraclass correlation coefficients assessed reviewer-related variance, and exploratory analyses examined reviewers' confidence and disagreement levels. 

Preregistered Stage 1 protocol: https://osf.io/jq84x/overview (date of in-principle acceptance: 20/01/2026).

Results: RR applications were not scored significantly higher than SA applications on Excellence (β= −0.08, 95% CI [−0.20, 0.03], p=.131) or Implementation (β= −0.04, 95% CI [−0.14, 0.06], p=.408). Excellence scores were slightly lower in the 2024/2025 calls than in the 2023 call (β= −0.08, 95% CI [−0.16, 0.00], p=.048), whereas Implementation scores did not change. Reviewer variability accounted for 18.3% of the variance in Excellence scores and 15.4% in Implementation scores, and was not greater for RR than SA applications. 

Conclusion: Findings do not support that choosing RR format yields higher assessed research quality at the application stage, but are informative for funders and journals developing their own RR models.

articles.title: Striking the Limits of the Rich-Get-Richer and the Poor-Get-Richer Hypothesis?  Trait Interpersonal Emotion Regulation and its Associations with Instant Messaging Emotional Support and Mental Health in Daily Life
articles.authors: Karen De Raeymaecker; Imke Baetens; Margot Bastin; Martijn Van Heel
articles.abstract: Up until now, the role of dispositions in the psychosocial effects of adolescent instant messaging (IM) remains inconclusive. While the straightforward rich-get-richer and poor-get-richer hypotheses do not allow for nuances about the individual-specific (dis)advantages of offline and online interactions, the literature on the dispositional tendencies for interpersonal emotion regulation shows a more complex picture. In this ecological momentary study (one week, 8 assessments/day), we adopted the rich-get-richer and poor-get-richer framework to test the social and psychological effects of IM with regard to the dispositional tendencies for co-rumination, co-dampening, and co-enhancing in 181 Belgian adolescents (n = 181; Mage = 15.04; 63% women). Adolescents with a higher tendency for co-dampening reported lower mean levels of momentary positive affect. Individuals with a clear tendency for co-enhancing experienced, on average, higher momentary IM emotional support. Regarding the tendency for co-rumination, no significant differences were found. Notably, (dis)advantageous social effects did not go together with similar psychological effects. Unexpectedly, IM behaviors (e.g., IM negative social exchange) were, regardless of the studied outcome and the level of analysis, systematically significant. Overall, this study endorses the importance of the abovementioned dispositional tendencies. Yet, their value was more limited than the rich-get-richer and the poor-get-richer hypotheses predicted.

articles.title: Personality Prediction from Moments to Lifetimes
articles.authors: Emorie D Beck; Adam Taylor Nissen; Eileen Kranz Graham; Dan Mroczek
articles.abstract: Personality is robustly linked to long-term outcomes, yet predicting momentary behavior (i.e., who does what, when, and where) remains challenging. We argue that personality and its outcomes can be understood at multiple levels within an emergent hierarchy, and that prediction requires identifying what level(s) is most informative for a given target. Broad traits reliably predict distal outcomes such as cognitive aging and mortality but reveal little about underlying processes. Within-person patterns capture shorter-term regularities, though heterogeneity is often overlooked. Momentary processes unfold as complex, multivariate systems that support personalized prediction but challenge generalization. We therefore propose a bottom-up integrative framework that derives comparable features from person-specific dynamics and tests whether they predict outcomes at other levels. Emerging evidence suggests that such features can bridge levels and support more integrative, explainable prediction.

articles.title: Building Connection Through Conversation: Linguistic Convergence and Neural Complexity in Dyadic Interaction
articles.authors: Grace Qiyuan Miao; Zachary P Rosen; Agnieszka Pluta; MATTHEW D. LIEBERMAN; Rick Dale; Yuwei Li
articles.abstract: Interpersonal connection emerges through conversation. Theories of interpersonal communication hold that conversational partners increasingly align in how they express meaning, build on one another’s contributions, and experience connection. Yet how such alignment unfolds during a conversation, and how it relates to the experience of a “good” interaction, remains largely untested. Seventy dyads of previously unacquainted individuals held naturalistic conversations while dual functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) recorded neural activity. We measured semantic alignment using convergence entropy and substantive exchange, the number of adjacent turns in which both partners contributed contentful talk. Contrary to a convergence account, dyads broadened their semantic range over time. Subjective experience was predicted not by semantic alignment but by substantive exchange, particularly in shallow-prompt conversations. Neurally, inter-brain synchrony tracked substantive exchange, whereas semantic alignment was reflected in partners’ matched turn-to-turn neural dynamics. First conversations build connection through reciprocal, substantive exchange, with distinct linguistic and neural signatures.

articles.title: Thought for food: Individual differences in how food decisions are made
articles.authors: Caitlin Lloyd; Zarrar Shehzad; Janet Schebendach; Akram Bakkour; Alice M Xue; Naomi Assaf; Rayman Jiliani; B. Timothy Walsh; Daphna Shohamy; Joanna Steinglass
articles.abstract: Daily food decisions accumulate to impact physical health, but making choices consistent with longer-term health goals can prove challenging. Prior research has focused predominantly on dampening preferences for highly palatable foods, or exerting self-control, as the mechanism for healthier food choices. Consequently, the range of cognitive strategies for healthy eating, and how they vary with demographic characteristics, remains unclear. Here, a large US sample (N = 1,052) completed an online food rating and choice task, and demographic and eating behavior questionnaires. Participants rated foods across 17 dimensions, which were reduced to three underlying core food attributes by factor analysis: Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami (capturing food savoriness). All attributes influenced food choices. A multi-attribute drift diffusion model quantified distinct yet latent choice processes, including the deliberation required prior to making a choice. The influence of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami on choice varied across the study population. Women, individuals endorsing higher levels of eating restraint, and individuals with lower BMI selected subjectively healthier foods more frequently. Making subjectively healthier choices was not dependent only on engaging self-control. Rather, individuals making subjectively healthier choices perceived subjectively healthier foods as tastier. In addition, individuals endorsing high levels of eating restraint required less deliberation when making choices, suggesting more automatic decision-making. These findings suggest multiple routes to making healthier food choices and question the narrative that food tastiness must be sacrificed to support physical health.

articles.title: What Are Situationships? Characteristics of an Ambiguous Relationship Type
articles.authors: Saffron Marli Costello; William Costello; Andrew G. Thomas; Martin Graff
articles.abstract:
Situationships are an emerging relationship type, yet quantitative research remains limited. Here we examined situationship characteristics and experiences, using sex and sociosexuality as theoretically relevant starting points for understanding individual variation. We conducted an exploratory, cross-sectional survey of 390 adults (68% women; M age = 27.41 years, SD = 8.66) from 48 countries who reported on current, or emotionally significant past, situationships. Participants endorsed proposed situationship characteristics and provided their own open-ended definitions which underwent structured content coding. These analyses informed a working definition of situationships as intimate, relationship-like connections lacking clarity about commitment, relationship status, or future trajectory. Although 56% of participants entered situationships hoping for a relationship, and 55% assumed sexual exclusivity, only 9% of reported past situationships progressed to a committed relationship. Compared with men, women more often emphasised ambiguity in their definitions, perceived greater long-term potential, and expressed stronger hopes for commitment. They also more strongly agreed that they would feel betrayed if their situationship partner saw other people. Relative to the reference sample, both sexes reported more unrestricted sociosexual behaviour, whereas women reported more restricted sociosexual attitudes. This pattern raises questions about incongruence between women’s sexual experiences and preferences, with potential implications for wellbeing. The observed sex differences also motivate future research to examine whether divergent mating goals between partners shape situationship experiences.
Keywords: situationships, romantic relationships, sex differences, sociosexuality

articles.title: The Governed Heart:  Institutional Emotion Regulation through Policy, Proclamation, and Proxy
articles.authors: Nicholas Paul Camp; Brett Quaid Ford
articles.abstract: Governments, schools, hospitals, companies, and myriad other organizations structure institutional life and mobilize large numbers of people to accomplish what they cannot do alone. Institutions also regulate something less visible, but equally consequential: the emotions of their constituents. We introduce institutional emotion regulation as the formal processes by which institutions, through organizations, seek to influence the emotions people have, when they have them, and how they experience and express these emotions. Research across the social sciences has examined how particular organizations attempt to shape affective experiences, but these literatures have largely developed in disciplinary silos or domain-specific settings. We propose that these phenomena reflect a distinct level of emotion regulation, characterized by emotion goals held by organizations and pursued through formal institutional means. We develop a framework that crosses four established stages of emotion regulation – targeting situations, attention, appraisals, and responses – with three distinctive vectors of institutional influence: policies, the rules and structures that shape people’s environments; proclamations, communications directed toward the public; and proxies, the agents who act on behalf of the organization. Our framework provides a common language for understanding how institutions influence emotional life at scale and suggests novel directions for psychological study while surfacing broader questions for society around the appropriate use of this influence.

articles.title: Own and others' confidence in social information use
articles.authors: Andrea Gradassi; Wouter van den Bos; Lucas Molleman
articles.abstract: The behaviour of friends, colleagues, television hosts and social media feeds affects what we buy, how we dress, and who we vote for. People tend to be more sensitive to social influence when unsure about their beliefs and when the source is highly confident. Less is known about the relative impact of the confidence of self and others’ on social information use, and how they jointly shape social transmission. We present results of two incentivized decision-making tasks (N=203 and N=213, samples from the U.S.A.) where participants could adjust their initial estimates upon observing estimates of peers and their confidence. Adjustments were most sensitive to the confidence of others when participants’ own confidence was low. Confidence also affected heuristic strategies: confident others prompted participants to compromise and copy social information more often, rather than to stick with their initial estimates. We discuss how following confident others when uncertain can improve decision-making, but also leaves people vulnerable to sources of misinformation.

articles.title: Disrupting social media habits: a one-week detox produces enduring reductions in use and automaticity
articles.authors: Tim van Timmeren; Suhaavi Kochhar; Mariek Magdalena Petra Vanden Abeele; Sanne de Wit
articles.abstract: This randomised controlled trial examines if a one-week social media abstinence intervention can reduce social media use by lowering automaticity of and craving for social media use. Participants motivated to reduce their social media use were assigned to an immediate one-week detox (N = 50) or a waitlist control condition (N = 64). Using a combination of smartphone usage logging and weekly surveys, we found that the detox produced significant reductions in social media use (d = 0.51), automaticity (d = 1.10), and craving (d = 0.58) one week post-detox relative to the waitlist group. Exploratory mediation analyses provided suggestive evidence that automaticity partially mediated the detox's effect on social media use. Furthermore, baseline automaticity predicted self-reported vulnerability to slips of action during the detox, i.e. spontaneous attempts to open removed apps. Pooling data from both groups after each had completed the detox (N = 108), we found that the reductions persisted across the three-week follow-up and that social media use remained below baseline at a six-month follow-up in a subsample (N = 46). The detox also shifted participants' subjective relationship with social media, increasing perceived control and reducing self-reported mindlessness, without changing how much they liked it or considered it purposeful. Together, these findings suggest that for those who want to cut back, taking a short break is an effective way to disrupt social media habits and restore a sense of control.

articles.title: Metacognitive Monitoring in Naturalistic Translation: a Signal Detection Approach
articles.authors: Aishvarya Raj
articles.abstract:
A novel signal detection approach was applied to translation behavioural data to assess
metacognitive sensitivity for complex, naturalistic tasks, using reformulation behaviour as an
implicit proxy for the confidence response. Existing units of segmentation (Production units
(PU)) were utilised to form trials made up of a Type-1 decision and a Type-2 response. By
using AUROC2, metacognitive sensitivity was estimated for two language-pair corpora under
a lower and upper bound on the response window: an English-Spanish group, where AUROC2
= 0.618 (upper bound) and 0.567 (lower bound), and an English-German group, where
AUROC2 = 0.625 (upper bound) and 0.539 (lower bound). Under the upper bound, estimates
were reproducible across both corpora, agreeing to within 0.007. Individual differences in
metacognitive sensitivity were dissociable from translation accuracy and varied considerably
between individual translators. Overall, reformulation behaviour during the drafting phase
carried information about the accuracy of individual productions, as judged against the
translator’s own post-revision translation, and this information was not reducible to their
overall accuracy.

articles.title: Recruiting families into preventive parenting programs: Messaging responses and participation barriers among Chinese-heritage and White parents
articles.authors: Katie Qintan Lin; Emma Marshall; Danhua Zhu; John W Toumbourou; Elizabeth Westrupp
articles.abstract:
Objective: Preventive parenting programs can reduce child mental health risks, but equitable reach requires effective recruitment. Little is known about how recruitment messaging can engage underserved culturally diverse families while retaining broad population appeal. We compared responses to recruitment messaging and participation barriers among Chinese-heritage and White parents. 
Methods: Parents of children aged 2-5 years (100 Chinese-heritage, 101 White) in English-speaking Western countries were recruited online. Participants rated six parenting program recruitment messages based on the Theory of Planned Behaviour, Goal-Directed Behaviour, Norm Activation Model, their combination, or Chinese cultural values (guan and harmony), and nine participation barriers. Mixed-effects regression models examined participation likelihood, perceived program usefulness, and barrier relevance by ethnicity and message/barrier type. 
Results: Chinese-heritage parents reported lower participation likelihood and perceived program usefulness, and higher average barrier relevance than White parents. Ethnicity-by-message interactions were not significant; descriptively, guan was highest rated among Chinese-heritage parents and Goal-Directed Behaviour among White parents, while the combined behavioural theory message was highly rated across groups. Ethnicity-by-barrier interactions were significant: Chinese-heritage parents rated seven of nine barriers as more relevant compared to White parents. Lack of time was most relevant among Chinese-heritage parents; concern about data security was most relevant among White parents, although its relevance did not differ significantly between groups. 
Conclusions: Findings extend research on cultural adaptation to recruitment, and highlight the need to balance cultural responsiveness with broad appeal while addressing families’ differing barriers to participation.

articles.title: Building Ethical Voice:  Students’ Self-Reported Experience of Expressing a Christian Perspective on Business Ethics through LEGO® Serious Play®
articles.authors: Todd Pfeifer; David Robert Dunaetz; Susan Barton; LaShan Epperson; Wendi Dykes McGehee
articles.abstract: LEGO® Serious Play® (LSP) is a methodology designed to help individuals and groups engage in meaningful problem-solving and communication as they address a variety of individual and organizational challenges. An LSP intervention was designed to help undergraduate students gain experience in expressing a Christian perspective on business ethics. Results revealed that the intervention significantly increased students’ self-reported experience of expressing a Christian perspective on ethics (Mdifference = .54, SDdifference = .68, d = .80, p < .001). The results suggest that LSP can effectively facilitate student experience in expressing a Christian perspective on business ethics and can potentially contribute to other learning outcomes.

articles.title: Be a Meditator Today: Testing Identity-Based Message Framing for Meditation in a Digital Field Experiment
articles.authors: Michael Bowen
articles.abstract:
Objectives. Brief in-app messages are commonly used to prompt meditation, but little is known about which message features influence engagement. Drawing on the reasoned action approach and research on self-identity, this study tested whether framing meditation as an identity (“Be a meditator today”) rather than a behavior (“Meditate today”) increases engagement, and whether any effect depends on prior engagement.

Methods. In a randomized field experiment on Spotify, 3,000 U.S. adults who had recently listened to a popular meditation teacher received one of two in-app messages that differed only in identity versus behavior framing. Outcomes were message click-through and listening to the teacher’s content during the treatment period, analyzed by intent to treat. Logistic regression tested moderation by prior listening.

Results. Click-through did not differ between conditions (8.2% vs. 8.2%; difference = −0.05 percentage points, 95% CI [−2.03, 1.92]). Identity framing did not increase listening during the treatment period (Mann–Whitney U = 1,106,605, p = .313; mean difference = 1.26 min, 95% CI [−5.72, 8.24]). Prior listening (median split) did not moderate the effect of framing (interaction OR = 0.93, 95% CI [0.55, 1.56], p = .77).

Conclusions. Identity-based framing did not increase engagement, even among an audience for whom the meditator identity was plausible. Consistent with the reasoned action approach, changing a message’s grammatical form without changing the beliefs it makes salient may offer little leverage over behavior.

articles.title: From Bulking to Cutting: Social Media, Self-Esteem, and Disordered Eating in Young Men
articles.authors: Jakub Smolinski; Jaynie Rance; Menna Price
articles.abstract: Bulking and cutting (caloric surplus and restriction) are increasingly common among young men but remain under-researched within disordered eating frameworks. This study examined social media use and self-esteem as predictors, as well as their association with disordered eating and bulking and cutting behaviours. Seventy-six physically active UK men aged 18-25 years (M = 22.07, SD = 2.07) completed online measures of social media use, self-esteem, disordered eating (restraint, eating concern, shape concern, weight concern), and bulking and cutting behaviours. Higher social media use predicted higher eating concern (p = .003), while lower self-esteem predicted higher eating and shape concerns (p = .029, p = <.001). Neither social media use nor self-esteem predicted restraint, bulking, or cutting. Exploratory mediation analyses showed that restraint fully mediated the association between shape concern and cutting behaviour (p = < .001). Social media use and self-esteem appear to relate to specific disordered eating symptoms, whereas bulking and cutting may be more closely linked to restraint processes. These findings support expanding conceptualisations of disordered eating in young men to include muscle-oriented dietary behaviours and their distinct psychological pathways.

articles.title: A “Human-Like” Stroop Effect No Longer Implies a Human Participant
articles.authors: Talha Özüdoğru; Christian Janssen; Silja Renooij; Christoph Strauch; Leendert van Maanen
articles.abstract: Researchers have long assumed that online behavioral experiments are completed by humans, an assumption AI agents can now violate. We asked whether agent and human data can be distinguished. We compared Stroop data from 51 respondents each: humans verified in person, an artificial experiment agent, and an online sample. All agent-generated respondents showed the congruency effect and passed six quality checks. A one-class support vector machine (SVM) trained only on human data achieved a median accuracy of 63%. A supervised SVM trained on human and agent data achieved 94%. At an assumed 5% contamination rate, most of its flags would be false alarms. The supervised SVM did not generalize to an agent it was not trained on. Neither plausible task performance nor the tested SVMs reliably distinguished human from agent data. These findings suggest that human participation should be safeguarded through study design rather than through screening afterward.

articles.title: Learning to Care More About Distant Others:  A Systematic Moral Reflection Intervention
articles.authors: Charlotte Riedl; Tao Burga; Erola Pons; Zeyiting Gao; Yichen Xu; Patricia Groß; Falk Lieder
articles.abstract: People's willingness to help others declines steeply with social distance: the more distant, different, or stigmatized those in need are, the less time, money, and consideration they receive — even when they need help the most. This article shows that moral learning from the consequences of past decisions can teach people to give more consideration to the welfare of outgroup members in future decisions and increase their outgroup prosociality. We developed a series of Socratic questions that guide people to systematically reflect on how their decision in a social dilemma affected distant others and how they reached it. Across four preregistered experiments (one reported in the Supplemental Materials), learning from a past decision through systematic moral reflection made participants more willing to donate their time and money to charities that help distant others, including real, incentive-compatible donations to charities helping a stigmatized group. Its effects transferred to outgroups the intervention never mentioned, persisted for more than one week, and exceeded those of two established prejudice-reduction interventions: empathy induction and perspective-taking. Process tracing methods and thematic analysis of the lessons participants learned indicated that these changes were mediated by participants learning to deliberate more and give greater consideration to how their actions affect distant others. These findings identify metacognitive learning as a promising pathway to expanding the reach of human generosity toward those who need it most.

articles.title: Use of communication channels in 2x2 strategic games
articles.authors: Veronica Boyce; Avidit Acharya; Michael C. Frank
articles.abstract: How do we use language to coordinate with each other? This question is of interest both from the cognitive science of language perspective as well as the game theory perspective. Here we attempt to bridge the gap between the empirical tradition of studying language use for coordination in reference games with the theoretical and analytic framework of game theory. We conducted a series of 5 real-time online experiments where pairs of participants were matched to play a sequence of 40 2x2 games together (total N=616). Across the experiments, we varied the exact structure of trials, but all experiments involved trials with reward structures modeled on Prisoner’s Dilemma (PD) and Bach or Stravinsky (BoS). We manipulated the presence or absence of a chat interface as a between-pairs manipulation. Despite low levels of use of the communication channel, we found slight differences in outcome between the chat and nochat groups, where pairs who could communicate were slightly more likely to reach coordinated beneficial outcomes in BoS games. In contrast to the predictions of rational actors, participants in both chat and no-chat conditions generally aligned on both cooperating rather than both defecting in PD. Overall, we were limited in our ability to discern the role of communication channels in game strategies due to low uptake in using the communication channels when available.

articles.title: Introducing the One-Shot Download Task: Testing the validity of a new and simple measure of online pro-environmental behavior
articles.authors: Daniel Farrelly; Tia Lippitt; Harvey Thompson
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Measures of actual pro-environmental behaviour are increasingly in environmental psychology due to their increased ecological validity over self-report measures. Here we introduce a new such measure, the One-Shot Download Task (OSD), a brief online behavioural measure in which participants choose between incurring personal costs (completing a tedious task) or environmental costs (downloading unnecessary files associated with carbon emissions). Two studies were conducted (Study 1: N = 104; Study 2: N = 96) that assessed the OSD’s criterion validity by examining associations with measures of eco-anxiety, environmentally minded consumer behaviour and environmental attitudes, while Study 2 also tested whether social influence in the form of exposure to “watching eyes” stimuli increased pro-environmental choices in the task. It was found that OSD scores positively correlated with environmentally minded consumer behaviour and the Preservation dimension of environmental attitudes, but not with eco-anxiety or Utilization attitudes. Furthermore, participants exposed to watching eyes selected significantly more environmentally friendly options (higher scores on the OSD). These findings provide initial evidence for the validity of the OSD as a measure of actual pro-environmental behaviour, demonstrating expected relationships with established environmental constructs and sensitivity to social influence. Given its simplicity, low cost, and accessibility, the OSD offers a practical addition to the growing range of behavioural measures available to environmental psychological researchers, although further validation is warranted.

articles.title: Daily life evidence against the general relieving function of conspiracy beliefs
articles.authors: Armin Gyarmati; Levente Rónai; Gábor Orosz; Lili Jakobovits; Péter Krekó; Bertalan Polner
articles.abstract: Conspiracy theories are assumed to provide psychological relief, reducing anxiety and uncertainty in the short term, at the cost of longer-term harms. Nevertheless, the temporal dynamics of conspiracy beliefs have rarely been investigated in naturalistic settings. Here, we tested whether fluctuations in conspiracy mentality are associated with changes in anxiety and sense of coherence in everyday life, using experience sampling data collected in a Hungarian (N = 77, Nobs = 2,905) and a pre-registered representative U.S. sample (N = 200, Nobs = 10,609). In both samples, we found moderate to strong evidence against a general association of conspiracy mentality with anxiety and sense of coherence across multiple timescales spanning from hours to weeks. However, among older adults, increases in conspiracy mentality were followed by lower anxiety and a higher sense of coherence, while individuals reporting no psychiatric diagnosis also benefited in terms of reduced anxiety. Together, these findings challenge the notion that conspiracy beliefs function as a universal buffer against anxiety and uncertainty, while the exploratory analyses point towards boundary conditions requiring further investigation.

articles.title: Personality Traits and Philanthropy Across Time
articles.authors: Lina Hungerbuehler; Michael Dominik Krämer; Peter Haehner; Christopher James Hopwood; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles.abstract: Philanthropic behaviors such as volunteering and charitable giving promote both societal welfare and individual well-being. Prior research has established cross-sectional links between broad personality domains and these behaviors, but it remains open whether and how personality differences prospectively predict philanthropic engagement (selection effects) and whether such engagement may, in turn, predict personality development over time (socialization effects). Furthermore, it is still unclear whether and how narrower personality aspects are linked to philanthropic behaviors. Drawing on five-wave nationally representative data from Switzerland (Nwave = 2,085 to 4,475), we extend prior research by testing prospective selection effects of personality traits on later philanthropic engagement and examining socialization effects of engagement on personality trajectories across broad personality domains and their narrower aspects. Results indicated that higher extraversion and lower neuroticism consistently predicted volunteering, whereas higher agreeableness and honesty-humility robustly predicted charitable giving. At the lower-order level of personality aspects, meaningful differences emerged within the domains of agreeableness and conscientiousness in predicting philanthropic behaviors, with compassion and industriousness showing more consistent and positive links than politeness and orderliness. Evidence for socialization effects was more limited. More time spent on volunteering was associated with smaller decreases in extraversion, although this effect differed depending on the included covariates. We discuss these findings in the context of theories on personality and prosociality and outline limitations and avenues for future research.

articles.title: Acoustic and visual cues to lexical stress interact with semantic predictions in Spanish lexical stress perception
articles.authors: Floris Cos; Matteo Maran; Hans Rutger Bosker; Esther Janse; Lieke van Maastricht
articles.abstract: Next to acoustic cues, lexical stress can be communicated visually through the timing of beat gestures. This study investigated for the first time how auditory and visual lexical stress cues are weighted in meaningful sentences. Minimal stress pairs of Spanish verb forms (clasiFIco, “I classify” vs. clasifiCÓ, “(s)he classified”) were embedded in sentence contexts that biased towards either member of the pair. Stress was manipulated acoustically along a continuum, and visually by aligning a beat gesture to the penultimate or last syllable. Native listeners selected the pronoun (yo “I” or ella “she”) they felt fit best with the sentence. Listeners were sensitive to acoustic cues, as indicated by both responses and response times. While gesture alignment did not significantly affect pronoun selection, response times were shorter when the gesture matched the semantic context bias. This study thus shows that in full sentences, congruent (vs. incongruent) gestural timing affects word recognition.

articles.title: Psychodiagnostic Markers and Linguistic Indicators of Psychological Capital: A Theoretical Model of Complementarity Within the Structural-Functional Paradigm of Human Capital
articles.authors: Dmytro Melnychuk; Oleksii Sabadukha; Iryna Kovalenko
articles.abstract:
Rapid epochal transformations call for rethinking human capital as a dynamic emergent entity with a complex architecture of endogenous components: educational-competence, health, social, and psychological capital. Within this architecture, psychological capital (PsyCap) acts as a cross-cutting moderator that determines the extent to which the educational-competence core is converted into socio-economic outcomes. This raises the significance of PsyCap psychodiagnostics while exposing the limitations of reflective self-report instruments, which capture momentary self-assessments and remain vulnerable to social desirability bias.
The article aims to substantiate the integration of linguistic indicators into PsyCap assessment and to develop a matrix model mapping the four HERO components (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) onto classes of linguistic indicators. Drawing on systemic, structural-functional, and interdisciplinary approaches, the study uses construct validity criteria to frame linguistic indicators as external correlates within the nomological network of PsyCap.
The model matches hope with achievement and goal-setting markers, efficacy with markers of confidence and control, resilience with register flexibility and reduced negative affect, and optimism with positive-emotional and forward-oriented language. Linguistic indicators cannot replace standardized instruments; rather, they constitute a complementary data source, provided that linguistic and cultural adaptation, control of socio-economic confounders, and ethical safeguards against profiling are ensured. The study builds a conceptual bridge between psychodiagnostics and psycholinguistics and outlines a pathway toward the culturally adapted operationalization of PsyCap assessment in Ukrainian psychology.

articles.title: Rethinking Smartphones and Sleep: A Fine-Grained Within-Person Analysis of Evening Smartphone Use and Sleep
articles.authors: Fenne große Deters; Katharina Salo; Jan A. Häusser; Anne Milek
articles.abstract: Inadequate sleep is a public health concern associated with adverse health and well-being outcomes. Evening smartphone use is frequently cited as a potential contributor, prompting widespread recommendations to avoid it. However, rigorous evidence to support these recommendations is limited. Using device-based smartphone use data and experience sampling data collected over 10 days, we examined within-person associations between evening smartphone use and five self-reported sleep-related outcomes: shuteye time, sleep latency, sleep duration, difficulty to fall asleep, and sleep quality. We examined these associations in two samples (N = 184 and N = 185) to test replicability. To investigate robustness and temporal dynamics, we assessed smartphone use across four equal-length time windows covering different segments of the evening. Across both samples and all time windows, greater-than-usual evening smartphone use was consistently associated with earlier shuteye time. Associations with the other sleep-related outcomes were less consistent, with most estimates indicating no significant relationship. Overall, our findings align with previous intensive longitudinal research that has likewise found little evidence of concerning associations between evening smartphone use and sleep. Our results challenge the assumption that evening smartphone use is inherently harmful to sleep and underscore the need to reconsider blanket recommendations to avoid it.

articles.title: Impact of Exergames on Cognition in Midlife and Older Age: A Bayesian Meta-Analysis
articles.authors: Marc Yangüez; Quentin Coppola; Esteban Lelo de Larrea-Mancera; Chloe Lee; Jessica Fan; Eesha Gangal; Sierra Hall; Pankil Bhatt; Aaron R. Seitz; Susanne M. Jaeggi
articles.abstract: Cognitive decline in older adulthood is a pressing global concern, prompting growing interest in scalable behavioral interventions. Exergames, which integrate physical activity and cognitively engaging tasks, have emerged as a promising approach to support cognitive health in aging. This Bayesian meta-analysis synthesizes 48 studies (181 effects; N = 2,605) on adults aged 50+, published up to May 31, 2024, examining the impact of exergames on cognition. Without adjustment for publication bias, exergames showed a small positive effect across cognitive domains. However, after adjusting for publication bias, the evidence for an overall effect was inconclusive, and no cognitive domain (i.e., attentional control, processing speed, working memory, cognitive flexibility, global cognition) showed more than anecdotal evidence for an effect. Moderator analyses provided no evidence that effects differed by factors such as age, population type (e.g., non-clinical vs. clinical), or intervention characteristics (e.g., exergaming modality, type of product, session frequency and duration, or intervention duration). These findings call for more rigorous, standardized, and well-powered trials to establish whether exergames benefit cognition in middle-aged and older adults.

articles.title: The Confidence – Information Quality Mismatch:  Low Quality Posts Use More Confident Language
articles.authors: Akshina Banerjee; Zhina Aghamohammadi; Matthew D. Rocklage; David Gertler Rand; Mohsen Mosleh
articles.abstract: Misinformation on online platforms is of great concern for democracy, public health, and civic discourse. In fast-paced feeds, users often rely on heuristics when deciding what to attend to, believe, and share. One such heuristic is confidence, which, prior research shows, is treated as a cue of knowledge and credibility. Yet, we show that in over 4 million posts across seven social media platforms and one messaging app, confidence is negatively associated with information quality: posts written with greater confidence are more likely to link to lower-quality news domains and to contain false claims — even controlling for user baselines, toxicity, political lean, emotionality, and valence. Furthermore, we find that confident posts receive more engagement. Together, these results reveal a problematic asymmetry in online information environments: a widespread linguistic cue that is likely to be read as a signal of knowledge, and to attract engagement, is in fact associated with lower-quality information.

articles.title: Motivation to Use Generative AI at Work: An Expectancy-Value Analysis of a National AI literacy program
articles.authors: Ivan Aslanov; Brayan Díaz; Charlotte Pearsall; Javiera Gonzalez-Arias
articles.abstract: AI-literacy training may facilitate workplace adoption of GenAI, yet little is known about how employees’ motivational beliefs change during training. Drawing on expectancy-value theory, we examined motivation before and after Hazlo con IA, a national adaptive AI-literacy program in Chile. The baseline sample included 9,835 working adults across public, healthcare, and small and medium-sized enterprise sectors (SME); 1,864 provided matched pretest–posttest responses. At both time points, attainment value (B = .231–.234), intrinsic value (B = .156–.173), utility value (B = .113–.185), and perceived workplace support (B = .153–.184) positively predicted intentions to use GenAI (all ps < .001). Self-efficacy was positively associated with intentions only at posttest (B = .086, p = .004), whereas perceived costs and anxiety were not significant independent predictors. Following training, all measured constructs except perceived workplace support declined significantly, although effects were small; the largest standardized decline was in intention to use AI (ΔM = −.193, dz = −.29, p < .001). Age (V = .016, p < .001) and employment sector (V = .020, p = .005) showed small multivariate associations with change: older participants reported slightly greater declines in workplace support (B = −.0054), and public-sector employees showed larger declines in intentions than SME employees (ΔM = −.240 vs. −.061, p = .004). Other demographic and experience variables were not significant. These findings highlight the central role of subjective value in workplace GenAI intentions and the relative stability of motivational beliefs across demographic and occupational contexts.

articles.title: The Allure of Simplicity: Framing Effects and Theoretical Virtues
articles.authors: Nick Byrd; Samantha Wakil; Jack Justus
articles.abstract: Are simpler explanations better, all else equal? Many people seem to think so. And many capitalize on this preference by claiming that their explanations are simple — perhaps the simplest! But some scholars have argued that the case for simplicity’s status as a theoretical virtue is quite thin. And some psychological studies raise questions about the reliability of simplicity’s benefits. Alas, once acquired, status as a theoretical virtue is rarely lost. To advance the debate, we conducted three experiments that test another way so-called theoretical virtues may impact reasoning (N = 1312). Merely labeling diagnoses ‘the simplest explanation’ made them more alluring in ways that were not warranted by relevant base rates, symptoms, or other causal information (experiment 1) — even when those diagnoses were not actually simplest! Neither the opposite label (‘most complex’) nor an alternative explanatory virtue label (‘most unifying’) had such consistent or reliable effects (experiment 2), suggesting simplicity itself is particularly seductive. The good news is that judgments and decisions were mostly unaffected by fallacious appeals to simplicity when we switched to other contexts and measures (experiment 3). That limited generalization suggests a variety of testable hypotheses about the boundaries and moderators of simplicity’s allure. For example, perhaps people rely more on intuitions about simplicity when diagnostic decision-making would otherwise require effortful reflection on technical terminology and difficult-to-compute probabilities. Together, our findings replicate and extend prior research on simplicity preferences, complement recent arguments and evidence about the risk of considering simplicity, and increase suspicion about simplicity’s virtuous status.

articles.title: Autism-Related Language Preferences of Turkish-Speaking Autistic Adults
articles.authors: Elif Bastan; Bahadir Turan; Esra Hoşoğlu; Beyza Ustun-Elayan; Ceymi Doenyas; Aynur Görmez; Ali Kandeğer; Yasemin Hoşgören Alıcı; Sophie Sowden-Carvalho; Connor Tom Keating
articles.abstract: Autism-related terminology is contested, and preferences vary across linguistic and cultural contexts. However, evidence from Turkish-speaking autistic communities is currently limited. This mixed-methods study examined terminology preferences among 127 native Turkish-speaking autistic participants aged 15–66 years. Participants selected all terms they felt comfortable using across seven categories of autism-related language. Eighty-one participants also provided open-ended responses, which were analysed using inductive reflexive thematic analysis. Participants most frequently endorsed otizm (“autism”; 79.30%) as the nomenclature of autism and nörolojik/beyin farklılığı (“neurological/brain difference”; 77.49%) as a broader conceptualisation. Farklılıklar (“differences”) was the most frequently endorsed term for both autism-related difficulties (82.45%) and strengths (71.19%). No single expression for an autistic person was endorsed by majority: otistik (“autistic”; 49.33%), nöroçeşitli kişi (“neurodivergent person”; 47.40%), and otizmli (“[person] with autism”; 45.48%) received similar support. Individual-difference measures showed few consistent associations with terminology endorsement after correction for multiple comparisons. Six qualitative themes concerned autonomy, social impact, identity, accuracy, context, and respect. Turkish-speaking autistic adults generally favoured direct and non-deficit-oriented language while emphasising individual choice. Researchers and professionals should therefore ask about personal preferences whenever possible and avoid imposing a single terminology on the wider community.

articles.title: Presaccadic Attention in Dynamic Scenes: Evidence from Hazard Localization in Road Videos
articles.authors: Ido Zivli; Benjamin Wolfe
articles.abstract: Presaccadic shifts of attention immediately prior to the movement of the eye have been extensively reported since the 1990s. However, all of these studies have used static images, often isolated objects on a neutral background, which do not much resemble the world we inhabit. Here, we use videos of rapidly-evolving road scenes to examine whether presaccadic attention operates in a similar manner when the observer needs to plan a speeded saccade to a target embedded within a complex, changing scene. Using a gaze-contingent paradigm, we isolated covert attention, presaccadic attention and overt attention, as well as manipulating the relative informativeness of the scene by varying the time at which the observer initiated their saccade. We find progressive improvements in localisation performance across our covert attention, presaccadic attention and overt attention conditions, but do not find evidence that the increasing informativeness of the scene over time modulates these effects, pointing to presaccadic attention as inherent to saccade planning and execution. This work represents a first step in extending our understanding of saccade planning processes to dynamic scenes, and lays the groundwork for future studies of what information is acquired prior to a saccade in daily life.

articles.title: Large language model agent simulations of individual differences in social interactions
articles.authors: Ole Hätscher; Leon Pielage; Pascal Kockwelp; Simon Mats Breil; Anna Junga; Jennifer Dabel; Benjamin Risse; Bernhard Marschall; Mitja D Back
articles.abstract: A key challenge in the behavioral sciences is the lack of formal models that capture individual differences in social interactions. At the same time, recent advances in artificial intelligence offer new opportunities to simulate and assess interpersonal behavior at scale. In this study, we introduce an agent-based modeling framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to simulate short-term social interactions. Within a dyadic interaction cycle, an LLM-based agent continually adjusts its interpersonal behavior (agency and communion) to its prior behavior, the partner’s behavior, and the combined influence of behavioral defaults (differences in default behavioral tendencies) and interpersonal reactivities (differences in reactions to partner behaviors). We derive a mathematical model that formalizes how interpersonal behavior unfolds across the interaction, evaluate the model in simulations, illustrate how the framework expresses these interpersonal dynamics in natural language, and outline the framework’s flexibility for simulating individual differences in practical applications across the behavioral sciences.

articles.title: Stable and Context-Sensitive Components of Interpersonal Complementarity
articles.authors: Kimberly J. Gilbert; Florian Bachofner; Maxim Trenkenschuh; Christopher James Hopwood
articles.abstract:
Objective: Interpersonal complementarity, in which warmth elicits warmth and dominance elicits submissiveness, is central to interpersonal theory. This study examined whether complementarity is stable across couples, varies across interpersonal situations, and relates to relationship satisfaction. 
Method: A total of 137 Swiss romantic couples completed four videotaped 5-min conversations about relationship strengths, relationship difficulties, and two persuasion conversations with alternating assigned roles. Warmth and dominance were coded using the Continuous Assessment of Interpersonal Dynamics, and both partners self-reported relationship satisfaction.
Results: Dominance complementarity was highly consistent across conversations, suggesting that one conversation can provide a useful estimate of a couple’s typical pattern. Warmth complementarity was less stable and varied by context, reaching its highest level during the positive conversation and decreasing during persuasion. Persuasion roles reversed which partner displayed greater dominance. Greater moment-to-moment warmth complementarity predicted higher relationship satisfaction, whereas dominance complementarity did not. 
Conclusions: Dominance complementarity appears to be a relatively stable couple-level characteristic, whereas warmth complementarity is more context dependent and more closely associated with relationship satisfaction.

articles.title: Prejudice in the Headlines: Anti-Trans Misinformation, Public Attitudes, and the Wellbeing of Trans and Gender Diverse People in the United Kingdom
articles.authors: Liam Cahill; Darel Cookson; Treshi-Marie Perera; Chase Staras; Bethany Jones
articles.abstract: Anti-trans misinformation is widely argued to drive an increasingly hostile climate for trans and gender diverse (TGD) people in the United Kingdom, yet its individual-level associations remain largely untested. Across two preregistered cross-sectional studies, we examined both sides of this intergroup relationship. In Study 1 (N = 400 cisgender adults), greater exposure to anti-TGD misinformation was associated with less positive attitudes towards TGD people and lower support for trans-inclusive policies, through trans-specific conspiracy beliefs but not populist attitudes and, in a separate model, through agreement with the misinformation claims. Neither social media information literacy nor parasocial contact moderated these pathways, although parasocial contact was directly associated with more positive outcomes. In Study 2 (N = 290 TGD adults), greater exposure was associated with higher mental distress over and above experienced trans-negativity, but not with social gender-role recognition, and neither community engagement nor disengagement moderated these associations. The same information environment may therefore be associated with harm through two routes: among cisgender people, through acceptance of its claims, and among TGD people, as a minority stressor. Correcting beliefs may help protect the attitudinal climate but is unlikely on its own to reduce harm to TGD people.

articles.title: Celebrity Endorsement and Meditation Intention: A Randomized Experiment
articles.authors: Michael Bowen
articles.abstract: Meditation offers well-documented health benefits, yet persistence with meditation is low. Drawing on the Reasoned Action Approach, we tested whether celebrity meditators as a descriptive-norm cue improve attitudes toward and intention to meditate. In this randomized survey experiment (N = 2,035), participants viewed one of four images captioned "Meditating for just a few minutes a day can transform your mind". Compared to same-gender non-celebrities, the celebrity images did not increase intention to meditate (female: OR = 0.88, 95% CI 0.64–1.21; male: OR = 1.18, 0.85–1.63) or change attitudes (female: b = −0.09, −0.19 to 0.00; male: b = 0.06, −0.03 to 0.14; all Holm-adjusted p ≥ .24). In conclusion, a single exposure to a celebrity meditator may be insufficient to shift attitudes or intentions toward meditation.

articles.title: Characterizing deaf and hard-of-hearing language experiences as arousal-regulation processes
articles.authors: Christina Kim; Laurel Aichler; Onudeah Nicolarakis; Shilpa Hanumantha Lacy; Rachel Sortino; Rachel Pizzie
articles.abstract: Empirical language research with deaf and hard-of-hearing (DHH) groups often includes proficiency, age of acquisition, or language background measures but excludes people’s socioemotional context. Measuring socioemotional context depends on characterizing the socioemotional experiences associated with DHH language development and use. We used the biopsychosocial model of arousal regulation as a theoretical lens to explore 11 qualitative interviews with DHH participants. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we developed three characteristic themes: 1) Deafness is not a monolith, 2) Name it to tame it – Language Anxiety, and 3) Positive roots for resilient shoots. These themes show that DHH language experiences are heterogeneous, that negative experiences can represent language anxiety, and that positive experiences modulate arousal regulation. Our study highlights new socioemotional considerations for language processing research like how emotions influence language use, how motivations support language skills, and how communication strategies impact social interactions within DHH communities.

articles.title: Eager inhibition, lagging enhancement: The time course of selective attention
articles.authors: Sizhu Han; Nancy Beth Carlisle; Anna Schubö
articles.abstract: Foreknowledge of target features biases attention toward those features even before search begins, indicating proactive activation of the target template. However, whether foreknowledge of distractor features leads to proactive inhibition remains debated, raising questions about whether target and distractor templates operate through similar mechanisms. The current study investigated this by presenting multiple task-irrelevant singleton probes before search display onset, combined with EEG. The probes either matched the color of the target, the distractor or had a neutral color. If a feature-specific template is activated proactively, we expect to see a reliable probe N2pc-modulation: With target template enhancement, probes matching the target color should elicit a more pronounced N2pc than neutral probes, whereas a distractor template inhibition should lead to an opposite pattern. In line with this prediction, results showed that the target-colored probes produced a more pronounced N2pc, with the largest amplitude for the last probe in the sequence, suggesting an increasing template activation from probe 1 to 4. Distractor-colored probes elicited a less pronounced N2pc than neutral probes at the first probe, suggesting an inhibited template activation at the start of the preparation. Both ERP and decoding results time-locked to search display onset showed that foreknowledge of the target color facilitated target selection, reaching its peak after 200 ms. Foreknowledge of the distractor color allowed active distractor inhibition within the first 200 ms and then vanished quickly. Taken together, separate temporal profiles during preparation and search support distinct mechanisms for target selection and distractor rejection in visual search.

articles.title: ‘Chemsex’ then and now – towards a ‘6Ws’ model for functional analysis and configurational assessment that embraces phenotypic diversity
articles.authors: Stephen Naulls
articles.abstract:
Background: Distinguishing problematic from non-problematic chemsex, or placing experience on a continuum of severity, generates limited information about why similar drug use can lead to different experiences and support needs. We propose considering how the circumstances of an encounter work together and change over time.
Method: This think piece presents a selective conceptual synthesis of chemsex research and assessment approaches, informed by minority stress theory, drug, set and setting, functional analysis, and addiction science. Empirical studies inform the domains and the proposed relationships between them.
Results: Six questions (who, what, why, with, where and when) describe the person, substances, functions, relationships, settings and timing within a changing chemsex configuration. Digital activity may connect these through partner contact, planning and support, and is an important emerging consideration. Three fictional vignettes illustrate different responses to comparable exposure. The person and therapist could each map the configuration, compare accounts and identify a focus for formulation and therapy.
Conclusions: Assessment should determine how pleasure, protection and harm arise through interacting circumstances. The six Ws direct attention to these relationships and to differences between the person’s and therapist’s accounts. Participatory development and longitudinal evaluation are needed to establish whether this approach improves shared understanding, decisions and care.

articles.title: Memory Overlap Shapes General and Specific Memory Differently in Adolescents and Adults
articles.authors: Merron Woodbury; Sagana Vijayarajah; Margaret Schlichting
articles.abstract: Over time we accumulate many interrelated memories which we draw upon to remember both generalities and specifics of our experience. While both aspects of memory improve through childhood, their maturation into adolescence remains poorly understood. Here, we compared how 39 adolescents (12-13 years old) and 36 adults managed differing levels of relatedness (“overlap”) among learned associations to remember shared (general) and unique (specific) features. Across age groups, greater overlap boosted memory for shared features but hindered memory for specifics. However, adolescents showed a reduced benefit of overlap for shared feature memory, suggesting they generalized across related memories differently than adults. Adolescents were also slower than adults to recognize unique features of highly overlapping memories, consistent with prolonged refinement of specific memory. Our results reveal continued maturation of both general and specific memory into adolescence while demonstrating how the overlaps among our experiences shape what we remember.

articles.title: Virtual Reality in Grief and Related Distress: A Systematic Review
articles.authors: Pelin Sila Gelmez; Ayala Licht-Handler; Clare Killikelly
articles.abstract:
Background: Virtual Reality (VR) might support grieving processes through therapeuFc
environments that encourage conFnuing bonds with deceased loved ones. In contrast, VR might
encourage avoidance of reality among bereaved individuals and interfere with their grieving
processes.
Objective: This systematic review of studies with mixed methodological designs (i.e.,
qualitative, quantitative, mixed methods) examines the acceptability, feasibility and efficacy of
Virtual Reality (VR) for bereaved individuals.
Methods: A systematic search identified studies published until May 2025 using terms related
to grief, VR and other immersive technologies (i.e., augmented reality, mixed reality) from 4
databases (OVID Medline, Web of Science, PsycINFO, and Scopus). Studies reporting the use of
VR or other immersive technologies for grief were included. Intervention elements, efficacy
outcomes, acceptability and feasibility were extracted.
Results: Out of 5’704 screened titles and abstracts, 9 studies met eligibility. Types of loss
included parental loss (k=1), patient loss (k=1), loss of a spouse (k=1), gestational loss (k=1), child
loss (k=1), loss of a significant person (k=1), and loss of a person (k=3). Seven studies used a web-based
VR intervention, and two studies used a non-web-based VR intervention. VR intervention
tools included Second Life (k=2), EMMA’s WORLD (k=5), AViR (k=1) and 3MDR-TG (k=1). Our
findings show modest support for preliminary VR efficacy, with three studies showing similar
significant changes compared to control groups and five studies showing reductions in grief and
related distress outcomes. VR was further shown to be feasible and acceptable for bereaved
people.

articles.title: Object-Based Priming and the Perceived Trustworthiness of Unfamiliar Faces: A Test of Home and Work Primes
articles.authors: Oliver Bazeley
articles.abstract: Research on material priming suggests that incidental encounters with everyday objects can activate the social meanings attached to those objects and bias subsequent judgements. It remains unknown whether objects belonging to a broad social domain, such as the home or the workplace, can shift how trustworthy an unfamiliar person appears. The present study tested whether briefly viewing home-, work-, or novel-object images altered trustworthiness judgements of unfamiliar faces, predicting that home objects would raise perceived trustworthiness and work objects would lower it. Thirty adults completed a within-subjects task in which each object prime preceded a facial trustworthiness rating on a continuous 0 to 100 scale; data from 28 participants were analysed. A trial-level mixed-effects analysis found no reliable category-specific priming. Relative to novel objects, both Home (b = 2.23, 95% CI [-0.10, 4.56], p = .061) and Work (b = 2.08, 95% CI [-0.21, 4.38], p = .075) primes produced small, non-significant increases in trustworthiness, the work effect running counter to the predicted decrease. Ratings did, however, closely track normative facial trustworthiness (b = 4.61, p < .001), indicating that the task captured the intended judgement. Exploratory analyses provided one weak and non-robust indication that Home primes were stronger among Home-leaning participants, and no evidence of moderation by workplace experience. The similar effects of home and work objects may instead reflect shared familiarity or overlapping meanings. Interpretation is constrained by the modest sample, and future research should establish whether such objects reliably activate their intended constructs.

articles.title: Science without scientists? In defence of human understanding
articles.authors: Jonathan Prunty
articles.abstract: Science has two grand goals, producing results and increasing human understanding, which have usually advanced together. Accelerating science by automating around human limits threatens to decouple them, as AI research output can scale with compute whereas humans can only read and digest new research at the pace biology allows, and some AI-generated results may be too opaque for anyone to follow. I argue that this could create a comprehension lag, a growing gap between what is discovered and what humans understand. This lag may begin inside individual labs, as scientists become "commissioners" directing their own teams of AI agents, but could extend to entire fields, as the frontier moves faster than people can follow. I discuss three costs of a comprehension lag: a loss of control over AI-accelerated research, a loss of capacity as aspects of training and apprenticeship are automated, and a loss of meaning that scientists find in their work. I then propose five measures to mitigate the comprehension lag, including new research directions for the cognitive and behavioural sciences, and argue that human understanding deserves protecting, both to keep oversight of AI-driven research and as an end in itself.

articles.title: Do people who care about their data and privacy know their data rights? Evidence from Estonia, 2023–2025
articles.authors: Tanel Mällo; Jaan Tulviste
articles.abstract:
European data protection law gives people rights over their personal data, but what mo-
tivates us to exercise those rights? In three surveys of Estonian adults (2023–2025), we
examined whether people who care about privacy also know their data protection rights.
Respondents valued privacy far more than they felt they had it and regarded all seven
types of personal data asked about as sensitive; valuing privacy, attention to privacy, ex-
perienced privacy and security, and perceived data sensitivity rose slightly over the period.
Knowledge of data rights, by contrast, was low, did not rise, and was unrelated to privacy
and data sensitivity. The same five combinations of sensitivity and knowledge recurred
in all three waves, and sociodemographic characteristics explained little of them. Caring
about personal data and privacy were thus unrelated to knowing one’s rights, so efforts
should be made to explain and bridge the gap between privacy/data concerns and the
individual opportunities to mitigate them.

articles.title: From Echo Chambers to Echo Machines? Endorsement, Evidence, and the Certainty of Belief in Conversations With AI
articles.authors: Olivier LE BON; Xavier Noël
articles.abstract: Randomized trials show that conversations with large language models (LLMs) can reduce conspiracy belief and, more modestly, political polarization. Yet the same systems can increase conspiracy belief when instructed to, and clinical reports describe chatbot conversations accompanying the escalation of implausible convictions. Prevailing accounts attribute both outcomes to the evidence a model supplies. We note that most experiments confound evidence about the world with endorsement of the person, and that the clearest attempt to separate them favors evidence. Drawing on research on attitude certainty, self-validation, and responses to flattery, we distinguish the position of a belief from the certainty with which it is held and formalize γ, an effect of endorsement on certainty at fixed factual content, interpretable as a validation gain. If higher certainty lowers responsiveness to later evidence, the account permits a conditional outcome: beliefs that become less extreme yet more rigid, without any misinformation. We specify two critical experiments, a factorial test of facts and endorsement that includes a source known to approve everyone and an endorsement-first design with counterevidence held constant, plus an articulation control. Conversational AI becomes a test bench for an old question: can social approval make subsequent evidence matter less?

articles.title: Personal and National Factors Predict Depression in Europe
articles.authors: Hannes Jarke; Robin van Kessel; Kai Ruggeri; Katarzyna Czabanowska
articles.abstract: Cross-national research has consistently documented sociodemographic gradients in depression across European countries. Most comprehensive analyses, however, predate the COVID-19 pandemic and its far-reaching consequences for population mental health and social hardship. Using data from the European Social Survey Round 11 (ESS 11, collected in 2023–2024), the most recent wave to include a measure of depression (CES-D 8), we examined the social patterning of depressive symptoms across 22 EU countries and the UK (N = 39,645) using multilevel modelling with sample design weighting. We confirm findings from prior ESS rounds of consistent gender, age, and income gradients in depression, confirming their persistence in the post-pandemic period. Women reported higher depressive symptoms than men across all countries, and income emerged as the strongest individual-level predictor, with those in the lowest income tertile scoring on average 2.09 points higher on the CES-D 8 than those in the highest (the scale ranging from 0-24). Critically, these associations are not uniform across national contexts. The gender gap in depressive symptoms was larger in Southern European countries—particularly Portugal and Spain than in Northern and Eastern Europe, while the protective effect of higher income was strongest in Bulgaria, Hungary, Belgium, and Greece. Country context alone accounted for only a small proportion of total variance in depressive symptoms (ICC = 0.033), indicating that differences in depression at the population level are driven primarily by sociodemographic factors, but that their magnitude is meaningfully shaped by where people live.

articles.title: Perioral motor stabilization without classical proprioception: a trigeminofacial force-balance model
articles.authors: Thomas Quettier; Paola Sessa; Luigi Cattaneo; Pier Francesco Ferrari
articles.abstract: Voluntary perioral movements, including speech articulation, deliberate lip posturing, and postural stabilization during oral closure, require motor precision despite the absence of muscle spindles and proprioceptive receptors in perioral musculature. The facial nerve is purely efferent, providing no direct sensory return. How the motor system achieves stable control under these constraints has remained unresolved. We propose the Orofacial Region as Integrated System (ORIS) model as a mechanistic candidate tailored to voluntary and automatic segmental perioral behaviors. The model identifies cutaneous mechanoreception via the trigeminal nerve as the primary afferent channel for perioral motor stabilization and proposes that the controlled variable is the spatial equilibrium of dermal surface tension across the perioral sheet, monitored by slowly and fast-adapting mechanoreceptors concentrated in the perioral region. The orbicularis oris sphincter provides circumferential tensile stability against which directional muscles act, with the modiolus anguli oris serving as the primary force-transmission junction. Three testable predictions follow from this architecture. Clinical implications for facial motor rehabilitation are discussed.

articles.title: Examining Individual Differences in Misinformation Engagement among Social Media Users in a Simulated Twitter Task
articles.authors: Dyuthi Dinesh; Michael Robert Haupt
articles.abstract:
Background 
Psychological traits and social identities have been linked to misinformation sharing, but most studies measure passive or low-effort engagement. Less is known about high-effort engagement that requires users to write a response. We examined whether cognitive reflection, motivated reasoning variables (political orientation, religiosity, trust in medical scientists) and personality traits are differentially associated with liking, retweeting, replying to, and quoting COVID-19 misinformation and public-health-unaligned tweets.
Methods 
US MTurk participants (N = 858; September 2021) engaged with real COVID-19 tweets in a simulated Twitter feed. Replies and quotes were manually coded as endorsive or combative. We fit OLS regressions for each engagement type (N = 851) and estimated relative importance using Shapley (LMG) decomposition of R².
Results
Endorsive replies and quotes were rare (7.3% and 4.3% of participants for misinformation). Political conservatism and religiosity were associated with endorsive misinformation replies, and motivated reasoning variables were the largest contributors in all reply and quote models, though these models explained little variance (adjusted R² ≤ .03). Cognitive reflection was negatively associated only with liking, and grandiose narcissism was the largest contributor to retweeting.
Conclusion
Classical reasoning, personality and motivated reasoning explanations of misinformation propagation were each supported, depending on the type of engagement. Simulation tasks that measure multiple engagement behaviors can help clarify inconsistent findings in the misinformation literature.

articles.title: Tracking vocabulary development as children start school: assessing measurement invariance in multilingual classrooms
articles.authors: Sonali Nag; Athina Ntalli; Gideon Arulmani; Joshua Aaron McGrane
articles.abstract: Receptive vocabulary, what is understood when hearing a word, underpins reading comprehension and wider learning. Yet, few tests have been validated to function fairly over developmental time and across diverse linguistic experiences. This study examined the Picture Test for Receptive Vocabulary (TalkTogether – Hindi), a 50-item test for four-to-nine-year-olds in multilingual north India. Words in the language of school instruction and linked images were drawn picture- and story books. Over one academic year (2023–2024), 1,949 administrations were collected from children (47% girls) at three time points across 40 schools. The test showed good reliability (Cronbach’s α = .82; Rasch reliability = .78) and captured variation across the proficiency range. Item properties remained stable across time, licensing its use as a fair tracking tool. Between-group differential item functioning (DIF) effects—by sex, home language(s), and a novel index of ambient peer language exposure—were small to negligible. The findings demonstrate that a contextually-situated vocabulary test, validated through rigorous psychometric evaluation, can meet the standards required for fair tracking of oral skills in the language of instruction. The reported protocol to inform item revision and evaluate dimensions of measurement invariance—demographic, contextual and developmental—are likely transferable to other similarly multilingual settings.

articles.title: An introduction to longitudinal multilevel and structural equation modeling approaches for examining change
articles.authors: Razieh Pourafshari; Miriam Brinberg; Joseph Bayer
articles.abstract: This chapter provides a practical introduction to two statistical frameworks for analyzing longitudinal data in quantitative communication research: multilevel modeling (MLM) and structural equation modeling (SEM). Focusing on intraindividual change and intraindividual variability, we illustrate how these methods can disentangle within-person processes from between-person differences. Using real-world data, the chapter demonstrates how to model daily patterns in social interaction desires and test dynamic relationships between social app use and interpersonal needs. Key considerations for choosing between MLM and SEM are discussed. The chapter also highlights advanced extensions, including nonlinear growth, mediation, and multivariate models, offering researchers a foundational guide for applying these approaches to their own questions examining change.

articles.title: From transdiagnostic compulsivity to clinical applications: a computational psychiatry approach to bridge research and clinic
articles.authors: Sean E Cavanagh; Toby Wise
articles.abstract: Compulsivity, the maladaptive persistence of behaviour despite adverse consequences, is central to obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and has been increasingly conceptualised as a transdiagnostic dimension spanning multiple neuropsychiatric disorders. Research within computational psychiatry has linked dimensional compulsivity to two candidate mechanisms: impaired goal-directed control and elevated metacognitive confidence.
