Here, we take a clinical perspective addressing how insights from these findings can be brought into practice. We first ask how dimensional compulsivity measures should be interpreted with respect to clinical presentations and discuss conflicts between the general population findings and clinical data. We highlight several challenges facing clinical implementation: effect sizes are small, goal-directed control has not been shown to change with either pharmacotherapy or psychological therapy, and the overconfidence associated with dimensional compulsivity contrasts with the reduced confidence reported in patients with OCD. We argue these discrepancies are informative rather than disqualifying and set out a translational roadmap for mechanistically informed detection and transdiagnostic intervention. Specifically, we suggest that screening and digital monitoring of dimensional compulsivity, combined with cognitive and mechanistic phenotyping to guide psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy, may ultimately improve outcomes across diagnostic boundaries.

articles.title: Children adjust behavior in novel social environments to reflect local prosocial norms inferred from brief exposure
articles.authors: Kari Britt Schroeder; Laura Nelson; Peter Blake
articles.abstract: Stark cultural variation in prosocial behavior, as elicited with economic experiments, is evident despite the high mobility of humans. Conformity to local norms has been posited to play an integral role in the maintenance of this variation. Experiments suggest that adults indeed rapidly infer pro- and antisocial norms in new or altered social environments and adjust their behavior to reflect the inferred norms. Studies of the ontogeny of prosocial behavior show that by middle childhood, children’s prosocial behavior conforms to that of local adults. Furthermore, by this stage, children are susceptible to the manipulation of explicit normative information. However, their propensity to extract or infer normative information from the environment and change their behavior accordingly has not been investigated. Here, we assess whether children 1) rapidly infer local prosocial norms in a novel, realistic social environment, 2) extend these inferences to norms for unobserved behaviors, and 3) alter their behavior in the novel environment to align with the inferred norms while still 4) maintaining their baseline prosocial behavior outside of the novel environment. We used questionnaires to measure children’s perceived pro- and antisocial descriptive norms in their Own Neighborhoods as well as in a novel “Neighborhood X,” to which they were introduced via a slideshow. Norms for Neighborhood X diverged drastically dependent upon which slideshow they witnessed (Prosocial or Antisocial condition), a result robust to the exclusion of questions about norms for behaviors observed in the slideshow. Children’s perceptions of prosocial norms in their Own Neighborhoods predicted their prosocial behavior (Dictator Game) in their Own Neighborhood. Moreover, even though information about giving behavior was not presented in the slideshow, inferred norms for Neighborhood X predicted children’s prosocial behavior in that neighborhood as well. These changes in prosocial behavior were transitory and specific to Neighborhood X; prosocial behavior in a separate “Helping Task” was best predicted by prosocial norms within the children’s Own Neighborhoods. Our results are consistent with the hypothesis that humans have a propensity to rapidly infer and conform to local prosocial norms, thus maintaining group differences in prosocial behavior, and further indicate that this propensity is in operation by middle childhood.

articles.title: Machines in the Middle: How AI Use Changes What Coworkers Think of, and Do for, One Another
articles.authors: Maxine Parker; Celine Huang; Sekoul Krastev
articles.abstract: Generative AI is now embedded in how coworkers, leaders, and organizations communicate, yet its effects on the relationships among them are still poorly understood. This review synthesizes recent research on how an individual’s AI use changes the way others perceive, judge, and behave toward them, and shows that these effects can be explained by established theories of human-human interaction, including attribution theory, computers-as-social-actors, the integrative model of organizational trust, social exchange theory, and resource-based theories. The evidence suggests that observers often read AI use as a sign of disposition rather than circumstance, judging AI users as less competent, motivated, warm, and authentic, and that disclosure does not repair the resulting loss of trust. These perceptions carry over into behavior: coworkers reciprocate less, share less knowledge, and show less prosocial behavior toward AI users, while AI-related job insecurity, loneliness, and work alienation further strain ties among colleagues. AI use also loosens moral standards and shifts how blame is assigned, making people more critical of others’ work but more lenient toward misconduct. These effects are conditional rather than uniformly negative. AI can reduce loneliness, improve coordination, and prompt employees to invest more in emotionally supportive ties, and relational buffers such as leader-member exchange, shared leadership, and supervisor support can offset its costs. The review concludes that AI’s costs to workplace relationships run mainly through indirect pathways, not through the technology itself. It outlines organizational implications, including clear norms for when and why AI is used and protection of socially valued tasks, and identifies priorities for future research: longitudinal designs, team- and network-level studies, intervention research, and more diverse samples.

articles.title: Do Sexual Beliefs Shape Relationship Quality Over Time? Evidence From Early Romantic Relationships
articles.authors: Jessica Caferri; Akshita Uppot; Stephanie Raposo; Emily Impett; Amy Muise; SHaRe Lab
articles.abstract: Satisfying romantic relationships are important for well-being yet are difficult to maintain, as sexual satisfaction and relationship quality often decline across early relationship development. Sexual growth and destiny beliefs reflect whether sexual satisfaction is viewed as something that develops through effort or depends on natural, inherent compatibility. Such beliefs may be associated with how couples navigate changes in their relationship. Using longitudinal data from 161 couples (N= 322) early in their relationship, followed over 18 months, we examined whether individuals’ and their partners’ sexual beliefs predicted trajectories of sexual satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, and commitment. Relationship satisfaction and commitment showed small declines over time, whereas sexual satisfaction and sexual beliefs remained relatively stable. Higher actor and partner sexual growth beliefs were associated with higher levels of all outcomes in general, and individuals with partners’ higher in sexual growth beliefs were buffered from steeper declines in relationship satisfaction and commitment over time. In contrast, higher actor, but not partner, sexual destiny beliefs were associated with lower relationship satisfaction and commitment in general. Overall, the findings suggest that sexual beliefs function as relatively stable cognitive frameworks, with partner sexual growth beliefs playing a role in protecting relationship quality and commitment during early relationship development.

articles.title: Minds Meet Machines: The Joint Role of Trust and Intellectual Humility in AI Persuasion
articles.authors: Devora Newman; Almog Simchon; Ruth Mayo
articles.abstract: Research shows that AI models have a remarkable ability to change people’s minds following a short conversation, a notoriously difficult task for human communicators. Such persuasive paradigms provide a unique opportunity to examine which psychological characteristics predict receptivity to counter-attitudinal information. We focus on two characteristics: intellectual humility (IH), reflecting openness to revising one’s beliefs following new information, and trust in the information source (AI). To establish the role of a-priori dispositions that determine acceptance of new information, we ran two online studies, sampling British participants with a negative attitude toward legal immigrants (N = 294). We replicated previous findings showing significant and lasting attitude change following a brief exchange with GPT, but crucially, this effect was not uniform. In Study 1, attitude change was greatest among participants with higher initial trust in AIs and higher intellectual humility. Study 2 extended this finding by measuring both dispositions a week before the conversation with GPT, revealing the same pattern: opinion change was greatest among those who were both open to new information and trusting of its source. These findings highlight the centrality of recipient dispositions, suggesting that the relationship between source trust and persuasion depends on recipients' intellectual humility. More broadly, source trust may function as more than a heuristic cue, and its relationship with attitude change may depend on recipients' willingness to recognize the fallibility of their beliefs. Together, these findings extend perspectives on persuasion by highlighting the joint role of source trust and recipients' epistemic dispositions in belief revision.

articles.title: Celebrity Endorsement and Meditation Intention: A Randomized Experiment
articles.authors: Michael Bowen
articles.abstract: Meditation offers well-documented health benefits, yet persistence with meditation is low. Drawing on the Reasoned Action Approach, we tested whether celebrity meditators as a descriptive-norm cue improve attitudes toward and intention to meditate. In this randomized survey experiment (N = 2,035), participants viewed one of four images captioned "Meditating for just a few minutes a day can transform your mind". Compared to same-gender non-celebrities, the celebrity images did not increase intention to meditate (female: OR = 0.88, 95% CI 0.64–1.21; male: OR = 1.18, 0.85–1.63) or change attitudes (female: b = −0.09, −0.19 to 0.00; male: b = 0.06, −0.03 to 0.14; all Holm-adjusted p ≥ .24). In conclusion, a single exposure to a celebrity meditator may be insufficient to shift attitudes or intentions toward meditation.

articles.title: It’s about time: Specifying time zero for target trial emulation in psychological research
articles.authors: Dongning Ren; Wen Wei Loh
articles.abstract: Psychologists often rely on observational studies for causal evidence, which raises the question of how to strengthen the design of observational studies for causal inference. One widely used approach in medical research is target trial emulation (TTE). In this tutorial, we introduce TTE to psychological research, with particular emphasis on its cornerstone concept that is routinely ignored in practice: time zero. Following a brief primer on TTE, we foreground time zero and highlight its critical role in improving valid causal inferences from observational data. Using examples drawn from psychological research, we systematically enumerate all possible permutations of the time zero components to show how their misalignment can introduce systematic biases, including selection bias, post-treatment confounding, treatment-dependent (in)eligibility, and immortal time bias, even when all baseline confounders are measured. To address this, we develop a decision framework for integrating time zero into research practices and offer practical recommendations. Through a running example of workplace AI use and employee burnout, we demonstrate how clearly specifying time zero clarifies causal questions, prevents many design-based biases, and strengthens internal validity. We further emphasize that time zero alignment is only one design feature of a strong observational study, and we delineate the boundaries of TTE, cautioning against the misconception that it is a magic fix that automatically delivers causal conclusions. We conclude that explicitly justifying time zero is a necessary step toward improving the rigor and transparency of causal research in psychology.

articles.title: Displayed judgment certainty reorganizes source selection in self-formed networks
articles.authors: Gaël Carniel; Valentin Guigon; Frédéric Moisan; Alain Barrat; Jean-Claude Dreher
articles.abstract: Collective intelligence in self-formed networks depends on which judgments people choose to observe, as well as on how they integrate those judgments. We tested whether displaying judgment certainty reorganizes source selection and improves subsequent accuracy. Across eight online sessions, 273 participants evaluated 14 true and false news headlines, formed costly directed observation networks, and revised their beliefs over five updates. During network formation, we manipulated the visibility of certainty, defined by the extremity of each source's private probability judgment, while belief direction and source accuracy remained hidden. Displaying certainty produced denser networks and redirected links toward more certain sources; current popularity also predicted selection. Visibility increased exposure to highly certain but incorrect judgments, without a clear improvement in the relative accuracy of selected sources. Accuracy increased across repeated judgments, but certainty visibility did not detectably increase this improvement and reduced reconstructed net scores under the task's payoff structure. Observations with selected sources showed greater improvement than those without, and improvement was associated with selected sources' initial accuracy. Belief revisions moved toward selected sources and decreased with participants' own certainty. Among six compact predictive models, certainty-reinforcing DeGroot provided the best penalized and aggregate held-out prediction, although it did not capture the large first update. These findings distinguish a cue's ability to attract attention from its ability to identify useful information: displayed certainty can reorganize costly information acquisition without a detectable average accuracy benefit.

articles.title: Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation for cognitive rehabilitation
articles.authors: Jamie Berry; Marc L. Copersino
articles.abstract:
This chapter describes a neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) approach to
cognitive rehabilitation (CR) following acquired brain injury (ABI), with primary
emphasis on traumatic brain injury and stroke. NIPE is conceptualised as more than
information provision: neuroscience-informed explanations are used to help patients
and families understand cognitive difficulties, recovery, rehabilitation strategies, and
their implications for everyday functioning. Neuropsychological feedback is presented
as a common context for NIPE, with attention to tailoring, functional translation,
multimodal support, and verification of understanding.
A dual-lens framework is proposed for NIPE delivery in CR. The therapeutic lens
emphasises alliance, empathy and warmth, person-centred collaboration, shared
explanatory models, and goal setting. The cognition-informed lens addresses how
cognitive difficulties may affect learning through adjustment of information load and
pacing, repetition, clear and concrete language, integration with existing knowledge,
teach-back, and multimodal delivery. Together, these lenses inform considerations of
timing and context and seven structural principles of NIPE: trustworthiness, interaction,
salience, motivation, intensity, repetition, and multimodal/multimedia delivery.
The chapter also considers NIPE content related to neuroplasticity, prognosis and
recovery, rehabilitation approaches, and factors that may influence functioning and
participation. Throughout, emphasis is placed on distinguishing established evidence
from plausible but untested mechanisms and on presenting recovery in probabilistic
rather than deterministic terms.

articles.title: A mind-body disconnection? Discordance between thoughts about stress and cardiovascular stress responses
articles.authors: Audrey Merwin; Brett J. Peters; Elizabeth Haudrich; Abriana M Gresham; Ashley Tudder; Nathan Stuart; Jessica Lang; Kylee Bernel; Parastesh Sattari; Peggy Zoccola
articles.abstract: Stress responses are defined by mind-body interactions that engage both psychological and physiological processes. We provide foundational research investigating the mind-body connection during stress to ask: how do individuals’ thoughts about stressors align with their cardiovascular responses? 925 dyads (N = 1,850) anticipated, engaged in, and recovered from stress-inducing social-evaluative tasks. Analyses revealed that individuals’ self-reported and cardiovascular indices of stress were not significantly associated at any timepoint, bolstered by post-hoc Inclusion Bayes Factors supporting the null (vs. alternative) hypothesis. Meta-analytic results suggested the association between measures is effectively zero, indicating findings may generalize beyond a social interaction context and our primarily White, female, college-aged sample. These findings suggest individuals’ perceptions of stress may be distinct from their physiological stress responses, carry significant implications for the way we conceptualize and measure stress, and indicate that multi-method, full-body approaches are critical for a holistic understanding of the human stress response.

articles.title: Distinct sensorimotor representations during combined action observation and motor imagery
articles.authors: Matthew Scott; David Wright; Nicola Jane Hodges; Justine Magnuson; Sarah N Kraeutner
articles.abstract: The human sensorimotor system can represent actions in the absence of movement, termed motor simulation. These motor simulations can be perceptually (externally) driven through observation of an actor or cognitively (internally) driven through imagining movement. Although there is evidence humans can represent multiple actions simultaneously, whether different motor simulations can concurrently be represented is unclear. We investigated the capacity of the sensorimotor system to simultaneously represent observed (action observation; AO) and imagined actions (motor imagery; MI). Two competing hypotheses were tested concerning whether AO and MI could co-exist or not, The Dual Action Simulation Hypothesis (DASH) and Visual Guidance Hypothesis (VGH), respectively. Fifteen participants completed a functional magnetic resonance imagining (fMRI) study, requiring them to complete four distinct conditions involving imagination or observation of a rhythmical hand tapping action. Conditions involved: AO, AO with a counting task (i.e., with cognitive load), MI, or simultaneous AO and MI of different actions (AOMI). Through representational similarity analysis, AO and MI motor simulations were evidenced in the right ventral premotor cortex, supporting DASH over VGH. Multidimensional scaling of representational similarity data indicated a unique representational pattern for AOMI, differing from AO and MI across different dimensions. Whole-brain analyses were conducted, showing descriptive support for greater engagement of sensorimotor regions during AOMI vs. the summation of independent AO and MI conditions occurred, complementing findings from our representational similarity analysis. While dual motor simulations appear possible, our data suggests that the representational pattern of AOMI is distinct, producing super-additive sensorimotor activity. Neither DASH nor VGH adequately explain these data.

articles.title: Disasters and Sports in Dreams: Unexpected Selectivity in Dream Incorporation
articles.authors: Marcin Florkowski
articles.abstract:
Population-level indicators of interest in dream-related topics were analyzed using Google Trends for California, Texas, the Philippines, and the United Kingdom—areas with a combined population of more than 250 million—as well as at the global level. Media-salient natural disasters are reflected in dreams. The relative representation of sports-related and disaster-related content was compared between ordinary searches and dream-related searches.
Although sports overwhelmingly dominated waking interest, disaster-related content was represented about 24 times as strongly in dream-related searches as expected based on its relative share of ordinary searches. 
This pattern indicates that content dominating conscious attention need not dominate dreams, a finding difficult to explain in terms of either classical predictors of incorporation. We propose that existing accounts fail to capture a mechanism that grants certain types of content privileged status as dream material. We introduce Phantom Anxiety Theory, which proposes that the human anxiety system assigns special priority to “safe threats”—objects or events that appear threatening but are remote and require no immediate action. The theory further posits that the anxiety system operates with relative autonomy in monitoring the environment and processing stimuli, including in the selection of dream content.

articles.title: Connected or drained? An experience sampling study on informal communication and well-being in hybrid work settings
articles.authors: Alicia Andrea Meier-Ernst; Leonard Reinecke
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Informal communication has been ascribed well-being functions. Yet in increasingly hybrid work settings, where employees work remotely, informal exchanges frequently occur via digital channels and may hinder relational bonds and drain rather than restore employees’ energy. Drawing on Communicate Bond Belong Theory, this study examines whether informal communication enhances or undermines employees’ well-being in hybrid settings by considering its perceived quality, relational benefits, and energy-related costs. Design/methodology/approach: A one-week experience sampling study (26 participants; 549 surveys) captured employees’ everyday communication episodes with co-workers and their subsequent experiences. Mixed-effects models estimated within-person relationships while accounting for between-person differences.
Findings: Episodes that were more informal than usual were associated with higher striving potential (e.g., more pleasantness or meaningfulness). In turn, higher striving potential was associated with more relatedness need satisfaction and a more favorable relatedness-to-energy ratio, though not with energy expenditure. Communication modality did not moderate these associations. However, text-based (vs. audio-visual) exchanges were significantly associated with lower relatedness and energy expenditure, and a higher relatedness-to-energy ratio. Originality: Adopting a situational perspective, this study moves beyond frequency-based and between-person approaches to everyday informal communication. It disentangles message- and channel-related effects and their distinct contributions in the relationship between informal talk and employee well-being. From this novel perspective, the findings provide evidence that informal communication is a resource for employees’ well-being, but can impose demands when it occurs digitally, an aspect that practitioners should recognize when designing informal communication initiatives.

articles.title: How to end a nightmare using ocular distress signaling
articles.authors: Remington Mallett; Norah Wolk; Daniel Morris; Yasmeen Nahas; Cameron Sandell; Karen Konkoly; Michelle Carr; Ken A. Paller
articles.abstract: Nightmares trap people in a unique state of helplessness. Whereas fear during wake can be resolved with downregulation strategies, fear during sleep typically coincides with a reduction in the cognitive and social routes to implement them. Here, we report a case in which a dreamer and a technician together overcame both limitations, ending a nightmare in real time. A participant experiencing frequent nightmares was enrolled in a protocol designed to induce lucid dreams (restoring cognition during REM sleep) and enable communication from the dream via eye movements (restoring a social connection). During a nightmare, they gained awareness and used the eye signal as a mayday to request extraction from the dream, all while in polysomnography-verified REM sleep. They were awakened by the technician 34 seconds after the help request and reported immediate relief. At 2- and 4-week follow-ups, lucid dream frequency increased relative to baseline, with lucidity reducing the distress of a subsequent nightmare. Together, these results suggest that real-time dream communication might offer an in somno approach to treating nightmares, a core symptom of PTSD and other psychiatric disorders.

articles.title: Trusting the Machine: Separating Trust in GenAI Authors from Trust in Their Content
articles.authors: Caroline Simpson; Clara Colombatto; Jonathan Albert Fugelsang
articles.abstract: As Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) becomes more sophisticated and widespread, it matters how its perceived humanness affects trust. Previous work shows that anthropomorphism increases an agent’s perceived trustworthiness as an advisor. We asked whether an author’s presentation also affects trust in the information it produces in a non-advisory role. In two experiments, participants read a science communication blog post attributed to an author with varying anthropomorphic cues. They rated the trustworthiness of the author (author trust) and the content (content trust). In Experiment 1 (N = 270), the post was attributed to a GenAI author described with low or high anthropomorphic cues, or to a human expert. The human author, who also differed in implied professional expertise, received higher author trust than either GenAI author. This effect was reliably larger than the effect on content trust. The low- and high-cue GenAI authors did not reliably differ, including in anthropomorphism ratings. In Experiment 2 (N = 148, preregistered), participants chatted with a GenAI chatbot, presented as the author, that used fewer (low condition) or more (high condition) anthropomorphic cues. The high-cue chatbot was rated more anthropomorphic and received modestly higher author trust. No reliable content trust effect was detected, and evidence that the two effects differed was inconclusive. Author and content trust were strongly correlated in both experiments. These results suggest that cues to an author’s humanness may shape trust in the author more than in what it communicates, although the clearest evidence came from comparing human and GenAI authors.

articles.title: Seeing a partner’s gestures in conversation increases referential but not form alignment: Evidence for distinct mechanisms of alignment in co-speech gestures
articles.authors: Sho Akamine; antje meyer; Asli Ozyurek
articles.abstract: People often align with one another’s sentence structures, lexical choices, and co-speech gestures during conversation. Such linguistic alignment has been attributed to both low-level priming and high-level collaborative efforts to establish mutual understanding (grounding). Although the contributions of these processes have been extensively investigated for verbal aspects of language use, their roles in co-speech gestural alignment remain largely unexplored. Here, we manipulated partner visibility in a video-mediated dyadic referential communication game (n = 45 dyads) to examine (i) whether priming and grounding contribute to the two dimensions of gestural alignment: referential and form alignment, and (ii) how lexical alignment relates to gestural alignment. We found that participants produced referentially aligned gestures more frequently when they could see their partner’s gestures than when they could not, irrespective of whether their own gestures were visible to their partner. This pattern provides evidence consistent with priming, but not with the predicted grounding effect. By contrast, visibility had little to no effect on Dynamic Time Warping (DTW)-based gesture form similarity, suggesting that the contributions of priming and grounding may differ between referential and form alignment. Furthermore, lexical alignment was positively associated with the frequency of referentially aligned gestures, even after accounting for control variables. This association is consistent with the possibility that shared conceptualization of referents contributes to gestural alignment. Taken together, these findings highlight that mechanisms underlying alignment may differ depending on the dimensions of gestural alignment and point to distinct roles for priming and shared conceptualization in the alignment of co-speech gestures.

articles.title: iOS Shortcuts as a Free, No-Code Tool for Event-Triggered Experience Sampling
articles.authors: Douglas A. Parry; Tilo Hartmann
articles.abstract: Event-triggered experience sampling prompts in situ surveys when specific behaviors or contexts occur. This approach is valuable for capturing infrequent or context-bound experiences but often requires custom or expensive software. This article describes how iOS Shortcuts, a pre-installed automation feature, can provide a free, no-code alternative for event-triggered surveys on iPhones. Using trigger-action programming, researchers can configure automations that launch survey URLs with embedded contextual parameters when designated events occur. We describe the procedure, outline a workflow of triggers, actions, and embedded variables, and illustrate the approach with worked examples and templates.

articles.title: Tales of Life: Curiosity for Positive and Negative Life Stories of Culturally Close and Distant Others
articles.authors: Esther Niehoff; Marret Noordewier; Malgorzata A Goclowska; Suzanne Oosterwijk
articles.abstract: Personalized stories about others’ life experiences are omnipresent in media, yet we know little about what drives people to engage with such narratives. Across two studies (N = 596 UK adults), we investigated how valence (positive versus negative life event) and cultural distance (experience from someone from a culturally close versus distant country) shape social curiosity. Consistently, participants reported greater curiosity for stories about negative life events, especially when the story’s protagonist was culturally close. Structural equation modelling revealed that the relationship between negative valence and higher curiosity was mediated through greater anticipated insight and – counterintuitive at first sight – greater anticipated distress towards negative stories. At the same time, curiosity for negative stories was attenuated through lower expected enjoyment. These findings suggest that curiosity is driven by anticipated emotional impact of either valence, and have implications for fostering empathy and meaningful engagement in media and public discourse.

articles.title: Age-related underestimation of smartphone screen time
articles.authors: Wenyu Wan; Maria G. Jol; Arko Ghosh
articles.abstract: There is growing evidence that self-reported media use poorly reflects real use, yet self-reports remain the dominant method in media research. Furthermore, the capacity to self-regulate smartphone use intuitively depends on how accurately one perceives that use. Here, we directly compared self-reported and objectively logged smartphone screen time in 304 participants aged 20 to 84 years. We found that reporting bias was strongly age-dependent: older adults underestimated their use while younger adults overestimated theirs. The age-related reporting bias was not explained by working memory performance (2-back task). Working memory did not mediate the association between age and reporting discrepancy. Our findings indicate that self-reported smartphone use carry little information on real use. We highlight the importance of objective measures of smartphone use and the need for understanding mechanisms which distort perceived use.

articles.title: From use perception to use behavior: Digitally traced smartphone use purposes and psychological well-being in daily life
articles.authors: Krisna Adiasto; Fenne große Deters; Lisanne Sarah Pauw; Katharina Salo; Anne Milek
articles.abstract: Research on smartphone use and psychological well-being has yielded ambivalent and generally small effects. Three methodological limitations contribute to this inconsistency: studies typically capture smartphone use through aggregate measures such as screen time, rely on self-reported estimates that are systematically biased, and focus predominantly on between-person differences while neglecting within-person dynamics. The present study addresses these limitations by examining the between- and within-person associations between digitally traced smartphone use purposes and psychological well-being. Using device logged app use data from a 10-day ecological momentary assessment study of romantic couples (N = 342 individuals), we examined five smartphone use purposes – active social use, passive social use, news consumption, entertainment, and practical use – in relation to positive affect, negative affect, and perceived stress. Analyses were replicated across two subsets to circumvent the dyadic structure of the data, and as an internal robustness check. Across both subsets, associations between digitally traced use purposes and well-being were overall modest and largely inconsistent. The only robust finding across subsets was a within-person association suggesting that days of higher than typical active social use were associated with lower positive affect. Notably, passive social use, which is among the strongest negative predictors of well-being in self-report studies, showed no reliable association under device logged measurement. Overall, these findings suggest that the psychological consequences of actual smartphone use behavior are more limited and more context-dependent than self-report studies imply, underscoring the importance of measurement methods in research on digital technology and well-being.

articles.title: Why Computational Cognitive Science? Specifying Social Science Theories as Cognitive Agents
articles.authors: Dohyun Ahn
articles.abstract: Social science theories about how people and environments change each other are mostly stated in words. Verbal statements leave open the quantities and functional forms needed to derive outcomes. Tests of association cannot distinguish the individual rules that could have produced an association, and causal structures established separately are rarely combined. Computational cognitive science offers a remedy: it specifies theories as rules that generate individual judgment and choice, runs the rules, and checks before data collection whether rival rules can be distinguished. Cognitive agent modeling adapts this practice to theories of person–environment relations. Four causal structures recur in social science: the environment changes people, people select their environments, the two change each other over time, and environmental effects differ across people. Cognitive agent modeling specifies these structures as four components of one agent: learning, choice, feedback, and individual differences. The article compares the approach with other computational approaches and works through media effects theories as a case, giving an example specification and four propositions. In a simulation, three rival explanations of crime viewing and fear yielded positive mean correlations, and a design alternating assigned and freely chosen exposure identified the generating specification in 96% to 100% of data sets.

articles.title: Navigating Digital Platforms in Adolescence: A Population‑Based Study of Online Sexual Experiences and Violations
articles.authors: Lia Ferschmann; Sjur Skjørshammer Sætren; Katrin Chauviré-Geib; Ann-Christin Haag; Miriam Rassenhofer; Olivia Dimitrijevic; Per Moum Hellevik; Else-Marie Augusti; Gertrud Sofie Hafstad
articles.abstract:
Background Digital platforms provide contexts for both normative adolescent sexual exploration and potential victimization. We lack understanding of the diversity of experiences adolescents encounter, and importantly, and how they subjectively appraise them. How a young person subjectively perceives an event may impact associations with health.
Methods This preregistered study used population-based self-report data from 3,675 adolescents aged 12–16 years to examine the prevalence of different online sexual experiences and violations, ranging from sharing sexual content to having nude images spread on social media. Additionally, the study probes several measures of subjective appraisals, including how distressing experiences were, regret and assessments of the extent to which one felt one was forced or tricked into the experience. Generalized linear models were used to examine associations between cumulative exposure to online sexual experiences and violations and mental health symptoms (Hopkins Symptom Checklist), somatic symptoms (Children’s Somatic Symptoms Inventory), and current and peak subjective distress related to these experiences. Regret was examined as a potential moderator. Logistic regression examined the history of offline sexual abuse by an adult as a risk factor.
Results By age 16, 49% of adolescents reported at least one online sexual experience or violation. Greater cumulative exposure was associated with more mental and somatic symptoms and higher current and peak subjective distress. Associations with symptoms remained even when accounting for symptoms from two years prior, family affluence, removing most severe items, and excluding participants reporting being coerced or tricked into the experience. Regret did not moderate exposure – subjective distress associations. Offline sexual abuse by an adult substantially increased the odds of having online sexual experiences or violations. Girls reported more coercion and subjective distress related to online sexual experiences, although boys were less likely to provide data on these measures.
Conclusions Digital contexts should be recognized as important developmental arenas in which adolescents navigate sexuality and intimacy, and where normative exploratory processes and potential risks co-occur. Future research should examine the socio-contextual factors that may render some online sexual experiences detrimental to health, informing efforts to create safer digital spaces that support adolescents’ exploration while protecting them from harm.

articles.title: The case for a developmentally-informed education system in the early years
articles.authors: Jenny Louise Gibson; Sally Hogg
articles.abstract: A developmentally-informed early years system is one that is underpinned by a clear understanding of children. In this chapter we argue that this involves integrating scientific insights into child development with expertise in how public policy, services and practices can influence this development. We present a framework of six core principles capturing essential knowledge about child development, which we propose should inform decisions about early childhood education and associated policies and services. We explore these principles in the context of the Early Years landscape in England. We consider challenges for this framework in the current system and explore what might be done to make the whole system – from front line practice to national policy – more developmentally- informed.

articles.title: Cheaper vegetarian meals reduce unhealthy add-on purchases without compensatory spending
articles.authors: Adéla Plechatá; Cecilie Fenja Strandsbjerg; Yanzhen Luo; Kristian Steensen Nielsen
articles.abstract: Price interventions are proposed to promote sustainable diets, yet real-world spillover effects are rarely tested. In three university canteens (94,740 transactions), one lowered vegetarian and increased meat buffet prices for 15 weeks. Unhealthy add-on purchases fell 1.09 percentage points relative to controls, a 26% relative reduction. Cheaper vegetarian lunches involved comparable portions and no more add-ons than meat lunches. We find no evidence that price differentiation shifts unhealthy consumption elsewhere.

articles.title: Political Ingroup and Outgroup Cues Condition How Large Language Models Refute Conspiracy Theories
articles.authors: Erin B. Fitz; Kyle L. Saunders
articles.abstract: Despite emerging literature on conspiracy theories (CTs) in human-AI interactions, whether large language models (LLMs) refute CTs and how political identities affect responses remains unclear. Drawing on AI system documentation, politeness theory, and motivated reasoning research, we hypothesize that LLMs refute most CTs but adapt responses to the political identities of the user and actor in the claim. In a preregistered study comprising 135,845 conversations, 57 CTs, 21 user-actor political identity condition combinations, and seven OpenAI LLMs, we find that 82% of responses refute the CT and 20% exhibit motivated responding, i.e., acknowledge the user's perspective and affirm their concern. While refutation is more likely for CTs implicating Democrats or Republicans, motivated responding typically accompanies refutation and is more likely when claims involve the user’s outgroup---for example, when a Republican user inquires about a CT involving Democrats, and the model refutes the claim. Although responses to CTs implicating Republicans vary more by user identity than CTs implicating Democrats, the former attenuates response differences between outgroup and ingroup claims. These findings raise broader questions about what it means for AI models to be capable and reliable if LLMs consistently refute conspiracy theories but do so in politically asymmetric ways.

articles.title: “I shape my world around my sensitivities”: Auditory environments and sound sensitivity in intermittently-/non-speaking autistic adults
articles.authors: Rebecca Poulsen; Ari Angel Star-McKenzie; Tim Chan; Melanie Heyworth; Liz Pellicano; Diana Weiting Tan
articles.abstract: Auditory environments shape autistic people’s everyday experiences and quality of life (QoL). However, existing literature tends to characterize these experiences primarily as ‘hypersensitivity’, lacking nuance in how everyday auditory environments shape lived experience. Studies focusing on the experiences of autistic people who are intermittently-/non-speaking are also scarce. This study examined auditory experiences in the presence or absence of competing background noise, operationalized through noisy and quiet everyday environments, among intermittently-/non-speaking and speaking autistic adults. 419 autistic adults (Mage=32.2 yrs, SDage=11.3) completed an online survey including a bespoke questionnaire on everyday sound experiences and a sound-related QoL measure. Of these participants, 383 (91%) predominantly used speech while 36 (9%) were intermittently-/non-speaking. Open-text responses from intermittently-/non-speaking participants were analyzed using content analysis. Statistical analyses revealed that intermittently-/non-speaking participants reported greater sound-related impacts on QoL, greater difficulty in quiet environments, and elevated pain hyperacusis compared with speaking participants. Content analysis contextualized these findings: participants often sought predictable environments to support regulation. Adaptive strategies, including selective withdrawal, preparation, and environmental modification, were framed as proactive self-regulation. Together, the findings position sensory accessibility as an environmental design consideration rather than an individual burden, while centering autonomy in managing auditory input to foster inclusion and wellbeing.

articles.title: Trail Making Tests in Extended Reality: A Critical Review with Implications for Cognitive Ageing
articles.authors: Panagiotis Kourtesis
articles.abstract: Extended reality (XR) versions of the Trail Making Test and Color Trails Test are promising for assessing and training cognition in older adults. However, each XR adaptation is a new instrument, whose display, interaction technique, timing rules and layouts may change what it measures. This critical narrative review maps these implementations by software lineage and appraises their evidence for assessment and training against common criteria. The Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality (TMT-VR), whose source code was inspected, serves as a measurement case. XR trail-making tests showed convergence with paper and computerised versions, varying by test part and sample, and clinical group differences (e.g., Parkinson's disease, mild cognitive impairment). However, gaps in reliability (e.g., randomised forms), validation (e.g., norms, prospective samples) and reporting (e.g., error handling, build identity) emerged, and no training benefit attributable to the trail-making component was identified. The TMT-VR case shows how interaction technique, timing rule, error handling and unlogged layouts shape a score's meaning. Future tests should log layouts and events, estimate alternate-form reliability and undergo prospective validation, and training trials should isolate the trail-making component. Several XR trail-making tests have moved beyond feasibility, and reported tolerability during supervised sessions supports further evaluation in older adults.

articles.title: Emotional and Cognitive Empathy as Predictors of the Levels and Changes in Well-being and Health
articles.authors: Rebekka Weidmann; Jillian Elizabeth Lange; Christie Perez; Joseph Romanelli; Brooke Soulliere; Ania Pathak; Alison Jane Martingano; Sara Konrath; William J. Chopik
articles.abstract: Previous research has been equivocal about whether empathy is associated with better or worse well-being and health. Much of this research used relatively small, cross-sectional samples to study a narrow range of well-being and health outcomes (often with a variety of different scales and types of empathy). The present study examined whether two distinct types of empathy—emotional empathy and cognitive empathy measured with the Basic Empathy Scale for Adults—were linked to average levels and trajectories of self-reported life satisfaction, mental health symptoms, physical health, and diagnoses of medical conditions across 9 years. Using a large, representative sample of Dutch participants (N = 3,974, Mage = 50 years, 53% female), growth-curve models revealed that emotional empathy was associated with lower levels of life satisfaction, higher levels of mental health symptoms and medical conditions, and lower levels of self-rated health. However, those higher in emotional empathy showed steeper declines in mental health symptoms over time (albeit they still reported more mental health symptoms overall). Many of these results replicated in two robustness tests, including a different measure of emotional empathy (based on the Questionnaire Measure of Emotional Empathy) and an independent sample of young adults. Understanding others’ emotions (i.e., cognitive empathy) was associated with reporting more medical conditions but was otherwise unrelated to the other well-being and health levels and trajectories. These findings provide impetus for further longitudinal research to clarify which specific types of empathy have a role in predicting well- being and health over time, and in what direction.

articles.title: Mental Health Conditions as Processes: Developmental Features and Clinical Implications
articles.authors: Vadim Pérez Koldenkova
articles.abstract: Mental disorders are typically approached as syndrome-defined states, and questions like why conditions outlast their triggers, why diagnoses overlap, why some resist treatment, how change occurs and what recovery should aim at are usually addressed separately. Here, we approach mental health conditions as processes within a person’s lifelong development, putting forward four propositions: 1) maintenance and development compete for a limited capacity for change; 2) repeated activity becomes structure; 3) self-maintenance can turn into entrapment, which depletes finite reserves; 4) reorganization is often abrupt and lasts only if consolidated. From this perspective, mental health appears as the preserved capacity to keep developing, whereas many persistent conditions appear as active entrapment—a pattern reproduced by the person’s own activity (avoidance, rumination). Therefore, entering a state, remaining in it, leaving it and stabilizing the outcome can depend on different conditions. For each of these phases we derive clinical implications and testable predictions.

articles_hidden.title: Reliability Exploratory Graph Analysis (rEGA): Nodal Variance Decomposition and Coefficient Gamma for Psychometric Networks
articles_hidden.authors: César Huerta-Huacchahuilca; Jano Ramos-Diaz
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychometric network analysis faces a foundational methodological divide: while rejecting the latent common-cause assumption, applied studies evaluate composite score reliability using classical common-cause coefficients (α, ω) or substitute metric precision with bootstrap partition frequencies (bootEGA), incurring indirect reliability induction under REGEMA guidelines and violating AERA/APA/NCME testing standards. We introduce Reliability Exploratory Graph Analysis (rEGA), an analytical framework grounded in support-constrained maximum likelihood refitting (K̂_refit) and the Neumann–Markov resolvent operator (Q = [I − Ω]⁻¹). rEGA establishes the Law of Conservation of the Nodal Triad, partitioning standardized item variance into Within-Community Communality (hᵢ²), Inter-Community Bridging Variance (βᵢ²), and Markov Nodal Uniqueness (ψᵢ²), such that hᵢ² + βᵢ² + ψᵢ² ≡ 1.000. From this decomposition, rEGA defines a purity-weighted adjacency matrix (A^rEGA), Within-Community (Γ_c) and Total Network (Γ_t) reliability coefficients, and the Graph Standard Error of Measurement (SEM^raw). Across a Monte Carlo simulation of 97,200 datasets (972 conditions), rEGA-Leiden outperformed Walktrap, Louvain, and Parallel Analysis in dimensionality recovery (87.65% vs. 64.81%–71.32%), eliminated ℓ₁-shrinkage bias (RMSE_ψ = .035), classified core, bridge, and noise nodes with 86.8%–99.4% accuracy, and yielded unbiased reliability estimates (Bias_Γ = −.007) immune to lexical doublet inflation. Multi-sample validation on the AAQ-II (N = 3,200) and DASS-21 (N = 2,751) demonstrated that the Nodal Triad Leakage Criterion (β̄² > h̄²) rules out spurious over-fragmentation while distinguishing noisy items (A1) from transdiagnostic bridges (D2, S3, S6) with high cross-sample invariance (r > .93). Separating structural validity from score error, rEGA prevents ad hoc scale pruning and reconciles network psychometrics with international measurement standards.

articles_hidden.title: MDMA-Assisted Therapy for Social Anxiety Disorder: A Qualitative Analysis of Patient Experiences of Change
articles_hidden.authors: Christina Chwyl; Malena Donas; Angelica Spata; Gabriella Gatto; Akeesha Simmons; Kim Hoffman; M. Kati Lear; Brian Pilecki; Jenna LeJeune; Jason B Luoma
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: This study represents the first qualitative analysis to explore experiences of 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA)-assisted therapy (MDMA-AT) for people with social anxiety disorder. 

Method: Following two MDMA (midomafetamine) sessions, participants (N = 20) completed semi-structured interviews of their treatment experiences. Team members derived themes pertaining to what aspects of treatment participants felt contributed to therapeutic benefit through reflexive thematic analysis.  

Results: Five themes were identified: 1) Healing Catalysed by Gently Facing Difficult Experiences (sub-themes: Moving from Criticism to Curiosity and Compassion; Enhanced Capacity to Access and Process Emotions); 2) Meaning Making through Broadened Perspectives of Self and Others (sub-themes: Clarity on the Origins of Distress; Deeper Understanding of Authentic Self; Interconnectedness and Oneness); 3) From Intellectual to Felt Knowing through Embodied States (sub-themes: Emotional Experiencing and Release; Feeling Safe and at Ease with Oneself); 4) Learning New Relational Patterns through Vulnerable Self-Expression; and 5) MDMA Experiences as Anchor for Ongoing Self-Discovery. 

Conclusion: Overall, participants felt that MDMA in the context of a safe therapeutic container facilitated them facing, deeply feeling and embodying emotions, which catalysed new insights and healing. By feeling more connected and at ease with themselves and with others, participants gained the motivation to show up authentically in their relationships.

articles_hidden.title: Appetitive Food Rewards and Cognitive Flexibility: Reward Transitions, Voluntary Task Switching, and Individual Differences
articles_hidden.authors: Beatrice Lomeo; Joseph M Orr
articles_hidden.abstract: Motivation shapes how people allocate cognitive control, including whether they persist with a current task or flexibly switch to another. Although reward transitions have been shown to influence this balance, prior work has largely relied on monetary incentives. We tested whether changes in appetitive food reward motivate voluntary task switching, and whether this effect varies with subjective reward valuation and eating-related traits. A total of 112 undergraduate participants completed a voluntary task-switching task in which cues signaled low (1 point) or high (10 points) rewards exchangeable for candy. Access to the candy rewards was manipulated between subjects, with a free access group and a restricted group that could see, but not access, the received candy rewards. Trial-level choices were analyzed with generalized linear mixed models. Participants switched tasks more often when reward value changed between trials than when it remained consistently low or high. This reward-transition effect was larger among participants reporting greater candy liking and wanting. It was also stronger among those more susceptible to external food cues and weaker among those reporting greater routine restraint. Candy-access condition and progress toward the next candy did not improve model fit in the primary choice model. These findings identify reward dynamics as a motivational influence on cognitive flexibility and extend reward-transition accounts of control allocation to primary food incentives. Individual differences in incentive valuation and eating-related tendencies further shape how reward cues guide flexible behavior.

articles_hidden.title: Can Human Verification Restore Felt Responsibility for AI-Assisted Knowledge Work?
articles_hidden.authors: Stefan Rose; Markus Weinmann
articles_hidden.abstract:
Generative AI (genAI) co-produces the work of hundreds of millions of people. Human
oversight, the default safeguard in AI governance, assumes that people still feel responsible
for the outputs they approve. Yet genAI assistance can lower psychological ownership of
such outputs, and whether the resulting loss of felt responsibility can be repaired remains
unclear. Drawing on the triangle model of responsibility and psychological ownership theory,
we propose that psychological ownership is how people experience the causal link between
themselves and an outcome, that genAI assistance weakens this link, and that a mandatory
verification step after generation can rebuild it. We derive five hypotheses on the erosion and
restoration of psychological ownership and felt responsibility and on revision after criticism,
and we outline a 3 × 2 experiment to test them.

articles_hidden.title: Fast Eyes, Sharp Eyes, or Good Eyes? What Links Visual Perception to Higher-Order Cognition
articles_hidden.authors: Shanglin Yang; Rean Du; Jeffrey N. Rouder
articles_hidden.abstract: Why do simple perceptual tasks predict higher-order cognition, such as working memory and fluid intelligence? We contrast three hypotheses. Fast eyes: individuals who extract visual information quickly do well on both perceptual and cognitive tasks. Sharp eyes: individuals who resolve targets clearly in visual noise do well on both. Good eyes: a general visual ability, specific to neither speed nor noise, underlies both. To distinguish them, we crossed three stimulus types (Pi, letter, Gabor) with two masking types. In temporal masking, a mask follows the target and limits processing time; in spatial masking, the same mask accompanies the target and limits visibility through noise. Each task’s temporal and spatial versions thus shared the same stimulus and mask, differing only in how the mask was presented. 79 participants completed these perceptual tasks and four cognitive tasks. A hierarchical psychometric structural equation model decomposed individual differences into general visual, masking, and stimulus factors and related each to cognitive performance. The results show that masking type accounted for relatively little variance and was unrelated to cognitive performance. Stimulus type accounted for more variance but was also unrelated to cognitive performance. Only the general visual factor, shared across all perceptual tasks, was strongly related to cognitive performance (*r* = .64), supporting the good-eyes hypothesis.

articles_hidden.title: An MDS-REM Model for Predicting Individual-Item Perceptual Old-New Recognition
articles_hidden.authors: Robert Nosofsky; Adam F Osth
articles_hidden.abstract: The Retrieving Effectively for Memory (REM) model (Shiffrin & Stevyers, 1997) is an extremely influential model of old-new recognition memory based on Bayesian reasoning principles that provides a comprehensive account of diverse memory phenomena.  However, a limitation of extant versions of the model is that it does not provide accounts of recognition memory at the level of individual items based on their precise positions in multidimensional similarity space and their possession of item-specific distinctive features.  Instead, it assumes a geometric probability distribution for generating hypothetical features and relies on computer simulation to generate predictions of patterns of results for large classes of items and experimental manipulations.  Here we move in the direction of filling that gap by proposing a REM-like model in which individual items are represented in one-to-one correspondence as points in multidimensional similarity (MDS) spaces and in which information regarding distinctive features possessed by individual objects is also provided.  Rather than using the geometric-probability distribution envisioned by Shiffrin and Steyvers, this “MDS-REM” model uses continuous probability density functions defined over the continuous-dimension MDS spaces.  The model is tested using data sets from three previously reported perceptual old-new recognition studies and provides reasonably accurate predictions of performance at the level of individual items or categories, including accounts of how both false-alarm and hit rates are influenced by detailed similarity relations among items and their possession of item-specific distinctive features.

articles_hidden.title: Conditional reasoning in preschoolers: The role of context and alternatives
articles_hidden.authors: Ebru Evcen; David Barner
articles_hidden.abstract: Understanding conditional inferences is fundamental to human reasoning, allowing us to evaluate possibilities and predict outcomes. For instance, the conditional, “If you eat your broccoli, you’ll get a candy” can be interpreted literally, meaning eating broccoli is one way to get a candy, or pragmatically, implying it is the only way. Past studies find school-aged children (ages 7-12) struggle to arrive at literal meanings but, interestingly, compute adult-like, pragmatic interpretations at this age. An important limitation of past research is the lack of testing in contexts that support literal meanings. We conducted two studies to examine whether children can derive literal interpretations when supported by context. We found that preschoolers as young as 4 years old are adult-like in computing literal meanings when they are able to judge that the antecedent is not the only way to bring about the consequent, either because discourse introduces salient alternatives (Exp 1) or because the stated antecedent is not causally related to the consequent (Exp 2). These findings suggest that preschoolers have the logical ability and processing resources required to make conditional inferences when provided with contextual support.

articles_hidden.title: Navigating Safety in Reproductive Health Self-Care Interventions in Ghana: A Qualitative Study
articles_hidden.authors: Kwasi Adu Manu; Sarah E. Stutterheim; Charles Adjei; Francine Schneider
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction
Reproductive health self-care interventions are growing rapidly in Ghana, but there is limited evidence on the quality-of-care provisions that ensure safety for end-users and health professionals. This study explored how quality of care and safety are experienced and maintained within reproductive health self-care interventions in Ghana, using a self-care-specific conceptual framework.

Materials and Methods
Using an exploratory qualitative approach, underpinned by the Quality-of-Care Framework for Self-Care, we interviewed 29 end-users and 19 professionals, comprising health providers, program managers, digital referral agents, and community facilitators across Accra, Tamale, Cape Coast, and Sunyani. The study spanned six sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) domains: family planning, abortion, HIV/STI, maternal and child health, general SRHR, and cervical cancer. Data was analysed using thematic analysis techniques in Dedoose, grounded in both deductive and inductive principles.

Results
Key outcomes include the following: Technical Competency – Despite barriers, end-users felt sufficiently empowered to access self-care services. although professionals required continuous capacity strengthening to keep pace with the evolving ecosystem; Client Safety – End-users preferred access to medical eligibility information, but professionals were while professionals expressed concerns about potential misuse; Information Exchange – Information on family planning self-care services was more openly available than across other SRHR domains; Interpersonal Connection and Choice – End-users reported more positive experiences with remote services than facility-based care, although professionals faced operational constraints that affected consistent delivery of quality care; Continuity of Care – Follow-up care was better integrated across health facilities than alternate service delivery points, with periodic stockouts disrupting continuity efforts.

Conclusion
In exploring how quality of care and safety are experienced and maintained within reproductive health self-care interventions in Ghana, this study found that end-users and professionals have adopted interim measures to maintain some level of safety amid policy and institutional inadequacies. However, the sustainability of these measures is uncertain, posing a serious risk to public health if not prioritised in the short term.

articles_hidden.title: Effects of active learning and talker variability on preschoolers' novel word learning
articles_hidden.authors: Federica Bulgarelli; Marina Rabideau
articles_hidden.abstract: Words sound different every time they are said, both by the same person and across people. This variability has been found to have mixed effects on learning. For example, 14-month-olds benefit from talker variability when learning minimal pairs, but struggle when learning distinct-sounding words. Talker variability is found to be particularly beneficial for learning to produce novel words. All of these previous studies have used passive exposure, presenting participants with predetermined orders or fixed types of variability. Here, we used an active learning paradigm wherein preschoolers could choose who to hear words from during word learning. Then, we tested whether participants seek out variability during word learning, how these talker variability choices influence word learning and whether actively making these choices results in different outcomes than passively receiving them. We find that preschoolers choose to hear words from multiple talkers, and talker variability choices interact with active learning to predict production, but not comprehension. Taken together, our results suggest that preschool aged children can make choices are benefit their own learning, informing theories of both talker variability and active learning.

articles_hidden.title: Factor Structure of the Auditory-Visual Abnormalities Questionnaire  and Development of a Brief Scale
articles_hidden.authors: Zach Hambrick; Elizabeth S. Eberlin; Katharine N. Thakkar
articles_hidden.abstract: Nikitova and colleagues’ Auditory and Visual Abnormalities Questionnaire (AVAQ) is the first comprehensive assessment of the type of perceptual abnormalities associated with the schizophrenia spectrum (Nikitova et al., 2019). The primary aim of this study was to investigate the factor structure of the AVAQ and develop a brief version of the scale. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses indicated that the AVAQ is multidimensional, capturing a general factor of perceptual abnormalities, along with more specific types of perceptual abnormalities. Through item-level analyses, we identified 23 items that capture this factor structure. A Brief AVAQ scale consisting of these 23 items exhibited good reliability and convergent validity in two relatively large samples. This scale could be used in both research and clinical practice.

articles_hidden.title: Delusion-like content emerges from common-cause inference over semantically disparate observations
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew Schafer; Emmett M. Larsen; Kiyohito Iigaya; Guillermo Horga
articles_hidden.abstract: Delusions are beliefs with extraordinary content, yet computational accounts of delusions have not explained how this content arises. We propose that extraordinary content emerges when an ordinary mechanism, common-cause inference, is applied to semantically disparate observations. We tested this with large language models (LLMs) by systematically manipulating semantic disparity between observations. Single causes inferred by these models from ordinary observations generally resembled true causes, yet became increasingly delusion-like as observations became more disparate. Observation disparity predicted delusionality, and this relationship could be explained geometrically via semantic analogues of common-cause properties. We further tested this idea in a large corpus of real-world delusions. In cases documenting pre-delusional observations, subsequent delusional beliefs were consistent with what LLMs would infer and exhibited corresponding common-cause properties. Together, our findings identify a computational route through which extraordinary delusion-like content can emerge from ordinary causal inference, and demonstrate its relevance to clinical delusions.

articles_hidden.title: Learning What Matters: Goal certainty shapes working memory prioritization
articles_hidden.authors: Cathy Zhang; Ata Baris Karagoz; Wouter Kool
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive resources are limited, yet people face an abundance of information. Often, which information matters is not stated and can change over time, so people must learn it through experience. This creates a tradeoff: uncertainty requires broad maintenance of multiple information sources, whereas certainty allows resources to be allocated more selectively. Does this reorganization of resources reflect enhancement of relevant information, degradation of irrelevant information, or both? Working memory provides a window into this process because differences in attentional priority should be reflected in what is remembered. To address these questions, we developed the Continuously Assessed Rule Inference Task, in which participants (N = 104) judged whether multidimensional stimuli followed a hidden rule that changed without warning, requiring them to continually update their beliefs about which information was relevant. On intermittent probe trials, participants reproduced the color, shape, and motion direction of the preceding stimulus. A reinforcement-learning model estimated trial-by-trial rule certainty from participants’ choices. As certainty increased, rule judgments relied more on evidence from the rule-defining (active) dimension, and memory for inactive features declined. A mixture model showed that active features became more likely to be retained, and inactive features less likely, with little evidence that the precision of retained features changed. These findings suggest that learning what matters reorganizes working memory by changing which information is retained, rather than how precisely it is represented. This shift from broad to selective maintenance may reflect a tradeoff between flexibility under uncertainty and efficiency once relevant information has been identified.

articles_hidden.title: Traveling back and forth through time: oscillatory brain patterns distinguish directional cued recall
articles_hidden.authors: Jeffrey D Johnson
articles_hidden.abstract: It is well established that episodic memory involves forming associations among stimuli within an event and between the event and its spatial and temporal context and that those associations can subsequently guide the strategies and search processes that lead to successful retrieval. While countless studies have characterized the neurocognitive correlates of relational memory, how retrieval precisely relies on the associations formed between consecutive events, as well as their correspondence with a representation of past time, is less understood. The current study sought to test how transitions are made across memories according to time by directly contrasting, behaviorally and neurally, retrieval in the forward versus backward directions. A list-learning paradigm was employed with immediate cued recall tasks in which subjects had to use cue words to recall those that came next (forward) or previously (backward) in the list. Scalp EEG data acquired just before the recalled words had to be reported was then used, in combination with multivariate pattern-classification analysis (MVPA), to distinguish neural activity related to retrieval deliberation and search processes. The main results provide novel evidence that, even while equating behavioral performance across retrieval direction, high-frequency (gamma-band) oscillatory EEG activity distinguishes forward and backward retrieval. Implications of the findings are discussed in relation to other, widely-used experimental and neuropsychological tasks (e.g., serial and free recall), as well as to work on understanding the broader role of time (i.e., past versus future) in episodic memory.

articles_hidden.title: Learning What Matters: Goal certainty shapes working memory prioritization
articles_hidden.authors: Cathy Zhang; Ata Baris Karagoz; Wouter Kool
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive resources are limited, yet people face an abundance of information. articles_hidden.title: Long-Term Predictors of Word Reading Fluency Beyond the Early Elementary Grades
articles_hidden.authors: Maria Psyridou; KATERINA KATOPODI; George K. Georgiou; Athanassios Protopapas
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose: Word reading fluency continues to develop after accuracy is achieved, yet which early skills drive this development beyond earlier attainment remains unclear. We examined the longitudinal development of word reading fluency in Greek from Grade 2 to 6 to find out (1) how stable fluency is across these grades, (2) which early cognitive and linguistic skills predict Grade 6 fluency beyond prior attainment, and (3) whether the suppression effects commonly reported in concurrent designs hold longitudinally.
Method: Greek children (n = 268) were assessed at the beginning of Grade 2 on serial and discrete naming (digits, objects, words, pseudowords), phonological awareness, orthographic knowledge, articulation rate, morphological awareness, vocabulary, and nonverbal ability, and on word reading fluency at the end of Grades 2, 3, and 6. Longitudinal structural equation models with autoregressive paths were used to identify unique predictors. 
Results: Fluency was highly stable (β = .88 from Grade 2 to 3; β = .64 from Grade 3 to 6). Grade 2 fluency was predicted mainly by discrete word naming. Beyond Grade 3 fluency, serial digit naming, orthographic knowledge, and articulation rate predicted Grade 6 fluency, accounting for an additional 13% of the variance, but only when discrete digit naming was included as a suppressor. General cognitive and linguistic measures made no contribution.
Conclusions: The predictors of word reading fluency appear to change across the primary school years, from word-level naming to sequential processing, orthographic knowledge, and articulatory speed. Word reading fluency may thus be better understood not as a unitary skill that simply improves quantitatively over time, but as a developmentally shifting construct.

articles_hidden.title: Cultural Distance between Geographic Regions is associated with Lower Mobility, Weaker Democracy, and Increased Risk of Civil Conflict
articles_hidden.authors: Cindel J. M. White; Michael Muthukrishna
articles_hidden.abstract: Stable nations require strangers to coordinate and cooperate despite cultural differences. Using the Cultural Fixation Index (CFST) on World Values Survey data (268,992 participants; 95 countries; 2005–2022), we quantify cultural distances between demographic groups within countries, including between regions, ethnicities, religious groups, education levels, and social classes. We test whether within-country cultural distances are associated with national indicators of social mobility, democracy, and civil conflict. A pre-registered multiverse analysis (54,600 model specifications; 100 model families; 6 demographic groupings; 6 outcome measures) shows that only cultural distance between geographic regions is associated robustly with institutional weaknesses, such as higher corruption, weaker democracy, lower social mobility, and greater risk of civil conflict. In contrast, distances between ethnic, religious, and socioeconomic groups show few significant associations with national indicators of governance, mobility, and conflict, and educational distance is often associated with lower corruption and stronger democracies. The results imply that what matters is not diversity per se, but whether culturally distinct groups are geographically segregated.

articles_hidden.title: Comparing physical literacy scores by sex and movement behaviour distributions across physical literacy profiles among elementary school students: an exploratory study
articles_hidden.authors: Henri Moncanis; Pierre-Yves de Müllenheim; Nicolas Hauw
articles_hidden.abstract: Current literature supports the idea that physical literacy may serve as a key concept for promoting, in children, physically active lifestyles over the long term. However, in France, few studies have focused on physical literacy levels among children, particularly when it comes to comparing scores between boys and girls. Building on a North American approach, the Canadian Assessment of Physical Literacy Second Edition (CAPL-2) framework provides classification of physical literacy profiles based on the overall physical literacy score across four main dimensions: physical, behavioural, affective, and cognitive. The association between these profiles and relevant indicators of movement behaviour distribution remains unclear in the literature. Therefore, the present exploratory study had two main aims: (i) to compare physical literacy scores by sex; and (ii) to compare, across physical literacy profiles, indicators of movement behaviour distribution (intensity gradient, tendency to spend time at higher intensities, and power-law exponent alpha, sedentary accumulation patterns). Ninety-nine final-year primary school students (Avrillé, Maine-et-Loire, France) were assessed using the CAPL-2. CAPL-2 total scores, multivariate combinations of CAPL-2 domain and item scores by sex, and multivariate combinations of movement behaviour distribution metrics across physical literacy profiles were compared using nonparametric analyses. The results encourage conducting confirmatory studies focusing primarily on sex differences in overall physical literacy and the affective dimension. It also supports conducting studies confirming the ability of physical literacy profiles to reflect the intensity gradient, that is, children's tendency to spend their activity time at higher intensities.

articles_hidden.title: Understanding, enacting, and adapting self-enactable behavior change techniques for physical activity: A qualitative study
articles_hidden.authors: Alexandre Mazéas; Keegan Phillip Knittle; Eleonoora Hintsa Figueiredo; Madalina Jäger; Magnus Kyed Meyer; Nelli Hankonen; Tina Dalager; Nikos Ntoumanis
articles_hidden.abstract: Self-enactable behavior change techniques (SE-BCTs) are actions individuals can apply independently to support their behavior change. Adults may use some techniques intuitively without formal instruction; however, little is known about how they understand, enact, and evaluate SE-BCTs in daily life. We examined middle-aged adults’ SE-BCT use, preferences, and perceived usefulness across physical activity initiation, action, and maintenance stages. Nineteen middle-aged adults with varying levels of self-reported physical activity participated in focus groups. Deductive framework analysis identified SE-BCTs in participants’ accounts. Inductive thematic analysis explored participants’ experiences of understanding, selecting, applying, adapting, and sustaining SE-BCTs across physical activity stages. We identified 216 technique-coded occurrences, representing 56 of the 123 techniques in the SE-BCT compendium. Of these occurrences, 66.2% were congruent with the compendium definitions. Goal setting and revision, self-monitoring, and problem solving were enacted only partially. Participants gave limited attention to some techniques (e.g., source credibility) and viewed others (e.g., environmental restructuring) as insufficient when used alone. SE-BCTs were perceived as interconnected strategies whose usefulness depended on personal fit, context, and phase of behavior change. SE-BCT education may therefore be most useful when it emphasizes practical implementation, combinations of complementary techniques, and flexible adaptation to individual needs and changing behavioral demands.

articles_hidden.title: CaliGaze: A Validated Webcam Eye-Tracking Framework for Attentional Drift-Diffusion Modeling
articles_hidden.authors: Qiang Shen; Qingyan Xiao; Shiguang Fu
articles_hidden.abstract: Eye-tracking has become central to process-tracing research in judgment and decision-making, yet access to this paradigm remains constrained by the cost and logistical demands of research-grade infrared systems. We present CaliGaze, an open-source webcam eye-tracking framework that uses geometric iris landmark estimation, individually calibrated piecewise spatial mapping, and a recorded single-eye eyelid-opening validity flag to support ROI-level gaze classification in binary choice experiments.
