In a within-subject validation study (N = 51), CaliGaze was evaluated against a Tobii Pro Spark infrared eye tracker while participants completed a risky binary choice task with simultaneous dual-system recording. CaliGaze showed strong cross-device agreement in ROI-level dwell proportions and reproduced the core fixation-choice signatures of the task. Both gaze streams consistently supported gaze-dependent over gaze-independent evidence accumulation, and attentional-weighting estimates showed strong cross-device correspondence in between-participant rank ordering. These results suggest that CaliGaze can support ROI-level process tracing and gaze-dependent computational modeling in binary choice tasks, offering a scalable and accessible alternative for decision researchers, with particular potential for large-scale, remote, or resource-limited settings.

articles_hidden.title: A simulation-based workflow and web app for matching self-generated identification codes in longitudinal surveys
articles_hidden.authors: Felix Dietrich; Sophie Mayen; Dora Weubel
articles_hidden.abstract: Longitudinal research links participants’ responses across waves, yet sensitive topics often require anonymity. Self-generated identification codes (SGICs) reconcile both, but participants may sometimes mistype, skip, or swap code parts. Most studies handle such mismatches with ad hoc rules of unknown accuracy. We present a simulation-based workflow and introduce the web app wavelink for choosing a customized matching procedure. To link waves, researchers must describe their design, SGICs, and expected errors; wavelink then simulates studies with known true links, compares exact, rule-based (tiered), and probabilistic procedures, recommends the procedure that misses the fewest links within a set false-link limit, and exports an R script for linking the researcher’s study data. To illustrate, we report a three-wave school panel of adolescents, for which error-tolerant procedures found 91–92% of true links versus 73% for exact matching. Simulations across conditions show that code length limits accuracy and that auxiliary variables compensate for short codes.

articles_hidden.title: Normative Reference Values for Saccadic and Fixation Eye Movements in Healthy Young  Adults: Centile Norms, Split-Half Calibration and Test–Retest Reliability from GazeBase
articles_hidden.authors: Bowen Fu
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Saccadic and fixation measures are widely used in psychiatry and neurology, yet no published centile norms exist for expressing a new recording as a centile or deviation score. We derived norms from GazeBase v2.0 (EyeLink 1000, 1000 Hz, left eye), using Round 1 recordings from 322 healthy young adults aged 18–46, most (284/322) aged 18–25. Twenty-nine features were extracted from three tasks—horizontal saccades (HSS), random oblique saccades (RAN), and central fixation (FXS). Norms are empirical centiles (5th–95th). We tested age and sex effects with generalized additive models for location, scale and shape (GAMLSS), assessed calibration with split-half resampling (50 random splits), and estimated 4-month test–retest reliability in 136 returners (ICC(2,1), absolute agreement). Median main-saccade latency was 121 ms in predictable HSS and 199 ms in unpredictable RAN, with median peak velocity 527 °/s and 440 °/s, respectively. Six of the 29 features differed by sex after Benjamini–Hochberg correction (q < .05), notably fixation small-saccade rate (female median 0.27/s vs. male 0.13/s). Split-half calibration was near-nominal except for ceiling and floor variables. Four features had good reliability (ICC ≥ .75), 8 moderate, and 17 poor (ICC < .50); fixation duration and small-saccade amplitude were least reliable (ICC = .11). At retest, HSS latency increased systematically (+53.0 ms), whereas RAN latency was unchanged. The HSS norms are therefore first-exposure norms. These frozen v1 norms allow new recordings on the same EyeLink tasks to be expressed as centiles and deviation scores, but their clinical validity requires prospective validation in patient samples.

articles_hidden.title: The influence of attention on visual statistical learning and vice versa: Insights from frequency-based grouping as revealed by EEG frequency tagging
articles_hidden.authors: Elena Greatti; Davide Crepaldi
articles_hidden.abstract: The human brain readily captures regularities in the environment. It is not clear, however, whether and how this skill—statistical learning—interacts with attention. We addressed this issue by leveraging neural entrainment, the synchronization of brain activity with statistical structure. In Study 1, we asked whether sensitivity to a frequency-based regularity, created by embedding low-frequency items among higher-frequency items, competes for attentional resources with a concurrent task. Participants viewed structured or random visual streams while performing a 3-back color matching task. Neural entrainment emerged only for structured streams, demonstrating sensitivity to the frequency structure. Improvement in the concurrent task, indexed by decreasing response times, unfolded more slowly when structure was present, suggesting that detecting statistical regularities drew attention away from the 3-back color matching task. In Study 2, we tested the reverse connection—whether taxing attention with a more difficult task impairs the neural tracking of statistical structure. We compared entrainment during an easier color-change detection task and a more difficult 3-back color matching task. We observed no detectable effect of attentional load on neural entrainment. These findings reveal an asymmetric relationship between attention and frequency-based statistical learning: detecting structure imposes a modest attentional cost on a concurrent behavioral task, whereas the online neural tracking of regularities appears to be unaffected by increased attentional demands.

articles_hidden.title: The shared basis of family wellbeing during middle childhood in the context of neurodevelopmental conditions in the MoBa cohort
articles_hidden.authors: Bernt Damian Glaser; Laura Hegemann; Adrian Dahl Askelund; José J. Morosoli; Knut Jørgen Bjuland; Daniela Bragantini; Alexandra Havdahl; Laurie John Hannigan
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Challenges associated with supporting a child with a neurodevelopmental condition (NDC) may mean that wellbeing among these families is subject to different dynamics than among other families.

Methods
In this study, we modelled a shared basis for family wellbeing in the Norwegian Mother, Father, and Child Cohort Study (MoBa) using measures of life satisfaction, depression, and anxiety. Next, we tested for structural differences in the shared basis of family wellbeing between different groups of families of children diagnosed with an NDC and comparison families without diagnoses using multi-group structural equation modelling. Finally, we examined how measures of children’s, mothers’, and fathers’ genetic liabilities to neurodevelopmental conditions and related traits were associated with wellbeing and whether these associations differed by group.

Results
We identified two well-fitting models that parameterised a shared basis for family wellbeing. Structurally, family wellbeing was similar between almost all NDC-diagnosis groups and the comparison group. The exception was the autism-diagnosis group, where the pattern of links between different family members’ wellbeing factors differed significantly to that of the comparison group. Any other group differences were related to the overall level of wellbeing or lower-level patterns of reporting on life satisfaction, depression, and anxiety. Mothers’, fathers’, and children’s indices of genetic liability to various traits were associated with wellbeing, typically via their own wellbeing or a shared family wellbeing factor. However, we did not observe any differences in genetic associations between NDC-diagnosis and comparison families. 

Conclusions
A similar, shared familial basis for wellbeing between families with and without children with NDC diagnoses indicates that the specific dynamics of wellbeing in families remain consistent, even as levels of overall wellbeing may differ. This finding may have implications for the kind of support that can be offered to improve wellbeing among families of individuals diagnosed with NDCs.

articles_hidden.title: Personality reveals distinct behavioral and neural patterns of social cognition in autism
articles_hidden.authors: Elisabetta Pisanu; Marco Zanon; Cristiano Stea; Luca Collari; Antonino Riolo; Raffaella I Rumiati
articles_hidden.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder is characterized by substantial heterogeneity in social-cognitive functioning, yet individual differences contributing to this variability remain poorly understood. Personality provides a normative framework for characterizing such differences across diagnostic boundaries. Here, we investigated whether personality, particularly agreeableness, relates to behavioral and neural variability in social cognition in autistic young adults without intellectual and language impairment. Thirty-eight autistic participants were compared with a large neurotypical sample for personality and with neurotypical individuals selected with high (HA) or low (LA) agreeableness during three EEG paradigms examining social-interaction perception, basic emotion recognition, and complex mental-state decoding. Autistic participants showed lower agreeableness, extraversion, and conscientiousness and higher neuroticism than neurotypical participants, with substantial interindividual variability. Their agreeableness scores were closer to those of LA than HA participants. Behavioral differences were selective: autistic participants showed lower accuracy than HA participants during complex mental-state decoding, whereas no significant difference was detected relative to LA participants or during the other social-cognitive tasks. Neural activity revealed a more nuanced pattern. No significant group differences emerged during social-interaction perception or basic emotion recognition. In contrast, decoding of complex mental states from the face revealed group differences in the ERP component N170 and a smaller Late Slow Wave (LSW) response in autistic participants. The LSW difference was more extensive relative to HA than to LA neurotypical participants. Overall, these findings highlight the importance of considering individual variability at both behavioral and neural levels, as similar behavioral outcomes may reflect distinct neural processing.

articles_hidden.title: Opening Hypothesis-Testing Flexibilities to Others Before Data Collection
articles_hidden.authors: Michael Höfler
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper introduces the concept of multiple, parallel specifications of hypothesis-testing flexibilities. Although its ideas are not entirely novel, the conception as a whole has not yet been fully explicated. It allows researchers other than the study conductors to test a given hypothesis according to their own specifications of how to formulate the hypothesis, collect data, and analyze them. In practice, Programmatic Registered Reports, which were originally designed for another purpose, already provide an implementation framework requiring only minor additions. Incorporating a priori specifications by others might necessitate small, feasible extensions to the study design, for example, collecting further outcome measures. Conceptually, allowing different specifications in hypothesis testing accommodates scientific pluralism while extending the epistemic benefits of preregistration to researchers beyond the study conductors. Further flexibilities in testing involve data processing and the decision rule for determining whether a hypothesis is corroborated. Existing approaches, including secondary data analysis, multiverse analysis, and sensitivity analysis, do not address the flexibilities that occur before data processing. They also have epistemic drawbacks because they rely on post hoc assessments. The paper discusses the value and scope of the resulting multiple test results, which are conditional on the specifications and their underlying substantive assumptions. It concludes with a brief discussion of flexibilities in exploratory research.

articles_hidden.title: Psilocybin-Assisted Therapy for Existential Distress in Serious and Life-Limiting Illness: Emerging Trial Evidence, Barriers to Access, and the Case for Individualized Eligibility
articles_hidden.authors: Janis Ancans
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Background. Existential distress and treatment-resistant depression are common and difficult to manage in patients with serious and life-limiting illnesses. Psilocybin-assisted therapy has shown early promise for these conditions, but access outside research settings remains narrow, inconsistent, expensive and often shaped by outdated eligibility rules. These include extremely limited lists of diagnosis- or just blanket age-based cut-offs, that are not grounded in evidence specific to palliative populations. Regulators slowly adjust to the state-of-the-art knowledge generated by psilocybin-assisted therapy, and overall, often present poor understanding of palliative populations specific needs.
Objective. To review current and emerging clinical evidence for psilocybin-assisted therapy in serious and life-limiting illness, highlighted with the examples of the EU “Horizon Europe” funded PsyPal project and a Johns Hopkins-led trial in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and to examine the regulatory, informational, and financial barriers that shape access for palliative populations.
Findings. Randomized trials in cancer-related existential distress report sustained reductions in depression and death anxiety. Furthermore, a majority of participants in the founding psilocybin studies rated their session among the most meaningful experiences of their life. Project PsyPal is currently the first randomized trial of psilocybin therapy in non-oncology palliative populations, enrolling patients with COPD, ALS, multiple sclerosis, and atypical parkinsonian disorders across four European sites with no upper age limit; a separate trial at Johns Hopkins is testing psilocybin for mood and hopelessness in ALS specifically. Real-world cohort data from Oregon's regulated program corroborate meaningful symptom improvement and low serious-adverse-event rates. Access, however, remains constrained by diagnostic and research-representation gaps, high out-of-pocket cost, and inconsistent regulatory pathways, illustrated by a Canadian patient refused psilocybin for existential relief who was approved for medical assistance in dying within weeks.
Conclusion. Clinical evidence relevant fort to palliative and serious-illness populations is accumulating rapidly. Eligibility frameworks for psilocybin-assisted therapy in palliative care should be built on individualized clinical assessment rather than systematic exclusions, paired with funding mechanisms that prevent access from becoming a function of wealth alone.

articles_hidden.title: Quality of Life and the Case for Consent-Based Psilocybin Access – Questions on the Regulatory Framework and Cost
articles_hidden.authors: Janis Ancans
articles_hidden.abstract: Legal access to psilocybin almost always requires a medical diagnosis first, usually treatment-resistant depression (TRD) or severe PTSD, as though informed consent alone was not sufficient. This article makes two connected arguments. Extending the autonomy argument already accepted for terminally ill patients, competent adults who understand the potential benefits and risks of a psilocybin experience should be able to choose it for reasons of psychological wellness or existential anxiety relief, not only because a clinician has certified a qualifying illness, a right the legal literature calls “cognitive liberty”. Just as important, the cost of access is not fixed; it reflects the regulatory framework under which psilocybin is provided. No jurisdiction has yet completed medicines authorisation pathway; the furthest-advanced clinical programme, Compass Pathways' COMP360, met its Phase 3 primary endpoint and reported six-month durability data for TRD by July 2026, and its developer has since signalled an annual cost close to that of esketamine nasal spray, USD 50,000–65,000, or roughly USD 17,000–22,000 per dose. Meanwhile, Australia's narrower authorised-prescriber legal route for TRD, using GMP-manufactured but unregistered psilocybin, already costs AUD $20,000 per course. Three distinct non-medical routes cost far less. Truffles in the Netherlands, sold under food law with no diagnosis and no supervision required, and Colorado and Oregon's state-licensed psilocybin services, which require no diagnosis but do involve a supervising facilitator, cost up to $3,000 per session. Removing the diagnosis requirement while leaving this cost structure untouched risks replacing the regulatory barrier with the wealth-based one, unless expanded access is paired with public subsidy. Article also briefly reviews the safety evidence, the political origins of psilocybin's scheduling, and the double standard in how its risks are treated. A Canadian case illustrates the institutional and regulatory framework dysfunction, a dying man denied psilocybin for existential relief while approved for medical assistance in dying within weeks, before the article closes with policy recommendations addressing both access and funding.

articles_hidden.title: The Infant and Toddler Curiosity Questionnaire: a German validation
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah F V Eiteljoerge; Elena C. Altmann
articles_hidden.abstract:
Curiosity plays an important role in early learning, but measures of trait curiosity in infancy and toddlerhood are still limited. The Infant and Toddler Curiosity Questionnaire (ITCQ) was recently developed as a caregiver questionnaire for children aged 5 to 24 months and validated in a UK sample. The present study examined the ITCQ in a German sample to test its applicability in a different cultural context and to support cross-national research on early curiosity. 
291 German-speaking caregivers completed the German version of the ITCQ and a temperament questionnaire. Items targeted young children’s observable exploration behaviour and were evaluated on a 7-point Likert scale. Factor analyses indicated an overall acceptable fit of the original three-factor structure, although the Investigative subscale showed weaker fit and may require further refinement. We further observed mostly good internal consistency for the overall scale and subscales, good test-retest reliability, and curiosity was positively associated with Surgency and Effortful Control, while Negative Affect was largely unrelated to the curiosity dimensions except for a small negative association with Interactive curiosity.
Taken together, the findings largely replicate the original results and extend them to an independent German sample. They enable further research on trait curiosity in young children, both locally and across cultures, while also highlighting the importance of remaining attentive to culture-specific nuances. More broadly, the current results provide a solid foundation for future work on how curiosity develops and shapes learning across early childhood.

articles_hidden.title: Correlation-Based, Parameter-Based, or Fixed-Effect? A Comparison of One-Stage Meta-Analytic Structural Equation Modeling Approaches
articles_hidden.authors: Julian F Lohmann; Oliver Lüdtke; Alexander Robitzsch
articles_hidden.abstract: Meta-analytic structural equation modeling (MASEM) is increasingly used in psychological research to evaluate multivariate models, such as path or factor models, across multiple primary studies. Several approaches to MASEM have been proposed that differ in whether and where they represent between-study heterogeneity, most notably the fixed-effect, correlation-based, and parameter-based approaches. This study investigates under which conditions these approaches target equivalent or divergent structural parameter estimates. We derive analytical conditions for equivalence and divergence and examine them in three simulation studies comparing one-stage implementations under parameter-based data-generating mechanisms. The results show that the approaches produce approximately equivalent estimates when the model-implied correlations depend linearly on the heterogeneous parameters. However, multidimensional, correlated parameter heterogeneity produces target discrepancies between the parameter-based and the other two approaches. These discrepancies increase with the magnitude of between-study heterogeneity. Nonlinear parameter transformations introduce additional discrepancies, even under unidimensional heterogeneity. Under the standard implementations used, almost no differences emerged between the fixed-effect and the correlation-based population targets. Two applications to psychological research further illustrate the model comparison. Overall, the findings show that the location of random effects can affect the target of structural parameter estimation in MASEM even when the study-specific structural models are correctly specified. It follows that the choice among the approaches constitutes a substantive decision for researchers between distinct statistical estimands: the mean of study-specific structural parameters (parameter-based MASEM) and a common parameter vector that best represents the mean correlations across studies (fixed-effect and correlation-based MASEM).

articles_hidden.title: “When AI Can Do the Task, Is Learning Still Worth It and Am I Capable?” Scales for Learning Value and Self-Efficacy in the Context of AI and Links to AI Use and Academic Outcomes
articles_hidden.authors: Soheil Behdarvandirad; Maryamsadat Mirpour
articles_hidden.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can now perform many academic tasks that students were once required to master, raising the question of whether learners still value learning for themselves and feel capable of learning without relying on AI. Available scales mainly focus on AI as the outcome of learning rather than the context of it. This study developed and validated brief scales measuring Learning Value in the Context of AI (LV-AI, the value of personally learning when associated tasks can be performed by AI) and Learning Self-Efficacy in the Context of AI (LSE-AI, the appraisal of ability to learn and perform academically without relying on AI) and examined their associations with AI use and academic outcomes (effort expenditure, persistence, GPA). Data were collected from 882 undergraduate students in the U.S. with approximately equal traditional-age and adult learners. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis supported a correlated two-factor structure. Both scales showed acceptable reliability (ω = .81 and .72), discriminant validity from classical task value and self-efficacy, and measurement invariance across student age type. When classical task value, classical self-efficacy, and AI use were controlled, LV-AI and LSE-AI incrementally predicted effort and persistence, but not GPA. Moreover, although AI use showed a significant negative association with academic effort, an exploratory mediation analysis indicated that this association no longer held when learners' LV-AI and LSE-AI were accounted for, with the indirect path carrying over half of the initial association. This highlights the important role these AI-embedded constructs play in preventing the disengagement tendencies.

articles_hidden.title: Keep It in Sight: Reward Function Compression Through Goal Visibility
articles_hidden.authors: Xitong Chen; Chaofan Li; Gaia Molinaro; Anne Collins
articles_hidden.abstract:
Humans often learn from outcomes defined by abstract goals rather than explicit rewards. This flexibility supports real-world behavior but typically causes slower and less efficient learning compared to directly observable rewards. We asked where the cognitive bottleneck arises as abstract goals are transformed into learning signals. 
The reward function compression hypothesis proposes that this inefficiency arises because evaluating abstract goal outcomes burdens limited cognitive resources otherwise directed toward learning, and that this cognitive cost can decrease over iterations when a specialized, efficient goal-dependent outcome evaluation function is learned. Alternatively, this cost could simply arise from an immediate dual-task effect, where goal maintenance imposes a cost on decisions.
To distinguish these two hypotheses, we manipulated the visibility of goal and non-goal information throughout learning and feedback. While the memory-offloading account predicts that this manipulation should immediately rescue goal-based learning, the reward function compression hypothesis predicts a gradually acquired benefit proportional to the compressibility of the match/mismatch rule. 
Our results (N = 61) supported the reward compression hypothesis. Visible goals gradually reduced learning efficiency costs, eventually approaching the point-based learning performance. An equivalent decrease in memory load (visible non-goals) did not boost learning as much, highlighting the role of outcome evaluation in goal-directed learning. Computational modeling revealed that outcome evaluation efficiency, proxied by participants' ``reward collection'' response time, specifically influenced participants' learning processes, rather than decision noise. These results show that learning from goals depends on our ability to train efficient estimators of outcome values, which is facilitated by keeping goals in sight.

articles_hidden.title: Computational Affective Science
articles_hidden.authors: Kate Petrova
articles_hidden.abstract: Affective science is the interdisciplinary study of phenomena such as emotions, moods, attitudes, and stress responses, which together make up a large part of the forces that energize and direct behavior. The field has developed rich theories of motivation and emotion and generated an impressively large empirical literature on affect in human and nonhuman behavior. In this paper, I argue that the field is now well poised for a systematic turn toward computational modeling. I begin by explaining what computational modeling is, trace how it has transformed neighboring disciplines, and lay out what affective science stands to gain from it. Many computational models of affect and motivation already exist, but this work remains scattered across fields that rarely speak to one another. I review this work across three interrelated domains: (1) models of specific, circumscribed affective phenomena; (2) applied models in computational psychiatry and affective computing; and (3) broader theoretical models that aim to explain what affect is and how it arises. Finally, I outline a vision for the new field of Computational Affective Science—one that transcends the boundary between affect and cognition in pursuit of a cumulative science of motivated behavior.

articles_hidden.title: Development and validation of a prognostic tool for antenatal depressive symptoms: Statistical analysis plan for a two-stage model integrating self-reported and biomarker measures
articles_hidden.authors: Ibrahim; Shahirose Sadrudin Premji; Shehzad Ali; Jaime Delgadillo
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Antenatal depression is common, under-detected, and harms mothers and infants. Pakistan has Asia’s highest perinatal depression prevalence and an estimated national economic burden of US$16.5 billion. About 9.7 million Pakistani women become pregnant each year, and roughly 3.6 million may experience antenatal depression. Routine detection relies on self-report scales (e.g., Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale [EPDS]); whether biomarkers add prognostic value is largely untested. 
Objective: Develop and validate a multivariable prognostic tool (MPT) to predict clinically significant depressive symptoms (EPDS ≥ 10) and assess the added value of biomarker data.
Methods: We will use secondary data (N = 1,621) from the Pakistani Pregnancy Cohort at the Aga Khan Hospital for Women and Children, Sindh. Self-reported predictors across eight domains (demographic, socioeconomic, behavioural, mental health, clinical history, pregnancy-related, and social network) plus biomarkers will inform MPT development. In Stage 1 we will compare supervised classifiers (regularized regression, decision trees, support vector machines, and neural networks) to logistic regression. Models will be trained with stratified five-fold cross-validation and nested L1 selection within folds to retain the smallest predictor set within 0.01 area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) of the full mode. External cross-validation on an independent hold-out sample will report ROC-AUC, area under the precision-recall curve (relative to prevalence), calibration, sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values. Decision thresholds will be set on training data and applied unchanged. In Stage 2 we will build a biomarker-augmented model and compare it to the optimized self-report model using paired AUC tests and reclassification metrics; exploratory clustering will identify participant subgroups. Pre-specified criteria (ROC-AUC ≥ 0.70; calibration slope 0.8–1.2; sensitivity ≥ 0.70; positive net benefit) will determine progression to prospective validation studies in new samples. 
Expected Outcomes: A pragmatic self-report prognostic tool and evidence on whether biomarkers meaningfully improve prediction and justify added complexity.

articles_hidden.title: Putting social, emotional, and behavioral skills to work: SEB skills are robustly linked with occupational attainment, attitudes, behaviors, interests, and values
articles_hidden.authors: Christopher J. Soto; Alexandra Glotzbach; Christopher Napolitano; Madison Nicole Sewell; Heejun Roy Yoon; Alex Casillas; Bo Zhang; Brent Roberts
articles_hidden.abstract: Personality traits are long-established correlates of occupational success. Recently, researchers have also begun to examine the role of social, emotional, and behavioral (SEB) skills in key life domains. Conceptualized as functional capacities rather than characteristic tendencies, SEB skills represent what individuals are capable of doing when wanted or needed. The present research examined how the five major skill domains assessed by the Behavioral, Emotional, and Social Skills Inventory (BESSI) relate with consequential work criteria and outcomes. Specifically, using a demographically representative sample of 1,064 working adults, we tested preregistered links of SEB skills with work performance, attainment, attitudes, intentions, behaviors, interests, and values. SEB skills related robustly with these criteria and outcomes, with different skill domains showing distinctive relationships. For example, Self-Management Skills were linked with self-perceived performance; Social Engagement Skills with occupational attainment; Cooperation Skills with prosocial interests and values; Emotional Resilience Skills with positive work attitudes; and Innovation Skills with creative interests and values. Short forms of the BESSI retained considerable predictive power, making them highly suitable for applied contexts. These findings highlight the key role of functional capacities in occupational experiences and provide a foundation for integrating SEB skills into personnel selection, career coaching, and organizational research.

articles_hidden.title: Reading Minds Beyond the Eyes: Conceptual Knowledge Structures Mental State Perception
articles_hidden.authors: Maryam Bin Meshar; Jonathan B. Freeman
articles_hidden.abstract: The ability to infer others’ mental states is central to understanding human behavior. Across four studies (total N = 827), we examined how facial information and perceivers’ conceptual knowledge structure mental-state inferences. In Study 1, participants identified 60 complex mental states more accurately from full faces than from faces with the eye region removed or isolated eye regions, demonstrating the importance of information beyond the eyes. Study 2 showed that mental states believed to co-occur were perceived as more similar in facial appearance. Crucially, perceivers’ idiosyncratic conceptual associations predicted their own facial-similarity judgments even after accounting for associations shared across participants. Studies 3 and 4 extended this correspondence from perceptual similarity to categorical identification: conceptually associated states were more likely to be confused with one another, both for standardized posed expressions and for naturalistic, unposed faces. On trials involving misidentification, participants’ unique conceptual associations predicted which incorrect mental-state label they selected above and beyond shared conceptual structure. Together, these findings suggest that inferring mental states from faces depends on both distributed facial information and the conceptual organization perceivers bring to the task. More broadly, they identify individual differences in conceptual knowledge as a source of systematic variation in how people read minds from the same facial expressions.

articles_hidden.title: Reliability Exploratory Graph Analysis (rEGA): Nodal Variance Decomposition and Coefficient Gamma for Psychometric Networks
articles_hidden.authors: César Huerta-Huacchahuilca; Jano Ramos-Diaz
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychometric network analysis faces a foundational methodological divide: while rejecting the latent common-cause assumption, applied studies evaluate composite score reliability using classical common-cause coefficients (α, ω) or substitute metric precision with bootstrap partition frequencies (bootEGA), incurring indirect reliability induction under REGEMA guidelines and violating AERA/APA/NCME testing standards. We introduce Reliability Exploratory Graph Analysis (rEGA), an analytical framework grounded in support-constrained maximum likelihood refitting (K̂_refit) and the Neumann–Markov resolvent operator (Q = [I − Ω]⁻¹). rEGA establishes the Law of Conservation of the Nodal Triad, partitioning standardized item variance into Within-Community Communality (hᵢ²), Inter-Community Bridging Variance (βᵢ²), and Markov Nodal Uniqueness (ψᵢ²), such that hᵢ² + βᵢ² + ψᵢ² ≡ 1.000. From this decomposition, rEGA defines a purity-weighted adjacency matrix (A^rEGA), Within-Community (Γ_c) and Total Network (Γ_t) reliability coefficients, and the Graph Standard Error of Measurement (SEM^raw). Across a Monte Carlo simulation of 97,200 datasets (972 conditions), rEGA-Leiden outperformed Walktrap, Louvain, and Parallel Analysis in dimensionality recovery (87.65% vs. 64.81%–71.32%), eliminated ℓ₁-shrinkage bias (RMSE_ψ = .035), classified core, bridge, and noise nodes with 86.8%–99.4% accuracy, and yielded unbiased reliability estimates (Bias_Γ = −.007) immune to lexical doublet inflation. Multi-sample validation on the AAQ-II (N = 3,200) and DASS-21 (N = 2,751) demonstrated that the Nodal Triad Leakage Criterion (β̄² > h̄²) rules out spurious over-fragmentation while distinguishing noisy items (A1) from transdiagnostic bridges (D2, S3, S6) with high cross-sample invariance (r > .93). Separating structural validity from score error, rEGA prevents ad hoc scale pruning and reconciles network psychometrics with international measurement standards.

articles_hidden.title: Data-driven recommendations for increasing reliability and validity in measures of infant word recognition
articles_hidden.authors: Veronica Boyce; Virginia A. Marchman; Heidi A Baumgartner; Claire Augusta Bergey; Mika Braginsky; Federico Giovannetti; George Kachergis; Jess Mankewitz; Stephan Meylan; Ben Prystawski
articles_hidden.abstract: Children’s early word recognition is both an important phenomenon in its own right and a key index of early language more broadly. A central paradigm for measuring word recognition in young children is the looking-while-listening paradigm (LWL), which tracks eye movements to the referent of a word as a measure of online language comprehension. Yet the analytic and design choices for LWL vary widely, and the consequences of these choices have rarely been investigated at a large scale. Here we use data from Peekbank, a repository of LWL data from studies with almost 4000 children (6 months--5 years), to search for analytic and design decisions that maximize the reliability and validity of LWL measures. Analytic recommendations include using long analytic windows for computing accuracy and avoiding baseline correction. We also find little or no benefit from excluding children or trials with low data. The recommended combination of analytic choices increased reliability (intra-class correlations and test-retest correlations) by approximately .20 and validity (correlations with productive vocabulary) by .07. Effects were generally consistent across age, but gains for reliability were more substantial than for validity. Design recommendations include building experiments with a minimum of 10 target trials per child per condition and matching stimuli for animacy. We hope that these recommendations lead to improved and unified standards for the measurement of children’s word recognition in the LWL paradigm.

articles_hidden.title: Perceived treatability is not evidence of diagnostic validity and benefit: A response to Hastings and Hahn on borderline personality disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Laurence Cobbaert
articles_hidden.abstract: Hastings and Hahn report that a borderline personality disorder (BPD) label can improve selected treatment beliefs among clinical psychology trainees. However, more favourable clinician expectations should not be interpreted as evidence that receiving the diagnosis benefits patients. Perceived treatability, treatment efficacy, treatment safety, and patient benefit are distinct constructs. This distinction is particularly important given documented negative effects associated with dialectical behaviour therapy and broader limitations in the systematic assessment and reporting of treatment-related harm in psychotherapy research. Hastings and Hahn's vignette design also presupposes rather than evaluates the legitimacy of the BPD construct and cannot address diagnostic bias, harms arising from classification, or the lived consequences of diagnosis and subsequent care. Their findings therefore demonstrate a change in selected clinician beliefs, not improved care or net patient benefit. Claims of diagnostic benefit require evidence addressing treatment safety, patient-defined outcomes, diagnostic validity and bias, and lived experience.

articles_hidden.title: Cognitive performance in young and middle-aged adults with obesity: a systematic literature review
articles_hidden.authors: Camille Sellier; Marie-Claude Brindisi; Léopold Fezeu; Cecilia Samieri; Valentina A. Andreeva; Stéphanie Chambaron
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective
This systematic review synthesizes prospective evidence on associations between obesity assessed in young or middle adulthood and subsequent cognitive performance before age 65.
Methods
A comprehensive search of PubMed, PsycINFO, and Web of Science identified prospective studies comparing adults with obesity to those of normal weight and assessing cognitive performance, using validated cognitive tests. Risk of bias was evaluated using ROBINS-E, and findings were synthesized narratively.
Results
Among 4,871 records screened, four publications representing three cohorts met the inclusion criteria. Two publications from Whitehall II reported small negative associations between obesity assessed in adulthood and global cognitive performance, whereas the MIDUS analysis found no longitudinal association for BMI. A modestly steeper 10-year decline in global cognition was reported among metabolically unhealthy adults with obesity compared with adults of normal weight in Whitehall II. Findings for executive function and memory were inconsistent and generally small. One study was judged at high risk of bias and the other three raised some concerns.
Conclusions
The available evidence is too sparse, heterogeneous, and methodologically uncertain to establish a meaningful independent association between obesity and cognitive performance before age 65. Future prospective studies should include cognitive assessment at baseline and repeated follow-up, report standardized effect estimates, use domain-specific cognitive outcomes, address confounding a priori, and assess central adiposity and metabolic health alongside BMI, particularly in younger adults.
PROSPERO registration: CRD42024573250
Keywords: Adults, Cognitive functions, Cohort studies, Executive functions, Obesity

articles_hidden.title: Perceived barriers and facilitators to recruitment in global surveillance of movement behaviours in the early years: Findings from the SUNRISE study
articles_hidden.authors: Hollie Miller; Andrew Woods; Kar Hau Chong; Mark Stephen Tremblay; Claudia Maddren; Anthony Okely; John Reilly; Farid Bardid
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Recruitment is often a challenge in health behaviour surveillance studies, especially when working with young children. The International Study of Movement Behaviours in the Early Years (SUNRISE Study) creates a unique opportunity to explore how barriers to recruitment and subsequent recruitment rates vary across countries. The present study aimed to examine global differences in recruitment rates, identify prominent barriers to recruitment, and explore researchers’ perceptions of recruitment practices. 
Methods: Research teams from 48 countries participating in the SUNRISE Study completed an online survey to examine perceived barriers and facilitators to recruitment of early childhood education and care (ECEC) settings, parents and preschoolers in the SUNRISE study. Descriptive analyses were performed to examine recruitment rates and barriers across countries, and directed content analysis, guided by the socio-ecological model were used to identify researchers’ perceptions of effective facilitators to overcome barriers.   
Results: Significant differences in recruitment rates and barriers were observed at both the country income and geographical region level for ECEC and parent/child recruitment with European and high-income countries reporting significantly lower recruitment rates. Across countries, the main barrier to ECEC and parent/child recruitment was time commitment concerns and parental concerns regarding accelerometer use, respectively. At the ECEC level, organisational barriers and centre beliefs regarding parent willingness were also identified to be prominent barriers by African & Eastern-Mediterranean, South-East Asia & Western Pacific, and Americas regions. These barriers were also considered prominent by low & lower-middle-income and upper-middle-income countries. Additional barriers to parent/child recruitment were time commitment concerns and lack of interest, as identified by European and high-income countries. Globally, facilitators at intrapersonal, interpersonal, and community level were found to be beneficial in overcoming recruitment barriers. This may involve providing education on the importance of movement behaviours to improve understanding, delivering participants in-person information sessions, and enlisting community organisations and professional networks to aid recruitment. 
Conclusion: Recruitment for child health surveillance and accelerometery research is inherently complex and may require context-specific approaches to overcome barriers. Our findings provide context-specific recruitment approaches to support the design and implementation of future global surveillance recruitment strategies, and to help ensure greater representativeness in global health research.

articles_hidden.title: Characterizing the input to racial category learning: Evidence from corpus analyses of children's books
articles_hidden.authors: Catarina Vales; Molly Niehaus; Anna Fisher
articles_hidden.abstract: Contemporary accounts of social category learning propose that children build social categories from experience. Despite the central role of experience in these accounts, we still know relatively little about how children learn social categories from their environment. Theories in other domains of developmental science have benefited from empirical work characterizing the structure of children’s experience; this work suggests that children’s environments contain regularities that shape developmental outcomes by structuring the information available for learning. We propose that a similar approach can advance theories of racial category learning: characterizing the regularities present in children's environments is critical to understand how racial category representations are formed. Using U.S. children’s books as a tractable, developmentally-relevant source of input to children, we employ corpus-analytic methods to examine two input properties known to influence category learning: frequency and contextual structure. We find that characters from minoritized racial groups are less frequent than their base-rate in the population (Study 1) and that there are systematic differences in the contextual themes associated with different racial groups (Study 2). Together, these findings suggest that children's books contain distributional regularities along dimensions known to shape category representations. More broadly, by characterizing the structure of children’s experience, this work contributes to a larger effort in developmental science to better understand the environmental regularities from which children learn.

articles_hidden.title: Bridging Perspectives: The Impact of Teacher and Student Ratings of Social-Emotional and Instructional Characteristics on Student Outcomes
articles_hidden.authors: Joyce Scheirlinckx; Sofie Dupré; Filip De Fruyt
articles_hidden.abstract: Teachers' social-emotional and instructional (SEI) characteristics shape classroom functioning and student outcomes, yet most research relies exclusively on teacher self-reports, potentially overlooking discrepancies between teachers' self-perceptions and students' lived experiences. This study addresses this gap by examining: (1) agreement between teacher self-ratings and student evaluations across 16 SEI characteristics, (2) associations between student-rated teacher characteristics and student well-being, and (3) optimal levels of teacher behaviors using Too Little/Too Much (TLTM) scaling methodology. Data were collected from 143 secondary school teachers and 1,993 students (ages 11-20) in Flanders, Belgium. Teachers completed self-evaluations of their SEI characteristics, while students rated their teachers using identical items and reported on their own well-being. Results revealed weak to moderate agreement between teacher and student ratings (ICCs: -.02 to .19), with teachers and students differing significantly in their latent mean ratings. Multilevel analyses showed that 9% of variance in student well-being was attributable to teacher-level factors. Four student-rated teacher characteristics showed significant curvilinear associations with student well-being: emotional self-regulation, teaching tempo, trust in students, and growth mindset beliefs. These inverted U-shaped relationships suggest that moderate levels optimize student well-being, while both deficits and excesses relate to poorer outcomes. Notably, teacher self-ratings did not predict student outcomes. These findings underscore the value of student perspectives in evaluating teaching quality and suggest that effective teaching requires balancing rather than maximizing certain behaviors.

articles_hidden.title: Lost in Mentalization? Revisiting the Mentalizing Construct
articles_hidden.authors: Moria Laznik Strauss; Julieta Piastro Behar
articles_hidden.abstract: Abstract: Over the past three decades, mentalization theory has captured the imagination and curiosity of clinicians, researchers, educators, and professionals across a broad range of disciplines. Alongside its growing influence, questions concerning the definition and measurement of mentalizing as a target construct have remained a recurring theme in literature. This raises two related questions: what are we measuring when we assess mentalizing, and what is the empirical basis for conceptualizing it as a four-dimensional construct? The four-dimensional formulation assumes that four distinct dimensions can be identified and measured, that their polarities form meaningful continuum, that balance and imbalance can be defined, and that the dimensions together form a coherent psychological structure. We propose distinguishing between the assessment of the mentalization theory and of mentalizing itself as a target construct. Adopting a curious, not-knowing stance, we revisit these assumptions and invite further consideration of the architecture and measurement of the mentalizing target construct.

articles_hidden.title: How can we achieve a good measurement of attentional control?
articles_hidden.authors: Alodie Rey-Mermet; Julia M. Haaf; Michelle C. Donzallaz; Gidon T. Frischkorn; Craig Hedge; Niels Oliver Kempkens; Klaus Oberauer; Anna-Lena Schubert
articles_hidden.abstract: Attentional control refers to the basic ability necessary to maintain a goal and goal-relevant features in the face of distraction. Many researchers conceptualize attentional control as a psychometric construct that can explain individual differences across experimental tasks and situations. However, recent research has challenged this idea by observing difficulties with establishing reliable and valid measures of attentional control. The goal of the present theoretical review is threefold: (1) to review and discuss the current methodological challenges that contribute to these difficulties, (2) to move beyond these methodological challenges to highlight theoretical challenges, and (3) to propose an approach combining formal modeling with experimental and correlational methods to address these methodological and theoretical challenges.

articles_hidden.title: Inhibitory functioning in Williams Syndrome: A scoping review on different types of inhibition
articles_hidden.authors: Raquel Baeza; José M. López-Frutos; María Sotillo Mendez
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Inhibitory control is a core component of executive functioning and plays an important role in cognitive, behavioral, and socio-emotional adaptation. It is commonly conceptualized as comprising three components: cognitive, motor, and perceptual inhibition. People with Williams syndrome (WS) frequently exhibit executive difficulties, including inhibitory impairments. However, findings remain dispersed across studies using different assessment approaches. This scoping review aimed to map the evidence on inhibitory functioning in WS, considering its three components and ecological functioning assessed through informant-based questionnaires.
Methods: Following Joanna Briggs Institute recommendations and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, searches were conducted in ProQuest, Web of Science, Scopus, and EBSCOhost. Empirical studies published between 2000 and 2026 involving genetically confirmed WS cohorts were included. Overall, 46 documents comprising 50 studies were reviewed.
Results: Studies were predominantly cross-sectional and evaluative, relying mainly on performance-based tasks. Samples were generally small and heterogeneous, and intervention studies were scarce. Findings indicate that inhibitory functioning is an area of vulnerability in WS, although difficulties vary across components. Most studies using informant-based questionnaires also reported clinically relevant difficulties in everyday inhibitory functioning. Associations with cognitive, behavioral, and socio-emotional variables were identified.
Conclusions: Inhibitory functioning represents an area of vulnerability in WS, with potential implications for everyday adaptation. However, evidence remains uneven across components, particularly perceptual inhibition. Further research using specific assessment measures is needed to clarify these difficulties. Longitudinal studies are also required to understand developmental trajectories, while intervention research should establish which inhibitory components may be amenable to improvement.

articles_hidden.title: How incarceration influences learning from reward and punishment: Longitudinal evidence from computational modelling and EEG.
articles_hidden.authors: Victoria RAMBAUD; Ilke Veeckman; Senne Braem; Louis Favril; Tom Vander Beken; Emilie A. Caspar
articles_hidden.abstract: Imprisonment intends to modify future behaviour partly through punishment. However, little is known about how incarceration alters reinforcement-learning and decision-making. This preregistered longitudinal study investigated behavioural and neural changes in reward and punishment processing during incarceration and release. Newly-incarcerated prisoners (Incoming; n = 61), newly-released individuals (Outgoing; n = 25), and community controls (n = 42) completed a probabilistic reinforcement-learning task at baseline and four months later. Hierarchical Bayesian computational modelling estimated reward and punishment sensitivities, learning rates, and lapse responding. EEG measured feedback-related negativity (FRN), feedback-locked frontal midline theta (FMθ), and delta activity during outcome evaluation. Compared to controls, incoming prisoners exhibited reduced reward sensitivity and learning rate at follow-up, whereas both incoming and outgoing participants showed greater punishment learning. Only controls showed the expected reduction in punishment learning rate across sessions. Behaviourally, controls made more optimal choices than prisoners at baseline, although outgoing participants improved to the same level as controls after release. Neurally, loss–win FRN differentiation strengthened across sessions in all groups. Delta activity was enhanced in both prisoner groups following reward and punishment, whereas FMθ was elevated overall in incoming prisoners. Computational and neurophysiological findings jointly indicate that incarceration is associated with alterations in reinforcement learning, characterized by reduced reward learning, sustained reliance on punishment, and altered neural feedback processing. This shift toward vigilance for negative outcomes may be adaptive within the restrictive prison environment, yet a reliance on punishment information also present after release could shape decision-making during community re-entry and could undermine successful reintegration.

articles_hidden.title: Why and How to Model Trends and Time-Varying Experimental Effects Using Mixed-Effects Models: A Simulation Study and a Tutorial
articles_hidden.authors: Salome Li G. M. Keintzel; Anna Nikolei; Florian Scharf
articles_hidden.abstract: ata from repeated-measures experiments (e.g., response time data, electrophysiological data) can show systematic changes in outcomes over time, so-called (temporal) trends. When analyzing experimental effects between conditions, different trends per condition can cause the experimental effect to vary with time, for example, to decline over the course of the experiment. Previous research has shown that ignoring time-varying effects in an analysis can influence results and distort conclusions, whereas explicit modeling yields more informative results and valuable insights into the underlying (psychological) processes. This article provides a systematic introduction to modeling trends and time-varying experimental effects in experimental data, accounting for fixed trends (across participants) as well as random (person-specific individual) trends. We consider different modeling approaches: exact parametric models, linear or polynomial growth curve models, generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) and the recently proposed random-effects-expectation-maximization (RE-EM) trees. We provide an overview of these different modeling approaches and compare their performance and data requirements in two simulation studies based on the characteristics of realistic data from a cognitive response time experiment. We conclude that polynomial models suffice for simple smooth trends. Otherwise, GAMMs and RE-EM trees are more suited. We derive specific recommendations for their application from our results, provide a tutorial on how these models can be applied in the open source software R, and explain how their results can be interpreted along with presenting annotated R-code. We conclude with a recommended workflow on how a combination of the investigated methods can help researchers better understand time-varying effects.

articles_hidden.title: Diverse Mechanisms of Adaptive Variability in Human Behavior
articles_hidden.authors: Janne Reynders; Tom Verguts; Senne Braem
articles_hidden.abstract: Adaptive variability in behavior is crucial when environments promote unpredictability, yet its underlying cognitive mechanisms remain poorly understood. Volatile and adversarial environments can elicit variability by abrupt rule switches and explicitly reinforcing variable choices, respectively; however, literature lacks paradigms, computational models, and data to investigate and compare how (human) agents address such challenges. We introduce a novel hide-and-seek paradigm and use computational modeling to disentangle five candidate cognitive mechanisms of variability: stochastic choice, fast reinforcement learning, action-frequency-based memory, sequence-frequency-based memory, and episodic memory. Across three experiments (N = 290), we show that participants flexibly increased learning rate in volatile environments, but stochasticity, action-frequency-based memory, and reliance on episodic memory in adversarial environments. For the first time, these findings uncover that adaptive variability is not a unitary phenomenon but instead emerges from the flexible recruitment of multiple cognitive mechanisms as environmental demands intensify.

articles_hidden.title: A comparison of state-of-the-art signal classification  algorithms in a locked-in end-user with a tactile P300 based BCI in long-term home-use
articles_hidden.authors: Maria Pfeiffer; Philipp Ziebell; Claudia Tröger; Wolfgang Tröger; Sebastian Halder; Thomas Giesler; Andrea Kübler; Matthias Eidel
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) constitute a last resort of communication for people with severe motor impairments. To date, several potential improvements of BCI-related hardware and software components have been investigated, for instance, classification algorithms for brain signals such as electroencephalography (EEG). These efforts focused on laboratory work with healthy participants. However, this is not representative for real-life conditions of potential motor-impaired end-users with diseases like amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Our study compares state-of-the-art classification approaches on a real-life dataset of an end-user with ALS and a tactile P300-based BCI, which was obtained in long-term home-use.
Approach: We applied state-of-the-art classification approaches, including Shrinkage Linear Discriminant Analysis (ShrinkLDA) and Riemannian Geometry Classifiers (RGC). Moreover, we tested effects of different calibration scenarios (i.e., amount of training data, time between calibration) and spatial filtering (using xDawn). These variations were compared to the classification results of a commonly used Stepwise Linear Discriminant Analysis (SWLDA). As a criterion for sufficient performance, we defined an accuracy of >70% (based on prior work). 
Main results: SWLDA could be outperformed, but without spatial filtering via xDawn, no classification algorithm was able to allow for sufficient independent home-use (with accuracies ranging between 33% to 66%; SWLDA: 59%). The addition of spatial filtering via xDawn notably improved classification results for all classifiers, with the best performance achieved by RGC_xDAWN and ShrinkLDA_xDAWN (both 72% accuracy; SWLDA_xDAWN: 70%).
Significance: This is the first study comparing classifiers on a large set of tactile P300-based BCI data obtained from an end-user in his own home. Of the state-of-the-art classifiers (established with healthy participants), only two reached slightly beyond a performance accuracy of >70%. Future work can build on our findings (e.g., implement spatial filtering) and further investigate the consequences of real-life conditions for potential end-users (e.g., disease characteristics, hardware and software optimization, environmental factors).

articles_hidden.title: Beyond comorbidity: cognitive decline, cardiometabolic dysfunction, depression and anxiety as a stress-related self-maintaining system in aging.
articles_hidden.authors: Matias M. Pulopulos; Maxime Bertoux; Fabien D'Hondt; Rudi De Raedt
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive decline, cardiometabolic dysfunction, and psychological disorders (particularly late-life depression and anxiety) are highly prevalent in aging, often co-occur, and predict each other over time. Importantly, stress exposure across the lifespan and dysregulation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis and the autonomic nervous system (ANS), the two main biological stress systems, are considered causes and exacerbators of these age-related conditions. However, the stress-to-disease pathway in aging has proven hard to demonstrate consistently, and health trajectories vary widely between individuals. We argue that this partly reflects how the problem has been modeled, with cognitive, cardiometabolic, and psychological health problems in aging studied as separate downstream outcomes of stress and HPA axis and ANS dysregulation. We review and propose several neurocognitive, neurovisceral, and psychophysiological mechanisms that may explain how these three conditions form a mutually reinforcing system. Importantly, these mechanisms also feed back onto the HPA axis and ANS, disrupting their circadian and context-sensitive regulation. We identify middle adulthood as the period in which these reciprocal influences strengthen. Moreover, we propose that the domain first affected and individual reserve shape the health trajectory and which conditions co-occur. In this framework, we argue that stress-system dysregulation in aging should be considered both a cause and a consequence of cognitive decline, cardiometabolic dysfunction, depression and anxiety, forming a self-maintaining loop that may provide a systems-level mechanism through which stress-related multimorbidity contributes to trajectories commonly associated with accelerated biological aging.

articles_hidden.title: Different Analyses, Same Conclusion: A Reply to Rahmadani and Putra (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Pauline Hartmann; Aleksandra E. Rupietta; Antonia Döring; Marcella Lydia Woud
articles_hidden.abstract: Rahmadani and Putra (2026) reanalysed the data originally published by Hartmann et al. (2026). In this reply, we address the points raised in their commentary. Importantly, all conclusions presented in Hartmann et al. (2026) were found to remain valid.

articles_hidden.title: When actions speak louder than words: Maintaining verbally instructed movement representations is driven by action imagery rather than verbal rehearsal
articles_hidden.authors: Carla Czilczer; Markus Martini; Pierre Sachse; Stephan Frederic Dahm
articles_hidden.abstract: When imagining actions based on verbal movement instructions, maintaining an evolving mental representation across successive instructions is important. We examined this process from a working memory perspective, asking whether maintenance of verbally instructed action imagery depends on verbal working memory or can be sustained by action imagery-related processes. In an adapted Final Position Judgment Task (FPJT), participants imagined three to six successive movements from listening to standardized movement instructions. They then judged whether an image of a human figure matched their imagined final position. Participants completed the FPJT in two conditions, once in baseline and once while repeating a syllable aloud to prevent verbal rehearsal. This articulatory suppression increased errors but performance remained above chance, suggesting that performance was not reducible to verbal rehearsal. Converging with this, FPJT errors were associated with visuospatial, but not verbal, working memory, with these associations not varying by FPJT condition. Articulatory suppression reduced reported verbal rehearsal and action imagery quality, whereas in both conditions, more than 80% reported visual rehearsal of instructed body parts to maintain imagery. Visual rehearsal was associated with fewer errors in baseline. Our results suggest that maintaining verbally instructed action imagery in the FPJT relies on action imagery-related visual rehearsal and visuospatial working memory, with verbal rehearsal playing a supporting role. Given that FPJT performance also covaried with mental body rotation and mental paper folding performance, the FPJT appears suitable for assessing action imagery ability.

articles_hidden.title: When risks add up: Cumulative psychosocial adversity and suicidality in an online sample of Latvian adults: a preregistered cross-sectional study
articles_hidden.authors: Edmunds Vanags; Marta Gēbele; Liene Sīle; Liene Konošonoka; Artjoms Soboļevs; Sibilla Krūmiņa; Elmars Terauds; Maris Taube; Romija Krezina
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Latvia has one of the highest suicide rates in the European Union, yet evidence on the psychosocial and mental health correlates of suicidality among Latvian adults remains limited. This preregistered study examined correlates of a composite suicidality outcome.

Methods: A cross-sectional nonprobability online survey of Latvian adults was conducted between May 2025 and February 2026. Of 1,018 participants in the analytic sample, 1,006 had an observed primary outcome. Measures included depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), workplace bullying (NAQ-R), alcohol use (AUDIT), and adapted UK Biobank items on trauma exposure, psychiatric symptoms, and substance use. The primary outcome was a binary composite of suicidal ideation or attempt in the past 12 months, or a lifetime suicide attempt. Hypotheses were tested using multivariable and hierarchical logistic regression, with estimates pooled across 20 multiply imputed datasets and complete-case sensitivity analyses. The protocol was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/8hjea).

Results: Lifetime suicide attempts were reported by 7.6% of participants (76/999), suicidal ideation by 61.9% (614/992), and self-harm by 21.4% (212/992). The composite outcome was present in 34.5% (347/1,006). Clinically significant depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 ≥ 10) were associated with higher odds of suicidality (OR = 5.33, 95% CI 3.97–7.16, p < .001). Compared with low perceived social support, strong support was associated with lower odds after adjustment for age, gender, and employment status (OR = 0.15, 95% CI 0.08–0.28, p < .001). Adding mental health variables to the demographic model increased Nagelkerke's R² from .095 to .345. Participants with four or more prespecified risk factors had higher odds than those with zero or one (OR = 21.53, 95% CI 11.07–41.88, p < .001). Complete-case analyses yielded broadly consistent results.

Conclusions: Depressive symptoms, lower perceived social support, and cumulative psychosocial adversity were associated with suicidality. The cross-sectional design and nonprobability sampling limit generalisability to the Latvian adult population. Nationally representative longitudinal studies are needed to clarify temporal associations.

articles_hidden.title: Face and eye gaze in preterm and full-term preschoolers during face-to-face interactions
articles_hidden.authors: Rowena Van den Broeck; Laura Tibermont; Lisa Gistelinck; Niilo Valtakari; Bieke Bollen; Els Ortibus; Gunnar naulaers; Bart Boets; Roy S Hessels
articles_hidden.abstract: Background: Preterm birth has been linked to atypical social development and difficulties with social orientation similar to those observed in autism. A fundamental component of social interaction is adequate gaze toward an interaction partner’s face and eyes. Preterm individuals have been reported to display atypical social gaze patterns, characterized by more frequent but shorter looks toward faces. Methods: We compared looking times to the face, as well as eyes versus mouth during face-to-face interactions in preterm (N = 45) and full-term (N = 29) five-year-olds, using a video-based eye-tracking set-up. Secondary, we examined number of dwells and mean dwell duration. Each child participated in four interaction tasks, including silent looking at their mother, silent looking at a female stranger, and a positive and negative conversation with their mother. Results: No statistically significant group differences were found between preterm and full-term children in percentage of total dwell times to either the face or the eyes, however small differences were observed with preterm children showing less dwells per minute with longer mean durations than full-term children. We observed a marginal effect of interaction partner, with children spending proportionately more time gazing at their mother’s face than at a stranger’s face. Conclusion: Preterm and full-term five-year-olds showed no differences in total social gaze to the face and the eyes of their interaction partner during face-to-face interactions, although subtle differences were observed in other gaze measures. Speculatively, these findings may reflect a developmental catch-up in social orientation following initial delays in infancy. Alternatively, advances in neonatal medical care, including infant-directed interventions in the neonatal intensive care unit, may have been successful in improving social gaze after preterm birth. Given the context-dependent and individual nature of gaze behavior, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Future longitudinal studies employing consistent methodological approaches are needed to investigate how social gaze develops over time following preterm birth.

articles_hidden.title: Selective maintenance of aversive memories as a mechanism of spontaneous recovery of fear
articles_hidden.authors: Isabel Berwian; Yongjing Ren; Sashank Pisupti; Jialing Ding; Seohyun Moon; Jamie C. Chiu; Deepta Chandrasekhar; Yael Niv
articles_hidden.abstract:
Return of fear after exposure poses a significant challenge for treatment of anxiety dis-
orders. In this study, we used computational modeling to test competing mechanisms
underlying spontaneous recovery of fear over time. We fit computational models of a
novel theory of spontaneous recovery—selective maintenance of aversive memories—
to behavior from a fear conditioning and extinction task (N=316), and showed that they
uniquely captured spontaneous recovery and quantitatively outperformed alternative
models embodying theories from the literature. The results were supported across mul-
tiple datasets, including a preregistered replication (N=355) and a sample with mental
health symptoms (N=520). The selective maintenance modeling framework addition-
ally offers mechanistic insights into overgeneralization and the development of anxi-
ety. Indeed, in the symptomatic sample we found that symptoms of generalized anxiety
disorder correlated with estimates of overgeneralization in the model. Through simu-
lations, we further demonstrated that insights from our model can explain how targeted
interventions such as retrieval cues and cognitive interventions can prevent the return
of fear. These results highlight selective maintenance of aversive events in memory as
a critical and testable target for improving anxiety treatments and preventing relapse.

articles_hidden.title: People Use Fluency Flexibly When Judging Creativity
articles_hidden.authors: Katherine Mae Allen; Nadia M Brashier
articles_hidden.abstract: People often resist innovation. Maintaining the status quo may involve fluency, or subjective ease of processing. Content that feels easy to understand seems true, inspires confidence, and is likable. Across four preregistered experiments (total N = 1002), we investigated whether repeated ideas also seem more creative than new ones. Participants saw uncommon uses for everyday objects (e.g., rolling out dough with a wine bottle; Experiments 1 - 3) or literary quotes (e.g., The richest plan is not to have one; Experiment 4). Later, they judged the creativity of these ideas and new ones. Repeated life hacks seemed less creative than new ones, but repeated literary quotes seemed more creative than new ones. When participants evaluated dimensions of creativity separately, repetition made uses for objects seem more useful without impacting perceived originality. Our findings support feelings-as-information theory, as people use fluency flexibly in domains like creativity, where novelty should be valued.

articles_hidden.title: Effects of Action Type on the Attentional Boost Effect
articles_hidden.authors: Xiangyu Li; Kanji Tanaka
articles_hidden.abstract: The attentional boost effect (ABE) refers to the enhancement of memory for concurrently presented information when a target is detected during a dual task. Although ABE reliably emerges with simple motor responses, such as button presses (i.e., taps), it remains unclear whether it generalizes to actions with higher cognitive demands, such as swipe actions. The present study investigated how action type (tap vs. swipe) and the visuospatial attention associated with each action task influence the ABE. Across three experiments, participants performed a Go/No-go task while encoding background images, followed by a recognition test. In the tap condition, participants pressed a key in response to Go cues, whereas in the swipe condition, they swiped in the direction indicated by the target. In Experiment 1, potential targets appeared at eight spatially distributed locations. The Result showed that the ABE emerged in the tap condition but not in the swipe condition. In Experiments 2 and 3, targets were presented at the center of the screen, and ABEs were observed for both actions. Reaction times were consistently shorter for taps than for swipes. These findings suggest that action-related cognitive demands do not attenuate the ABE; rather, visuospatial attention linked to specific action environments may modulate its magnitude.

articles_hidden.title: Proactive Control and the Processing of English Wh-Dependencies: A Web-Based Behavioral Study
articles_hidden.authors: Keng-Yu Lin; Edith Kaan
articles_hidden.abstract:
Previous studies have found that the engagement of domain-general cognitive control facilitates the solution of sentence ambiguities. This web-based behavioral study investigated the interplay between general cognitive control and linguistic processing. We examined the interactions between proactive control and processing of English wh-dependencies. We reasoned that if processing English wh-dependencies engages proactive control, we should observe differences in reaction times and/or accuracy during processing when proactive control is exercised to different extents.
To this end, we manipulated participants’ proactive control mode by asking them to perform one of the two variants (less vs. more proactive versions) of the AX-Continuous Performance Task (AX-CPT), right after which they read English wh-dependency sentences in a self-paced manner. We also manipulated the gap type (filled vs. control) of the English wh-dependency sentences: filled gaps induce parsing disruptions while control gaps do not. Our AX-CPT results revealed that participants were in distinct proactive control modes under our manipulation; however, such differences did not modulate the subsequent sentence reading task. We did observe a filled gap effect at the subject position, in contrast to previous studies. This suggests that our participants were more proactive than those in prior studies, possibly due to the proactivity manipulation task.

articles_hidden.title: Depressive symptoms are associated with weaker evidence accumulation and greater caution during social decision-making
articles_hidden.authors: Jinil Kim; Yuan-Wei Yao
articles_hidden.abstract: Depression is often characterized by reduced reward sensitivity, slowed responding, and altered social functioning. Prior drift-diffusion modeling studies have linked depression to less efficient accumulation of decision evidence and to greater decision caution in non-social decision-making tasks. However, it remains unclear whether similar process-level alterations extend to social decision-making tasks, such as the ultimatum game, which involves weighing monetary reward against emotional reactions to another player’s offer. To address this question, we applied drift-diffusion models to a publicly available dataset in which 351 adults, grouped by the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D), responded to offers in the ultimatum game. Participants with elevated depressive symptoms accepted offers at a rate comparable to those with lower symptoms but responded more slowly. In a standard time-stationary diffusion model, the high depressive-symptom group showed weaker evidence accumulation and greater decision caution, indexed by lower drift rate and wider decision thresholds, respectively. In an exploratory time-varying model that allowed different attributes to enter the decision process at different times, the same group differences in drift rate and decision threshold were observed. Additionally, the difference between reward and emotion information was estimated to enter the decision process later in the high depressive-symptom group. These findings suggest that depression-related slowing during social decision-making may arise from weaker evidence accumulation and greater decision caution, which are not apparent from acceptance rates alone.

articles_hidden.title: Divergent trajectories of autonomic and affective responses during a real-world contemporary art viewing exhibition visit
articles_hidden.authors: Ami Yamazato; Atsuya Fujimoto; Nobuko Demura; Asuka Nishida; Jun Tamura; Emi Kamono; Kenkichi Takase; Mizuki Ohashi; Yuichiro Yano; Tomoyuki Miyazaki
articles_hidden.abstract: Although viewing art reportedly elicits profound physiological and psychological responses, few studies have examined both domains concurrently in ecologically valid real-world exhibition settings. This study aims to investigate the temporal trajectories and concurrence of autonomic responses—specifically heart rate (HR) and heart rate variability (HRV)—and affective responses across pre-, during-, and post-viewing phases of a naturalistic art-viewing experience. This observational study was conducted at the Yokohama Triennale 2024. In total, 86 adults participated in the on-site procedures; 73 participants with valid HR data across all three on-site phases were included in the primary analytic sample. HR was recorded continuously, from which HRV (indexed by the root mean square of successive differences: RMSSD) was derived.
