Self-reported affect, well-being, resilience, and interest in art were assessed at prespecified time points before, during, and after the visit, as well as at 1-day and 1-week follow-ups. The results revealed divergent trajectories between autonomic and affective responses across the exhibition visit. Mean HR decreased from pre-viewing to post-viewing, while RMSSD increased—a pattern consistent with lower autonomic arousal and greater parasympathetic modulation. Conversely, self-reported negative affect increased (mean change = 5.29, 95% confidence interval [3.91, 6.67]), whereas positive affect exhibited little descriptive change. Broader psychological states—including well-being, resilience, and interest in art—exhibited no consistent patterns of change. Decreases in mean HR, increases in RMSSD, and increases in self-reported negative affect were observed over the same pre- to post-viewing period during a real-world contemporary art-viewing experience. This contrasting pattern may reflect the multidimensional complexity of naturalistic aesthetic experiences, in which physiological and affective measures may exhibit different patterns of change over the same observation period. Future studies should incorporate control conditions, standardized measurement periods, and additional physiological and experiential measures to clarify the mechanisms underlying these divergent patterns.

articles_hidden.title: Psychometric validation of the Spanish-language version of the Power of Food Scale in adults: convergent, discriminative, and trait–state associations with eating behavior and hunger
articles_hidden.authors: Sofia Abrevaya; Delfina Sarciat; Sofia Stancanelli
articles_hidden.abstract: The Power of Food Scale (PFS) is a widely used measure of hedonic hunger — the psychological impact of food environments on motivation to eat. No validated Spanish version exists for South American populations. This study adapted and validated an Argentine Spanish version of the PFS in 810 adults. Item analyses showed adequate variability and acceptable corrected item–total correlations. Internal consistency was high (α = .91). Parallel analysis and exploratory factor analysis supported the original three-factor structure. Confirmatory factor analysis indicated acceptable fit; a bifactor model showed improved fit with an Explained Common Variance of .73, supporting use of the total score. Measurement invariance across biological sex was established. Item response theory analyses confirmed adequate discrimination for most items. Convergent validity was supported by strong associations with hedonic eating, binge eating, and eating disorder symptoms, and negative associations with intuitive eating. PFS scores differentiated binge-eating severity groups (AUC = .86) and showed incremental validity over established measures. Regression-based normative data are provided. The Argentine Spanish PFS is a reliable and valid instrument for assessing hedonic hunger in adults.

articles_hidden.title: Predictors of knowledge of ticks, tick-borne diseases and engagement in protective behaviours: an analysis of survey data from England
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah Masterton; Lee Chan; Anna Middlewick; Janie Olver; Kayleigh Hansford; Louise E Smith
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Ticks pose a considerable threat to both animal and human health, with tick-borne diseases presenting substantial economic and public health burdens. Although engaging in protective behaviours can reduce the risk of tick bites, and subsequently disease risk, factors that are associated with uptake of such behaviours, and knowledge of ticks and tick-borne diseases, are underexplored within England. 
Method 
An online survey was conducted with 1,400 adults residing in England. Multiple linear regression analyses were performed for the outcomes of knowledge of ticks and tick-borne diseases, and engagement with protective behaviours. 
Results 
Participants had a mean knowledge score of 20 out of a possible 35 (57.14% correct responses), and participants engaged in fewer than two protective behaviours on average. Many participants provided ‘don’t know’ responses to questions, with 62.05% of participants providing at least one ‘don’t know’ response. 
Among those who had heard of ticks, knowledge of ticks was associated with higher perceived severity of disease, self-efficacy, social norms and self-reported knowledge. Engagement with protective behaviour was positively associated with belonging to a Black ethnic group, a suspected previous tick encounter, seeing or hearing information about ticks and higher knowledge about ticks and tick-borne diseases. There were no other sociodemographic factors associated with knowledge of ticks, or engagement in protective behaviours.
Conclusions
These findings provide insight into the factors associated with knowledge of ticks and engagement in protective behaviours in a sample of adults from England. However, these results also highlight that knowledge about ticks and tick-borne diseases is incomplete in the English population. Further work is needed to design and evaluate interventions aimed at increasing knowledge about ticks and TBDs and assess their impact on engagement in protective behaviours.

articles_hidden.title: I Remember That Question: Using Eye Tracking to See How Prequestions Shape Reading
articles_hidden.authors: Jason Geller
articles_hidden.abstract:
Answering questions before learning (prequestions) improves memory for the information they
address, but how it does so is unclear. A common proposal is that prequestions direct attention to
that information. We tested this account by recording eye movements while participants read a
text about polio and tuberculosis after answering prequestions about one topic or none, so that
every target sentence was read both with and without prequestions. Prequestions improved
memory only for the prequestioned information, and eye movements showed the same
specificity. Ex-Gaussian models, which separate typical reading time from occasional unusually
long readings, showed that prequestions did not change typical reading of the answer sentences.
Instead, these sentences received more unusually long readings, were looked back to more often,
and were re-read for longer; other sentences were unaffected. Prequestions thus guide attention
selectively rather than heightening it, consistent with additional processing when readers
recognize an answer.

articles_hidden.title: Does Numerology Foretell a Life? Preregistered Tests on Legislators, Olympians and Laureates, and a Lesson on Identity Leakage When Language Models Judge Blind
articles_hidden.authors: TSUTOMU YAHAGI
articles_hidden.abstract: Numerology, sun-sign astrology and the Japanese system sanmeigaku claim that the date of birth (and, for numerology, the name) shows whether a person will rise and when their life will turn. We tested 33 such predictions (excluding the blind matching test described below), preregistered on the Open Science Framework, on four populations with third-party records: 3,308 members of the Japanese House of Representatives, 120,798 national legislators worldwide, 156,386 Olympic athletes, and 8,296 nominees for the Nobel Prize or an Academy Award and Japanese Persons of Cultural Merit. None was supported. Leadership numbers and signs did not predict becoming a leader, an Olympic champion or a laureate, and beginnings, endings and deaths did not cluster in the predicted years; in the largest samples, several differences from chance lay within preregistered bounds of practical equivalence. A positive control, the relative-age effect among Olympic football and ice-hockey players, was detected with the same data and methods (30.0% born January–March against 24.7% of days; p = 1.8 × 10⁻²⁴). In a preregistered blind matching test, one language model wrote a numerology reading and a model from another provider picked the person's life summary out of five. When the reading model was given names, the judge matched readings to summaries well above chance, largely because the reading model wrote the names into the readings against its instructions. Given only the numbers, the judge matched at chance worldwide (20.4%) but at 28.0% in Japan. A follow-up, registered after the first submission, asked the judge to identify each person from the summary alone. In trials in which the judge had not identified the target by both name and exact date of birth, hit rates were 18.5% worldwide and 25.5% in Japan (95% CI 19.0–32.8%), and the judge chose summaries whose recalled birth dates reproduced the reading's numbers more often than chance. The systems did not foretell lives. A language model asked to judge readings blind can appear to succeed by recognising the person, and instructions alone do not prevent this.

articles_hidden.title: The Generalized Price Equation: A Unified Approach to Behavioral Selection Theory
articles_hidden.authors: Matthias Borgstede
articles_hidden.abstract: Behavioral selection theory is an overarching framework that describes behavior as the target of several simultaneous selection processes acting at different aggregate levels, including evolution, culture, and learning. I propose a formal theory of behavioral selection building on a generalized version of the Price equation. The theory provides an overarching account of behavioral selection that can be used to describe various selection processes at different levels of analysis - including natural selection, cultural selection, and operant selection. Focusing on behavioral selection occurring within individuals, I propose a theory-driven strategy for the construction and evaluation of specific behavioral selection models and sketch its empirical application using example data from a published learning experiment.

articles_hidden.title: Selection by Consequences and Psychological Measurement: A Behavioral Account of Rating-Scales
articles_hidden.authors: Matthias Borgstede; Frank Eggert
articles_hidden.abstract: We present a theory-based approach to psychometric rating-scales based on the hypothesis that their putative measurands are internal discriminative stimuli that are shaped by operant selection of relational responding. According to the formal requirements of representational measurement theory, we argue that a measurable internal discriminative stimulus emerges, if and only if relational responses are selected such that the resulting structure is homomorphic to a numerical structure such as the real numbers. We further embed the concept of internal discriminative stimuli in the theory of operant selection, where selection is understood as a multilevel process that shapes behavior with regard to its expected fitness consequences. The theory has wide implications for the interpretation of psychometric rating-scales, as well as for the experimental study of measurement in psychology.

articles_hidden.title: Pattern Completion of Occluded Objects Transforms Retrieval into Learning
articles_hidden.authors: Jennifer Gove; David E. Huber; Rosemary Cowell
articles_hidden.abstract: Recognizing a partially occluded object is effortless and automatic: visual cortex fills in the missing parts to infer a recognizable whole. We tested whether part-to-whole visual pattern completion constitutes not just a retrieval operation, but also a learning mechanism. Participants studied whole objects, after which each object was assigned either to retrieval practice, cued by a circular aperture offering a “peephole” view, or to restudy. At final test, retrieval-practiced (peephole-cued) objects were better remembered than restudied objects – a visual testing effect. The task eliminated the utility of conceptual information, suggesting that this testing effect occurs without semantic mediation, contrary to prominent theories. Critically, when retrieval no longer required pattern completion—retrieval without a peephole cue—the testing effect disappeared. Thus, we report a non-semantically mediated visual testing effect driven by occlusion-induced pattern completion. We suggest that visual pattern completion supports not only occluded object recognition, but also robust visual learning.

articles_hidden.title: Reducing Concerns about Falling in Older Adults: Evaluation of a multi-component intervention and the role of stress and inflammation markers - Long-term effects of the FEARFALL randomized controlled trial
articles_hidden.authors: Sabine Britting; Anja Müller; Robert Kob; Ellen Freiberger; Nicolas Rohleder
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Concerns about falling (CaF) are common in older adults and associated with reduced activity and poorer health. This study investigated, for the first time, the long-term effects of a multi-component intervention targeting CaF on psychological, functional, biophysiological, and anthropometric outcomes. 
Methods: 160 community-dwelling older adults (≥ 70 years) were randomly assigned to a 4-month intervention featuring exercise and cognitive-behavioral training or to a sham control group. CaF and related psychological outcomes were assessed using validated questionnaires. Salivary cortisol and α-amylase, physical function, activity, body composition and inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein [CRP]-, interleukin-6 [IL-6], interleukin-10 [IL-10], interleukin-1 [IL-1] and tumor necrosis factor-alpha [TNF-α]) were analyzed at baseline, post-intervention, and 8-month follow-up.
Results: All estimates represent T0–T2 estimated marginal mean differences. There was no intervention effect or long-term superiority between the groups. Significant time effects were observed for CaF and physiological biomarkers for stress axis activity and inflammatory markers. Functional outcomes changed only marginally.
Conclusion: CaF improved similarly in both groups. Changes in basal stress system activity and inflammatory cytokines were highly comparable between groups. Contrary to our hypothesis, the intervention did not confer additional benefits over the sham control intervention in reducing CaF.
Trial registration: German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS): DRKS00029171. Registered 22 July 2022, https://drks.de/search/de/trial/DRKS00029171.

Keywords
Older adults, concerns about falling, inflammation, community-dwelling, stress, cortisol

articles_hidden.title: Effect-Based Assessments of Intergroup Comparability  – The Practical Impact of Measurement Non-Invariance & Differential Item Functioning on Psychological Tests and Scales
articles_hidden.authors: Tizian Maria Benedikt Schuhbeck; Melanie Viola Partsch; Philipp Sterner; David Goretzko
articles_hidden.abstract: To assess psychological tests and scales for violations of intergroup comparability – termed Measurement Non-Invariance (MNI) in factor analysis and Differential Item Functioning (DIF) in item response theory – statistical testing has emerged as the dominant approach, but inherently fails to differentiate between major and negligible violations. In response to this, upwards of 37 effect size measures for both MNI and DIF have been proposed over the last decades, using vastly different conventions in naming and notation, with no clear consensus on interpretation. This arguably constitutes a severe hindrance for the much-needed popularization of non-dichotomous assessments of intergroup comparability. We address this by systematically deriving a unified framework for a large class of measures from the theoretical definition of first-order measurement invariance. This yields a rich and interpretable taxonomic framework derived from just four fundamental types: Expected Difference (ED), Expected Absolute Difference (EAD), Total Expected Difference (TED) and Total Expected Absolute Difference (TEAD), which are universally applicable, irrespective of the underlying measurement model. Seen as instances of these four measures, this framework includes the 37 identified measures, uncovering both a notable `Jangle' and vast taxonomic gaps in the literature. Finally, we show the relations between measures of this framework and provide a step-by-step guide for practical applications, which we illustrate using models of both factor analysis and item response theory on real-world data.

articles_hidden.title: Measuring Cognitive Demands in Professional Esports
articles_hidden.authors: Cui Zhou; Boyu Qiu
articles_hidden.abstract: Practice may improve certain cognitive skills more than others because those skills are called upon more frequently during an activity. Professional esports provides a means of measuring these demands during gameplay because match records capture the information available to players and their responses as events unfold. This study introduces the Telemetry and Replay Analysis of Cognitive Exposure (TRACE) framework, which measures seven dimensions of cognitive demand in professional esports. The analysis used records from 314 professional DOTA 2 matches, covering 558 distinct player accounts and approximately 2,184 player-hours of competition. TRACE defines four measures at the player level (cognitive control capacity, task switching, inhibitory control, and dynamic attention) and three measures at the team level (visuospatial working memory and updating, decision-making under uncertainty, and feedback learning). Hierarchical Bayesian models estimated each dimension in its original units and on a common percentile scale, accounting for differences among teams, matches, and hero-role combinations. By identifying comparable situations across matches, TRACE can quantify how often players encounter a given demand and how they respond when it arises. This transforms routinely recorded match replays into a source of large-scale behavioral data for cognitive psychology.

articles_hidden.title: Cue-guided attention modulates neural responses to distracting features
articles_hidden.authors: Sizhu Han; Anna Schubö
articles_hidden.abstract: The impact of prior knowledge about an upcoming distractor (i.e., a negative cue) on performance in a subsequent search task has yielded mixed results. A central question is whether negatively cued features can be preemptively suppressed (i.e., before distractors capture attention) or whether they initially capture attention followed by reactive distractor handling (i.e., after distractors capture attention). Notably, negative cueing benefits tend to emerge when the search task is difficult, yet most prior electrophysiological studies have employed easy search tasks that may discourage negative cue use. Therefore, direct neural evidence for negative cueing effects under difficult search is rare. To address this gap, we conducted two experiments. Experiment 1 manipulated task difficulty by varying the number of task-relevant items while keeping the overall set size constant. Results revealed that negative cues enhanced search efficiency in difficult search (8 task-relevant items), but not in easy search (4 items), suggesting that negative cueing benefits depended on the number of items requiring attention rather than overall set size. Experiment 2 employed EEG during difficult search to delineate the neural underpinnings of distractor processing. ERP results showed that negatively cued distractors elicited a reliable early distractor PD in participants showing a cueing benefit in RT but a distractor N2pc on slow-response trials in participants showing RT cost. While preparatory alpha activity did not differ by cue type, stronger alpha lateralization was associated with larger cueing benefits at the individual level. Collectively, these findings suggest that negative cue use is a flexible, strategic and active process, with its deployment contingent on both task demands and individual differences in control capacity.

articles_hidden.title: Tuning flexibility of target templates, not of distractor templates
articles_hidden.authors: Sizhu Han; Lea Marie Schmitt; Anna Schubö
articles_hidden.abstract: Attentional templates guide visual search by biasing attention toward target features and away from distractors, yet how these templates adjust as a function of cue precision and directional deviation remains poorly understood. In two experiments, we manipulated cue precision to assess how imprecise color-based templates guide voluntary attentional selection. With positive cues (indicating the target template), robust benefits were stable at small cue–target deviations (≤36°), but shifted to an optimal tuning pattern at larger deviations (≥48°), where selection favored cues displaced away from distractor features. In contrast, negative cues (indicating the distractor template) yielded little benefit and no systematic modulation by cue precision or direction. These results indicate that target templates flexibly shift from coarse, category-like representations to optimally tuned configurations when target-distractor discriminability is challenged. Together, these findings reveal distinct mechanisms and varying degrees of flexibility underlying target versus distractor templates in voluntary visual search.

articles_hidden.title: TO MONETIZE OR NOT: INFLUENCE OF INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES AND GENDER IN MONETARY VALUATION OF MEANINGFUL EXPERIENCES
articles_hidden.authors: Jude A. Beale; Anne Z. Murphy
articles_hidden.abstract: Money is a universal measure of value that influences most decisions. For centuries, humans have used it to exchange goods and experiences. Research in psychology and behavioral economics, however, shows that there may be limits to what individuals are willing to exchange for money. This study examined the monetary values people assign to personal experiences, and whether willingness to engage in monetary valuation differs between males and females. Five hundred and twenty-nine participants completed an online survey in which they provided the minimum amount of monetary compensation it would require to complete ten separate hypothetical scenarios, with the option to refuse any task. The hypothetical tasks ranged from temporary restrictions and social isolation to public disclosure, loss of memories and permanent identity changes. Based on the results from previous economic decision-making studies, we hypothesized that females would refuse to price tasks more than males and that males would request higher compensation for priced tasks. We also hypothesized that permanent or identity-altering tasks would result in higher refusal rates than temporary ones in both genders. Whether resistance to monetary valuation is a consistent individual tendency was also examined. Our results showed that participants who refused to price one hypothetical task were more likely to refuse other tasks. While no gender differences were observed for any task regarding the monetary value requested, females refused significantly more tasks than males (4.43 vs. 3.17, p < .001). Refusal rates were highest for permanent or identity-altering tasks and lowest for temporary tasks. Lastly, refusal rates for loss of digital pictures/videos were nearly identical to losing contact with friends and family. Together, these findings suggest that monetary valuation involves two separate decisions: whether or not to assign a monetary value and, if so, how much to request. Individuals differ consistently in their willingness to engage in monetary valuation, and gender influences the decision to engage rather than with the amount requested.

articles_hidden.title: Simultaneous detection of patterned and random responses using unsupervised methods
articles_hidden.authors: Wenshuo Li; Carl F. Falk; Michael John Ilagan
articles_hidden.abstract: Careless responding poses a growing threat to data quality in the social sciences. Conventional detection methods often fail when data quality deteriorates or when multiple types of careless respondents coexist. To address these challenges, we propose and study several new methods that require neither measurement models nor labeled data, yet have the potential to detect random and patterned respondents simultaneously. In two simulation studies, we compare these methods to each other and to recently developed alternatives that are designed to detect only random or patterned responses. Empirical examples are provided to shed additional light on algorithm performance and possible boundary conditions. Methods that performed well in simultaneous detection were those that combine generation of a null distribution for each respondent (either by permutation or use of an n-gram model) with certain combinations of outlier statistics for detecting random or patterned responses. However, such approaches were affected by sample size, the number of items, and length of patterns. Through this work, we provide new insights into detecting multiple types of carelessness and provide practical recommendations for improving data quality.

articles_hidden.title: A Crucial Source of Psychological Certainty in Human Cognition: The Certainty Signature of Central Form
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Haward
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans often exhibit more certainty than is justified. Drawing on recent work in Form Theory, a theory of conceptual structure, the present paper proposes and tests a novel hypothesis about one important source of psychological certainty. On Form Theory, concepts have a central form: a core structure within each concept that stores a subset of its information, gives that information default influence in cognition, and activates a distinctive set of strong form-generated beliefs. The present paper tests the proposal that psychological certainty is one such form-generated belief. In Experiment 1, participants judged which properties would be present in newly encountered instances of familiar concepts. While they generalized both form and non-form properties to new instances, they reported being certain only for form properties. In Experiment 2, participants showed the same pattern for newly learned concepts. As soon as a property had been encoded as part of a concept’s central form, participants were much more likely to report being certain of its presence in a new instance than when the same property had been introduced in a generic sentence, but not as part of the concept’s central form. These findings help reveal a deep connection between psychological certainty and the structure of human concepts. Further, they suggest that conceptual structure is one important source of psychological certainty and provide a framework for investigating whether strongly held beliefs documented in research on stereotyping, memory, clinical depression, and conflict may sometimes derive from how concepts have been structured.

articles_hidden.title: A Tutorial on Multilevel Generalized Structured Component Analysis Using GSCA Pro
articles_hidden.authors: Sunmee Kim; Gyeongcheol Cho; Silvia Martelo-Landroguez; Gabriel Cepeda-Carrión; José L. Roldán; Heungsun Hwang
articles_hidden.abstract: Hierarchically structured data are common in behavioral and social science research, yet ignoring nested structures can lead to misleading statistical inferences and obscure meaningful variation in measurement and structural relationships across groups. Multilevel generalized structured component analysis (GSCA) extends component-based structural equation modeling to hierarchical data by allowing measurement loadings and structural path coefficients to vary across higher-level units while retaining common component weights. This tutorial introduces two-level GSCA and demonstrates its practical implementation using GSCA Pro, free software with a graphical interface. Data from 5,014 customers across four corporate chains provide a worked example. We guide readers through model specification, estimation, fit assessment, and interpretation of average and group-specific measurement and structural parameters, highlighting between-group heterogeneity.

articles_hidden.title: Mathematical Relationships Between Brains and Consciousness
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander Maier
articles_hidden.abstract: A chief aim of the neuroscience of consciousness is to derive how states of conscious experience (i.e., qualia) are related to supporting brain states (e.g., patterns of neural activation within patterns of neural connectivity). This aim goes beyond identifying neuronal correlates of consciousness (NCC) on the one side, and beyond structural descriptions of conscious experience (e.g., qualia structure) on the other side. The ultimate goal is to link these two sides by mapping specific neuronal states or mechanisms to specific conscious experiences. Relating two or more phenomena in science often takes the form of mathematical mappings, such as equations (e.g., E = mc^2). This raises the possibility that there also are mathematical mappings that relate conscious states to brain states. Here we review empirical work on mapping neuronal spiking activity to conscious contents. We specifically contrast pioneering paradigms aimed at identifying “bridge loci”, in the form of NCC, with paradigms aimed at identifying “bridge laws”, such as relating psychometric to neurometric functions. We then examine how these paradigms are augmented by mapping structural descriptions of conscious experience to structural descriptions of neuronal activity.

articles_hidden.title: The Effect of an ADHD Diagnostic Label: Stigmatizing or Protective?
articles_hidden.authors: Gabrielle Geist; Ronald Auguste; Marilyn Chege; J. Bruce Morton; Ryan A Stevenson
articles_hidden.abstract: Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a highly prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by clinical symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. These symptoms are often accompanied by social stigmatization, including negative descriptors, animalistic characterizations, emotional reactions of anger, and desired social distance from individuals with ADHD. Stigmatization can negatively impact diagnosis, treatment, and behavioural functioning. This study investigates how diagnostic labels and the gender of individuals with ADHD influence stigma-related responses. Specifically, it examines whether the presence of an ADHD diagnostic label reduces or exacerbates stigma and how gender affects these perceptions. Utilizing a 2x3 factorial design, participants were presented with vignettes describing a 12-year-old child with ADHD behaviours. These vignettes varied by diagnostic label (Label vs No Label) and gender (Female, Male, and Gender-Neutral). Stigma was assessed through four outcome variables: positive-negative attitudes, humanistic-animalistic attitudes, emotional reactions, and social distance. Findings indicate that the presence of a diagnostic label significantly reduced negative attitudes, anger, and social distance. Gender effects were observed but were not statistically significant. Notably, the female vignette condition showed the strongest trends, suggesting that a diagnostic label may be particularly beneficial for females, who often go underdiagnosed. These findings highlight the potential of diagnostic labels to reduce stigma and promote social acceptance.

articles_hidden.title: The Forecasting Proficiency Test: A General Use Assessment of Forecasting Ability
articles_hidden.authors: Mark Himmelstein; Sophie Ma Zhu; Nikolay Petrov; Ezra Karger; Jessica Helmer; Sivan Livnat; Page Hedley; Amory Bennett; Phil Tetlock
articles_hidden.abstract: Accurate predictions about the future are crucial for optimizing policy choices, but finding skilled forecasters is challenging. Prior work relied on forecasting tournaments to identify generalist "superforecasters" who made accurate predictions across domains, but these tournaments take months to complete and require large concurrent samples to compare performance among individuals. We solve these problems by developing a one-hour Forecasting Proficiency Test (FPT) that explains 75% of the variance in forecasters' accuracy about a wide variety of events. The FPT provides standardized percentile scores normed to a large (N=1,147) test development sample based on a combination of reusable real-world forecasting questions and standalone cognitive tests. Which questions and tests are included is highly customizable. Forecasting questions are the best predictors of forecasting proficiency, but cognitive tests help stabilize score distributions and facilitate score exchangeability across different custom test versions even as forecasting questions and resolution dates change. The FPT is primarily a practical tool for decision-makers who rely on accurate predictions to make decisions. However, it is based on one of the largest dedicated psychometric studies ever conducted on human forecasting, which also provides insight into the cognitive mechanisms that drive forecasting proficiency and guidance for future researchers interested in studying the psychology of forecasting.

articles_hidden.title: Boys and Things, Girls and People?  Gender-Related Interest Patterns in Elementary School
articles_hidden.authors: Benjamin Goecke; Jessika Golle; Ingo Zettler; Ulrich Schroeders
articles_hidden.abstract: Gender-related interest patterns are well documented in adolescence and adulthood, but little is known about comparable patterns in elementary school and their relation to subject-specific interests. We assessed RIASEC-based activity preferences in 1,150 third graders in Germany (50.6% girls; mean age = 8.62 years), with interest data for 835 children approximately six months later. A 24-item version selected using T1 data showed good circumplex fit for boys and girls in temporal cross-validation at T2. Boys showed stronger things-oriented profiles (d = 0.77), whereas girls showed stronger ideas-oriented profiles (d = −0.37). The People-Things difference remained largely unchanged over six months. Domain-level retest correlations ranged from .38 to .52. Associations with academic interests were small to moderate (r = .04 to .44), whereas associations with grades were small (r = −.16 to .13). Gender-related differences in broad activity preferences are thus already visible in middle childhood, well before children make consequential educational choices.

articles_hidden.title: Language and Terminology Preferences in Greek-speaking Autism Communities
articles_hidden.authors: Themis Karaminis; Despina Papoudi; Stavroula Stavrakaki
articles_hidden.abstract: The language used to discuss autism both reflects and shapes perceptions of Autistic people, yet research on terminology preferences has largely been confined to English. This study examines autism-related terminology in Greek. A sample of 1,006 Greek-speaking adults (124 Autistic adults, 434 parents/caregivers, and 448 professionals) completed an online survey, selecting, from a list of 61 terms, those they use to refer to autism, Autistic people, autism-related difficulties, and non-autistic people, and explained their choices. Data were analysed using demographics-adjusted group comparisons, principal component analysis, and thematic analysis. The groups shared a core vocabulary (“autism”, “difficulties”, “is on the autism spectrum”) but differed in their use of 39 terms, with small effects, and the main contrasts persisted after demographic adjustment. Autistic adults preferred identity-first and neurodiversity terminology, professionals favoured clinical terminology, and parents/caregivers resembled professionals on identity terms and Autistic adults on clinical terms. Identity and clinical vocabularies were independent dimensions on which every group was represented. Open-ended responses tied these choices to identity among Autistic adults, others’ reactions among parents/caregivers, and audience and setting among professionals. We discuss these findings in the context of autism research and their implications for practice and public discourse.

articles_hidden.title: Potential Brain Predictors of Stroke Risk: A Structural, Functional, and Central Autonomic Network Framework
articles_hidden.authors: Jianhua Chen; Melanie Wilke; Mathias Bähr
articles_hidden.abstract: Stroke risk is assessed using factors such as hypertension, diabetes, smoking and atrial fibrillation. However, these factors describe sources of risk but do not reveal how long-term vascular, metabolic and cardiac stress has affected the brain. Structural MRI can show accumulated brain injury, whereas functional MRI reflects dynamic brain states and may provide complementary information about vulnerability. Their temporal sequence and predictive value require longitudinal validation. This Review evaluates brain imaging features as candidate stroke-risk markers and proposes the central autonomic network as a mechanistic framework linking brain function with cardiac rhythm, blood pressure, inflammation and metabolism.

articles_hidden.title: LifeDive: Cross-kingdom phenotype estimates for 35,856 species
articles_hidden.authors: Tyler Maxwell Moore
articles_hidden.abstract:
Dense, standardized species-by-trait matrices support comparative biology and ecology, but their
coverage remains uneven. LifeDive uses a general-purpose, web-search-enabled language model
within a scripted annotation pipeline to estimate traits across animals, plants, and fungi. The
workflow assembled 35,856 species by 196 phenotype questions, yielding 7,027,776 entries in a
completed matrix; 16.6% of entries were imputed from other machine-derived annotations. Four
ordered substantive responses express model judgments about trait statements, with a separate
code for unknown or inapplicable cases. An exploratory 14-factor representation summarized broad
biological contrasts, although statistical factor-retention criteria suggested substantially more
dimensions. A benchmark screened 168 external criteria, with selected results reported for 44;
many biologically direct associations were strong, particularly for taxonomy and selected ecological
traits. A separate model-assisted audit reported 96.5% directional agreement in a selected
taxonomy-rule subset and approximately 237 agreements among 240 selected species-specific
checks. These audit subsets do not estimate accuracy across the whole matrix, and the
AmphiBIO-derived benchmark results require qualification because unrecorded categories were
treated as negative indicators. Trait profiles also produced recognizable taxonomic and functional
groupings. LifeDive offers a broad computational phenotype resource for exploration, hypothesis
generation, and prioritizing expert review. Individual values remain estimates, and downstream
inference requires attention to imputation, sampling, source dependence, and trait-specific
verification. The reported application programming interface and computing expenditure was
approximately US$10,000.

articles_hidden.title: Rapid processing deficits in children with dyslexia: Influence of stimulus, modality, and genes of interest
articles_hidden.authors: Tracy M Centanni Rosen; Vishal J Thakkar; Logun PK Gunderson; Remington Crossnoe; Abby S Engelhart
articles_hidden.abstract: Rapid automatized naming (RAN) performance is highly predictive of reading outcomes when administered prior to the start of formal reading instruction. Children with dyslexia struggle with this task and RAN difficulties are described as a main deficit in this population. Perhaps unsurprisingly, some children with dyslexia also exhibit deficits in rapid auditory temporal processing of tones. Given that automaticity tasks rely on speed, the goal of the current study was to evaluate rapid processing tasks, their relationship to RAN, and associated genetic variants of interest. Children with or without dyslexia completed an assessment battery, provided a saliva sample for genotyping, and completed self-paced tasks of rapid auditory and visual perception online. Children with dyslexia were significantly slower to respond during tasks that included a linguistic element (speech sounds or letters). Performance on the visuospatial working memory task was correlated with rapid digit naming. Among children with dyslexia, there was a significant main effect of a KIAA0319 variant previously associated with neural inconsistency on reaction times in the rapid speech task and a nominally significant effect on RAN performance. Overall, we provide evidence for general processing speed deficits in dyslexia, though more research is needed to determine the relationship to candidate-dyslexia genes.

articles_hidden.title: Problem gambling and physical blind box and card pack and digital loot box spending: a Mainland Chinese survey
articles_hidden.authors: Leon Y. Xiao; Loïs Fournier; Charlotte Eben
articles_hidden.abstract: Gambling-like products share structural and psychological characteristics with legally regulated traditional gambling but are generally not regulated as gambling. Virtual gambling-like products include video game loot boxes, whilst physical gambling-like products include blind boxes and card packs. Stakeholders are concerned about the potential harms of these globally popular products, including overspending and the normalization of gambling amongst children. We surveyed Mainland Chinese video game players (final N = 913) to investigate whether spending on various gambling-like products is associated with problem gambling severity. Replicating previous results, we found weak—but practically meaningful—associations between problem gambling severity and both digital loot box and physical card pack spending. In contrast, the association between problem gambling and physical blind box spending was very weak and arguably not practically meaningful. Fundamental differences at the product characteristic-level mean that some gambling-like products, like blind boxes, may be less risky, but further research is warranted. Thus, a cautious and balanced approach with a focus on product transparency and child protection should be taken when regulating gambling-like products. Blind box regulation may justifiably be light-touch, whilst loot box and card pack regulations could be stricter and more restrictive, given a greater potential for harm. Preregistered Stage 1 protocol: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/PYFQV (date of in-principle acceptance: 18 March 2026).

articles_hidden.title: From the app to the lexicon: Neurocognitive markers of word integration in a second language
articles_hidden.authors: Ramón Igarreta; Luz Bavassi; Laura Kaczer
articles_hidden.abstract: The consolidation of newly learned vocabulary into semantic memory networks is a critical process in word learning, including second-language (L2) acquisition. However, most neurocognitive studies of lexical-semantic integration rely on short, artificial learning paradigms, leaving open the question of whether naturalistic, app-based learning produces comparable neural outcomes. In this study, we combined an ecological learning environment with controlled electrophysiological testing to examine whether vocabulary learned through Duolingo shows neural signatures of semantic integration. Native Spanish speakers studied Guarani vocabulary for five weeks and subsequently completed a semantic decision task during EEG recording that included both L1 (Spanish) and L2 (Guarani) word pairs. Critically, L2 targets were classified as remote (learned earlier during the five-week training and not practiced in the final stage) or recent (learned in the final training stage and tested approximately 10 days later), allowing us to assess consolidation-related differences. Behaviorally, participants responded more accurately and faster to L1 than L2 words, and accuracy for related items was higher for remotely than recently learned items, consistent with consolidation-related strengthening. Electrophysiologically, robust N400 priming effects emerged for remotely learned words—whereas no facilitation was observed for recent words. This graded pattern suggests that only words with extended consolidation time exhibited neural markers of lexical–semantic integration. Together, these findings demonstrate that combining real-world digital learning with controlled neural testing can reveal how naturalistic language experience shapes the neurocognitive dynamics of word learning and consolidation.

articles_hidden.title: Bonobos and chimpanzees: revisiting the aggression dichotomy
articles_hidden.authors: Ulrich Maloueki; Bekeli Nseu Mbomba
articles_hidden.abstract: Aggression in the genus Pan (including bonobos and chimpanzees) remains a central puzzle in primatology and anthropology. Traditionally framed as a dichotomy between “peaceful bonobos” and “violent chimpanzees,” recent findings challenge this view by documenting coalitionary aggression, maternal cannibalism, and lethal intergroup encounters in bonobos, alongside evidence that captive chimpanzees and bonobos exhibit comparable aggression levels. These observations highlight the importance of ecological context, demographic composition, and behavioral plasticity in shaping aggression. We propose that species identity is a weaker predictor of aggression in Pan than socioecological, demographic, social, and neuroendocrine context. While captivity offers methodological control, it also introduces confounds such as reduced group size, absence of fission–fusion dynamics, and enforced proximity. Conversely, wild studies reveal the ecological pressures, territorial defense, resource distribution, and interspecies competition that drive variation in aggression. Future research must integrate captive and free‑ranging data through hybrid protocols, quantify ecological and demographic drivers, and explore neuroendocrine mechanisms underlying sex‑specific aggression. An integrative review on Pan aggression will refine our understanding of adaptive strategies, illuminate the evolutionary roots of human social conflict, and advance comparative models of primate behavior.

articles_hidden.title: A Hierarchical Dynamical Model of Learning, Forgetting, and Relearning
articles_hidden.authors: Howard Smith
articles_hidden.abstract:
The model developed here provides a quantitative account of a range of well-known findings on 
learning, forgetting, and relearning, spanning delays from seconds (e.g., Peterson & Peterson, 
1959) to weeks (e.g., Ebbinghaus, 1885/1964; Perkins, 1914). The model tracks the probability of 
recall of individual items as they are learned, forgotten, and relearned over time. During study, 
recall probability increases, whereas during retention intervals it declines exponentially. Crucially, 
the rate of this decline is not fixed but is governed by a forgetting exponent that itself changes 
across study and delay periods. These changes are organised within a hierarchy of interacting 
processes operating over multiple timescales, allowing recall dynamics to evolve systematically 
across study and delay. This structure allows the model to capture effects of serial position, list 
length, spacing, and long-term retention within a single framework. Although classic studies such 
as those of Ebbinghaus, Peterson and Peterson, and Perkins are often treated as demonstrations 
of separate phenomena, the present model shows that they can be understood as arising from a 
common set of underlying processes.

articles_hidden.title: Bayesian Predictive Ensembles for Random Effects Specification Uncertainty: Capturing Individual Heterogeneity in Large-Scale Assessments
articles_hidden.authors: Mingya Huang; Weicong Lyu
articles_hidden.abstract: A common challenge in multilevel modeling is determining which predictors should have random effects, especially in educational and psychological research where several theoretically plausible model specifications exist. Choosing a single specification ignores information from the alternatives and can lead to understated uncertainty in later inference. Popular Bayesian ensemble methods, including Bayesian model averaging (BMA), Bayesian stacking (BS), and Bayesian hierarchical stacking (BHS), combine predictions across candidate specifications but constrain model weights to sum to one, implicitly assuming that the candidate model set collectively accounts for all systematic variance in the outcome. This assumption rarely holds when each candidate captures only a portion of the true random effects structure. To address this, we propose to apply the Varying Coefficient Bayesian Additive Regression Tree (VCBART; Deshpande, Bai, Balocchi, Starling, & Weiss, 2024) with an adaptive intercept that absorbs variance not captured by any candidate model. The approach estimates individual-specific ensemble weights as nonparametric functions of individual-level and cluster-level covariates without imposing a sum-to-one constraint. The posterior distributions of these weights indicate which random-effects structures are most relevant for each individual and quantify the associated uncertainty. We evaluate VCBART using simulations calibrated to the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2018 mathematics data and an empirical application to the same data. Among the methods compared, VCBART achieves near-nominal prediction interval coverage with the lowest prediction error. It even outperforms the correctly specified oracle in out-of-sample prediction under high within-cluster variability.

articles_hidden.title: Longitudinal and cross-sectional perspectives on elementary school children's post-error slowing in reading and arithmetic
articles_hidden.authors: Claudia M Roebers; Daniela Menath; Hülya Özmen; Ebru Ger
articles_hidden.abstract: This study investigated the development of primary school children’s error-related adjustments in reading and arithmetic. N = 622 children from 2nd and 4th grade were tested on two tablet-based academic tasks twice in six months: an arithmetic task composed of addition and doubling items with two answer options and a silent word reading task matching words with four pictorial answer options. Children in both grades showed robust post-error slowing (PES) in both reading and arithmetic, indicating reliable monitoring and strategy use in the form of upregulating cognitive control mechanisms. Overall, post-error slowing was larger in arithmetic than in reading, independent of grade and measurement point. Fourth graders showed larger PES than 2nd graders, especially at T1, and both grades’ PES increased from T1 to T2, suggesting that task experience, improving monitoring skills, and strategy discovery play an important role. In terms of the benefits of PES for performance accuracy, PES was linked to better accuracy after the error in the arithmetic task, particularly for younger children. This was not the case for reading. Results are discussed in terms of often overlooked educationally relevant strategies in arithmetic, possible strategy’s utilization deficiency, developing monitoring and cognitive control skills in this age range and differing processing demands across academic domains.

articles_hidden.title: The Influence of Parental Cultural Values on Preschool Children's Over-Imitation
articles_hidden.authors: Esmee Miron Aalders; Moritz M. Daum; Joanna Maria Rutkowska
articles_hidden.abstract: Over-imitation, the copying of irrelevant actions, is driven by causal, affiliative, and normative processes. Because these processes develop in the environments in which children grow up, parental values likely shape them through cultural practices and interaction patterns.  Yet, how children's environments shape their over-imitation remains unexplored. Following the dual-process perspective \parencite{schleihauf_dual-process_2020}, this study examined whether three variables from children's environments are associated with their over-imitation of pseudo-instrumental and noncontact actions: parental cultural values, cultural diversity, and language status. We tested 133 monolingual, bilingual, and bidialectal 4-year-old children. Parents completed questionnaires on 9 dimensions of cultural values, and their child's language exposure. Two parental cultural values were associated with children’s over-imitation, but in opposite directions: Higher parental institutional collectivism was associated with less over-imitation; higher parental in-group collectivism was associated with more over-imitation. Children's language status was not associated with their over-imitation, but the distance between parents' cultural values was. Children whose parents had similar cultural values over-imitated pseudo-instrumental actions more than children whose parents' cultural values differed. Notably, cultural values were more consistently related to over-imitation of pseudo-instrumental than to noncontact actions, suggesting that preschool children do not yet apply blanket copying to pseudo-instrumental actions, or that culture has an effect above and beyond children's normative motivation to over-imitate. Overall, the results indicate that children’s over-imitation reflects both action properties and cultural environments, emphasising the importance of cultural context in theories of social learning.

articles_hidden.title: Neural evidence for intact statistical learning in Developmental Dyslexia in the absence of conclusive behavioral results: an individual differences approach to cognitive correlates
articles_hidden.authors: Iris Maria van der Wulp; Marijn Eefje Struiksma; Frank Wijnen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Individual differences in Statistical Learning (SL) are associated with reading ability, yet evidence on whether SL is impaired in Developmental Dyslexia (DD) is inconsistent. Furthermore, DD is associated with impairments in Rhythmic Ability (RA) and Working Memory (WM). This study examined SL in adults with self-reported diagnoses of DD compared to Typical Readers (TR), and explored whether individual differences in RA, WM, and vocabulary related to individual SL ability in speech segmentation.
	A total of 143 participants (N_DD = 25, N_TR = 118) were exposed to an artificial language of trisyllabic nonsense-words while neural entrainment to the words assessed SL via electroencephalography (EEG), followed by behavioral SL outcome measures. Aiming to assess individual differences, we linked the neural measure of SL to a battery of tests measuring musicality, RA, WM, and vocabulary size. 
	Results indicated neural evidence for SL in both groups, with similar neural entrainment to the structure during exposure. Behavioral performance in the DD group on SL seemed below TR, though Bayesian analyses rendered this inconclusive. The DD group obtained lower scores on tasks measuring RA, WM and vocabulary size, which was primarily driven by the latter two. Comparison of relations between neural SL and these tasks indicated no group differences therein. Exploratively combining the groups into one population resulted in anecdotal Bayesian evidence that individual differences in SL related to WM and RA measured by sensorimotor synchronization, which was rendered inconclusive in sensitivity analyses. Our results emphasize the importance of an individual differences approach, moving beyond group comparisons.

articles_hidden.title: Investigating associations between food insecurity and eating disorder pathology: A systematic review and meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Akansha Naraindas; Georgia Pickford; Caroline West; Vivienne Hazzard; Francesca Solmi; Fidan Turk
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective
Food insecurity is increasingly recognised as an important social determinant of eating disorder (ED) pathology. Although research in this area has grown substantially, evidence remains fragmented across ED pathology, diagnoses, age groups, and clinical and non-clinical populations. This review aims to update and synthesise the literature on the relationship between food insecurity and eating disorder pathology.
Method
Relevant studies were identified by searching PubMed/Medline, Web of Science, PsycINFO, Scopus, and the grey literature up to September 2026. Random-effects meta-analyses and narrative synthesis were carried out. The methodological quality of the included studies was evaluated using Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Public and patient involvement and engagement informed the process throughout. The protocol for this review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261291381).
Results 
We included 140 articles in the review (n=628,090 participants) and, of these, 72 in the meta-analysis. Food insecurity was associated with greater overall eating pathology, with pooled eORs ranging from 1.75 (1.18–2.58) to 2.36 (0.15-0.31) across the three effect-size measures. Positive associations were also observed for binge eating, dietary restriction, purging, vomiting, and laxative use, although effect sizes varied across outcomes and analyses. Findings were mixed for excessive exercise and negative body image, with some studies reporting significant associations with food insecurity and others finding no evidence of an association. Overall, the included studies were of moderate to high methodological quality.
Conclusion
To date, the existing literature supports the role of food insecurity in the aetiology of eating disorder pathology and highlights the need for future theoretical frameworks and prevention interventions.

articles_hidden.title: Environmental Exposures and Brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging Phenotypes in Cognitively Healthy Ageing: A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Kelly E Perry; Breanna Watterson; Jenna Louise Merenstein
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Air pollution and built environment features are increasingly associated with negative health outcomes, yet their relation to brain health in cognitively healthy older adults remains unclear.

Methods: To synthesise the extant literature, we conducted a systematic review, searching MEDLINE (PubMed) and Web of Science (Core Collection) from inception to February 23, 2026. Eligible studies assessed a natural or built environmental exposure against brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) measures in cognitively healthy older adults (ages 65+). Reviewers screened and extracted summary data from published reports in Covidence; no individual patient data were sought. The main outcome was brain health; findings were synthesised narratively using an effect-direction approach, as heterogeneous exposures, outcomes, and effect metrics precluded pooling.

Findings: Of 2,496 records screened, 27 studies met eligibility, comprising >84,000 older adults across 10 countries: United States, South Korea, United Kingdom, France, Spain, Sweden, Netherlands, Taiwan, Germany, and Japan. Thirteen studies were cross-sectional and 14 were cohort studies (nine observational and five longitudinal). Higher air pollution exposure—particularly PM2.5, NO2, and PM10—was associated with altered brain structure: smaller total, grey matter, and white matter volumes, greater white matter hyperintensities, cortical thinning, and smaller medial temporal and hippocampal volumes; greenspace was associated with more favourable brain structure in several mostly cross-sectional studies, though findings were not uniform. Thirteen studies met criteria for high methodological quality and low though not uniform risk of bias; outcome assessment was a recurring source of bias (12 of 27 studies), and four of the five longitudinal studies did not meet criterion for follow-up adequacy.

Interpretation: This review synthesises emerging observational evidence that air pollution is associated with differences in brain structure in cognitively healthy ageing. Because the included evidence is predominantly cross-sectional, these associations are hypothesis generating; if confirmed in longitudinal studies, this modifiable exposure could serve as a potential target for policymakers aiming to protect brain health in the fastest growing segment of the global population.

articles_hidden.title: Processing spoken prefixed words with obscured morphological identity and boundary: An auditory masked priming experiment
articles_hidden.authors: Dave Kenneth Tayao Cayado; Samantha Wray; Adam J. Chong; Linnaea Stockall
articles_hidden.abstract: To comprehend speech, the auditory system segments a continuous input stream at various levels (e.g., sounds, words). Previous studies have shown that listeners also segment complex spoken words like treatment into their morphological units /ˈtriːt/+/mənt/, where there is a clear morphological boundary between /stem/+/affix/. Here, we report an auditory masked priming experiment in Tagalog investigating whether complex spoken words with obscured morphological identity and boundaries are segmented into morphemes. We compare the processing of prefixed words [1] without morphophonological alternations (NOCHANGE, e.g., /maŋ/+/híla/ becomes maŋhíla ‘to pull’), [2] with nasal ASSIMILATION obscuring prefix identity (e.g., /maŋ/+/búlag/ becomes mambúlag ‘to blind’), and [3] with nasal SUBSTITUTION obscuring both prefix and stem identities and their phonological boundary (e.g., /maŋ/+/túlak/ becomes manúlak ‘to push’). Crucially, these morphophonological alternations exhibit variability: nasal SUBSTITUTION is more likely for VOICELESS-initial stems than for VOICED-initial stems. We found significant priming effects of similar magnitude across NOCHANGE, ASSIMILATION, and SUBSTITUTION conditions. These effects are morphological in nature since no reliable priming was observed for monomorphemic word pairs with phonological overlap. Further, similar priming was found for both VOICELESS and VOICED SUBSTITUTION conditions. These findings unambiguously show that spoken complex words are decomposed into morphemes, thereby supporting auditory processing models and morphological theories which argue that morphologically complex words are stored and accessed as morphemes in the mental lexicon. Ultimately, we provide clear evidence that automatic decomposition in speech comprehension is robust in the face of variable morphophonological alternations that obscure prefix identity and morphological boundaries.

articles_hidden.title: “He did not want to tell me and so I did not push”: Researchers' experiences of navigating ethnographic data collection in a special school
articles_hidden.authors: Astrid Bowen; Laura Fox; Kayleigh Doyle; Kathryn Asbury
articles_hidden.abstract: Learning-disabled children and young people experience systemic barriers to their inclusion in research, and researcher expertise and experience can either act as one of those barriers or as a facilitator. Researcher accounts of conducting research with learning-disabled children and young people can provide useful insights into practices that facilitate inclusion, yet such accounts are scarce. This study presents a secondary analysis of ethnographic data collected by four researchers during a study exploring the communication preferences of learning-disabled students in a special school setting in the North of England. It focuses on the researchers’ reflections on their own experiences of data collection, as captured in their fieldnotes.  Four themes were developed using thematic analysis: (1) Moving beyond a "one size fits all" approach; (2) The importance of relationships; (3) Researching as an outsider/insider; (4) Why it matters who does the research. Findings highlight the positive, yet sometimes challenging, experiences of working with learning-disabled students in a special school setting, and contribute to the knowledge base on supporting inclusive practices for qualitative research with learning-disabled participants. Suggestions for how researchers can develop strategies to navigate the challenges they may encounter during data collection are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: GEMScapes: linking acoustic features to aesthetic emotions in ambient and cinematic music using the GEMS-9 scale
articles_hidden.authors: Javier Marín-Murillo; Irene Fondón; María Luz Montesinos
articles_hidden.abstract: Ambient and cinematic music are widely used in behavioral and immersive multimedia paradigms, yet standardized stimulus sets with computational acoustic norms remain scarce. We introduce GEMScapes, an open-access dataset of 38 original, high-fidelity instrumental tracks designed to elicit aesthetic emotions free from familiarity or semantic bias. We combined computational acoustic profiling across temporal, spectral, cepstral, tonal, harmonic–percussive, rhythmic, and stereo spatial domains with 816 trial-level ratings of 36 of the tracks, provided by 65 participants in 68 listening sessions on the Geneva Emotional Music Scale (GEMS-9). To account for stimulus- and participant-level dependencies, we fitted crossed linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) and validated them with ordinal models across 171 candidate pairs, identifying nine predictor–emotion associations (Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate [FDR]-adjusted p < 0.05) involving six acoustic and spatial descriptors across six emotional dimensions. Temporal variability and soundstage spatialization were the main predictors: variability of spectral tilt predicted Tension, variability of percussive energy predicted Joyful Activation, Transcendence was associated with wider stereo width and smoother, non-percussive onsets, Peacefulness and Nostalgia with spectral stability, and Sadness with lower spectral brightness and reduced timbral modulation. Variance partitioning revealed a continuum from strongly stimulus-driven states (Tension: 46% stimulus vs. 9% listener variance) to predominantly listener-dependent ones (Wonder: 8% vs. 32%). GEMScapes provides an acoustically characterized resource for music perception, affective computing, and neurocognitive research.

articles_hidden.title: Recognizing versus valuing curiosity: Cross-country similarities and differences in parental judgments of early curious behaviors
articles_hidden.authors: Elena C. Altmann; Lizhi Ma; Mikako Ishibashi; Yaying (Tiffany) Bai; Keiya Taguchi; Gert Westermann; Hiromichi Hagihara
articles_hidden.abstract: Cross-cultural research has examined whether parents differ in how they value curiosity as a developmental characteristic, but it remains unclear whether they understand the concept in the same way. Because early curiosity must be inferred from behavior, concrete behavioral judgments offer a direct test of this question. Parents in Germany, China, and Japan were randomly assigned to judge age-appropriate behaviors from a published infant-toddler or early-childhood curiosity measure, rating each either as an expression of curiosity or as socially desirable. The 689 parents (142 German, 425 Chinese, and 122 Japanese; ethnicity not explicitly collected) reported on children aged 5 to 71 months (344 girls, 345 boys) between July 2025 and March 2026. Candidate curiosity items clearly outperformed non-curiosity fillers in every country (differences of 1.19 to 2.84 points on a 7-point scale), and behavior orderings were strongly similar across countries (Spearman ρ = .67 to .88). Ratings were near-identical for individual items such as poking and probing, with country differences in curiosity attribution occurring much less compared to desirability differences (for 4 versus 19 items). These findings suggest that cultures may differ less in what curiosity looks like than in which behavioral expressions of curiosity are welcomed and reinforced.

articles_hidden.title: Multiplying Bayes Factors Across Studies: Which Hypotheses Are We Testing?
articles_hidden.authors: Laura Groot; Daniel W. Heck
articles_hidden.abstract: Bayesian evidence synthesis (BES) is a method for evaluating the empirical support for a common theory across multiple studies. In each study, the theory predicts a set of order constraints on the parameters of interest. Evidence is aggregated by multiplying the Bayes factors of the individual studies, yielding the product Bayes factor (PBF). The numerator of the PBF corresponds to the joint predicted hypothesis that the theory holds across different contexts, implying that the predicted order constraints are correct in each study. Since the Bayes factor is a relative measure of evidence, interpreting the PBF requires a clear understanding of the alternative hypothesis. The joint alternative is represented by the denominator of the PBF and states that the respective study-specific alternative hypothesis holds in each study. However, this joint alternative may lack both a clear substantive interpretation and a theoretical justification. We investigate how different combinations of study-specific alternative hypotheses give rise to distinct joint alternatives, focusing on three alternatives common in order-constrained inference: the null, the unconstrained, and the complement hypothesis. In particular, we show that multiplying Bayes factors involving study-specific complements does not test the theory against its complement (i.e., the hypothesis that the theoretical predictions are false in at least one study). Finally, we provide recommendations for specifying meaningful joint alternative hypotheses that support a clear interpretation of BES results and are useful for theory testing.

articles_hidden.title: Can GenAI Boost Writing Scores? Another Robust Bayesian Meta-Analysis (RoBMA) of Writing Ability
articles_hidden.authors: Shawn Hemelstrand
articles_hidden.abstract: A new meta-analysis (Teng, 2026) has shown that genAI has a strong impact on writing with similar effects as another recent meta-analysis (Dong, 2026). The current analysis instead shows a much weaker effect after correcting for entry errors and heterogeneity.

articles_hidden.title: Designing AI-Agents with Personalities: A Psychometric Approach
articles_hidden.authors: Muhua Huang; Xijuan Zhang; Christopher J. Soto; James Evans
articles_hidden.abstract: We introduce a methodology for assigning quantifiable and psychometrically validated personalities to AI-Agents using the Big Five framework. Across three studies, we evaluate its feasibility and limitations. In Study 1, we show that large language models (LLMs) capture semantic similarities among Big Five measures, providing a basis for personality assignment. In Study 2, we create AI-Agents using prompts designed based on the Big Five Inventory-2 (BFI-2) in different format, and find that AI-Agents powered by new models align more closely with human responses on the Mini-Markers test, although the finer pattern of results (e.g., factor loading patterns) were sometimes inconsistent. In Study 3, we validate our AI-Agents on risk-taking and moral dilemma vignettes, finding that models prompted with the BFI-2-Expanded format most closely reproduce human personality-decision associations, while safety-aligned models generally inflate ‘moral’ ratings. Overall, our results show that AI-Agents align with humans in correlations between input Big Five traits and output responses and may serve as useful tools for preliminary research. Nevertheless, discrepancies in finer response patterns indicate that AI-Agents cannot (yet) fully substitute for human participants in precision or high-stakes projects.

articles_hidden.title: The Association between Climate Anxiety and Nature Connectedness: A Systematic Literature Review and Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Angus D. E. Faul; Léan V. O’Brien; Teaghan Hogg
articles_hidden.abstract:
Nature connectedness (NC) refers to an individual’s subjective sense of connection with nature and has a well-established link to overall health and well-being. NC shows potential for being incorporated into future climate anxiety (CA) management interventions. However, no study has reviewed the literature investigating the association between NC and CA. Therefore, we conducted a systematic literature review to: 1) synthesise the empirical research and assess the evidence for associations between NC and CA using meta-analytic methods; and 2) identify factors that may influence this relationship, and the nature of their influence. Following a systematic search of eight electronic databases from inception to April 2026, fifty studies met inclusion criteria. Substantial heterogeneity was identified in NC and CA operationalisations. We conducted random-effects meta-analyses using restricted maximum likelihood estimation (REML), using correlation coefficients (r) as the effect size metric and pooled across studies using inverse-variance weighting. Meta-analysis indicated a significant positive moderate mean association between NC and CA. NC and CA measurement instruments/items were selected as categorical moderators. Subgroup analyses revealed 15 CA instruments significantly influenced the relationship between NC and CA. Based on our findings we recommend: (a) the development and refinement of CA instruments and their conceptual alignment, (b) more diverse population contexts in this research area, and (c) the development of a clear theoretical framework for defining and conceptualising NC and its relationship with CA. This review was registered on the PROSPERO International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (Registration ID = CRD420251063755). 
Keywords: Nature connectedness (NC), climate anxiety (CA), meta-analysis, measures, operationalisations.

articles_hidden.title: Which Distortion gets confused? A Controlled Comparison of Language Models for Dominant Cognitive Distortion Classification
articles_hidden.authors: Rishi Gnanasekar; Caleb J. Siefert
articles_hidden.abstract:
Cognitive Distortions are unhelpful thinking
patterns that Cognitive Behavioral Therapy
(CBT) aims to identify and restructure, so
classifying cognitive distortions is a crucial
process for reframing. The classification
becomes difficult as the data is limited, and
the data are imbalanced most of the time. We
study dominant distortion classification on
the publicly available Therapist Q&A dataset
(Shreevastava and Foltz, 2021) where the anno-
tator agreement on the dominant distortion is
low (34%). Using the annotated distorted span
as input, we compare TF-IDF baselines with
RoBERTa, DeBERTa-v3 and MentalBERT
(with and without focal loss) over three seeds,
reporting accuracy, macro F1 and Cohen’s
kappa with significance tests. The encoders
reach 0.39 to 0.44 accuracy, well above the
majority-class baseline (0.15), the three cross-
entropy encoders are not significantly different
from each other, while the weighted focal loss
is worse. An error analysis shows that errors
concentrate on a small group of overlapping
distortions, mainly All-or-nothing thinking,
Magnification and Mental filter, which
suggests that unclear category boundaries limit
performance more than model choice.

articles_hidden.title: The social ecology of trustworthiness inferences: Cultural gradients in emotion overgeneralization
articles_hidden.authors: Yuqing Shi; Ryutaro Uchiyama; Shuxian Jin; Yin Wang; Steve M. J. Janssen; Daniel DongWon Oh
articles_hidden.abstract: Judgments of trustworthiness from faces guide critical social decisions. It remains debated whether these judgments reflect shared features of human perception or are shaped by cultural experience. One prominent explanation is emotion overgeneralization: faces that structurally resemble emotional expressions elicit corresponding impressions, even when no emotion is displayed. Although often treated as universal, emotion overgeneralization may reflect ecological learning shaped by culture-specific norms. We propose a cultural gradient: where emotional expressions are more informative, the link between happiness resemblance and perceived trustworthiness should be stronger. Participants from 32 countries (N ≈ 6,400) will evaluate the trustworthiness of unfamiliar individuals from standardized resting facial photographs and complete a measure of emotional expressivity, with each face’s resemblance to happiness quantified computationally. We will test whether emotional expressivity is associated with greater emotion overgeneralization at both country and individual levels. Null results would favor perceptual invariance, whereas positive associations would support ecological calibration.

articles_hidden.title: The Governed Heart:  Institutional Emotion Regulation through Policy, Proclamation, and Proxy
articles_hidden.authors: Nicholas Paul Camp; Brett Quaid Ford
articles_hidden.abstract: Governments, schools, hospitals, companies, and myriad other organizations structure institutional life and mobilize large numbers of people to accomplish what they cannot do alone. Institutions also regulate something less visible, but equally consequential: the emotions of their constituents. We introduce institutional emotion regulation as the formal processes by which institutions, through organizations, seek to influence the emotions people have, when they have them, and how they experience and express these emotions. Research across the social sciences has examined how particular organizations attempt to shape affective experiences, but these literatures have largely developed in disciplinary silos or domain-specific settings. We propose that these phenomena reflect a distinct level of emotion regulation, characterized by emotion goals held by organizations and pursued through formal institutional means. We develop a framework that crosses four established stages of emotion regulation – targeting situations, attention, appraisals, and responses – with three distinctive vectors of institutional influence: policies, the rules and structures that shape people’s environments; proclamations, communications directed toward the public; and proxies, the agents who act on behalf of the organization. Our framework provides a common language for understanding how institutions influence emotional life at scale and suggests novel directions for psychological study while surfacing broader questions for society around the appropriate use of this influence.

articles_hidden.title: Simulated Survival: A Theoretical Framework for Using Immersive Virtual Reality Challenge to Target Ideation-to-Action Mechanisms of Suicide Risk
articles_hidden.authors: Mohammad Sheraz Akbar; Fatima Afsar
articles_hidden.abstract: Ideation-to-action theories explain how suicidal desire develops and how some people come to act on it, but they give little guidance on interventions for the physiological state that accompanies suicidal crises. This article proposes Simulated Survival, a theoretical framework for using controlled, demanding experiences in immersive virtual reality (VR) as an adjunct to suicide-specific care. Drawing on the Three-Step Theory, the Integrated Motivational-Volitional model, and the Interpersonal Theory of Suicide, together with research on autonomic regulation, interoception, attention under pressure, challenge appraisal, adventure-based interventions, and VR, the framework specifies three hypothesized mechanisms: interruption of suicide-specific rumination through attention captured by demanding, embodied tasks; repeated stress-recovery cycles that train autonomic and interoceptive regulation; and the pairing of high arousal with successful protective action, intended to strengthen self-preservation rather than tolerance of death-related fear. Expectation violation is proposed as the learning process that turns short-term effects into lasting change. Because repeated exposure to danger could raise fearlessness about death, the framework sets design rules (no suicide-method cues, no virtual death states, graded difficulty) and treats fearlessness about death as a primary safety outcome. Eight testable propositions and a staged research path are set out.
