Simulated Survival offers a testable basis for body-based digital interventions in suicide prevention, and its value depends on experimental work that tests each mechanism against active VR control conditions before any clinical trial.

articles_hidden.title: From Bulking to Cutting: Social Media, Self-Esteem, and Disordered Eating in Young Men
articles_hidden.authors: Jakub Smolinski; Jaynie Rance; Menna Price
articles_hidden.abstract: Bulking and cutting (caloric surplus and restriction) are increasingly common among young men but remain under-researched within disordered eating frameworks. This study examined social media use and self-esteem as predictors, as well as their association with disordered eating and bulking and cutting behaviours. Seventy-six physically active UK men aged 18-25 years (M = 22.07, SD = 2.07) completed online measures of social media use, self-esteem, disordered eating (restraint, eating concern, shape concern, weight concern), and bulking and cutting behaviours. Higher social media use predicted higher eating concern (p = .003), while lower self-esteem predicted higher eating and shape concerns (p = .029, p = <.001). Neither social media use nor self-esteem predicted restraint, bulking, or cutting. Exploratory mediation analyses showed that restraint fully mediated the association between shape concern and cutting behaviour (p = < .001). Social media use and self-esteem appear to relate to specific disordered eating symptoms, whereas bulking and cutting may be more closely linked to restraint processes. These findings support expanding conceptualisations of disordered eating in young men to include muscle-oriented dietary behaviours and their distinct psychological pathways.

articles_hidden.title: Multilingualism WithOut Words: A non-lexicalist model of bilingualism
articles_hidden.authors: Alexandra Krauska; Danielle Fahey
articles_hidden.abstract: Standard models of bilingualism are primarily concerned with how words in multiple languages are stored and associated in the mind. However, there is growing consensus in linguistic theory that language cannot be organized around words, given that meaning, syntax, and form do not always align at the word level. We propose the Multilingualism WithOut Words (M-WOW) model to realign models of bilingualism with current linguistic theory and account for a broader typology of languages. In contrast to other models, M-WOW allows more flexibility in how features are realized across languages and expands the possibilities for code-switching. Because the model does not rely on a word level, it accommodates a broader set of linguistic phenomena and provides new insights into bilingual language processing and the dynamic and variable processes of L2 acquisition and attrition.

articles_hidden.title: Multiple Methods for Visualizing Human Language: A Tutorial for Social and Behavioural Scientists
articles_hidden.authors: Veerle Celine Eijsbroek; August Nilsson; Leon Ackermann; Zhuojun Gu; Clara Wiebel; Adithya V Ganesan; Katarina Kjell; H. Andrew Schwartz; Oscar Nils Erik Kjell
articles_hidden.abstract:
Humans use language to communicate psychological experiences. Advancements in Natural Language
Processing have enabled researchers to quantitatively study and assess psychological states and
behaviors through language (e.g., well-being and mental health). Insights from language analyses are
often best conveyed through visualizations. Data-driven visualizations of how language statistically
relates to psychological dimensions can help interpret assessment scores, uncover meaningful patterns,
and understand the intricate relationships between language use and mental states. Visualizations can
be used to differentiate between related constructs (e.g., How does language related to depression versus
anxiety differ?), understand the validity of assessment tools (e.g., Does the language related to high
depression severity match with depression theory?), and explain language-based assessments (e.g.,
Which language is indicative of higher depression severity in a language-based assessment?).

This tutorial demonstrates how to transform language data into visual insights using the text and topics
packages in R. We provide practical guidance on creating four types of visualizations based on different
language analysis techniques, examining how language use patterns are statistically associated with a
psychological construct. We visualize 1) individual words and phrases (n-grams), 2) topics (word
clusters), 3) words in the word embedding space, and 4) relevant language examples. These different
visualizations offer complementary perspectives, visualizing linguistic elements from individual words
to overarching topics and text examples. The underlying methods range from correlations between
individual words to more advanced techniques, including topic modeling and Large Language Models.
By making these methods accessible, this tutorial aims to empower researchers to use language
visualizations for meaningful, data-driven insights.

articles_hidden.title: Noun memory advantage drives sentence internal primacy and recency at clause boundaries
articles_hidden.authors: Sebastián Mancha; Ellen Lau
articles_hidden.abstract: Classic research in psychology has shown that comprehenders in recall tasks ‘chunk’ word lists in order to facilitate later retrieval. Here we ask how chunking mechanisms apply in grammatically structured sentence stimuli. How do comprehenders make use of this grammatical structure to guide chunking of a sentence’s component words in memory? In previous studies of multi-clause sentence recall, many researchers have argued that chunking is clause-based, as evidenced by scalloped serial accuracy curves in which primacy and recency effects are observed within each clause. Here we suggest that these previous findings may have been driven by the correlation of sentence boundaries with nouns, a lexical class known to demonstrate an independent accuracy advantage in recall. Using immediate serial recall of naturalistic biclausal English sentences and manipulating noun placement, we find evidence that nouns indeed confer a large accuracy boost at the internal clause boundary that can explain prior results. We discuss the difficulty of applying serial position logic to highly structured representations such as those that underlie sentence forms.

articles_hidden.title: A Placebo Cannot Be Psychedelic: Why psychedelic trials need dose, not mimicry, as their control
articles_hidden.authors: Wolfgang Liedtke
articles_hidden.abstract: In a recently published Viewpoint, Yang-et-al propose masking high-dose psilocybin trials with a multidrug comparator engineered to reproduce the psychedelic experience. Their objective, restoration of the gold-standard of randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled standard, is well-intentioned, but the proposed approach dissolves the concept it aims to rescue. A placebo permits to understand the impact of expectation because it is inert. Recent neural circuit-level results in mice shows how concretely expectation affects behavior, relying on in-vivo experimentation that separates placebo effect from active treatment. A comparator that recreates the psychedelic experience must engage the circuits that generate it, becoming a second active treatment whose own pharmacology confounds any eventual difference placebo-active, possibly in both directions. Some interventions, from topical TRP-channel activators (capsaicin, menthol) to classic psychedelics, cannot be matched by an inert control. Dose-controlled designs represent the remaining option where well-intentioned mimicry fails: their main possible bias might work against the drug. Dose-controlled designs can be paired with external controls and approval tied to mandatory postmarketing evidence.

articles_hidden.title: Comparing Logit and Probit Coefficients From Same-Sample Nested Models: Adapting the (Revised) KHB Method to an SEM Framework
articles_hidden.authors: Wolfgang Wagner; Benjamin Nagengast
articles_hidden.abstract: Karlson et al. (2012) suggested an estimation strategy for logistic and probit regression models, the so-called KHB method, which allows differences between regression coefficients in same-sample nested regression models to be interpreted. We introduce the pseudo mediation model (PMM), which implements the KHB method in a structural equation modeling (SEM) framework. The PMM has several advantages over the “standard” KHB method: First, missing data can be handled under less restrictive assumptions. Second, predictors can be included as latent variables to avoid bias due to measurement error. Finally, nested data structures and survey weights can be accounted for. We illustrate the method with empirical examples.

articles_hidden.title: Not passive sponges: When attention wanes, our brains are less synchronized with the environment
articles_hidden.authors: Elena Greatti; Laura Batterink; Davide Crepaldi; Amy Finn
articles_hidden.abstract: Without even being aware, humans are amazingly sensitive to the structures around them. Is this sensitivity constant or does it fluctuate along with our attentional states? To answer this foundational question, we deployed temporally sensitive measures that allow us to track neural entrainment—the synchronization of brain activity to environmental regularities—alongside fluctuations in attentional states. Participants (n = 78) viewed both random and structured visual streams while performing a task to index fluctuating attentional states. Structured streams evoked robust neural entrainment and reduced attentional lapses. Moreover, attentional states varied with neural entrainment. Across participants, those who displayed greater neural entrainment had reduced attentional lapses. And critically, even within individuals, greater entrainment was observed during periods of greater attentional focus. Our sensitivity to structure and attentional states are therefore inextricably linked: structures stabilize our attentional states and our sensitivity to structure dynamically mirrors the ebb and flow of human attention.

articles_hidden.title: A systematic review of recruitment and retention within randomised controlled trials of adults with Down Syndrome
articles_hidden.authors: Aimee Wilkinson; Jade Eloise Norris; Nicola Mills; Victoria Nimmo-Smith; Angela Hassiotis; Dheeraj Rai; Alba X Realpe
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Adults with Down Syndrome (DS) face significant health inequalities. Evidence from high-quality randomised controlled trials (RCTs) for interventions are lacking, and there is a perceived difficulty regarding recruiting and retaining participants with DS. 
Aims: This systematic review aimed to examine planned vs. actual recruitment and retention rates of RCTs involving adults with DS, summarising reported facilitators of and barriers to participation.
Method: MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and EMBASE databases were searched systematically to retrieve RCTs of any intervention involving adults with DS =>16yrs, published to 07/12/2023, with a second search in April 2025. Searches were also conducted on trial registries, and reference lists reviewed. Trial design, planned and achieved sample size, retention rate, and recruitment and retention strategies were extracted 26/02/2024-18/03/2024 for the first search, and in August 2025 for the updated search (Prospero: CRD42023447126; registered: 04/09/2023). 
Results: After deduplication, 1,622 articles underwent title and abstract screening, with 89 full texts reviewed. Five additional papers were identified from reference lists. 1,785 adults with DS were randomised to 44 included RCTs. Most studies did not pre-register their protocol nor target sample size (n=16 reported target N; 36.36%) and typically recruited small samples: 13 recruited N ≥40 (29.55%; N range=8-337, median N=25, IQR 21.75). Attrition by primary outcome also varied widely (0-47%).
Conclusions: There is a paucity of high-quality, large-scale RCTs involving adults with DS, and challenges related to participation rates (e.g., stringent exclusion criteria, consent challenges, and study burden). Strategies to overcome challenges in recruitment and retention to such trials are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: How do time of day and location influence affect experience? A passive sensing study
articles_hidden.authors: Simon M. Li; Molly Patapoff; Aanika Schueler; Qimin Liu; David E. Gard; Carlos Busso; Jukka-Pekka Onnela; Daniel Fulford
articles_hidden.abstract: Momentary emotional experience is shaped by the contexts in which individuals are embedded, yet little is known about how time spent in certain locations (e.g., at home versus in public spaces) relates to affect in daily life. In the current study, 74 young adults completed 14 days of smartphone-based ecological momentary assessment and GPS-based geolocation. We examined three contextual dimensions in relation to momentary affect (happiness, anxiety, and sadness) in young adults: environmental context (at home versus outside), recent exposure duration (time spent at home in the preceding three hours), and temporal context (time of day and day of week). Multilevel models indicated that participants reported higher happiness and lower anxiety in the evening relative to morning, and higher happiness on weekends than on weekdays. Within individuals, being at home (and time spent at home) was associated with lower happiness than being outside the home. Furthermore, the exploratory analysis suggested that the association between time spent at home and lower happiness was stronger among individuals who typically spent less time at home. These findings suggest that temporal and environmental contexts are associated with momentary happiness, whereas environmental context was not associated with anxiety or sadness.

articles_hidden.title: Humans adaptively delay planning using cognitive maps
articles_hidden.authors: Paul B. Sharp; Eran Eldar
articles_hidden.abstract: Planning is an expensive computational operation that easily exhausts our cognitive resources. For this reason, it is critical to learn strategies to initiate planning wisely. To understand how humans adaptively initiate planning, we developed a task where humans can learn to delay planning at certain timepoints when all actions are equally likely to reach an instructed goal. Across two pre-registered studies, we show that humans adaptively delay planning, and improve in their ability to do so with experience. To explain this behavior, we formalize a model of the underlying meta-control computations. Our model demonstrates how strategies to delay planning are not learned from experienced outcomes, but rather, from searching a cognitive map of the task to determine at which points it is more valuable to delay control. We thus establish that humans can adaptively delay planning, and learn to do so by means of a cognitive map.

articles_hidden.title: Background music isn’t just background noise: Evidence from speech comprehension
articles_hidden.authors: Mine Muezzinoglu; Rochelle Suzanne Newman; L. Robert Slevc
articles_hidden.abstract: Understanding speech amid other sounds is challenging because background sounds can mask target speech and draw on attentional and memory resources. Yet people frequently encounter and seek out background music in everyday settings, from cafes and classrooms to offices. Prior work suggests that background music may engage reward systems and enhance concurrent learning, but most of that evidence comes from performance on visual tasks where acoustic masking is not a concern. Here, we asked whether background music affects comprehension of spoken stories, and which musical characteristics matter. Participants listened to short stories in silence and with five background conditions: intact, reversed, pitch-scrambled, rhythm-jittered, and combined pitch-scrambled and rhythm-jittered music. Performance was best in silence, but also better with intact music than with the combined pitch- and rhythm-disrupted music. Performance in music disrupted in only one dimension (pitch or rhythm) did not differ reliably from intact music. These findings suggest that music may be less disruptive than other background sounds when at least one dimension of predictability, pitch or rhythm, remains intact. Liking ratings and individual sensitivity to musical reward did not reliably predict outcomes, suggesting that structural predictability, rather than subjective preference, influences how background music affects speech comprehension.

articles_hidden.title: Perceptual distinctiveness underlies apparent emotion-specific advantages in facial expression detection
articles_hidden.authors: Erika Bucci; Giacomo Handjaras; Giada Lettieri; Luca Cecchetti
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans are assumed to prioritize facial expressions because of the evolutionary significance of their affective content. Here, we show that this assumption does not survive rigorous control of perceptual structure. Across three studies integrating preregistered visual search experiments, geometric modeling of facial expressions, and eye-tracking data, we tested whether detection advantages for happy and angry faces reflect low-level visual salience rather than emotion. To this end, we combined frequentist interval testing with a predefined smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) and Bayesian region-of-practical-equivalence (ROPE) analyses. Behavioral and oculomotor measures reliably predicted emotion category when expressions were presented at full, perceptually unbalanced intensity. By contrast, when expression intensity was matched, both interval testing and Bayesian ROPE analyses supported the absence of a practically meaningful effect. In addition, detection speed and accuracy were best explained by geometric deviation from a neutral face, independent of emotional category. These findings indicate that apparent emotion advantages in visual search arise from perceptual salience rather than privileged access to emotion, challenging evolutionary accounts of attentional prioritization.

articles_hidden.title: Child Multilingualisms Beyond WEIRD Contexts: Evidence from Asia and Africa
articles_hidden.authors: Alexandra Paquette; Leher Singh
articles_hidden.abstract: Who is the language learner represented in language acquisition research? Despite the prevalence and diversity of multilingual childhoods, theories of early language development remain grounded in monolinguals from Euro-American contexts, while multilingual research has concentrated on limited populations/settings. This review examines multilingual language development during the first three years across Asia and Africa, attending to diversity within and between regions. Research on input, speech perception, word recognition, and vocabulary indicate that multilingual infants flexibly adapt to linguistic ecologies, but vary in developmental pathways. We argue that multilingualism should be conceptualized not as a categorical characteristic, but as a multidimensional ecology structured by language combinations, caregiving arrangements, social functions, socioeconomic conditions, and colonial histories. We conclude with a research agenda that broadens empirical and linguistic coverage, improves measurement of multilingual experiences, and centers community-informed priorities. A globally adequate science of language development requires building theory from children’s diverse multilingual realities.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluating the Parental Burnout Assessment in parents of children with and without complex care needs: Measurement invariance, group differences, and the correlates of sociodemographic characteristics
articles_hidden.authors: Nathalie Patty; Caro Henrica Catharina Lemmen; Carlo Schuengel; Karen van Meeteren; Marjolijn Ketelaar; Maartje Luijk; Agnes M. Willemen
articles_hidden.abstract: The study aim was to evaluate the measurement invariance of the Parental Burnout Assessment (PBA), across parents of children with complex care needs (CCN) and parents of children without CCN, compare burnout scores between these groups, and explore how sociodemographic characteristics relate to parental burnout within each parenting context. The PBA was completed by 337 parents of children with CCN and 329 parents who did not have a child with CCN. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) supported the theoretically proposed four-factor structure of the PBA, encompassing exhaustion in the parental role, feelings of being fed up, contrast with pervious parental self, and emotional distancing. A subsequent second-order CFA indicated that these four dimensions could be explained by a single overarching factor, parental burnout. Multigroup CFA supported scalar invariance across groups for both the four-factor model and the second-order model, indicating that the observed group differences in PBA scores reflect true differences rather than measurement bias. Parents of children with CCN reported significantly higher PBA scores than parents of children without CCN (d = 1.33, p < .001). Among the sociodemographic characteristics examined, we found that being a mother of a child with CCN was associated with substantially higher PBA scores compared to being a father of a child with CCN. This gender difference was smaller among parents of children without CCN. Parental age, ethnicity, educational attainment, being single parent, the number of children, and minimum and maximum age of the child were not associated with higher parental burnout scores. Findings underscore the heightened vulnerability for parental burnout among parents of children with CCN compared to parents of children without CCN while also providing further evidence for the suitability of the PBA as a research instrument for assessing parental burnout across the caregiving context of being a parent of a child with CCN or not.

articles_hidden.title: Facilitation by Irrelevant Distractors Under High Perceptual Load: Suppression or Controlled Distractor Prioritization?
articles_hidden.authors: Greta Manini; Francisco Garre-Frutos; Fabiano Botta; Elisa Martín-Arévalo; Juan Lupiáñez
articles_hidden.abstract: Perceptual load theory is a key framework in visual attention research, demonstrating that under high-load conditions, fully irrelevant distractors are no longer processed and do not disrupt task performance. In our recent work (Manini et al., 2026), we replicated this effect. However, we also found that under high load, the distractor not only failed to impair performance but actually led to faster reaction times (RTs) in distractor-present trials. In the attentional capture literature, this reversed effect is typically considered to reflect distractor suppression. However, in the perceptual load task, where the distractor is placed outside the relevant search array, suppression should not logically lead to faster responses. Furthermore, the faster responses were accompanied by increased error rates, leading us to hypothesize that this reversed effect may reflect some form of distractor prioritization rather than distractor suppression. To test this hypothesis, we first analyzed the consistency of this effect across all available open-data resources using the Forster and Lavie (2008b) task. We then reanalyzed the same data, incorporating the spatial proximity between target and distractor as an additional variable: distractors appearing near the target strongly drove the reversed RT effect, while distractors presented far from the target led to increased error rates. These findings challenge the idea that high perceptual load prevents the processing of irrelevant stimuli. Moreover, they suggest that faster RTs in distractor-present conditions do not necessarily indicate distractor suppression, as commonly assumed in attentional capture research, offering new insight into the interpretation of behavioral observations in this field.

articles_hidden.title: Mapping Leadership in Teams: An Empirically Grounded Taxonomy of Formal and Peer Leadership Roles.
articles_hidden.authors: Charlotte Marie Edelmann; Filip Boen; Jeroen Stouten; Katrien Fransen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose: Formal and peer (informal) leaders play crucial roles in fostering team effectiveness and member well-being. Although leadership research has examined a wide range of leader behaviors, it remains fragmented and typically focuses on either formal or peer leaders rather than both. Moreover, no empirically grounded taxonomy captures the breadth of leadership behaviors across hierarchical levels.

Design/methodology/approach: To address this gap, we developed an inductively derived, literature-integrated taxonomy of leadership functions. We first conducted qualitative interviews with 35 employees varying in hierarchical level, education, sector, and gender. Qualitative content analysis identified leadership functions enacted by formal and peer leaders. Participants then completed individual and group card-sorting exercises to cluster these functions into higher-order leadership roles.

Findings: The taxonomy comprised 10 formal and 10 peer leadership roles. Comparison with existing leadership frameworks showed where prior research converges with and extends the leadership functions identified by participants.

Originality: This integrative taxonomy provides a practice-informed framework for advancing leadership theory and informing leadership development across organizational contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Testing Socio-Perceptual Equigenesis with Biophilic Interventions: A Virtual Reality Eye-Tracking Study Across Neighborhood Socioeconomic Status
articles_hidden.authors: Paula Latorre; Cleiton Pons Ferreira; Aurora Molina-Muñoz; Sergio Castaño-Castaño; Miguel Morales Navas; Francisco Nieto-Escamez
articles_hidden.abstract:
Inequity in access to urban green spaces perpetuates marked disparities in psychological well-being in cities. The present study evaluates whether micro-scale biophilic interventions in virtual environments act as a socio-perceptual equalizer (Environmental Equigenesis Hypothesis) and modulate attention through oculomotor patterns of soft fascination (Attention Restoration Theory). Within this framework, 60 Hz eye-tracking integrated into Immersive Virtual Reality (IVR) was used to capture implicit attentional dynamics objectively. Framed within a mixed methods project registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) after data collection and before any inferential analysis, and given the density of the data obtained, this manuscript reports exclusively the quantitative block focused on oculomotor and psychometric triangulation, reserving the qualitative analysis for a subsequent report. A sample of 75 participants exposed to 360° virtual tours evaluated low-, medium-, and high-socioeconomic-status (SES) neighborhoods under Original and Enhanced conditions. Eye-tracking revealed that the biophilic design did not alter the total volume of fixations but significantly reduced the average fixation duration, a pattern compatible with the attentional coupling of soft fascination. In parallel, subjective increases in positive affect, liking, esthetic evaluation, and relaxation were observed, while perceived stress did not change significantly overall. No significant differences in esthetic evaluation between neighborhoods remained after the intervention, and the areas-of-interest (AOIs) metrics showed a different allocation of gaze across neighborhoods, partly because the interventions applied were not the same in each one. Eye-tracking complemented the self-report data, although the main equigenesis findings rest on the psychometric measures.
Keywords: virtual reality, eye-tracking, biophilic design, attention restoration theory, environmental equigenesis, socioeconomic status

articles_hidden.title: Don’t throw the baby out with the bathwater! Why "preregistration" is still a useful term: Commentary on Mayo-Wilson et al. (2025)
articles_hidden.authors: Priya Silverstein; Lisa Spitzer; Lukas Wallrich; Josefina Weinerova
articles_hidden.abstract: This is a commentary on Mayo-Wilson et al. (2025), published in Avances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science (AMPPS). As per AMPPS submission guidelines, no abstract is included for commentaries.

articles_hidden.title: Gamblers' behavior in a self-exclusion system with social barriers to revocation: evidence from Chile
articles_hidden.authors: Omar D. Perez; José Rafael Arenas Rojas; Mario Sanclemente Villegas; Steve Sharman
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background and aims: In most self-exclusion programs, leaving is the gambler's own decision. In Chile, by contrast, revocation requires the consent of a sponsor whom the participant nominates at enrollment and may later replace. We investigated whether the relationship with the first sponsor, and later changes of sponsor, relate to how long participants remain excluded.

Methods: We analyzed records from Chile's self-exclusion registry (2019–2025; N = 3,825 participants; 1,753 revocations). Time to first revocation was examined using Kaplan–Meier curves and time-varying Cox models including the relationship with the first sponsor, the direction of replacements, and prior rejected requests, accounting for the three-month waiting period after a replacement.

Results: Participants whose first sponsor was a close family member had a lower revocation hazard than those who nominated a partner (HR = 0.67, 95% CI 0.59–0.76); their median time to revocation was 40.4 months, against 20 to 22 months in the other groups. More importantly, replacing a non-family sponsor with a close family member was followed by a lower hazard (HR = 0.59), whereas the reverse change showed no detectable difference. Each rejected request, and each replacement once the waiting period had ended, was associated with a higher hazard, with many revocations right after that period.

Discussion and conclusions: Having a close family member as sponsor, whether from enrollment or after a replacement, is associated with longer exclusions. These results are discussed in the light of the sponsor's role as a social commitment device and the points at which participants may benefit from support.

articles_hidden.title: How Self-Location Predicts the Degree and Quality of the Felt Sense of Connection
articles_hidden.authors: MARIE SESTER; Glenn Hartelius; Michaël Dambrun
articles_hidden.abstract: Research has typically examined how self-location in the head or heart is associated with traits and behavior, yet its link to relationality—specifically the felt sense of connection—remains underexplored. This study investigated how dispositional self-location predicts the embodied experience of being relationally linked to others and the world. We initially developed the Dispositional Self-Location Questionnaire (DSLQ), an association-based instrument designed to minimize potential subjective bias in participant reporting of self-location. Using this measure, we categorized a U.S. sample of 218 adults who had reported a strong experience of connection as head-locators or heart-locators and assessed them on self-construal, self-expansiveness, connectedness, and perceived qualities of connection. Head-locators reported firmer self-boundaries, emphasizing independence, rationality, and decision-making. In contrast, Heart-locators scored significantly higher on connectedness to both self and world, and on metapersonal self-construal, describing their connections as close, warm, caring, and authentic. These findings suggest that self-location functions as a somatic attentional stance that anticipates the experiential boundary between self and other: the head favors separation and autonomy, while the heart favors openness and expanded belonging.

articles_hidden.title: Cognitive Polyphasia and Cognitive Dissonance: An Integrative Model for Understanding Inconsistency Management Within Social Representations Theory
articles_hidden.authors: Thiago Mikael Silva; Adriano Roberto Afonso do Nascimento
articles_hidden.abstract:
The aim of this study was to explore the interrelationship between cognitive
polyphasia and cognitive dissonance in the management of contradictions. We argue
that both concepts maintain a circular relationship. To support this position, we
establish a theoretical path structured around four core axes: 1) the recognition that
Festinger and his followers already considered dissonance management mechanisms
that, much like cognitive polyphasia, maintain inconsistency; 2) from a diachronic
perspective, dissonance can stem from cognitive polyphasia; 3) from a synchronic
perspective, the varieties of cognitive polyphasia can be systematized within the
functional approach to cognitive dissonance; 4) this systematization raises questions
regarding the self and identity, bringing Social Representations Theory closer to
contemporary models of the self. Throughout this path, we outline an integrative
model for the study of inconsistency management, offering brief considerations on the
challenges that future research must overcome.

articles_hidden.title: Mediterranean-style dietary components and self-reported depression: a cross-sectional analysis of 502,359 UK adults in the UK Biobank cohort
articles_hidden.authors: Haidi Martinidou; Donald M Lyall
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Mediterranean-style diet adherence has been associated with lower depression prevalence, but studies are typically small and adjust for few confounders. We aimed to estimate cross-sectional associations between individual Mediterranean-style dietary components and reported depression, and how far they attenuate with broader sociodemographic and lifestyle adjustment.
Methods: Cross-sectional analysis of the UK Biobank cohort (N=502,359). Six self-reported dietary variables - oily fish, non-oily fish, fresh fruit, salad and raw vegetables, cooked vegetables and processed meat - were tested against self-reported depression using binary logistic regression, modelled individually with progressive adjustment (full adjustment: age, sex, smoking, medication, Townsend deprivation index, month of assessment, educational attainment), then all together in one multivariable model.
Results: 28,194 participants (5.6%) reported depression. Fully adjusted, higher intakes of oily fish (odds ratio[OR]=0.900, 95% CI [confidence intervals] 0.888 to 0.912), non-oily fish (OR=0.931, 0.917 to 0.945), fresh fruit (OR=0.974, 0.966 to 0.982), salad and raw vegetables (OR=0.970, 0.964 to 0.976) and cooked vegetables (OR=0.967, 0.960 to 0.974) were each associated with lower odds. 
Conclusion: Individual components of a Mediterranean-style diet showed small, consistent associations with lower odds of self-reported depression, not explained by the measured confounders. The design does not support causal interpretation. For researchers, prospective designs with repeated dietary measurement and diagnosed outcomes are needed; for practitioners and policymakers, these estimates do not support dietary components as a substitute for established treatment or as a stand-alone prevention target.

articles_hidden.title: Looping effects and the cognitive source of epistemic injustices: A simulation study
articles_hidden.authors: Axel Constant; Christophe Gauld; Ana Gomez-Carrillo; Laurence Kirmayer; Karl Friston
articles_hidden.abstract: Patient–clinician interactions are central to diagnosis and treatment in mental health care. They involve inferential processes grounded in patients’ reports of symptoms and clinicians’ interpretations of signs. These processes are liable to microdynamic looping effects that drive diagnostic belief formation. In facing the hermeneutic challenge of reaching a shared ascription of the patient’s condition, such looping effects can lead to misalignment and give rise to epistemic injustice if a credibility deficit exists between the patient and the clinician. In this paper, we use the active inference framework to develop a computational model of looping microdynamics that captures how patients and clinicians reciprocally interpret symptoms, attribute causes, and negotiate diagnostic categories over time. We present a simulation study showing how specific interactional patterns can amplify or mitigate credibility deficits, depending in part on clinicians’ attributional attitudes toward patients’ self-interpretations. Our results suggest that, in contexts of diagnostic disagreement, positive disconfirmation—offering an alternative explanatory framing rather than simply negating the patient’s perspective—may reduce the risk of epistemic injustice. Overall, the model highlights how looping microdynamics structure mutual belief formation in clinical encounters and how attention to these dynamics can support more epistemically responsible clinical communication.

articles_hidden.title: Data Transparency in Industrial, Work, and Organizational Psychology: A Primer on Data Sharing and Documentation of Data Reuse
articles_hidden.authors: Maie Stein; Richard Janzen; Cort W. Rudolph; Hannes Zacher
articles_hidden.abstract: Data transparency is fundamental for evaluating the validity of empirical findings, supporting cumulative knowledge building, and strengthening the credibility of science in society. However, data sharing (i.e., making research data available to others) and transparent documentation of data reuse (i.e., reporting the use of the same data across multiple publications) are not yet standard practice in industrial, work, and organizational (IWO) psychology. The aim of this primer is to discuss the important role of these data transparency practices in advancing open science and to provide practical guidance for the adoption of these practices in IWO psychology. We review the benefits and challenges of data sharing and outline recommendations for researchers, reviewers, and journal editors in IWO psychology to support its implementation. We also examine the implications of data reuse for the interpretation and accumulation of empirical evidence and propose several approaches for transparently documenting data reuse.

articles_hidden.title: Moral Preferences for Avoiding Non-Lethal Human Injury over Property Damage in Autonomous Vehicle Accidents
articles_hidden.authors: Kiichi INARIMORI; Yuri Tanaka; Takashi Hikasa; Tsutomu Sawai
articles_hidden.abstract: Given the rapid development of autonomous vehicle (AV) technologies, recent studies, such as the Moral Machine Experiment, have examined people’s moral judgments in trolley-style dilemmas, where AVs must choose between unavoidable outcomes, often involving whether to change course to save a greater number of lives. However, fatal injuries represent only a subset of harms caused by traffic agents; most traffic accidents are non-fatal or involve only property damage. The present study focuses on trade-offs between human harm and property damage, examining whether the principle of the priority of human over property (PPHP)—reflected in some ethical and legal guidelines—is consistently supported by the public. Across a series of online experiments, we investigated whether people’s path preferences in scenarios where an AV must choose between avoiding human harm and avoiding property damage align with PPHP. We manipulated several factors, including the severity of harm to the pedestrian, the value of the property, the observer’s perspective (first-person vs. third-person), the gender of the potential victim, and whether the passenger would bear legal liability. The results indicate that participants are more likely to prioritize avoiding property damage when the expected harm to humans is relatively low compared to the value of the property. This tendency is amplified when passengers are held legally liable and among participants with more utilitarian moral attitudes. These findings suggest that AV behavior strictly guided by PPHP is not always supported by lay moral judgments.

articles_hidden.title: Excitation-inhibition imbalance in depression and the limits of observability: cohort-level inference from resting-state EEG with an amortised three-region Wilson-Cowan model
articles_hidden.authors: peng yu; ze yang; Shiqi Zhang; Cui Ruolin; Liu Yijun; cheng kang; lu cao; ning ma
articles_hidden.abstract: Depression is widely thought to involve an imbalance between neuronal excitation and inhibition, but the idea has rarely been tested quantitatively at the level of macroscopic brain networks, because dynamical models are hard to fit to EEG spectra and fitting them person by person is prohibitively slow. We present a complete, reproducible pipeline that makes such a test possible, and we report where it succeeds and where it does not. Using eyes-closed resting-state EEG from 117 participants (22 with lifetime major depressive disorder, 95 without), we fitted a three-region excitatory-inhibitory network model with an amortised Bayesian method, in which a single shared library of simulations serves every participant and reduces inference to milliseconds per person. Depressed participants showed a consistent shift towards excitation in three core networks, together with a stronger inhibitory loop gain and a lower operating-point drive. The model's default-mode resonance frequency rose with symptom severity, whereas the conventional peak-frequency estimate computed from the same recordings did not. We then asked what the model actually buys. For distinguishing groups it did not outperform simple spectral measures, and its per-person low-frequency predictions were poor, so we restrict our claims accordingly. A real-time state observer detected sudden shifts in the network's operating point within milliseconds, yet could not reconstruct the moment-to-moment state, a limit set by the model's intrinsic randomness rather than by our algorithm. Finally, a dose-matched control showed that closed-loop stimulation is no more accurate than a fixed stimulus at the same dose, so we report the real-time feasibility of the loop without claiming an accuracy advantage. The contribution of the paper is therefore a reusable, calibrated inference pipeline together with an explicit map of its limits, including negative findings that we deliberately kept as results.

articles_hidden.title: Altered pre-supplementary motor area recruitment during semantic inhibition in individuals with elevated obsessive–compulsive traits
articles_hidden.authors: Rebeca Villarroel; Francisco Marcano; José Luis González-Mora; Manuel de Vega; Iván Padrón González; Mariano Díaz-Rivera; Damián Jan; Cristián Modroño
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Inhibitory control dysfunction has been implicated in obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD), but neuroimaging research has focused predominantly on motor response inhibition. Whether obsessive–compulsive traits are associated with altered neural recruitment during semantic inhibition remains unclear.
Methods: Forty right-handed participants with lower or elevated obsessive–compulsive traits performed an fMRI adaptation of the Hayling Sentence Completion Task. Participants either selected an expected sentence completion (initiation) or suppressed this strongly prepotent response to select an unrelated word (inhibition). Whole-brain and anatomically defined region-of-interest (ROI) analyses examined task-related activation and Group × Condition interactions, with particular interest in the pre-supplementary motor area (preSMA) and SMA proper.
Results: Semantic inhibition produced a robust behavioural cost in reaction times and error rates, with no significant differences between groups. Whole-brain analysis identified the strongest inhibition-related activation in the left preSMA. The exploratory Group × Condition analysis also yielded its peak interaction in this region. Anatomically defined ROI analysis showed a significant Group × Condition interaction in the preSMA after family-wise error correction (t = 2.56, pFWE = .012), reflecting a larger inhibition-related increase in controls compared to individuals with elevated obsessive–compulsive traits. The corresponding interaction in SMA proper did not reach statistical significance (t = 1.74, pFWE = .084).
Conclusions: Elevated obsessive–compulsive traits were associated with altered preSMA recruitment during semantic inhibition in absence of behavioural impairment. This extends neural markers of obsessive–compulsive alterations from the domain of motor inhibition to that of semantic inhibition.

articles_hidden.title: Number personification and imaginary companions: Concurrent rather than developmental links in school-age children
articles_hidden.authors: Eiko Matsuda; Acer Yu-Chan Chang; Yusuke Moriguchi; Osamu Sakura
articles_hidden.abstract: Number personification (NP), the attribution of gender, age, or character to digits, is common among 9- to 12-year-olds, but its relationship to other forms of childhood personification remains unknown. Because NP and imaginary companions (ICs) share the attribution of personhood to non-living entities and high idiosyncrasy, we hypothesized that NP is a developmental extension of ICs. In a web survey, 2,193 Japanese mothers of children in grades 1--6 reported their child's current and past IC and NP status and fantasy orientation. Current ICs were reported for 15.1¥% of children, and current NP for 1.2¥%. Contrary to our hypothesis, past IC did not predict current NP; instead, children with a current IC had four times the odds of NP (odds ratio = 4.16). Grade, gender, and fantasy orientation were related to ICs but not, or only weakly, to NP. NP appears to co-occur with ICs rather than to follow them developmentally.

articles_hidden.title: Are Workplace Tolerance and Individual Autonomy associated with Work Engagement? —Mediation analyses with Psychological Safety and Intrinsic Motivation
articles_hidden.authors: Takazumi Ono; Ryota Shin; Aoba Tamura; Yukihiko Okada; Hiroko Costantini; Misato Nihei
articles_hidden.abstract: There is growing recognition of the importance of designing work environments that promote the well-being of diverse employees. Although the Job Demands–Resources (JD–R) model has contributed substantially to work engagement research, there remains scope to extend it to address the challenge of creating inclusive work environments. We examined the associations of workplace tolerance and individual autonomy with work engagement, including the potential mediating roles of psychological safety and intrinsic motivation. We used data from 1084 Japanese workers collected across four waves of online surveys and conducted causal mediation analyses. As a result, the presence of tolerant coworkers was associated with work engagement through workplace psychological safety (total effect = 0.296; proportion mediated = 29.7 %), whereas the absence of intolerant coworkers was not clearly associated with work engagement. Individual autonomy was also associated with work engagement through intrinsic motivation (total effect = 0.444), although the proportion mediated was modest (14.5 %). These findings suggest that positioning workplace tolerance and individual autonomy as social and personal resources, respectively, may extend the JD–R model by enabling it to describe the conditions under which employees with diverse characteristics and circumstances can engage in their work on an equitable basis.

articles_hidden.title: A Computational Approach to Search in Visual Working Memory
articles_hidden.authors: Aditi Singh; Andra Mihali; Wen-Chuang Chou; Wei Ji Ma
articles_hidden.abstract: Search in visual working memory (VWM) is  an important  process in everyday life, but it has so far not been investigated sufficiently using psychophysical and computational approaches. Here, we examine whether computational process models from the study of VWM and of visual search also apply to search in VWM. Participants performed a two-alternative VWM-based color localization task in which set size and color similarity were varied. We tested models with a resource-limited encoding stage and a Bayesian decision stage. We found that a variable-precision model fit the data well and that adding an item limit did not improve the fit. Next, we took a resource-rational approach, in which mean precision at each set size is set by optimizing a combination between behavioral performance and encoding cost. We found that a resource-rational model with an ad-hoc cost function captures behavior well, but not better than the best non-resource-rational model. Our results, albeit unsurprising, contribute to the evidence that search in VWM is very similar to search in perception.

articles_hidden.title: Benchmarking an automated speech recognition pipeline for Spanish-English bilingual preschoolers: Quantifying language input and output in daylong recordings.
articles_hidden.authors: Gaurab Subedi; Marvin Lavechin; Jorge Fonseca; Sarah Surrain
articles_hidden.abstract: Measuring how much of each language bilingual children hear and use in their daily lives requires transcribing long, naturalistic recordings, which is too costly to do by hand at scale. We benchmarked four WhisperX-based automatic speech recognition pipelines, differing in how speech is located and attributed to speakers, against expert transcripts of 168 five-minute clips (14 hours) drawn from daylong home recordings of 14 Spanish--English bilingual preschoolers. Word error rates across pipelines were high (69.5% to 82.0% overall), compared with 35.4% (key child) and 53.9% (adults) between expert coders. Running a child-centered voice type classifier (VTC2) before transcription attributed words to speakers far better than labeling speakers afterwards; we retained this pipeline (WER = 71.4%). Despite word-level errors, it preserved the rank order of clips; automated and manual counts of total and distinct words correlated at r = .83 to .93 for adults and the key child in each language. Agreement rose further at the recording level. Lexical diversity was recovered best: slopes for distinct words (0.79 to 0.88) were closer to one than for total words (0.53 to 0.77). The proportion of Spanish was underestimated (adults: 77% vs. 89%; key child: 70% vs. 90%), largely because WhisperX output short English phrases on brief, unclear audio. Open, inspectable pipelines can yield language-specific measures of bilingual adult input and child output, but precise word counts and language proportions require correction before direct interpretation. These estimates, from one Spanish--English community, will need re-estimating in other populations.

articles_hidden.title: Decisions About Expressing Subjective States Generalise Across Psychological Domain
articles_hidden.authors: Jess Grimmond; Scott Brown; Quentin Frederik Gronau; Guy Hawkins
articles_hidden.abstract:
People routinely make decisions about how to express their internal psychological states to the
outside world. These communication choices can systematically influence the meaning observers
extract about the internal states of others. In psychological science, this is frequently observed in
the way people respond to self-report surveys. Quantitative cognitive models of these
communication choices, such as the Latent State and Response Style (LASARS) model, translate
continuous psychological states into Likert-type responses. In doing so, the model can separate
internal experiences (latent states) from preferences for (or against) certain response options in
self-report scenarios. A key assumption of the LASARS model is that response style reflects a
stable individual characteristic that generalises across contexts. The present study tested this
assumption by examining whether response styles remain consistent across theoretically distinct
psychological domains. A sample of 145 adults completed four survey instruments assessing
sensation seeking, thinking styles, dark personality traits, and perceived control. We compared a
model in which response style parameters were estimated separately for each instrument with a
more parsimonious model in which response style was assumed to be identical across all
instruments. Response style parameters exhibited strong cross-instrument correlations, exceeding
the magnitude of correlations observed among latent states. Furthermore, constraining response
style to be shared across instruments produced virtually identical predictions of observed scores
and latent state estimates while reducing model complexity substantially. These findings provide
strong evidence that response style is a stable, domain-general characteristic. They also support
the conclusion that people use similar decision strategies to express their internal psychological
states across the different constructs they may wish or be asked to communicate.

articles_hidden.title: Linguistic Markers of Self-Representation Reflect Daily Emotional Experiences in an Expressive Writing Study
articles_hidden.authors: Emily Huang; Claire Whiting; Steven Mesquiti; Sofia S. Baran; Erik C Nook
articles_hidden.abstract: The words people use provide important insights into their emotional experiences. Several measures for tracking emotions through language have been developed, including sentiment (i.e., the positivity and negativity of language) and I-usage (first-person singular pronoun use, thought to reflect negative self-focus). However, emerging research using large language model embedding techniques has quantified not just if people use “I” but how they use it, yielding a measure of self-representation (i.e., how strongly people see themselves as “good” and “able” rather than “bad” and “unable”). This measure tracks mental health outcomes in psychotherapy. Given that emotions and emotion regulation are intimately connected to how we view ourselves, linguistic self-representations may also offer a means for assessing emotional experiences. Here, we examined the associations between participants’ linguistic self-representations and daily emotional experiences in a 14-day expressive writing study (N = 53). Within-person associations showed that on days when participants’ self-representation embedding scores were closer to “good” or “able,” they reported more positive and less negative emotions. At the between-person level, people with self-representations overall closer to “good” experienced lower negative emotional reactivity to expressive writing. These findings suggest that linguistic markers of self-representation hold promise as a tool for assessing emotional experiences, extending prior work linking it to mental health. Translations of these findings could contribute to earlier identification of changes in emotional functioning and provide new ways of assessing metrics of mental health through everyday language.

articles_hidden.title: Comment on Suresh et al. (2026): Drug-level sample size, validation and embedding confounds in receptor–semantic mappings
articles_hidden.authors: Tim Kmecl
articles_hidden.abstract: Suresh et al. (2026, Psychopharmacology) related GloVe embeddings of 4,496 first-hand reports of 21 psychedelic drugs to receptor affinity profiles using partial least squares regression (PLSR), and reported associations between specific receptors and experiential themes. Because affinities vary only between drugs, every report of a drug carries the same profile. I show algebraically that within-drug variation drops out of every cross-product with the affinities. The published loadings can be reproduced from the drug means alone (r ≥ 0.998), so the analysis rests on 21 drugs, with a Kish effective sample size of about 11, rather than on 4,496 reports. The model is near-saturated at the drug level. The cross-validation, receptor subset selection and loading interpretation have not been assessed at the drug level, and the associations have not been tested against chance or for generalisation beyond the few heavily weighted drugs, within the sample or to new ones. A reanalysis of published values shows that the first three components closely follow the DMT–MDMA contrast (r = 0.93), mean report length (r = 0.96) and the LSD–DMT contrast (r = 0.97). The length component follows from summing word vectors. I propose drug-level validation, permutation and resampling analyses that can be run on the existing data. Code reproducing all numbers is publicly available.

articles_hidden.title: Innateness is (still) an orienting principle for language development
articles_hidden.authors: Leher Singh; Marisa Casillas; Shanley E. M. Allen; Michael C. Frank; Caroline F Rowland
articles_hidden.abstract:
How humans come to acquire language has been a persistent object of philosophical and scientific inquiry, in part because it bears on fundamental questions about the nature of human cognition.
Classically, this field of inquiry has centered innateness as a critical component of language acquisition, traditionally characterizing innate capability in terms of richly specified, biologically endowed linguistic structure, such as Universal Grammar. Contemporary theories have evolved considerably from these earlier formulations and now present several differing candidates for innateness in language. Throughout this evolution, though, questions of innateness have remained central to theories of language acquisition, even as the nature of those questions has shifted in response to new sources of evidence. In this Perspective, we consider evidence from three complementary sources of evidence—linguistic diversity, human social interaction, and language models (LMs)—that together inform the question of what children must bring to the task of language learning. We conclude by identifying desiderata for theories of language acquisition that seek to specify the nature, scope, and explanatory role of innate contributions to language development.

articles_hidden.title: Revisiting the Radius of Trust Problem: Who Counts as “Most People”?
articles_hidden.authors: Anu Realo; Jüri Allik
articles_hidden.abstract: General trust in social surveys is usually measured with a Single-Item General Trust (SIGT) question that asks whether “most people” can be trusted. The concept of the radius of trust challenges this approach by highlighting that trust may vary with the social distance between those who express trust and those who are trusted. This has led to the addition of six specific trust questions to the World Values Survey (WVS) questionnaire since Wave 5, which ask respondents to rate their trust in their family, neighborhood, and people they know personally, as well as in people of another religion, people of another nationality, and people they meet for the first time. Analyzing respondents’ answers to the SIGT and six specific trust items in the Integrated Values Surveys (IVS) dataset (1981-2022) across 88 countries and territories and the three most recent survey waves, we find that trust is a complex construct whose invariant property across cultures is a fixed-length vector composed of the squares of its two components: ingroup and outgroup trust. The phrase “most people” in the SIGT question appears to refer to “familiar strangers”—people whom respondents do not know personally but are likely to encounter in everyday life. It is trust in these familiar strangers, rather than in more distant outgroups, which is most strongly associated with the Human Development Index. This association, however, becomes pronounced only at very high levels of human development.

articles_hidden.title: Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex Causally Supports the Memory Advantage of Reading Aloud
articles_hidden.authors: Lihui Hu; Wenjie Chen; Travis Morgan Seale-Carlisle; Agnieszka Konopka; Manuela Macedonia; Brian Mathias
articles_hidden.abstract: Reading words aloud improves later recognition relative to reading them silently, a phenomenon known as the production effect. This advantage may reflect not only the distinctive sensorimotor information generated by production, but also cognitive control processes that prioritise this information during encoding. Given the central role of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) in supporting cognitive control, we tested whether this region causally contributes to the production effect using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). In a preregistered within-participant study, 40 adults completed three sessions in which TMS was delivered bilaterally to the DLPFC. They received continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS), expected to reduce DLPFC excitability; intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS), expected to increase it; or sham stimulation. Participants then read words aloud or silently before completing an old/new recognition test with confidence and recollection judgements. There was a clear production effect: words read aloud were recognised more accurately and quickly, with greater confidence and more frequent recollection ratings, than words read silently. Crucially, cTBS reduced the accuracy advantage for aloud words relative to sham and iTBS. Exploratory receiver-operating-characteristic (ROC) and unequal-variance signal-detection (UVSD) modeling approaches provided converging evidence that cTBS reduced the memory advantage for words read aloud. Stimulation did not reliably affect responses to new words. These findings provide the first causal evidence that the DLPFC helps make words read aloud more memorable, consistent with a role for cognitive control in prioritising the distinctive information generated by speaking.

articles_hidden.title: Noradrenaline-centric bias in the pupil-linked arousal literature
articles_hidden.authors: Simon van Gaal; Lola Beerendonk; Haoyue Zhang; Tobias H. Donner; Jan Willem de Gee
articles_hidden.abstract: The literature on pupil-linked arousal shows a pervasive bias: it often attributes findings to the noradrenergic locus coeruleus while overlooking other neuromodulatory systems. Here, we quantify the extent of this bias and emphasize that correcting it is essential for refining theoretical models and improving interpretability in this rapidly evolving field.

articles_hidden.title: Multidimensional Analysis of Personality Prediction from Electroencephalographic Representations
articles_hidden.authors: Seyed Mahan Mohajerani; Moein Esghaei
articles_hidden.abstract: Associations between personality and resting brain activity have proved difficult to reproduce, leaving unresolved whether electrophysiological information is broadly absent or selectively detectable across personality dimensions. Here, we investigated this question in 254 adults undergoing clinical assessment, examining 15 personality-pattern scales of the Millon Clinical Multiaxial Inventory–IV using resting-state electroencephalography (EEG). We evaluated eight complementary EEG feature families across four representations of personality scores—continuous, two binary thresholds and ordinal—using nested participant-level cross-validation. Most of the 60 scale–formulation combinations showed little predictive performance beyond chance. The strongest evidence concerned Masochistic scores dichotomized at a base-rate score of 60 (area under the curve, 0.630 and 0.594 across two model-aggregation widths), the only combination meeting the within-formulation false-discovery-rate criterion at both widths in fixed-candidate permutation tests. Weaker evidence emerged for continuous Turbulent scores and thresholded Negativistic scores, while an ordinal Histrionic association was identified in a post hoc three-class analysis. Although particular EEG feature families recurred among better-performing configurations, the exact configurations varied across folds. These findings do not support broadly accurate prediction of clinically oriented personality dimensions from resting EEG. Instead, they reveal modest, selective associations whose detection varies across personality dimensions and their operational definitions. Whether these associations generalize, reflect enduring individual differences or provide clinically useful information remains to be established.

articles_hidden.title: Developing human-AI complementarity: Augmenting everyday decision making with Large Language Models
articles_hidden.authors: Adrian Paul Banks; David M Gamblin
articles_hidden.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can improve human judgement, but human–AI systems rarely achieve complementarity: combined performance exceeding that of both humans and AI alone. Across three longitudinal studies (N = 671), we tested whether large language models (LLMs) could support complementarity by contributing to the construction and revision of everyday decision representations. Participants reported real, personally meaningful decisions involving two options and the decision outcome success one week later. As decisions were participant-generated rather than predefined, LLMs dynamically generated considerations and alternative evaluations tailored to each decision. We compared the predictive validity of AI, Human, and augmented evaluations. AI evaluations were standalone LLM predictions of decision outcome success. Human weighted-additive evaluations combined participant-generated attributes, importance weights, and option ratings. Augmented evaluations incorporated LLM-generated attributes and, in later studies, suggested weights and ratings, while participants selected attributes and retained control over evaluations. Augmented evaluations consistently predicted experienced outcomes and showed the strongest observed associations across all three studies. Evidence for complementarity was clearest in Study 2, where fully augmented evaluations outperformed both standalone approaches and explained additional variance in expected and experienced outcomes beyond the standalone evaluations considered together. Across studies, augmentation expanded the attribute set, with participants retaining human and AI contributions. These findings show that human–AI complementarity can emerge in predicting success of real decision outcomes and suggest that decision architecture matters. A distributed cognitive system that integrates AI contributions across all stages of decision making while humans remain responsible for selection and judgement of personally relevant considerations offers a promising architecture for evaluating diverse, personally meaningful real-life decisions.

articles_hidden.title: Reciprocal Relationships between Machiavellianism and Workplace Competition: A Six-Year Longitudinal Study
articles_hidden.authors: XIAOHAN XU; Bart Wille; Louisa Vofrei; Sofie Dupré; Jasmine Vergauwe
articles_hidden.abstract: Machiavellianism is linked to workplace competition, yet it remains unclear whether this association reflects personality-driven activity effects, environment-driven reactivity effects, or a combination of both. This study examined the reciprocal relationships between Machiavellianism and workplace competition across six years of early career development among 1,513 Belgian university graduates. Using both Cross-Lagged Panel Models and Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Models, we tested longitudinal activity and reactivity processes at the between-person and within-person levels, respectively. To this end, workplace competition was evaluated using both objective occupational characteristics and subjective perceptions. Regarding activity effects, results showed that higher levels of Machiavellianism at career start positively predicted increases in workplace competition (both objective and subjective), but only at the between-person level of analysis. Additionally, results provided evidence for reactivity effects whereby higher workplace competition predicts increases in Machiavellianism, but only for subjective evaluations of competition and when analyzed at the between-person level. Implications for theory and practice are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Cognitive performance in young and middle-aged adults with obesity: a systematic literature review
articles_hidden.authors: Camille Sellier; Marie-Claude Brindisi; Léopold Fezeu; Cecilia Samieri; Valentina A. Andreeva; Stéphanie Chambaron
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective
This systematic review synthesizes prospective evidence on associations between obesity assessed in young or middle adulthood and subsequent cognitive performance before age 65.
Methods
A comprehensive search of PubMed, PsycINFO, and Web of Science identified prospective studies comparing adults with obesity to those of normal weight and assessing cognitive performance, using validated cognitive tests. Risk of bias was evaluated using ROBINS-E, and findings were synthesized narratively.
Results
Among 4,871 records screened, four publications representing three cohorts met the inclusion criteria. Two publications from Whitehall II reported small negative associations between obesity assessed in adulthood and global cognitive performance, whereas the MIDUS analysis found no longitudinal association for BMI. A modestly steeper 10-year decline in global cognition was reported among metabolically unhealthy adults with obesity compared with adults of normal weight in Whitehall II. Findings for executive function and memory were inconsistent and generally small. One study was judged at high risk of bias and the other three raised some concerns.
Conclusions
The available evidence is too sparse, heterogeneous, and methodologically uncertain to establish a meaningful independent association between obesity and cognitive performance before age 65. Future prospective studies should include cognitive assessment at baseline and repeated follow-up, report standardized effect estimates, use domain-specific cognitive outcomes, address confounding a priori, and assess central adiposity and metabolic health alongside BMI, particularly in younger adults.
PROSPERO registration: CRD42024573250
Keywords: Adults, Cognitive functions, Cohort studies, Executive functions, Obesity

articles_hidden.title: What Drives Leaders to Serve? The Joint and Interactive Effects of HEXACO Personality Traits and Implicit Motives on Servant Leadership
articles_hidden.authors: Justine Amory; Sofie Dupré; J. Malte Runge; Bart Wille
articles_hidden.abstract: Drawing on the channeling hypothesis (Winter et al., 1998), this study examines the role of leaders’ explicit personality traits, implicit motives, and their interaction in predicting servant leadership. Using a dyadic design (N = 219), supervisors completed measures of their HEXACO personality traits and implicit motives, while subordinates rated their servant leadership behavior. Contrary to expectations, neither personality traits nor implicit motives explained unique variance in servant leadership. However, interactions between explicit traits and implicit motives significantly improved prediction. Specifically, leaders high in affiliation motivation were perceived as more servant when they scored high on extraversion and, contrary to expectations, low on agreeableness. These findings highlight the value of considering both implicit motives and explicit traits, as well as their interplay, in understanding servant leadership.

articles_hidden.title: Mapping and Understanding Employees’ Perceived Personality–Work (Mis)Fit: a Mixed-Method Approach
articles_hidden.authors: Sofie Dupré; Jasmine Vergauwe; Bart Wille
articles_hidden.abstract: Although perceived person–environment (P–E) fit has been extensively studied and linked to important workplace outcomes, it has not been examined with the same level of attribute specificity as objective fit. This study addressed that gap by introducing and empirically examining perceived personality–work (mis)fit. Employing a multi-method, multi-informant design with 734 employees and 521 supervisors, we aimed to (a) operationalize perceived personality–work (mis)fit using the too little/too much scale, (b) explore the workplace experiences that shape these perceptions, and (c) examine how they relate to supervisor-rated job performance. We found a high prevalence of perceived misfit, with both deficiency (30%) and excess (42%) commonly reported, while perceived fit was observed across a range of personality trait levels. Thematic analysis revealed that negative experiences associated with perceived misfit extended beyond task performance, encompassing well-being concerns and interpersonal difficulties, with distinct patterns across traits. Finally, perceived personality–work (mis)fit showed modest associations with supervisor-rated job performance. Theoretically, these findings provide insight into how employees experience the fit of their personality at work and highlight the value of examining perceived fit with respect to specific personal attributes. Practically, they inform efforts to better support employees’ fit experiences in the workplace.

articles_hidden.title: Bayesian Treed Regressions for Estimating Heterogeneous Trajectories of Test Scores in Large-scale Educational Assessments
articles_hidden.authors: Mingya Huang
articles_hidden.abstract: In large-scale educational assessment, students’ academic outcomes can evolve over time, due to various effect modifiers. For instance, parents’  education level, a common modifier, has been found to have time-varying effects on children’s test scores, leading to heterogeneous academic trajectories. To model these varying trajectories, parametric models like hierarchical linear models (HLMs) are commonly deployed. While these highly parametric methods are interpretable, their predictive capacities have not been rigorously compared to those of more flexible nonparametric approaches. We present the results of systematic simulation studies and empirical analyses comparing traditional parametric models to Bayesian nonparametric models based on Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART). Our findings indicate that BART-based alternatives can (1) achieve comparable out-of-sample prediction as HLMs, after accounting for individual variability over time; (2) provide a reasonable amount of interpretability and uncertainty quantification; and (3) do not incur much more computational burden. This work contributes to the existing social science literature by demonstrating that Bayesian treed regression methods are viable and feasible alternatives to conventional HLMs for predicting heterogeneous trajectories across time.

articles_hidden.title: Taxing working memory shifts the balance from goals to stimulus-response habits
articles_hidden.authors: Tim van Timmeren; Poppy Watson; Irene van de Vijver; Sanne de Wit
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite our familiarity with the concept of habits, eliciting and measuring habitual “slips of action” experimentally in humans has proven to be difficult. A possible explanation is that participants in psychological experiments actively recruit goal-directed control and therefore make few habitual slips-of-action in the presence of stimuli signalling devalued outcomes. In the current experiment we used the symmetrical outcome-revaluation task in combination with a working memory load in an attempt to tip the balance from goal-directed control to stimulus-response habit. During the instrumental learning phase, participants learned to make a Go response to stimuli signalling valuable outcomes (and points) while not responding (NoGo) to stimuli signalling not-valuable outcomes. During the subsequent test phase, the outcomes signalled by the stimuli were either value-congruent with training (still-valuable and still-not-valuable), or value-incongruent (devalued and upvalued). Participants had to flexibly adjust their behaviour on value-incongruent trials where the stimulus-response association learned during training was no longer appropriate. For half the participants, a concurrent working memory load was imposed during the test phase. In line with our preregistered hypotheses, participants showed evidence for habitual slips of action across two experiments, but those under working memory load showed increased habit tendencies (specifically failures to inhibit prepotent Go responses in the presence of stimuli signalling devalued outcomes). This central finding suggests that a working memory load can be used to reveal habits in humans.

articles_hidden.title: Supporting Early Career Development Through Volitional Personality Change: A Multi-Layered Evaluation of a Digital Intervention
articles_hidden.authors: Sofie Dupré; Bart Wille; Barbara De Clercq; Janne Vanhalst; Joeri Hofmans
articles_hidden.abstract: Personality change interventions (PCIs) offer promising opportunities for personal development, yet little is known about how different psychological layers of personality—thoughts, feelings, behaviors, skills, and identity—respond to intentional change efforts. This study addressed that question through a six-week smartphone-based intervention tailored to students' preparation for entering the workforce, an applied setting in which PCIs remain understudied. Final-year undergraduate clinical psychology students (N = 565) participated in one of three interventions designed to enhance resilience, social boldness, or punctuality, with a quasi-experimental control group for comparison (N = 99). Participants in all three conditions showed meaningful growth in the targeted facet, with gains exceeding changes in non-targeted facets, surpassing those observed in the control group, and persisting at the four-week follow-up. Moreover, perceived feasibility of change moderated intervention effectiveness. Finally, participants targeting resilience and social boldness showed significant growth across psychological layers, whereas those targeting punctuality changed primarily in the behavioral and skill layers. The identity layer—representing how participants see themselves—exhibited the smallest degree of change. Collectively, these findings enrich volitional personality change (VPC) theory by illuminating how personality change unfolds across different psychological layers, while also demonstrating the feasibility of PCIs in supporting the school-to-work transition.

articles_hidden.title: PsyScale Studio: A Guided, Browser-Based Application for Developing and Validating Measurement Scales
articles_hidden.authors: Assis Kamu; Nicholas Tze Ping Pang; Ho Chong Mun
articles_hidden.abstract: Validating a measurement scale requires a long sequence of analyses, from content validity and item analysis to factor analysis, item response theory, fairness and relations to other variables. These analyses are spread across several programs, and many applied researchers find them difficult to choose, run and report. PsyScale Studio is a free web application that guides users through this sequence. Users describe their study purpose and response format (ten formats, from dichotomous tests to forced-choice and formative indices); the application then builds a purpose-specific roadmap, runs each analysis and explains every result in English or Malay with criteria, references and reporting text. Classical, exploratory and Rasch analyses run in JavaScript. Confirmatory factor analysis, measurement invariance, polytomous item response theory, differential item functioning and cognitive diagnostic models run in R compiled to WebAssembly (webR), using lavaan, semTools, mirt and CDM, while the data stay on the user’s computer. Outputs include an APA-style Word report with references and a reproducibility package with the exact R code and input of each analysis.
