articles.title: She Is Anyway: The Chatbot as Compliant Auxiliary in a New Psychodramaturgy for Voice-Hearers
articles.authors: John Hawkins
articles.abstract: This paper proposes a new therapeutic modality I am calling psychodramaturgy, and a new role for the large language model within it which I am calling the compliant auxiliary. The method extends narrative therapy (White & Epston, 1990) into dramatic writing, with the chatbot held in the role Moreno (1946) called the auxiliary ego, and the voice-hearer held in the role of playwright. The modality is proposed as homework between group meetings, for clients already in the stabilization phase of the Maastricht approach (Romme & Escher, 2000), with the group's embodied performance of the client's chatbot-authored script as the necessary completion of the work. Drawing on Boal's Forum Theatre and Levinas's ethics of the face as a strained but useful rung, the paper argues that the voice-hearing community is uniquely placed to develop the phenomenology of address that this kind of instrument will require. Risks are named candidly: sycophancy, session closure, surveillance, and externalization without integration. A protocol sketch and a brief illustrative session transcript are offered. The paper is written from a Lived Experience Expert standpoint and engages directly with Read (2019) on the inversion of the diagnostic question.

articles.title: Minimum Attainment Cost: National Benchmark Framework for Measuring Healthcare Accessibility in Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias-Related Services
articles.authors: Kyusik Kim; Amber DeJohn; Weining Kan
articles.abstract: A threshold represented as travel time or distance is a key concept for determining catchment areas in cumulative opportunity and Two-Step Floating Catchment Area methods. As destinations included in a catchment area are determined by the threshold, it is a primary factor affecting spatial accessibility. In many cases, thresholds are arbitrarily determined or fixed values are used. The resulting accessibility based on these arbitrary or fixed thresholds makes it challenging to compare accessibility scores across heterogeneous geographic contexts (e.g., urban and rural areas). In this paper, we propose the Minimum Attainment Cost (MAC) as a context-sensitive spatial accessibility measure using the national average facility-to-population ratio as a benchmark and explore how fixed thresholds can over- or underestimate accessibility compared with MAC in a nationwide U.S. analysis. Using the national benchmark, MAC measures the minimum travel time required to reach the national average level of a given resource in each zone, accounting for the geographic distributions of demand and resources. By comparing MAC with multiple fixed thresholds (i.e., 30, 60, 90, and 120 minutes), we find that MAC is sensitive to geographic contexts in terms of the distributions of demand and resources. This approach enables direct geographic comparisons of spatial accessibility to different resources and provides evidence to support effective policy interventions by providing more context-sensitive accessibility estimates.

articles.title: Physician-Led Research Infrastructure in a Private Equity–Backed Musculoskeletal Network: An Organizational Case Study
articles.authors: Tesheia Howard Harris; Gary W. Stewart; Kenneth Ellinger; Melissa Murphy
articles.abstract:
Background: Clinical research programs are often described from the perspective of academic departments with established infrastructure. In contrast, large private musculoskeletal practice networks face a different challenge: how to build a durable research structure while maintaining high-volume clinical operations, distributed leadership, and day-to-day practice efficiency.
Objective: To describe an early-stage model for building a clinical research structure within a busy physician-led musculoskeletal practice network and to identify the operational, governance, and partnership strategies used to make research feasible in routine practice, including how physician decision-making authority over research was structured within a private equity–backed management services organization. 
Methods: This descriptive organizational case study drew on a 2024–2025 clinical research infrastructure assessment, including document review, semi-structured interviews with 12 UMP leaders, and two site visits, together with a structured, iterative review of internal strategic planning materials, leadership presentations, quality and patient-reported outcome (PRO) dashboards, and organizational documents from United Musculoskeletal Partners (UMP), interpreted against prior literature on orthopaedic research team development. Interpretations were checked through author consensus and face-validity review by market-level leaders.
Results: UMP’s emerging model rests on five practical design choices: 1) starting with a focused research vision tied to patient outcomes and quality benchmarks; 2) placing physician leadership at the center of governance; 3) using external partners strategically to supplement internal capacity; 4) integrating research activities with existing clinical and operational workflows rather than creating a parallel academic structure; and 5) sequencing the work into short-term proof-of-concept projects and longer-term infrastructure building. Participation grew from a three-person founding team to 21 surgeons serving on a cross-site research council without additional compensation. Existing PRO infrastructure had captured 2,721,144 PRO scores by June 2026, with 2025 baseline compliance of 77.23% across participating practices.
Conclusion: For high-volume musculoskeletal groups, durable research infrastructure may be most feasible when built as an extension of clinical operations rather than as a separate academic enterprise. A pragmatic, partnership-enabled, physician-led model may allow busy practice networks to generate publishable data, strengthen quality measurement, and create a sustainable pathway toward broader participation in innovation and clinical trials. Within a private equity–backed platform, documented governance preserved physician authority over research priorities, offering a counterexample to the assumption that such ownership necessarily limits physician direction of research.

articles.title: Spirit-Masters, Supernatural Punishment, and Religious Cooperation Among the Altai Uriankhai of Mongolia
articles.authors: Attila Mateffy; Daniel Major-Smith; Benjamin Grant Purzycki
articles.abstract: Whether supernatural punishment beliefs promote cooperation has been studied extensively, yet much remains to be understood. For instance, most previous work has focused on “moralistic” religious traditions (e.g., Christianity, Hinduism), and how this may facilitate cooperation with distant co-religionists. Here, we use data from the Altai Uriankhai of Western Mongolia to examine whether punishment and omniscience beliefs regarding local deities (here, spirit-masters) promotes cooperation among distant co-religionists of this spirit-master tradition. Cooperation with distant co-religionists was assessed using two experimental games, the Random Allocation Game and Dictator Game. A formal causal inference approach was employed to specify our estimand of interest – i.e., the joint causal effect of punishment and omniscience beliefs on cooperation with distant co-religionists – and the assumptions required for a causal interpretation. Across most models a negative relationship between spirit-master beliefs and cooperation with distant co-religionists was observed, although many were also consistent with a null relationship. To the extent these results can be given a causal interpretation, they suggest that supernatural beliefs regarding local deities do not promote cooperation beyond parochial boundaries in this population, although whether the relationship is negative or null is equivocal.

articles.title: Measuring Rohingya children’s happiness through fathers’ eyes: Revisiting validity with a culturally responsive lens
articles.authors: Fatima Tuz Zahra; Sabiha Sultana
articles.abstract: Accurately assessing happiness among displaced Rohingya children is essential for designing effective psychosocial and educational interventions. This study reports the cross-cultural adaptation and Rasch validation of an existing children’s happiness instrument — originally developed in Western contexts — using father-report proxy methodology for use in Rohingya camps in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. A total of 14 dichotomous parent-report items were translated, back-translated, expert-reviewed, and pilot-tested through cognitive interviews to ensure linguistic and cultural appropriateness. Following administration of the instrument to 392 fathers of children aged 2 to 6 years, we analyzed the data using the Rasch one-parameter logistic model to examine item fit, person–item targeting, dimensionality, and differential item functioning (DIF) by fathers’ education and employment status. Eleven of 14 items fit within a priori criteria (0.79–1.20 MNSQ), yielding a person reliability of 0.68. Dimensionality analyses supported a primarily unidimensional structure with closely related social–emotional components. Three items showed a small uniform DIF by education and one by employment. A 9-item short form, refined through item-fit and DIF review, achieved improved person reliability (0.71) and retained conceptual coverage. Overall, the adapted instrument demonstrates promising internal structure and fairness evidence, supporting its use as a culturally grounded tool for humanitarian research and policy evaluation.

articles.title: Bringing Citizen Science into Deliberative Democracy: Insights from Climate Citizens’ Assemblies
articles.authors: Julian Vicens; Ferran Bertomeu; Kyriaki Maria Fameli; Anna Maria Kotrikla; Amalia Polydoropoulou; Nil Alvarez; David Laniado
articles.abstract: This paper explores the integration of citizen science into climate citizens’ assemblies as a pathway to democratise not only decision-making but also knowledge production. While citizens' assemblies enable citizens to deliberate on policy, they typically rely on expert-defined evidence, limiting participants’ epistemic agency. Conversely, citizen science empowers lay publics to generate and interpret data but often lacks deliberative structures for collective reflection. We present the co-creation and testing of a Citizen Science Toolkit for Climate Assemblies, developed through participatory workshops in Living Labs and field deployments across two European climate citizens' assemblies, in Riga and Edermunde. Using mixed methods, including surveys, focus groups, and qualitative coding, we analyse participants’ and organisers’ perspective. Results from those two assemblies show that integrating citizen science fosters knowledge uptake, citizen empowerment, and trust in the process, but also increases organisational demands. We argue that structurally embedding citizen science within deliberative formats expands the epistemic legitimacy of democratic innovation. The paper concludes with design principles for future citizens' assemblies and outlines a framework for citizen science as a climate adaptation governance tool.

articles.title: The Quality of Resources Used in Google AI Overviews for Health Topics
articles.authors: Adéla Jarolímková
articles.abstract:
Background: The growing number of consumers seeking health information online are increasingly offered Google AI Overviews atop their searches. Recent research has identified pitfalls of using large language models for health information generation. 
Objectives: To examine sources employed in generating AI overviews for minority-language queries and evaluate their quality. 
Methods: Query topics were derived from the Czech National Medical Library's patient information portal, entered in Google, and information about sources linked to AI overviews was collected and statistically analysed. 
Results: Of 145 distinct queries, 40 (27.6%) did not yield AI overviews. The remaining 105 queries produced 1,231 unique URLs (mean=11.7). General web pages were most frequent (68.9%, n=848), followed by Wikipedia (5.4%, n=66) and peer-reviewed articles (2.9%, n=35). Private-sector entities owned 55.7% of sources, public sector 29.5%, and non-profits 14.8%. Quality scores ranged from −1.5 to 7.0 (mean=1.85). Poor-quality sources comprised 28.4%, while 10.6% were excellent. 
Discussion: Quality variability strongly correlates with sector ownership. Public sources and structured initiatives demonstrate best practices, while private entities often introduce commercial bias and non-evidence-based content. 
Conclusion: Source quality for Czech health AI overviews is highly variable and sector-dependent. Rigorous quality control measures are essential for consumer safety.

articles.title: Who Speaks Matters More Than How: Automated Accounts, Account Reach, and Message Features in COVID-19 Vaccine Tweets Around the Delta Wave
articles.authors: Abdallah Sayed Ali Essa; Sergey V. Kovalchuk
articles.abstract: Studies of crisis communication on social media often infer which message features drive engagement from large public tweet corpora, yet such corpora can contain automated accounts and are rarely adjusted for who is posting. We re-examine Media Richness Theory and the feature-based operationalization of Dialogic Communication Theory using 180,278 deduplicated English-language COVID-19 vaccine tweets from a public Kaggle corpus, covering windows before (April–June 2021), during (July–September 2021) and after (October–November 2021) the Delta wave. Automated vaccine-slot notification accounts produced 34.0% of Delta-window tweets and attracted almost no engagement. A naive negative binomial model of all Delta tweets suggested that a link or attached media multiplied engagement 4.71-fold. After removing automated accounts, adjusting for account reach and clustering standard errors by account, the association fell to 1.40 (95% CI 1.19–1.64). Positive sentiment remained positively associated with engagement (IRR = 1.48), questions (0.85) and hashtags (0.91 per tag) were modestly negative, and @mentions were unrelated to engagement. Follower count was the strongest predictor: doubling an account's followers was associated with about 36% more engagement. Across windows, the link and sentiment associations were stable in direction, whereas the dialogic cues shifted, and we found no evidence that the link effect reverses after the peak. The results suggest that who speaks matters more than how a message is designed, that counting dialogic features captures little of what dialogue theory describes, and that auditing corpora for automation is a precondition for drawing communication lessons from public tweet data.

articles.title: Media Framing of the Rohingya Crisis and Its Implications for Regional Diplomacy in South Asia, 2017-2026
articles.authors: Mohammad Mohtasim Rahman; Jannatul Ferdous Lamia; Junayed Hosen; Shahnoor Mridul
articles.abstract: Nearly nine years after the 2017 mass displacement of Rohingya from Myanmar, the crisis remains one of the world's largest and most protracted refugee situations. This article examines how media framing of the Rohingya crisis in Bangladesh, Myanmar, and selected international outlets evolved from 2017 to 2026, and how these frames have shaped regional diplomatic responses. Using a mixed-methods design, the study combines quantitative analysis of UNHCR, IOM, and UN OCHA data on refugee populations, humanitarian funding, and maritime movements with qualitative framing analysis of a comparative corpus of 1,071 English-language reports from nine outlets, as coded by Islam and Shuchy (2026), and of later 2025-2026 coverage. Results show a clear shift from atrocity-centred reporting in 2017 toward humanitarian-managerial and securitised frames by 2026, even as the registered Rohingya population in Bangladesh grew to 1,204,492 and funding shortfalls deepened. The framing patterns sit beside diplomatic stagnation: Myanmar's repeated symbolic repatriation pledges without implementation, Bangladesh's rising security and fiscal costs, and a 96 percent increase in embarked refugees in early 2026. The article argues that humanitarian visibility without sustained genocide recognition depoliticises state responsibility and weakens pressure for durable solutions. It concludes with recommendations for newsrooms, donors, and regional bodies.

articles.title: Rapid Exploratory Maps and their potential role in supporting evidence-to-policy dialogues and processes
articles.authors: Gareth J Hollands; Ian Shemilt; James Thomas
articles.abstract: Producing useful evidence syntheses requires clearly formulated research questions linked to an understanding of their optimal scope. When policymakers (or other end users) commission or steer the production of systematic reviews or other evidence syntheses to fulfil a demand for evidence, these parameters are rarely specified sufficiently for production to proceed. Instead, these details are typically developed via a collaborative dialogic process involving evidence producers and users to ensure the resulting synthesis will meet users’ needs. This process is informed by scoping and (more-or-less formally) mapping the existing evidence base, which can take many weeks or months, slowed by applying mostly manual processes to identify and characterise the evidence. Recent developments in artificial intelligence (AI) technologies have opened up new opportunities for more rapid, iterative, and responsive mapping of relevant evidence to support such early-stage evidence-to-policy dialogues and processes. In this article, we outline and characterise this emerging approach, termed Rapid Exploratory Maps (REMs). We also present two illustrative case studies drawn from first-hand experiences within a programme of evidence reviews production to inform government policy in England. While this approach could be transformative for the mapping process, its broader potential is as yet largely unassessed, and it confers important challenges and likely risks, as well as benefits. Determining whether REMs could usefully support more efficient ways of working with end users when developing and designing evidence syntheses will require continued development and careful evaluation.

articles.title: Probing Computational Video Representations with MAVIC: A Multimodal Assessment Vocabulary for Interpretability and Coverage
articles.authors: David Wegmann; Marcus Olesen; Kristoffer Nielbo; Anja Bechmann
articles.abstract: When researchers analyze thousands of videos, their choice of computational representation shapes which similarities and differences they can detect. However, standard model benchmarks do not show whether a representation captures the visual, audio, and linguistic properties relevant to a particular study. We present MAVIC, the Multimodal Assessment Vocabulary for Interpretability and Coverage, which assesses video representations against 133 observable features grounded in communication research. These comprise 86 visual, 13 audio, and 34 linguistic features. We apply MAVIC to 20,180 videos sampled from 1,009 donated YouTube watch histories and compare three representation pipelines using images, audiovisual content, or metadata. For each pipeline, linear probes predict every MAVIC feature from its representation, producing an interpretable coverage profile. The three profiles differ markedly: pipelines tend to capture features from the modalities they receive most strongly, but they also encode indirect associations across modalities. Some features that vary across demographic groups’ observed video exposure are captured only weakly, indicating possible substantive blind spots. MAVIC therefore enables researchers to evaluate whether a representation preserves the distinctions their research question requires, rather than selecting pipelines based on general performance alone.

articles.title: Thin Markets, Thick Ties, and Thinking Machines: Institutional Environments, IPO Markets, Technological Disruption, and New Venture Performance in Central Europe
articles.authors: John Stanly
articles.abstract: New ventures in Central Europe grow up inside institutional environments that are neither fully mature nor fully void. Formal rules have converged on European Union standards, yet capital markets remain thin, informal ties remain consequential, and successful technology ventures frequently exit to foreign exchanges. At the same time, artificial intelligence and related digital technologies are altering what a new venture is, who acts on its behalf, and how investors evaluate it. This conceptual paper integrates institutional theory, signaling and legitimacy perspectives on initial public offerings, and research on technological disruption to explain how these forces jointly shape new venture performance in the region. We develop seven propositions. We argue that the IPO operates as a legitimacy substitute whose value rises where market-supporting intermediaries are weak, that positive media sentiment exhibits a too-much-of-a-good-thing effect that is sharper in thin markets, and that founder drive pays off most when paired with political skill in particularistic settings. We further propose that category-breaking ventures face an initial valuation discount but superior long-run performance, that artificial intelligence acting as an entrepreneurial actor weakens the dependence of performance on local institutions, and that organizational scope and supranational harmonization condition these relationships. We conclude with a research agenda and implications for founders, investors, exchanges, and policymakers.

articles.title: Reading the City: Urban Sentiment, Technological Disruption, and the Exporting and Performance of High-Growth Firms in China
articles.authors: Xiaoqing Wang; Kaifu Zhang
articles.abstract: High-growth firms are disproportionately responsible for job creation and productivity gains in emerging economies, yet little is known about how the urban environments in which they operate shape their decisions to sell abroad and the returns they earn from doing so. Integrating real options reasoning with an institution-based view of urban task environments, we argue that city-level sentiment about economic development and technological disruption functions as a collective signal that shapes how high-growth firms value and exploit international opportunities. We combine a simulated firm-level survey dataset calibrated to the World Bank Enterprise Survey design for 25 Chinese cities (N = 2,700 firms; 540 high-growth firms) with city-industry sentiment scores produced through large language model text classification. Economic development sentiment is positively associated with export intensity, whereas technological disruption sentiment displays an inverted U-shaped relationship with export intensity. Exporting is associated with higher productivity and growth, but these returns are amplified by favorable development sentiment and attenuated by intense disruption sentiment. A multiverse analysis of 72 specifications supports the robustness of the core moderation result. The study advances research on emerging-market internationalization, high-growth entrepreneurship, and text-based measurement in international business.

articles.title: Newspapers Blocking AI Crawlers Expose Their Voters to a Partisan Flood
articles.authors: Sho Miyazaki
articles.abstract: Major newspapers block AI crawlers, while parties and partisan sites leave their text open. This paper builds a game-theoretic model of the hold-out and asks what voters hear while it lasts. In the model, an AI that cannot grade its sources pools the text it can read; two persuaders choose how much nearly free text to publish; and an AI lab may license a newspaper's reporting for its lost revenue. Neither the newspapers nor the lab has a political aim. Three results follow. First, the persuaders flood the AI, and the lab licenses each newspaper once a fixed share of the voters closest to it asks the AI, whatever the AI says. Second, newspapers whose voters dislike the AI's answers more hold out longer, and their voters hear the flood longer. Third, licensing bends the persuaders' contest by a small tilt from where the costs alone put it: patient persuaders tilt the AI's answers against the voters' average ideology, and impatient ones toward it. Business decisions with no political aim thus set how long each group hears the flood and which way the AI's answers tilt.

articles.title: Meaning through Relations: Lévi-Strauss and Large Language Models
articles.authors: Ulrich Mansmann
articles.abstract: Claude Lévi-Strauss’s structuralism offers a useful perspective on large language models (LLMs) through its emphasis on relationships within systems of meaning. This paper recalls relational meaning, oppositions and mediation, transformations, and bricolage, illustrating these ideas through Lévi-Strauss’s analysis of myth and an everyday example of gift-giving. It then examines their connections with contextual representations and generative processes in LLMs. These connections support a productive comparison, although similarities do not establish that language models implement or validate structuralist theory. Practical implications include assessing whether models preserve relevant relationships across reformulations, examining the cultural categories expressed in their responses, and distinguishing coherent explanations from empirically justified claims. Structuralism can inform the interpretation and evaluation of LLM behaviour, while LLMs offer opportunities to investigate how relationships are learned, represented and transformed. The comparison therefore provides a basis for exploring meaning and creativity, with attention to the differences between linguistic competence, cultural understanding and knowledge of the world.

articles.title: Scientists held their ground, science did not: public trust in 95 countries before and after the Covid-19 pandemic
articles.authors: Michael James Ireland
articles.abstract: Trust in science, an institution, and trust in scientists, its practitioners, are usually read as one. In Wellcome Global Monitor microdata for 95 countries surveyed in the same mode in 2018 and 2025, with nearly four billion adults, I compared the two questions each respondent answered. Strong trust in scientists rose slightly, tracking trust in doctors, nurses and journalists. Strong trust in science fell from 34% to 30% in the average country, losing ground relative to every other group asked about. Science led scientists in 2018; by 2025 the order had reversed, a 5.5-point swing (95% CI 4.1 to 6.9), about 150 million adults; 112 alternative analyses pointed the same way. Telephone interviewing was associated with about 6 points higher strong trust in science, a caution for mixed-mode trends. Scientists were judged like other institutions; science lost standing on its own. Surveys asking only about scientists would miss it.

articles_hidden.title: Metrics by Default: Bibliometric Gatekeeping, Institutional Logics, and Early-Career Research Evaluation in India
articles_hidden.authors: Moumita Koley; Yogesh Vijay Krishna
articles_hidden.abstract:
Journal-based bibliometric indicators continue to dominate research evaluation globally despite sustained advocacy for reform. However, the mechanisms by which they become institutionally entrenched, and the structural conditions that make them difficult to dislodge, remain poorly understood. Particularly in rapidly expanding research systems in the Global South. This article addresses that gap through a systematic qualitative investigation of how bibliometric indicators are operationalized as institutional gatekeepers within India's national post-doctoral fellowships and early-career selection processes in STEM. India represents a critical and underexamined case. It’s the world's third-largest producer of scientific publications, combining quantitative growth imperatives with limited evaluation infrastructure capacity and facing structural asymmetries in international publishing. These situations amplify reliance on metrics and shift their costs onto those who are unfavorably positioned to resist them.
Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 25 early-and mid-career researchers, and fellowship administrators across four case settings - the INSPIRE Faculty Fellowship, the National Postdoctoral Fellowship (NPDF), institutional postdoctoral fellowships, and retrospective accounts from mid-career researchers in STEM. The study reveals a metrics-governed gatekeeping architecture, where quantitative screening serves as the primary filter before any qualitative assessment. This logic generates field-specific distortions, reproduces structural inequities under the guise of objectivity, incentivizes volume over significance, and creates systemic vulnerabilities to metric manipulation and research misconduct.  We theorize these dynamics through the lens of commensuration, institutional logics, and the sociology of quantification. Despite policy discourse emphasizing quality and societal impact, operational evaluation infrastructures continue to rely on bibliometrics because metrics reduce administrative complexity and create the appearance of objectivity & transparency. The article concludes with evidence-based recommendations for context-sensitive reform appropriate to India's research ecosystem and transferable to other rapidly expanding research systems in the Global South.

articles_hidden.title: Keep on Keeping On, With a Machine: Artificial Intelligence and the Calibration of Entrepreneurial Persistence
articles_hidden.authors: Jiaju Justin Yan; Xiaqing Nancy He; Alan Boss
articles_hidden.abstract: Entrepreneurs increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI) when deciding whether to continue a struggling venture, yet persistence theory locates the antecedents of persistence either within the entrepreneur or within human social networks. We theorize AI as a distinct, non-human antecedent of entrepreneurial persistence. Building on the psychological resource approach to persistence, escalation and threshold theories, and the AI Entrepreneurial Agency Framework, we distinguish two pathways. Through a resource pathway, AI supplies psychological resources that raise persistence intensity and loosen its dependence on the entrepreneur's internal resources. Through an epistemic pathway, AI shapes the feedback on which persistence decisions rest and thereby governs persistence calibration, which we define as the responsiveness of persistence to diagnostic disconfirming evidence. Five propositions specify when the pathways combine into AI-amplified escalation, how the Knightian uncertainty of the decision widens a gap between confidence and calibration, and how agentic AI attenuates the decision points at which founders confront adversity. A temporal extension explains how sustained AI scaffolding can render persistence fragile. The framework reconciles optimistic and pessimistic accounts of AI in entrepreneurship and offers testable implications for small business owners, advisors, and AI designers.

articles_hidden.title: The Justice Engagement Gap: Comparative Institutions and Anti-Trafficking Enforcement in the United States, Brazil, and China
articles_hidden.authors: Caye Lee; Mayank Kejriwal
articles_hidden.abstract: Human trafficking is nearly universal in law but highly uneven in prosecution. Existing cross-national research usually examines either trafficking prevalence or anti-trafficking enforcement, leaving unclear whether states respond at levels proportionate to estimated need. This article introduces the Justice Engagement Gap (JEG) framework to compare estimated trafficking prevalence with observable prosecutorial engagement while avoiding false numerical precision. The framework classifies trafficking prevalence levels and prosecutorial engagement separately, then evaluates whether their relationship indicates a narrow, moderate, high, or severe justice gap. I apply the framework to three institutionally contrasting cases: the United States, Brazil, and China. The comparison identifies three distinct pathways linking formal criminalization to uneven enforcement. In the United States, a narrow gap coexists with strong prosecutorial capacity but persistent underenforcement of labor trafficking. In Brazil, a high gap reflects fragmented federal coordination, dual legal tracks for trafficking and “slave labor,” and judicial bottlenecks that prevent investigations from yielding timely convictions. In China, a high gap reflects a qualitatively different problem: state perpetration, data suppression, and the absence of independent accountability. The article argues that anti-trafficking outcomes are best under- stood as institutional products shaped by capacity, coordination, transparency, and regime incentives rather than by statutory criminalization alone.

articles_hidden.title: Social Acceptability Smart Glasses and Social Acceptability: Reassessing User Responsibility and Controllership under EU Data Protection Law
articles_hidden.authors: Mark Leiser
articles_hidden.abstract: This article critically examines the European Data Protection Board’s initiative on the social acceptability of camera-enabled smart glasses, analysing the commissioned qualitative research alongside the Board’s October 2026 statement and the Hamburg DPA’s technical and legal assessment. It evaluates the relationship between the social evidence and the legal conclusions advanced, then reconstructs documented operating modes and data flows from the available technical evidence. Tracing processing across the device and connected services grounds a doctrinal analysis of user responsibility and controllership under the GDPR, situated within the wider law governing image capture and disclosure. The analysis distinguishes the wearer’s personal photography from the provider’s independently determined service processing and any separately established further use. It concludes that an ordinary request for visual assistance does not itself establish joint controllership; the provider’s commercial purpose likewise does not automatically remove the household exemption from the wearer’s private activity. Separating capture from publication also clarifies the interference requiring justification and the actor responsible. Effective safeguards retain legal significance without achieving absolute anonymity, while legitimate interests can support defined processing that satisfies necessity and the balancing test. These findings produce a materially different legal picture from the broader regulatory concerns and restrictive implications of the EDPB and Hamburg materials. Social acceptability can inform the assessment, but cannot replace attributing responsibility or create an independent condition of lawfulness. The article argues for supervision grounded in identifiable processing and applicable duties, with practical guidance explaining how lawful uses can proceed.

articles_hidden.title: How normative claims guide engineers under value pluralism: The “Portasello” model of collaborative viability and value interfaces
articles_hidden.authors: Martin Baumers
articles_hidden.abstract: How can normative claims guide engineers under conditions of value pluralism? Existing approaches in the engineering and engineering management literatures, including value engineering, value management, and value-sensitive design, explain how values inform decision-making but leave underdeveloped how practitioners act when multiple legitimate values remain in tension. This paper develops a contextual account of action guidance drawing on Raz's theory of exclusionary reasons, Tomasello's account of socially stratified intentionality, and a conception of engineering as participation in collaborative value chains derived from Porter. It argues that engineers confront value pluralism not by resolving conflicts through value ranking or optimization, but committing to a higher-order norm of collaborative viability, which functions as a constitutive condition of engineering collaboration rather than as a competing substantive value. Building on this insight, the paper introduces the “Portasello” model, a framework of how engineers organize, communicate, and reconcile values through the management of intra-agent and inter-agent value interfaces. The model shows how values acquire action guiding force within collaborative practice by being translated into workable courses of action through coordination across the value chain. Rather than treating engineering as the application or pursuit of pre-given values, the paper reconceptualizes engineering as a practice of interface management through which diverse values become actionable. The framework further develops a typology of normative failure modes and argues that knowledge of how to sustain collaboration under conditions of persistent value pluralism constitutes a core dimension of engineering expertise.

articles_hidden.title: Civic Architecture: A Statement of the Research Program
articles_hidden.authors: Robert M Ceresa
articles_hidden.abstract: Civic architecture is a design science of democratic life. It holds that democratic capacity is produced by institutions that convert participation into binding civic consequence through durable pathways, and that where those pathways are absent, participation erodes the capacity it is meant to build. This statement sets out the research program as it stands in November 2026: its account of hollowness and managerial professionalism; the two dimensions of one civic ontology; standing, office, and structural cognition; four design elements and the rules that combine them; repair, trust, and the outside order; a consent standard; the method and the evidence standard, applied first to the program's own case; and the questions that remain open. It replaces nothing in the 2025 deposits, names what has changed since them, and states what the program claims and what it does not.

articles_hidden.title: Two Varvaras: Was Semennikova the Oldest Documented Woman in Russian History?
articles_hidden.authors: Nikolay Zak
articles_hidden.abstract: Varvara Konstantinovna Semennikova (née Dyakonova; registered as Androsova at her 1944 marriage), a resident of the Anabar ulus of Yakutia, died on 9 March 2008. The birth year 1890 attributed to her in the 2000s would make her 117 years old at death. The attribution rests on an 1890 parish-register entry for a daughter of Konstantin Stefanovich Dyakonov of the 2nd Khatyga nasleg. This paper examines, for the first time, an alternative entry recording the birth on 28 September 1907 (O.S.) of Varvara, daughter of Konstantin Nikolaevich Dyakonov and Feodosia Petrovna of the 3rd Khatyga nasleg. Her earlier passport age, family recollections, the 1944 marriage certificate and a 1926–1927 household census card found by the author are compared. Of particular weight is a 2005 newspaper report that Varvara herself believed her second husband (born 1917) to be 11, not 27, years younger than she was. Had she been born in 1890, she would have been 53 at the 1944 wedding, while by her own reckoning she was about 37 and her husband about 27; an error of this size in adulthood is unlikely. As shown by Zak and Gibbs [15], deeming a claimed age unvalidated does not require proving the alternative hypothesis: it suffices to establish a plausible alternative scenario whose probability, given the available evidence, is incompatible with the degree of certainty required for validation. In the present case the evidence as a whole agrees substantially better with Varvara Semennikova's birth in 1907 than in 1890. At the same time, the identification of the claimant with the specific 1907 register entry remains unproven.

articles_hidden.title: The wealth of algorithms: generative AI, jobs and inequality in a global dynamic CGE model
articles_hidden.authors: David Radi
articles_hidden.abstract:
This paper models how generative artificial intelligence (AI) affects jobs, wages and inequality across the
world economy. Few doubt that it will change the economy; what nobody yet knows is how. Workers, firms
and governments want to know whose jobs and pay will change, who will capture the gains and which
countries will come out ahead, well before the evidence can tell them. This paper does not try to forecast that
future. Its contribution is a quantitative framework for understanding what drives AI’s economic effects, what
they depend on, and what follows for policy. We add AI to a global dynamic computable general equilibrium
(CGE) model that tracks production, trade, investment and employment year by year to 2040 in 23 regions. AI
does some tasks inside each occupation and makes workers more productive in others. When AI does a task, we
start from a 27% saving on its labour cost, the average Acemoglu (2025) draws from two workplace
experiments. We run a central scenario and 68 alternatives that vary how fast and how widely AI is adopted,
what it costs, how far it replaces rather than helps workers and how labour markets adjust.

How cheap and capable AI becomes, and how widely firms adopt it, decide the size of the gain: by 2040 world
GDP ends about 1% to 15% above a path without AI in our main scenarios (about 7% in the central case). It
reaches about 35% in an extreme case where AI becomes 30% a year more efficient (15 to 25% if AI keeps
improving but more slowly over time). Most of the gain goes to owners of capital in almost every scenario.
Who shares in it depends on who owns capital and on the extent to which AI replaces rather than helps
workers. In the central case capital’s share of world income rises by about 4 points, clerks’ real pay ends
roughly 13 to 22% below the no-AI path in the large economies, and within rich economies the Gini coefficient
of household income rises by about 2 to 3.5 points. If job losses last, the world gain against the no-AI baseline
in 2040 is 5.4% against 6.8%, and labour income falls further everywhere.

Based on these results, we then test several illustrative AI policies to see how they change the outcomes and
their distributional effects. Each does a different job: support for changing jobs mainly protects workers’ pay,
keeping AI cheap mainly protects output, and only sharing AI’s capital income narrows inequality noticeably.
The policies are illustrative and largely unfunded in the model, so their gains are likely inflated.

articles_hidden.title: What Makes Policy Fair? Evidence from U.S. Immigrant Integration Policy and Public Opinion
articles_hidden.authors: Taylor Trummel
articles_hidden.abstract: Immigration attitudes research is often centered on cultural and economic threat debates. However, this focus has missed an important mechanism that guides our everyday judgments: fairness. Very limited work has engaged with fairness and little has done so in the context of immigration. To address this, I construct a theoretically grounded method for measuring different dimensions of fairness. Using an original conjoint experiment, I test how varying state-level policy attributes such as eligibility requirements, intended beneficiaries, and assistance types influence perceptions of fairness. Agreement with different dimensions of fairness and policy support increase when policies include social services and exclusion criteria. I find limited evidence for xenophobic cultural threat and sociotropic economic threat in motivating policy support. The results offer a reevaluation of immigration attitude debates and demonstrate opportunities for broader use of a multidimensional measurement of fairness, as well as suggest a framework for democratically popular subnational immigrant integration policy design.

articles_hidden.title: Algorithmic Gatekeepers: Artificial Intelligence, Financial Intermediation, and the Disruption of China’s IPO Market
articles_hidden.authors: Jin Yang
articles_hidden.abstract: Initial public offerings in China pass through a dense chain of gatekeepers: sponsors, auditors, exchange reviewers, the securities regulator, and a retail-dominated investor base. Artificial intelligence now enters every link in that chain at once. It writes disclosures, verifies them, screens them for regulators, informs the investors who price them, and increasingly forms the core of the issuers that seek listing. This paper develops a theory of how AI disrupts an IPO market that operates as a state-orchestrated certification system. Drawing on signaling theory, the economics of certification, institutional theory, and the view of AI as an entrepreneurial actor, we argue that AI lowers the cost of producing information while leaving the cost of producing credible information intact. Seven propositions trace where the residual cost of credibility moves: toward an inverted U-shaped link between AI-generated disclosure and informativeness, a shift in intermediary rents from reputation to verification, an advantage for algorithmically legible issuers, an earlier inflection point in the effect of positive sentiment on IPO performance, attribution-dependent penalties for AI issuers, scope-contingent gains for intermediaries, and state pacing as a boundary condition. The theory explains why AI can raise market throughput and lower signal informativeness at the same time.

articles_hidden.title: Wealth Inequality and Public Support for Financial Stabilization in Economic Crises
articles_hidden.authors: Björn Bremer; Jeffrey Chwieroth; Andrew Walter
articles_hidden.abstract: Wealth provides private insurance, investment opportunities, and social status, shaping citizens' policy preferences. Citizens therefore have a stake in policies that stabilize financial markets and protect private wealth during economic crises. However, by disproportionately benefiting asset-rich households, such policies often reinforce wealth inequality. Using information treatment and conjoint survey experiments with more than 5,000 respondents in Australia and the UK in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, we examine how concerns about wealth inequality shape support for financial stabilization and compensation for disadvantaged households. We find that informing respondents about the regressive impact of financial stabilization on wealth inequality decreases support for such policies, but highlighting their effects on wealth disparities between ethnic groups has a much weaker effect. Furthermore, respondents prefer compensation targeted by economic disadvantage to compensation targeted by ethnicity: targeting poor households raises the probability of choosing a policy package by nearly 12 percentage points relative to no targeting, whereas targeting ethnic minorities lowers it by roughly 6 percentage points. Together, these findings underscore a key political economy challenge in addressing wealth concentration in contemporary multiethnic societies.

articles_hidden.title: Persistent Rating Disagreement, Measurement Robustness, and Information Reliability in Sustainable Finance: Implications for ESG Transparency and Evidence-Based Sustainability Governance in Chinese Listed Companies
articles_hidden.authors: Stephen Kamran; Farah Saman
articles_hidden.abstract: This study investigates cross-provider environmental, social, and governance (ESG) rating disagreement, temporal persistence, and measurement robustness, with particular emphasis on improving the reliability of sustainability information for ESG management and financial decision-making. Using an unbalanced panel of 1,323 firm-year observations representing 377 Chinese listed companies during 2019–2024, the study compares MSCI- and FTSE Russell-attributed assessments. Disagreement is operationalised through percentile-rank, standardised-score, and min-max transformations. The analysis integrates descriptive statistics, consecutive-year Spearman correlation, exploratory panel regressions, firm-clustered inference, multiple-testing adjustments, and reproducible computational verification. The mean absolute percentile-rank disagreement is 0.2493, indicating appreciable differences in relative corporate assessments. A consecutive-year Spearman correlation of approximately 0.493 demonstrates moderate temporal persistence. Alternative harmonisation procedures produce different inferential conclusions concerning exploratory financial associations, particularly firm size, highlighting the importance of measurement-sensitive interpretation. The study integrates disagreement magnitude, temporal persistence, and measurement robustness within a reproducible framework, extending ESG divergence research beyond isolated provider comparisons. Drawing on Institutional Theory and information asymmetry, it positions ESG disagreement as an information-governance challenge rather than direct evidence of inaccurate sustainability performance. The findings support systematic provider comparison, transparent rating harmonisation, and sensitivity assessment in ESG information management. Such practices offer a basis for improving evidence scrutiny and decision transparency, subject to limitations concerning secondary-data provenance, panel composition, and observational inference.

articles_hidden.title: LLM-Based Measurement of Latent Attributes in Trade Data
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew DiGiuseppe; Xuelong Fu; Michael E Flynn
articles_hidden.abstract: Trade data are available at a high level of disaggregation, allowing scholars to examine flows of highly specific goods. Yet the sheer number of goods classifications (5,000+) makes it difficult to analyze trade flows and tariff policy at a mid-level of aggregation beyond a few existing categorizations. Here, we outline a method that can scale---not merely classify---traded goods on researcher-defined dimensions that are orthogonal to existing classification schemes. We propose that the embedded knowledge in large language models (LLMs) can be used to conduct pairwise comparisons (PWCs) of Harmonized System (HS) product descriptions by determining their relative proximity to a specific concept. A Bayesian Bradley--Terry model then uses these PWCs to place individual items on a latent scale of interest. These estimates and their associated uncertainty can then be used for downstream descriptive or causal analysis.

articles_hidden.title: Towards a Scientific Theory of Vipassana Meditation: Integrating Buddhist Psychology into Contemporary Psychological Science
articles_hidden.authors: Lukas Neuwirth; Ajay Raghunath Nair
articles_hidden.abstract: Vipassana meditation in the tradition of S. N. Goenka proposes a detailed psychological model of how suffering is generated, maintained, and potentially reduced. Although meditation and mindfulness have received considerable scientific attention, the original effect pathways proposed within this tradition have rarely been translated into contemporary psychological terminology or systematically compared with established psychological mechanisms. This theoretical paper reconstructs the psychological model underlying S. N. Goenka’s Vipassana tradition and examines its potential correspondence with contemporary psychological science. Central propositions include that (1) psychological suffering is amplified through reaction patterns of craving and aversion; (2) repeated reactions to experiences strengthen conditioned dysfunctional patterns of responding (saṅkhāras); (3) equanimous observation is proposed to interrupt these maladaptive reaction patterns, allowing a natural process of permanent dissolution to unfold (purification); (4) bodily sensations provide an interface through which mental reactions can be modified; and (5) reduced ongoing mental activity may allow previously conditioned psychological material to surface and to become accessible. Research on memory accessibility, acceptance, interoception, and learning supports aspects of this account, without establishing that these processes jointly produce the proposed “purification.” We conceptualize purification as reduced maladaptive influence of stored psychological material, with (a) natural dissolution, (b) extinction learning and (c) memory reconsolidation as candidate mechanisms. Seven propositions guide empirical investigation of this pathway, distinguishing temporary relief from lasting psychological change. Testing these propositions could establish whether concentration and equanimous bodily observation provide trainable skills for accessing difficult psychological material and changing habitual responses, thereby supporting well-being and reducing suffering.

articles_hidden.title: An Analytical Framework for the Assessment of Employment Impacts of Energy Transition
articles_hidden.authors: Rudeena Jabar; Anjali Sharma; Haritha Songola
articles_hidden.abstract: The potential employment generation is an important co-benefit and policy motivation to pursue energy transition. Empirical evidence suggests that energy transition leads to net employment gains. However, the job estimates vary across studies due to methodological choices, underlying modelling assumptions and scope of analysis. In this study, we present a systematic review of the studies that have examined labor impacts of energy transition to understand the underlying mechanisms that impact employment estimates. Using the Context-Interventions-Mechanisms-Outcome framework, we selected 236 papers for the study. The paper identifies multiple factors that explain these variations: first, the type of assessment used in the study impacts the projected job numbers. Gross assessment (42% of studies in our sample) provide optimistic results without accounting for the potential job losses. Second, ambitious climate action scenarios in an economy leads to the increase in projected jobs. We find that 25% of studies are dependent on the scenario assumptions. Third, employment details such as employment factors, learning effects, job quality and skills determine the intensity of the job estimates. The review suggests that only 12% of the studies have included learning effects in their assessment and 15% have assessed the skill requirements for the manufacturing of renewables. Based on these limitations in the existing literature, we have developed an analytical framework that can serve as the benchmark for studying the labor impacts of energy transitions. The framework systematically identifies and highlights the importance of integrating different elements previously discussed in the labor assessment studies to avoid the over-estimation/underestimation of employment numbers.

articles_hidden.title: Shared Answers, Different Paths: Gender and University Plans among Japanese Adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: Yuko Nozaki
articles_hidden.abstract: Educational expectations are often compared by gender as if shared responses denoted shared goals. Using Japan’s Longitudinal Survey of Newborns in the 21st Century, I examine 10,227 adolescents who selected a university plan in grade 9, when the questionnaire offered no separate junior college option. I classify their grade 10–12 reports by whether a four-year university plan was maintained or which alternative was first named, and decompose the gender gap in four-year university entry at ages 19–20. Boys’ entry exceeded girls’ by 3.01 percentage points. The composition component rises from 0.88 points under a binary classification to 2.77 under three categories and 3.09 under five. Girls more often named junior college or college of technology; a majority of them later entered junior colleges. Without identifying when intentions formed, the results show how aggregating response categories can make gendered postsecondary pathways look like unequal realization of shared plans.

articles_hidden.title: Reconciling Diverging Meanings of Just Transitions in a Fragmented World
articles_hidden.authors: Rudeena Jabar; Arohi Patil; Anjali Sharma; Juhi Chatterjee
articles_hidden.abstract: Just transition, an integral part of climate action, has become increasingly popular in both academic discussions and global climate negotiations. In 2022, the Just Transition Work Programme (JTWP) was established with the aim of discussing pathways to just transition in a climate-constrained world. However, the negotiations at JTWP have been slow due to fundamental disagreements in the interpretation of just transition between the Global North and Global South countries. The just transition (JT) scholarship has paid limited attention to explain the reasons for the starkly different understandings of JT across countries. In this paper, we first review academic literature on JT frameworks to understand whether and how they discuss the tensions that emerge when applying JT theories in practice. As we find limited academic literature on this topic, we develop a conceptual framework that focuses on highlighting and understanding the tensions that emerge in operationalizing academic JT frameworks in the real world. In particular, we focus on explaining tensions across different types of justice, geographical scales, and time. We then apply this framework to analyze JTWP negotiation proceedings. Our findings suggest that the existing justice frameworks do not consider the interactions between different types of justice, geographies, and time scales. This often leads them to ignore the tensions that could arise and the trade-offs that are involved in achieving a comprehensive vision of justice for all parts of the world at the same time. Through our framework, we are able to explore these tensions and explain the slow progress on JTWP negotiations. In the end, we provide examples to illustrate strategies that could be used to highlight and potentially resolve these tensions and, in turn, contribute to globally just low-carbon energy transitions.

articles_hidden.title: Expanding Mortality Research:  The Demography of Bereavement
articles_hidden.authors: Emily Smith-Greenaway; Ashton M. Verdery
articles_hidden.abstract: The study of mortality is the oldest enterprise in demography. Despite centuries of advancements, mortality research has long expanded within a monolithic framework of death as an individual demographic outcome. Yet, in recent decades, social demographic research emphasizing family relationships and linked lives, matched with the development of computational and formal demographic kinship methods, has set the stage for new perspectives on mortality, which are coalescing into a new demography of bereavement. In this review, we argue this new subfield has expanded mortality research, and demography more generally, in notable ways. Specifically, the demography of bereavement has recalibrated our sense of the significance and scope of mortality conditions; aided the development of the concept of demographic memory; produced experiential perspectives of mortality regimes; facilitated understanding of the cumulative inequality in mortality conditions; and centered mortality as a cause, not merely consequence, of inequality. We identify future directions that could advance these conceptualizations further.

articles_hidden.title: Diverse Paths After First Birth: Maternal Employment Trajectories in Hungary, East Germany, and West Germany, 1991–2012
articles_hidden.authors: Lili Vargha; Antonino Polizzi; Anette Eva Fasang
articles_hidden.abstract: East Germany shares a socialist legacy of full-time maternal employment with Hungary and, since 1990, a family-policy framework with West Germany. Did these shared conditions lead to similar maternal employment pathways after first birth? Comparing these contexts requires following mothers longitudinally, capturing the diversity of their pathways, their employment intensity and stability, and separating them by subsequent childbearing, which can prolong interruptions and differs across contexts. Using panel data on first births in 1991–2012, we apply group-based multi-trajectory models and bias-adjusted regressions to six years of monthly employment, separately for mothers with one child and mothers with additional children. In both groups, Hungarian mothers were concentrated in one dominant pathway, whereas German mothers spread across several. Among one-child mothers, no or very late return became similarly uncommon across contexts by 2007–2012, but mothers returned through different pathways: late full-time in Hungary, part-time in West Germany, and mixed pathways in East Germany. Among mothers with additional children, no return within six years remained at two thirds in Hungary but fell to about one fifth in both German contexts, first in the East and then in the West. East-West differences in employment intensity persisted and were larger among mothers with additional children.

articles_hidden.title: Complete-Association Factorizations of Discrete Copulas: Existence, Tree Characterization, and Log-Linear Representations
articles_hidden.authors: Melissa Bora; Pablo A. Mitnik; Junchao Tang
articles_hidden.abstract: For multivariate categorical variables, the discrete-copula and log-linear approaches provide two different representations of dependence: the former uses probability distributions with discrete-uniform one-way margins, and the latter uses interaction parameters computed from full-table or marginal distributions. This article studies the exact division of the dependence represented by a positive discrete copula into factors that are themselves complete associations among disjoint groups of variables treated as composites. Although no nesting, tree, ordering, or binary structure is imposed in defining admissible factors, every rooted tree on the component variables generates a regular complete-association factorization: the map from the positive discrete-copula space to the product of the individual factor ranges is a smooth bijection with a smooth inverse, and the node factors are globally variation independent. Conversely, every regular complete-association factorization necessarily has this rooted-tree structure. The article also establishes several connections with log-linear analysis. Saturated full-table interactions and discrete copulas encode the same margin-free dependence information, while tree-induced marginal log-linear blocks provide complete, smooth, variation-independent coordinates for individual association factors. Such a factorwise representation cannot be obtained by directly partitioning saturated full-table interactions for a nontrivial tree. The tree factorization guarantees that complete-association factors can be manipulated independently, through recursive application of iterative proportional fitting. A regular parameterization permits direct implementation of such manipulations by substituting parameter blocks if and only if each block is a smooth, invertible transformation of the corresponding tree-induced marginal log-linear block. The article also shows that every multifurcating node admits an exact binary refinement without loss of dependence information, and that refinement, local rotation, and collapse provide smooth transformations between the factor values associated with different rooted trees. The article’s results support structured dependence models, sensitivity analysis, simulation, and counterfactual-based decompositions, including Shapley decompositions.

articles_hidden.title: Polyphemus in the Cave and the Absence of Public Persuasion: An Institutional Analysis of Status-Demographic Codes from Early Joseon to Colonial and Post-Colonial Surveillance Enclosures
articles_hidden.authors: Hyun-nam Im
articles_hidden.abstract: This study investigates a foundational void in the constitutional and legal history of the Korean peninsula: the structural non-existence of political persuasion. In comparative state formation, deliberative persuasion functioned not as moral benevolence, but as a formal transaction cost extorted by the material capacity of direct producers to execute systemic rupture—exemplified by Roman republican plebeian secessions. Across five centuries of the Joseon dynasty and its twentieth-century transformations, peninsular state power operated upon an inverse trajectory. The governed were never constituted as horizontal negotiating subjects possessing juridical standing; rather, they were regimentally quarantined within patriarchal units of production under centralized bureaucratic oversight. By examining the institutional continuity of status codes, colonial cadastral dispossession, the reception of Bismarckian-Meiji Pandectist jurisprudence in the 1958 Civil Code, and the permanent reproduction of extraordinary penal regimes, this monograph demonstrates that the post-colonial republic preserved and refined the coercive machinery of the inherited state apparatus. Rather than fulfilling an emancipated compact among co-legislating citizens, this historical development culminated in an unbroken bureaucratized enclosure. Perfected through the 1968 universal biometric registration system and managed by a credentialed technocratic caste, the contemporary state definitively fixed the direct producer where peninsular statecraft has always confined him: an administered asset, governed entirely without the procedural friction of persuasion.

articles_hidden.title: Human Capital Management: Principles, Functions, and Priorities in the Context of the Structural-Synergistic Paradigm / Менеджмент людського капіталу: принципи, функції та пріоритети у контексті структурно-синергетичної парадигми
articles_hidden.authors: Dmytro Melnychuk
articles_hidden.abstract: Peer-reviewed author’s accepted manuscript, accepted for publication on November 4, 2026, in Economics, Management and Administration (scheduled for Q4 2026).The article is devoted to the development of scientific and theoretical foundations and human capital management practice. The study is based on the author’s approach, according to which human capital in its traditional dimension – as an accumulated stock of knowledge, skills, abilities, and professional experience – is defined from the perspective of the educational and competency-based core belonging to a content-wise significantly broader polystructural complex. The latter, being human capital in its full sense, also includes other types of capitals, forming an emergent whole that has an investment nature, is capable of generating income, and contributes to improving the quality of life of employees and society as a whole through a set of economic and social effects. Under such a paradigm shift, along with the educational and competency-based component as a key subsystem, the architecture of the studied economic phenomenon is structurally and functionally complemented by health capital, social capital, and psychological capital, the nature of interaction between which is determined by the regularities of moderated mediation as a condition for the emergence of systemic synergy. The fundamental difference of the proposed theoretical and methodological framework lies in the fact that within the defined systemic framework, the concept of human capital acquires a holistic rather than fragmentary content, which, inter alia, should be reflected in managerial activity. The purpose of the article is to uncover the properties of human capital under its expanded interpretation, as well as to clarify the principles, functions, and priorities of management in the context of the structural-synergetic paradigm. The methodological basis of the study includes systemic, structural-functional, and synergetic approaches. The article analyzes the processes of formation, actualization, and externalization of human capital subsystems and determines their properties, which became the basis for updating scientific and theoretical foundations and formulating practical recommendations for human capital management as an integral part of management processes in the era of the knowledge economy.

articles_hidden.title: Convergence and continuity of time use for housework and childcare in German couples, 1991–2022
articles_hidden.authors: Florian Schulz
articles_hidden.abstract: This study provides a descriptive account of trends in the gendered division of unpaid labor in Germany over three decades, drawing on all four waves of the German Time Use Study (1991/1992, 2001/2002, 2012/2013, and 2022). Using a sample of coupled women and men aged 25–64, the analysis reports trends in total, core, and occasional housework time on weekdays and weekend days, assesses key determinants, decomposes changes into a part explained by compositional change and an unexplained part, and compares trends in West and East Germany. The results show substantial but incomplete gender convergence. Women’s total housework time on weekdays declined by more than one third, from 241 to 153 minutes per day. Men’s total housework time on weekdays declined slightly, from 100 to 92 minutes, because their time spent on occasional housework declined while their time spent on core housework increased. The gender ratio in core housework on weekdays fell from 6.89 to 2.49. Blinder-Oaxaca decompositions show that compositional change, mainly women’s rising employment, accounts for about one third of the decline in women’s housework time, whereas men’s increase in core housework remains almost entirely unexplained. The unexplained parts may reflect normative change but also factors not observed in the data. Between West and East Germany, differences in women’s housework time and in gender ratios largely disappeared, as both regions moved toward a common pattern. Among parents, childcare time increased by about 50 minutes per day for both mothers and fathers, and fathers’ weekday childcare time more than doubled.

articles_hidden.title: Forecasting Cohort Fertility with a Simple Neural Network
articles_hidden.authors: Paige Park
articles_hidden.abstract: Forecasting completed cohort fertility (CCF) helps resolve ambiguities in total fertility rate (TFR) trends, yet conventional cohort forecasting methods perform little better than a freeze-rate baseline (Bohk-Ewald et al., 2018). Inspired by deep learning advances in mortality forecasting, this paper tests whether an untuned ensemble of Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), named CCF-Net, can improve cohort fertility forecasts. Using data from the Human Fertility Database and the models and evaluation criteria of Bohk-Ewald et al. (2018), CCF-Net ranks first among established methods. On average across jump-off years 1985–2013, CCF-Net forecasts higher CCF than other methods; it appears to better capture rises in fertility among some cohorts born in the late 1970s and early 1980s. However, its accuracy varies considerably across jump-off years, and it falls behind other methods in 2006–2011. When trained on data through 2019, CCF-Net forecasts substantially and perhaps unrealistically lower CCF than all benchmarks, which raises doubts about whether its historical performance will continue.

articles_hidden.title: Recycling fabricated narratives about an early-career researcher is not a valid defence: a reply to Caruso et al.
articles_hidden.authors: Saul Newman
articles_hidden.abstract: Here, I respond to Caruso et al. regarding their recent paper defending the Sardinian blue zone. Despite the brevity of the work, the paper relies on an extensive set of straw-man arguments, falsehoods, and libels. These appear deployed as little more than a coping mechanism in the absence of arguments, and the errors and misrepresentations are tallied below. However, rather than restrict the reply to raising these issues, it seems appropriate to use this venue to highlight some of the far deeper problems with the blue zones concept as a scientific, social, and financial enterprise. That is, it seems worthwhile to address this paper on a few scientific failings first, and its many logical and ethical failures second.

articles_hidden.title: Building climate resilience in Australian homes and households
articles_hidden.authors: Michaela Lang; Subhadarsini Parida; Priya Rajagopalan; Ralph Horne; Lyrian Daniel; Megan Robinson
articles_hidden.abstract: This project defines climate-resilient housing in Australia, develops climate-ready housing guidelines (CRHG) outlining adaptation measures for a range of environmental threats, and establishes a framework for government and industry action to future-proof the nation’s homes. It is part one of an AHURI Inquiry into making Australia’s housing climate-resilient by 2050. Climate change is making heatwaves, bushfires, floods and storms more frequent and severe, and risks are expected to increase as global temperatures rise. Such events can damage or destroy homes and make them uncomfortable or unsafe. Many Australian homes are not designed for current and future climate conditions, and regulations to improve resilience are inadequate. This research provides guidelines for policy and practice to strengthen climate resilience in all homes and improve the community assets that help residents cope with climate change.

articles_hidden.title: Immigrants and their descendants as supporters of the populist right: Finding a coherent narrative
articles_hidden.authors: Gianni D'Amato; Camilla Bilò; Simon Mastrangelo; Leonie Mugglin; Didier Ruedin
articles_hidden.abstract: Observers are often surprised to find immigrants and their descendants who support the populist right with their exclusionary conception of the demos. This article explores the internal contestation of the demos and how immigrants and their descendants cope with boundaries and exclusion. We show how immigrants and their descendants construct coherent narratives through which they reconcile their political engagement with exclusionary conceptions of the demos. Drawing on interviews with party representatives and activists in the Swiss People’s Party (SVP/UDC), we outline their experience and reasoning. We compare these experiences to other representatives of the populist right and party representatives in the left-wing Social Democrats (SP/PS). This comparison shows that the left offers a readily accessible and widely shared narrative where immigrants and their descendants can feel at home. However, there are different internally coherent narratives through which immigrants and their descendants present their support for the populist right as coherent and non-contradictory. We conclude that narratives offer opportunities to better understand political participation in a world of changing cleavages, and that narratives are a central symbolic mechanism in the contestation over the demos.

articles_hidden.title: Incidental Perceptions Shape Strategies for Responding to Violence: Evidence from a Lab-in-the-field Experiment in Kenya
articles_hidden.authors: Aidan Milliff
articles_hidden.abstract: What shapes people's behavior during violence? Choices made in dangerous environments accumulate into a range of political outcomes, from refugee crises and mass riots to civilian resilience during conflict. I argue that decision-makers' perceptions of control and certainty influence preferences for dealing with violence, and that those perceptions can carry over from unrelated sources. Using a large lab-in-the-field experiment in Kenya where participants' perceptions of control and certainty were manipulated through a financially incentivized video game and non-violence-related information treatments, I show that participants primed to feel more ``in control'' are 4 percentage points per choice more likely to respond to locally-relevant violence scenarios by engaging threats (rather than avoiding them). Participants encouraged to feel more certainty are 12.6 percentage points per choice more likely to select conservative, less disruptive strategies (rather than drastic strategies like fighting or fleeing). This study contributes to research on civilian agency and strategic decision-making during violence by showing that manipulating perceptions changes strategy preferences even when people face identically-presented threats, and that perceptions formed in other domains can ``intrude'' on high-stakes decisions

articles_hidden.title: Complete-Association Factorizations of Discrete Copulas: Existence, Tree Characterization, and Log-Linear Representations
articles_hidden.authors: Melissa Bora; Pablo A. Mitnik; Junchao Tang
