articles_hidden.title: Legal interpretation and AI: From expert systems to argumentation and LLMs
articles_hidden.authors: Vaclav Janecek; Giovanni Sartor
articles_hidden.abstract: AI and law research has encountered legal interpretation in different ways, in the context of its evolving approaches and methodologies. Research on expert systems has focused  on  legal knowledge engineering, with the goal of ensuring that human-generated interpretations can be precisely transferred into knowledge bases, to be consistently applied. Research on argumentation has aimed at representing the structure of interpretive arguments, as well as their dialectical interactions, to assess the acceptability of interpretive claims within argumentation frameworks. Research on machine learning has focused on automated generation of interpretive suggestions and arguments, through general and specialized generative AI tools, now being increasingly deployed in legal practice.

articles_hidden.title: Computing The Incomputable? Artificial Intelligence and Entrepreneurial Decision Making Under Uncertainty
articles_hidden.authors: Miles Robin; Leo Will; M Pyad
articles_hidden.abstract: Artificial intelligence promises to reduce the uncertainty that surrounds entrepreneurial decisions by predicting demand, scanning environments, and evaluating strategic alternatives at negligible cost. We argue that this promise is conditional on the type of uncertainty a decision involves. Drawing on real options reasoning and research distinguishing risk from Knightian uncertainty, we theorize that AI reduces uncertainty that can be resolved through information but cannot resolve uncertainty that is revealed only through action. When decision makers fail to distinguish the two, AI produces uncertainty compression, a condition in which perceived uncertainty falls faster than actual uncertainty, leading entrepreneurs to abandon flexibility and commit prematurely to irreversible investments. We contrast two modes of AI use. In oracle mode, AI is used to resolve uncertainty and select a single course of action. In generator mode, AI is used to expand, stage, and monitor a portfolio of real options. We develop propositions specifying when each mode improves decisions and how entrepreneurial theorizing and competitive diffusion of AI condition these effects. The framework reframes AI not as a substitute for entrepreneurial judgment under uncertainty but as a technology that changes the economics of flexibility.

articles_hidden.title: ‘The more the merrier?’ Do earnings trajectories following fathers’ parenting leave uptake vary by contextual support?
articles_hidden.authors: INVEST Flagship; Anna Erika Hägglund; Satu Helske; Simon Chapman
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite policy reforms extending fathers’ parenting leave rights, many fathers still refrain from taking longer leaves. While fear for career disadvantages provides a prominent explanation for men’s limited use, empirical evidence on earnings consequences remains mixed. The extent to which leave uptake shapes fathers’ post-birth earnings trajectories could differ depending on how normalized leave-taking is within a given context. In this study, we ask whether potential negative implications decrease if leave entitlements targeted towards fathers expand and uptake becomes more widespread. We examine this question both at the national policy level and in the local workplace context. Empirically, we draw on Finnish register-based data for the period 2000–2020, and analyse hourly earnings among first-time fathers using stacked regression estimators. Our findings suggest that interruptions beyond the period earmarked to the father may be associated with lower earnings, if the policy and workplace context are less supportive; yet selection is also crucial.

articles_hidden.title: Meritocratic Ideals and Beliefs: Social Divides in Normative–Descriptive Alignment across Europe
articles_hidden.authors: Raphaël Piters
articles_hidden.abstract: The persistence of meritocratic beliefs despite enduring social inequalities raises a central question about the legitimation of inequality: why do people perceive social outcomes as deserved when opportunities are unequally distributed? One possible explanation is that individuals who endorse meritocratic principles are also more inclined to perceive existing outcomes as deserved, a form of normative--descriptive alignment consistent with just-world reasoning. Yet the strength, social distribution, and contextual variability of this association remain unclear. Using Round 9 of the European Social Survey, we analyse 33,811 respondents in 29 European countries through multilevel models distinguishing within- and between-country variation in normative support for meritocracy. We find a positive but modest average association, substantially smaller than differences linked to education, political orientation, and subjective economic circumstances. Crucially, alignment is socially and contextually differentiated. It is particularly strong among respondents experiencing comfortable economic circumstances, a pattern robust across alternative specifications and more consistent with position-justification interpretations than with stronger alignment among disadvantaged groups. Higher education is also associated with stronger alignment, despite lower overall levels of descriptive meritocratic belief. At the contextual level, alignment is stronger in countries with higher human development and GDP per capita, whereas income inequality shows no significant moderating association. Political orientation, meanwhile, strongly differentiates levels of descriptive belief but not the strength of alignment. These findings demonstrate that the social determinants of meritocratic beliefs cannot simply be inferred from those of normative--descriptive alignment. Understanding meritocratic legitimation therefore requires examining not only whether ideals correspond to perceived reality, but also the social positions and national contexts in which this correspondence is strongest.

articles_hidden.title: Model Praktik Eco Social Work dalam Perlindungan dan Pengelolaan Lingkungan Hidup di Indonesia: Sintesis Konseptual
articles_hidden.authors: Andri Biantara; Feri Setiadi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Environmental issues have social dimensions that affect livelihoods, health, community relations, access to resources, and the social functioning of individuals and groups. Environmental protection and management therefore require more than technical and administrative instruments; they also require approaches that assess social impacts, strengthen participation, protect vulnerable groups, and build community capacity.

This article develops a conceptual practice model of Eco Social Work to explain the contribution of social work to environmental protection and management in Indonesia. It uses a conceptual synthesis of literature on ecological social work, community development, participation, collaborative governance, and the practice domains addressed in the developing Eco Social Work book. The synthesis proposes a six-stage model: socio-ecological context, socio-ecological assessment, intervention planning, implementation and collaboration, monitoring-evaluation-learning, and socio-ecological outcomes and sustainability.

The model positions social workers as professionals who integrate social dimensions into environmental processes through planning, social impact assessment, environmental education, community empowerment, advocacy, mediation, and institutional strengthening. The proposed model remains a conceptual framework and requires empirical examination and refinement. Its contribution is to articulate a practice pathway connecting the mandate of social work with environmental governance while respecting the technical and legal authority of other professions.

articles_hidden.title: Constitutional Unilateralism and Federal Fragmentation in Somalia: Contested Constitutional Change, Intergovernmental Consent, and the 2024-2026 Amendments
articles_hidden.authors: Ismail H Warsame
articles_hidden.abstract:
Somalia's federal settlement rests on the 2012 Provisional Constitution, which deferred central questions concerning the allocation of powers and resources, the structure of the judiciary, the status of the capital, and the relationship between federal and state constitutions. The constitutional amendments adopted in March 2024 and March 2026 were presented by the federal government as the completion of a review that had run for more than a decade. They were opposed by significant political actors, by the administrations of Puntland and Jubaland, and later by the leadership of South West State. This article asks whether the resulting disputes share a common mechanism, described here as constitutional unilateralism: the alteration of constitutional terms, electoral rules, or intergovernmental arrangements without the participation or agreement reasonably required of the units whose authority or status is affected.
The article distinguishes three questions that are frequently merged: whether the required amendment procedure was followed, whether consultation and agreement obligations were satisfied, and what institutional consequences followed. It examines the record for Puntland, Jubaland, South West State, and Hirshabelle; the November 2026 confrontation between the Presidency and the Supreme Court over the judicial treatment of term extensions; and the implications for the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia and the wider security transition.
The evidence supports a narrower claim than a single causal story. Contested constitutional change did not create Somalia's political disputes, and in several cases it intersected with conflicts that were already under way. It nevertheless made cooperation harder where it overlapped with unresolved disputes over power, leadership, representation, and security, and it narrowed the space for negotiated settlement. The article concludes that the durability of Somalia's federal order depends less on the formal adoption of a text than on procedures capable of sustaining intergovernmental consent, and on an authenticated constitutional and electoral record that all parties accept as authoritative.

articles_hidden.title: Written as ‘he’: Colonial inheritance, constitutional language, and women’s representation in Anglophone Africa
articles_hidden.authors: Amartey Laryea
articles_hidden.abstract: Anglophone African constitutions retain masculine-default language inherited from British legal drafting, a register many of the region’s own languages cannot reproduce. Reform advocates and parts of the scholarship assume that gender-inclusive constitutional language supports women’s political representation. This article measures that assumption for the first time. A systematic census of gendered pronouns in the constitutions of Ghana, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, The Gambia, Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, and Rwanda reveals three drafting regimes: masculine-default texts (Nigeria 524:0 masculine-to-feminine tokens; Tanzania 373:0; Sierra Leone 439:1; Ghana 427:8), paired-inclusive texts (The Gambia, Uganda, Rwanda), and Kenya’s pronoun-avoidant 2010 text. Set against representation data for 2000–2023, textual inclusivity does not track women’s parliamentary presence. The weak cross-national association rests on Rwanda alone, while states with enforceable gender quotas average 36.8 per cent women against 9.0 per cent without. The masculine default emerges as a removable colonial inheritance that half the sample has already discarded. Constitutional text marks who a republic imagines holding office; allocation rules decide who takes the seats. Language reform is a dignitary and decolonial measure that complements structural provision and never substitutes for it.

articles_hidden.title: Tolerance for Inclusion: Scale Development, Psychometric Evaluation, and Initial Examination of Cross-Contextual Applicability
articles_hidden.authors: Takazumi Ono; Hiroko Costantini; Misato Nihei
articles_hidden.abstract: The inclusion of people with diverse circumstances and needs is an important goal of contemporary society and building such an inclusive society requires mutual tolerance among its members. This study aimed to develop a scale measuring individuals’ attitudes and behaviours based on the concept of tolerance for inclusion and to evaluate its psychometric properties. The study comprised three major steps involving four surveys. First, we developed the Individual-level Tolerance for Inclusion Scale (ITIS) based on a conceptualization in previous qualitative research. Second, we conducted three online surveys in Japan. Survey 1 (n = 165) was conducted to explore the factor structure of the newly developed scale. Survey 2 (n = 2,526) and Survey 3 (n = 428) were conducted to evaluate its construct validity, internal consistency, test–retest reliability, and standard error of measurement. Third, we conducted Survey 4 (n = 1,114) in Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States of America and examined the cross-cultural validity of the new scale and its concurrent validity with an existing measure of individual-level tolerance. The results of present study support the validity of the ITIS for assessing tolerance for inclusion and its reliabilities may also be acceptable. In addition, the findings provide initial support for the applicability of the concept of tolerance for inclusion in a combined sample from three English-speaking countries.

articles_hidden.title: Electoral Systems and Resistance to Democratic Backsliding
articles_hidden.authors: Sean Gailmard; Andrew T. Little; Carlo Prato
articles_hidden.abstract: We study how electoral institutions affect incentives for elected elites to resist democratic backsliding by a chief executive or party leader. Conventional wisdom suggests that party-centered systems, such as list PR with centralized candidate selection, should weaken co-partisan resistance by making legislators more vulnerable to the leader’s retaliation. Using a formal model, we show that this logic is incomplete: legislators do not solely respond to the electoral cost of resisting but also to the leader’s capacity to retaliate after successful resistance. In candidate-centered systems such as single-member districts with primaries, leaders may still be able to punish dissenters after removal. In party-centered systems, punishment is more severe if the leader survives but weaker if resistance succeeds, in which case the leader loses control over the party. So, party-centered systems produce stronger complementarities in the incentive to resist. We show that equilibrium resistance decreases with the effectiveness of punishment (highest under closed-list PR), but increases with its contingency on the leader’s own survival (highest under centralized candidate selection). As a result, party-centered institutions can generate more co-partisan resistance and offer stronger protection against backsliding.

articles_hidden.title: Corporate Governance, Audit Transparency, and Task Environment: An  Integrative Framework for Understanding Financial Outcomes in Chinese Public Firms
articles_hidden.authors: Andrea Ting
articles_hidden.abstract: This essay develops an integrative framework linking corporate governance, audit transparency, and the task environment to the financial outcomes of Chinese publicly listed firms. Drawing on agency theory, resource dependence, and real options reasoning, I argue that governance mechanisms and audit-related transparency are complements whose effectiveness is contingent on the munificence, dynamism, and complexity of the environment in which firms operate. Because China's listed firms combine concentrated and state-linked ownership, an evolving legal system, and politically shaped information incentives, the marginal value of governance and transparency differs systematically from that observed in Anglo-American settings. By synthesizing evidence from the accounting, finance, and management literatures, I advance seven propositions, including non-monotonic relations in which additional signals of quality or favorable external attention yield diminishing, and eventually negative, returns. Ultimately, the essay concludes with measurement guidance, identification challenges, and a concrete research agenda for scholars studying transparency and performance in transition economies.

articles_hidden.title: Medical Mesocosms of Cohort Differences in Spousal Abuse Victim Decisions in Sub-Saharan Africa.
articles_hidden.authors: patricia elungata
articles_hidden.abstract: Background: Contradictory evidence exists on whether medicine explicates social disparities in health perceptions. This study evaluates healthcare systems as mesocosms to understand social differences in spousal violence perceptions in sub-Saharan Africa, concretely, cohort differences in victim decisions in spousal violence (VDSV). Conceptual framework: Medical dominance theory criticizes medical power asymmetry, while socio-ecological theory illuminates social disparities in human behavior. This study investigates socio-behavioral patterns in medicine as parallels to spousal violence behaviors, analyzing how power asymmetry influences VDSV in sub-Saharan Africa. Methods: A cross-sectional study analyzed data from the latest Demographic and Health Surveys (2001–2024) across 31 countries, focusing on 193,232 women aged 15–49 years and their VDSV patterns: none, Discordant, and Other types. Unadjusted odds ratios (ORs) examined associations between VDSV patterns and birth cohorts (BCs) while adjusting for confounders. Interaction terms assessed the impact of neighborhood ethnic diversity, relationship power differences, and healthcare access. A two-level hierarchical multinomial logistic regression model analyzed VDSV variation, considering individual, cluster, and household-level confounders with random country effects. Spatial interpolation addressed geographical clustering. Analyses were performed using the McLogit package in R (Version 4.4.0). Results: Across BCs, a greater percentage change in predicted marginal probabilities was observed for Other type VDSV compared to Discordant VDSV. Overall, women with recent healthcare access had smaller percentage changes; those with a large relationship power difference, especially, showed the opposite trend. Notably, observed healthcare access effects persisted beyond socioeconomic disparities. Discussion: Higher VDSV amongst younger birth cohorts suggests lower SV-accepting attitudes. VDSV differences across healthcare access intimate anti-violence intervention exposure effects; relationship power differences play moderating roles. Persistent adjusted healthcare access effects suggest roles for narrowing socio-health inequalities in SSA. Conclusion: The study results advocate for macro-societal policies within healthcare that address social issues, particularly through theory-based approaches. Future research may evaluate the potential influence of healthcare funding cuts.

articles_hidden.title: Local Pachamama Beliefs and the Expansion of Cooperation among the Amazonian Kichwa
articles_hidden.authors: Connor Wood; Lexi Carver; Daniel Major-Smith; Benjamin Grant Purzycki
articles_hidden.abstract: Religious beliefs regarding deities’ punishment and knowledge breadth may facilitate the expansion of cooperative behaviour towards distant co-religionists. However, most previous research in this area has targeted so-called “moralistic” religious traditions (e.g., Christianity, Buddhism), and thus the extent to which these findings apply to other religious traditions is unclear. Here, we aimed to explore this question among the Kichwa, an indigenous group in Amazonian Ecuador, focusing on religious traditions regarding a pan-Quechua nature spirit, Pachamama. Our estimand of interest was the joint causal effect of beliefs about Pachamama’s punishment and omniscience on cooperation with distant Pachamama co-religionists, with cooperation assessed via two experimental games (the Random Allocation Game and Dictator Game). Across all models and sensitivity analyses to different causal assumptions regarding the structure of confounding, we found little evidence for a relationship — either positive or negative — between Pachamama beliefs and cooperation. Assuming a causal interpretation, these results suggest that, in this population, beliefs regarding local deities do not motivate cooperative behaviour towards distant co-religionists.

articles_hidden.title: Finnish Court-Ordered Foster Care  Placement Data (LASTU)
articles_hidden.authors: INVEST Flagship; Mikko Hertzig; Mika Pihlajamäki; Henri Salokangas
articles_hidden.abstract:
This paper describes the construction of LASTU, a new individual-level dataset
covering all Finnish court-ordered out-of-home placement decisions from 2000
to 2025 (n ≈ 14000). The dataset was built by digitising, pre-processing, and
structuring the free-text content of administrative court records, and linking the
resulting case-level variables to the INVEST Full Population administrative regis
ters. We document the data structure, the text-partitioning and variable-extraction
pipeline, and the multi-stage validation protocol. The pipeline follows a rules
based approach exploiting the highly consistent structure of Finnish court deci
sions to partition text into thematically defined segments before conducting ex
traction of variables . The resulting dataset enables causal analysis of placement
effects on children’s long-term educational, health, and labour market outcomes
as well descriptive evidence, and supports research on the determinants of court
decisions and regional variation in child welfare practice.

articles_hidden.title: The Cooperative Scope of Local Gods: Punishment, Omniscience, and Distant Cooperation among the Sihanaka of Madagascar
articles_hidden.authors: Anders Norge; Daniel Major-Smith; Benjamin Grant Purzycki
articles_hidden.abstract: Do supernatural beliefs in punishment and omniscience promote cooperation among distant unrelated individuals? Previous cross-cultural research – predominantly among “moralistic” religious traditions – suggests it might, although numerous open questions remain. Foremost among these are: “Do these results replicate among local religious traditions?” and “Is the relationship causal?” Here, we take a causally-informed approach to explore these questions among the Sihanaka from Madagascar. Our research question is: Do punishment and omniscience beliefs about a local god - zazavavindrano, an aquatic deity - promote cooperation towards co-religionists of this tradition? We assessed cooperation using Random Allocation and Dictator Games. Bayesian regression models were used, adjusting for plausible confounding factors, with g-computation methods to estimate our counterfactual causal effects of interest (i.e., the joint effect of zazavavindrano punishment and omniscience beliefs on cooperation with distant co-religionists). Across all games, conditions, and confounding assumptions, we found little evidence for a relationship between these zazavavindrano beliefs and cooperation. While zazavavindrano beliefs may not promote cooperation with unknown distant co-religionists, whether these beliefs facilitate cooperation in other domains – such as ecological management of wetlands, which is of greater concern to zazavavindrano than moral behaviour towards strangers – is an interesting open question for future research.

articles_hidden.title: Parental occupational configurations and changing occupational expectations: Evidence from PISA, 2000–2022
articles_hidden.authors: Tamilka Bonjeer
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on occupational expectations has largely examined mothers' and fathers' occupations separately, paying less attention to how they combine within families. Using six PISA waves (2000–2022) across 20 countries, this study examines changes in parental occupational configurations and adolescents' expectations of entering Technical STEM, Health, and Education. Four configurations are distinguished: Both-parent, Mother-only, Father-only, and Neither-parent. Descriptive analyses, a symmetric Kitagawa decomposition, and survey-weighted logistic regressions examine changes in configuration prevalence, expectations within configurations, and their associations over time. Results show declining Technical STEM expectations, increasing Health expectations, and modest changes in Education. Within-configuration changes accounted for most historical change in Technical STEM and Health, whereas compositional changes contributed more substantially in Education. Parental configurations remained associated with occupational expectations after socioeconomic and achievement adjustments, with limited evidence of systematic changes in these associations over time. The findings show that changing occupational expectations can coexist with continuing differences associated with parental occupational backgrounds.

articles_hidden.title: The Pricing-by-Design Matrix: Classifying Resort Activities by Experience Design and Pricing Status
articles_hidden.authors: Mohammed Ali Sharafuddin
articles_hidden.abstract: Maldivian resorts operate in an island setting characterised by lagoons, reefs and a tropical climate. Differentiation can arise from how each resort combines accommodation, facilities, service delivery and the experiences offered to guests. This paper proposes the Pricing-by-Design Matrix, an activity-level instrument for examining experience design and pricing within that service-product mix. The design dimension assesses evidence of five principles: theme, positive cues, removal of negative cues, memorabilia and sensory engagement. The pricing dimension records whether an activity carries an additional charge or is included in a specified reference plan. Crossing the design score with pricing status produces a two-by-two matrix that classifies each activity as a background activity, priced service, designed but given away, or experience offering. A coding protocol specifies how to record the evidence and calculate the Experience Design Completeness Index (EDCI). The pilot examines 17 activities identified in published descriptions and plan terms from two Maldivian resorts. It assessed theme, memorabilia and sensory engagement through a provisional three-principle text index. Positive cues and the removal of negative cues could not be assessed from the published material. Thirteen activities were provisionally classified as priced services and four as background activities. No activity met the text-index design threshold. At the all-inclusive resort, separate pricing was inferred for seven activities absent from the published inclusion list. The paper develops four propositions for further research. Further testing should assess coding reliability, threshold sensitivity and relationships with guest outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Response to matters raised on the MEECC
articles_hidden.authors: Lavanyaa V P; Tejal Kanitkar; T Jayaraman
articles_hidden.abstract: This reply responds to the notes by Schaeffer et al. (2026) and George and McJeon (2026) on the Model for Energy Equity and Climate Compatibility (MEECC), introduced in Kanitkar et al. (2026). It addresses the main conceptual issues; a more detailed response to methods- and coding-related questions is provided in the Supplementary Material (SM).

articles_hidden.title: Does Inflation Shape the Phillips Curve? Panel Evidence from the Next-11 Economies
articles_hidden.authors: Asma Ul Hosna mim; Zakia Sultana; Sumiya Akter Sua; Sabiqun Nahar Mily
articles_hidden.abstract: This study re-examines the Phillips Curve in the Next-11 (N-11) economies using annual panel data for 1991–2024. Because unemployment rate is non-stationary while inflation is stationary, the trade-off is specified in terms of the change in unemployment within an expectations-augmented framework. The model also includes lagged inflation, output growth, foreign direct investment, broad money growth and exchange rate depreciation. Panel diagnostics reveal strong cross-sectional dependence, heteroskedasticity and serial correlation, so we estimate dynamic fixed-effects models with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors. For the panel as a whole, a one percentage point rise in unemployment lowers inflation by about 2 percentage points in the same year and inflation is highly persistent. The trade off, however, differs sharply by inflation regime. In high inflation economies (Egypt, Iran, Nigeria and Turkey), the short run slope is −2.72 and inflation is driven by money growth. In low inflation economies the slope is only −0.75 and not robust. But inflation responds mainly to exchange rate movements in these countries. An interaction model confirms that the difference between the two groups is statistically significant at the 1% level. The result holds with year effects with unemployment in levels and the exclusion of the COVID-19 years. The findings suggest that the inflation–unemployment trade off is high where inflation is high and monetary discipline is weak. Policymakers in the two groups should therefore set different priorities.

articles_hidden.title: Energetic Affordances: Climate Change and Industrial Transformation
articles_hidden.authors: Benjamin H. Bradlow
articles_hidden.abstract: Climate change is reorganizing the material foundations of economic life. Why do some countries coordinate low-carbon industrial change while others stall? This article argues that the answer lies in “energetic affordances,” defined as what inherited energy infrastructures make politically possible. Drawing on interviews with 116 informants (including automotive executives, union officials, and policymakers), factory visits, and documentary analysis, I compare efforts to shift from manufacturing internal combustion to electric vehicles in Brazil and South Africa. Despite similar levels of development, democratic institutions, and integration into global automotive value chains, the cases diverged because their energy infrastructures made different responses politically viable. Brazil’s renewable grid and ethanol infrastructure afford multiple technologies that can credibly meet its emissions goals, enabling coalitional alignment among automakers, labor, and agricultural producers; institutional coordination across administrations; and sovereign partnerships with Chinese manufacturers. South Africa’s coal dependency forecloses those options: zero-sum conflicts fragment coalitions, paralyze institutions, and channel the country toward restrictive climate finance. Energetic affordances thus specify a cross-sectoral form of path dependence, in which the energy base shapes downstream industrial change, working through markets, coalitions, institutions, and geopolitics. The concept reorients the sociology of climate change toward classic questions of industrial transformation.

articles_hidden.title: Spirit-Master Beliefs and Cooperation Among the Buryat of Mongolia
articles_hidden.authors: Byambabaatar Ichinkhorloo; Daniel Major-Smith; Benjamin Grant Purzycki
articles_hidden.abstract: Previous cross-cultural research suggests that beliefs in punitive and omniscient deities may promote cooperation among distant co-religionists. However, much of this work is limited by: i) predominantly focusing on “moralistic” religious traditions (e.g., Christianity, Hinduism), rather the beliefs towards less moralistic “local” deities; and ii) not taking a formal causal inference approach, leaving potential causal interpretations unclear. We aimed to overcome these limitations here among the Buryat of eastern Mongolia. Our focal estimand was the joint causal effect of punishment and omniscience beliefs regarding local deities (spirit-masters) on cooperation towards distant co-religionists of the same local religious tradition. Cooperation was measured using two experimental games, the Random Allocation and Dictator Games, with distant co-religionists the target recipients. Overall, results were consistent with there being no relationship between spirit-master beliefs and cooperation towards distant co-religionists. Assuming a causal interpretation, these results suggest that – in this Inner Asian population – local punishment and omniscience beliefs regarding spirit-masters do not promote cooperation with distant co-religionists. However, as cooperation was overwhelmingly fair, there may have been insufficient variation in behaviour to detect meaningful differences by religious beliefs (or anything else).

articles_hidden.title: Climate Change as a Securitizing Factor  in the Kashmir Water Dispute
articles_hidden.authors: Malik Muhammad Umair Afzal
articles_hidden.abstract: Climate change as a securitizing factor in the Kashmir water dispute is examined here through the lens of the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) of 1960 has been characterised as one of the world's longest water-sharing treaties, as it has endured the wars in 1965, 1971 and 1999 between the two nations. The recent glacial melting in the Karakoram and western Himalaya that has intensified over the years and the decision by India to keep the treaty in abeyance after the attacks at Pahalgam on 23 April 2025 has added another underexamined dimension into the Kashmir water dispute: the securitization of climate change. This paper argues that glacial melt and hydrological uncertainty are strategically framed not as a technical or territorial problem or even as a socio-economic one, but as a 'securitization' of water as an 'existential security threat' according to the framework developed by the Copenhagen School (Buzan, Wæver, and de Wilde, 1998), and the hydro-hegemony approach developed by Zeitoun and Warner (2006). While the Kashmir issue was viewed as simply a territorial and/or ideological dispute, the paper examines how glacial retreat, glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs), and variability in monsoon patterns become incorporated in political and strategic discourse, providing justification for extraordinary measures including the suspension of the treaty and the unilateral release of water. Based on official documents, treaties, arbitration records, glaciological information from ICIMOD and peer-reviewed hydrological modelling, the paper provides a climate-integrated assessment of the post-2025 suspension and highlights that the scholarly discourse has been primarily centred on the episode as a political-strategic development, rather than one of environmental securitization involving ongoing processes. It concludes that integrating glacial and hydrological variability into the IWT's dispute-resolution framework would otherwise enhance the scope for renegotiation, arbitration and regional water diplomacy in a basin that is becoming more climate volatile in a manner that is likely to be articulated in terms of security as well as technicalities.

articles_hidden.title: The Cloud-Pattern Illusion: Falsifiability, Transferability, and the Market for Discretionary Trading Education
articles_hidden.authors: Bahram Rakhshani Pourfard
articles_hidden.abstract:
Traders who ask for a method that works do not receive, in the usual sense, a method. They receive a repertoire: a chart-reading practice that is described only by example, a lexicon of pattern names, and a repertoire of reasons why any given application of the pattern did not work. This paper argues that that repertoire is not a theory of markets. A theory must state conditions under which it is wrong and must show that its competence is stable across a residue of cases rather than undefeated only by its own redescription. Discretionary pattern trading fails both requirements. The pattern's content is indexed to the trader's discretion: the same configuration is readable as a valid signal, a transitional form, or a counter-example depending on what happened next, while the method's defence proceeds by attributing failure to the trader's application rather than the method's falsity. The paper shows that a single empirical success cannot absorb the failures implied by that asymmetry because the repertoire's asymmetry is systematic. The contribution is conceptual: to distinguish a pattern's descriptive appeal and the trader's experienced competence from the informational and institutional conclusions that a market for trading education draws from them, and in a companion paper to show how the translation of that competence into a disability claim functions as an institutional mechanism of attribution shifting.

AI assistance disclosure: The author used AI tools for translation from Persian and copy-editing. The ideas, analysis, data and conclusions are the author's own. The author reviewed the full text, verified every cited source, and takes full responsibility for the content.

articles_hidden.title: The Geometry and Dynamics of Power II : Interacting Political Path Integrals: Collective Dynamics and Probabilistic Futures
articles_hidden.authors: Caesar Edward
articles_hidden.abstract:
This study develops a mathematical framework for interactions among alternative political trajectories represented as an evolving ensemble of weighted stochastic paths. The model combines pairwise attractive–repulsive forces, replicator-type weight dynamics driven by a mean-field effective action, absorption, and statistical elimination. The effective action approximates the Onsager–Machlup path measure; it is not the exact likelihood of the coupled system.
Simulations of Ethiopia, Kenya, Rwanda, South Sudan, Tanzania, and Uganda over ten years show strong concentration of path weights: effective path counts approach one and path entropy approaches zero. Jamming diagnostics show a strong but transient early signal. Its decline is driven primarily by loss of path density through absorption and elimination, not by demonstrated recovery of collective mobility.
At the reference interaction parameters, the leading terminal-state share shifts by at most about 0.06. The pooled difference is detectable at 1,500 replications per country (p = 2 × 10⁻⁵), but not reliably in blocks of 300. Interactions nevertheless alter path-loss mechanisms, while substantially stronger coupling or longer interaction ranges can change terminal distributions. A 2016-calibrated historical hindcast matches the pre-registered outcome classification for five of six countries, missing Tanzania. The interacting and non-interacting models obtain comparable hindcast scores, so this result does not establish an advantage from path interaction.

articles_hidden.title: La monetización de la intimidad: juventud, plataformas y economía sexual en Onlyfans
articles_hidden.authors: Ignacio Ceinos Fernández; Camila Gonzalez Veleiro
articles_hidden.abstract:
Presentado como la mayor investigación realizada en España hasta la fecha sobre OnlyFans, este estudio impulsado por la Fundación Child Heroes y financiado por el Ministerio de Igualdad, examina la plataforma no como un entorno digital cerrado, sino como la superficie visible de un complejo macro-ecosistema de explotación y mercantilización articulado por el capitalismo de plataformas. La investigación profundiza en cómo este modelo instrumentaliza redes sociales de acceso masivo no concebidas originalmente para el contenido adulto (Instagram, TikTok, X, Reddit, Telegram, Youtube), aprovechando algoritmos diseñados para premiar la hipersexualización y maximizar la retención de audiencia para captar tráfico y normalizar su consumo. Asimismo, se cartografía el entramado comercial emergente de agencias de representación, gestores de cuentas y «gurús» digitales que reproducen dinámicas tradicionales de intermediación y extracción de rentas bajo un opaco modelo de negocio.

El informe sitúa estos mecanismos en la confluencia entre la precariedad socioeconómica estructural que atraviesa a las personas jóvenes y la penetración de las narrativas del femineoliberalismo, las cuales resignifican la autoexplotación y la cosificación como formas de libertad, autonomía y emprendimiento individual. Por último, se contextualiza el auge de este mercado dentro de una cultura sexual fuertemente pornificada y permeable a los discursos misóginos de la manosfera. Con todo ello, el estudio de Child Heroes evidencia que OnlyFans opera como un engranaje donde la captura algorítmica de la intimidad y la mercantilización del cuerpo terminan legitimándose socialmente como falsa agencia económica.

articles_hidden.title: La comprensión del mundo desde una modernidad incierta:  Sociología de la Incertidumbre y el Riesgo existencial
articles_hidden.authors: Ignacio Ceinos Fernández
articles_hidden.abstract: This research paper analyzes, from the perspective of contemporary sociology, the causes and consequences of the rise in risk and existential uncertainty in advanced modern societies. Through a literature review based on key theorists such as Ulrich Beck, Anthony Giddens, Zygmunt Bauman, and Richard Sennett, existential uncertainty is conceptualized as a loss of control and a lack of certainty regarding one's own biographical trajectory and traditional support institutions. The study argues that the shift from external to manufactured risk, the processes of individualization and reflexivity, the social acceleration driven by consumerism, and global interdependence have created a paradox: the relentless pursuit of technoscientific safety and control ultimately exacerbates subjective insecurity and "liquid fear". Furthermore, it examines the impact of this phenomenon across four critical dimensions of everyday life: the fragilization of romantic bonds, the corrosion of character within flexible work environments, vulnerability in personal identity formation, and the progressive erosion of institutional trust. The paper concludes that late modernity places individuals in a state of continuous negotiation with instability, highlighting the need for interdisciplinary approaches combining sociology and psychology to mitigate the disruptive effects of existential risk.

articles_hidden.title: Identifying numbers in the archaeological record
articles_hidden.authors: Karenleigh A. Overmann
articles_hidden.abstract: Numbers are one of the longest-lived cultural systems the world has ever known, but we still do not know how old numbers might be, or where and why they might have first emerged or in what form. Contemporary number systems have implications for examining and interpreting the archaeological record for signs of pre-Historic numeracy. To define what we should be looking for in the archaeological record and how we might recognise numbers in markings on pre-Historic artefacts, current assumptions, evidence, methods, and issues are reviewed, and recommendations are offered for incorporating interdisciplinary data and insights into archaeological investigations and interpretations.

articles_hidden.title: Multi-Cohort  Behavioral  Telemetry  and Longitudinal  Attrition  Metrics  Across Gated LMS and Open-Access Streaming Environments (2014–2025)
articles_hidden.authors: Aimar Rollán-González
articles_hidden.abstract: This data descriptor documents a unified collection of four longitudinal datasets capturing user interaction telemetry, retention dynamics, and attrition boundaries across self-paced digital mind-body interventions (relaxation, mindfulness, physical yoga, and yoga philosophy) recorded between May 2014 and December 2025. Telemetry was extracted from two parallel technological architectures: a gated, structured Learning Management System (LMS, Udemy) and an ungated, algorithmically driven video streaming environment (YouTube). Collectively, the repository comprises 1,787 anonymized individual student progression logs in the LMS environment, aggregated country-level demographic distributions across up to 52 territories, granular video-level retention and sequential playlist drop-off metrics across 107 instructional modules, and multi-year annual view timelines. The data architecture is specifically structured to support survival analysis (e.g., Kaplan-Meier estimation), activation gap modeling, gaming/speeder detection, and cross-platform attrition comparisons. All tabular files strictly enforce Tidy Data principles, include automated schema validation  via  Frictionless  Data  specifications  (datapackage.json)  alongside  semantic  manifests  (ai-manifest.jsonld), and are publicly released at Zenodo under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license.

articles_hidden.title: A Transdisciplinary Research Agenda for the Sharing Economy in BRICS: Co-producing platform knowledge with workers, users, communities, and public institutions
articles_hidden.authors: Carson Duan
articles_hidden.abstract:
This paper develops a transdisciplinary agenda for BRICS sharing-economy scholarship. It
asks how bibliometric mapping can be connected to knowledge co-produced with workers,
users, communities, firms and public institutions. The evidence is a Web of Science corpus of
443 records, mapped with VOSviewer, together with the earlier bibliometric work of Duan and
Sandhu (2023). Three observations shape the agenda. First, the maps show a field with
economic, sustainability, tourism and digital concerns, and each BRICS country is tied to a
different set of topics: environmental and business terms for China, consumer adoption for
Brazil and India, and tourism and ride-hailing for South Africa. Second, formal co-authorship
and keyword ties cannot stand in for community participation. Third, the five BRICS countries
fall into five separate clusters in the country coupling map, so comparison cannot assume a
shared body of knowledge. The paper therefore treats maps as prompts for choosing questions
and stakeholders, and it proposes a staged process for validating constructs and outcomes with
affected groups. A next phase should give local participants a defined role in research
governance and interpretation.
Keywords: sharing economy, BRICS, bibliometrics, interdisciplinary research,
transdisciplinary research, sustainability

articles_hidden.title: A Multidisciplinary Account of the Sharing Economy in BRICS Countries: Multiple disciplinary perspectives on platforms, markets, society, and sustainability
articles_hidden.authors: Carson Duan
articles_hidden.abstract:
This study treats the BRICS sharing economy as a multidisciplinary research problem. Platform markets in Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa have to be understood through economics, management, information systems, public policy, labour research and sustainability science. The evidence is a Web of Science corpus of 443 records, mapped with VOSviewer. Three conclusions follow. First, the topic has several disciplinary homes: business and management, environmental sciences, sustainability, tourism and transport sources all carry weight in the co-citation and source-coupling maps. Second, closeness in a network shows shared references or shared terms and does not show integrated theory. Third, country comparison needs attention to institutional and sectoral settings, because the international co-authorship network is centred on China and the USA, with the other BRICS members in smaller roles. The paper proposes a multidisciplinary evidence matrix that links concepts, methods, settings and outcomes, and suggests testing it against country-level platform cases.
Keywords: sharing economy, BRICS, bibliometrics, interdisciplinary research, transdisciplinary research, sustainability

articles_hidden.title: Towards an Age of Transdisciplinary Research: An Inaugural Statement for the International Journal of Disciplinary Studies
articles_hidden.authors: Carson Duan
articles_hidden.abstract: The International Journal of Disciplinary Studies is launched with an enduring task: to support rigorous inquiry into questions that cross the boundaries through which knowledge is commonly organized. Its transdisciplinary orientation does not promise a universal method or a final synthesis of different ways of knowing. It asks for deliberate engagement, honest accounting of difference, and careful explanation of how a study’s parts contribute to its whole. These standards are demanding because the problems at stake are demanding, and because the authority of scholarship depends on the quality of the work rather than the breadth of its claims.

articles_hidden.title: A Lacanian Interpretation of the Authoritarian Personality
articles_hidden.authors: Geoff M Boucher
articles_hidden.abstract: In this chapter, I present a Zizekian interpretation of the authoritarian personality that I think provides an intellectually satisfying, sociologically plausible and politically effective alternative to the classical theory.  Although Zizek is in general highly critical of Adorno, in his critique of the category of “totalitarianism,” he develops a theory of perverse political subjectivity that is effectively coextensive with the concept of the sado-masochistic character. However, Zizek’s concept of totalitarian subjectivity foregrounds the role of transgressive fantasy in supporting identification with the leader figure in a way that the classical theory does not. Because the Zizekian concept of perversion reframes it in terms of the disavowal of transgressive desires constructed in fantasy scenarios, rather than the denial of castration, it is alert to the political implications of rightwing authoritarian conspiracy theories and dystopian speculations. Furthermore, by reframing the basis for the authoritarian personality, not as the violently erotic expression of a sado-masochistic character, but as the eroticised violence resulting from a perverse form of subjective structuration, Zizek develops a psychodynamic model of contemporary authoritarianism. Central to this mechanism is the Lacanian understanding that the return of the repressed causes anxiety because of the transgressive nature of the political desire. It is this which leads to the characteristic “deterioration” of ego identity seen in cases of authoritarian meltdown. Finally, Zizek’s insight that the root of totalitarian subjectivity is a kind of self-instrumentalisation, designed to force absolute authority to become manifest, clarifies the logic of pre-emptive violence motivating authoritarian personalities.

articles_hidden.title: Separating Campaign-Level Threat from Incident-Level Attribution: A Bayesian Framework for Assessing Russian Hybrid Operations in Europe
articles_hidden.authors: Johan G.L. Verheyden
articles_hidden.abstract: European debate about Russian “hybrid war” tends to collapse three different questions into one: whether Russia is conducting hostile activity below the threshold of armed conflict, whether that activity forms a centrally coordinated campaign, and whether a given incident was directed by the Russian state. This article develops and applies a Bayesian framework that keeps these questions apart. At the incident level, six exhaustive hypotheses distinguish Russian state operations, state-sponsored proxies, autonomous pro-Russian actors, other states, non-hostile causes, and non-incidents; evidence enters through explicit likelihoods with dependence weights, and uncertainty in those likelihoods is propagated by simulation. At the campaign level, eight evidence blocks are weighed against three hypotheses: coordinated campaign, fragmented activity, and over-attribution. Applied to five cases spanning the evidentiary spectrum—the Wagner-tasked Leyton arson, Nord Stream, the Eagle S cable damage, the December 2025 Polish grid attack, and the November 2025 Dutch drone sightings—the model yields posterior probabilities of state direction ranging from below 0.05 to above 0.99. At the campaign level, the probability of sustained Russian activity exceeds 0.97 under every prior and dependence assumption tested, whereas the probability of central coordination ranges from 0.56 to 0.87 and is driven chiefly by assumptions about source dependence. The framework shows which conclusions are robust, which are assumption-dependent, and which evidence would most reduce uncertainty. A census of all 255 incidents in a recent open-source dataset, coded against a tiered evidentiary standard, shows that a Russian link is established for 41% of covert incidents and state direction for 24%, that none of 28 drone sightings is established, and that roughly one in five recorded incidents is overt or lawful state activity. The findings support graduated public attribution and investment in forensic and financial evidence over the accumulation of incident counts.

articles_hidden.title: Coastal Flooding Resilience in Sitio Kagang and Sitio Tapusok of Barangay Utod: Integrating Local Worldviews and Futures Thinking for Adaptive Management
articles_hidden.authors: Marloudiza McMillan; Jedess Miladel Salomon; Ma. Kresna Mansueto; Anna Rossini Parcero; Mohaliden Mohammad; Ulysses Nolan Paredes; Erick Glenn Juanich
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examines how sustainability worldviews shape residents' understanding of coastal flooding and their preferred management responses in Sitio Kagang and Sitio Tapusok, Barangay Utod, Baybay City, Philippines. Using a convergent mixed-methods design, we surveyed 99 coastal residents (87.6% of households), conducted 8 focus group discussions with residents using causal mapping, and consulted 9 expert key informants through individual interviews and a focus group discussion with environmental scientists. Survey responses classified 90 residents (90.9%) into three worldview orientations: hybrid (n = 50), primary ecocentric (n = 27), and primary anthropocentric (n = 13). Residents across all groups agreed that poor waste management (M = 4.60), upland deforestation (M = 4.58), and climate change (M = 4.51) drive flooding, with no significant group differences. Groups differed, however, on whether inadequate drainage (p = .014) or mangrove destruction (p = .042) is the primary cause. Support for stronger seawalls (M = 4.58), upstream reforestation (M = 4.41), mangrove restoration (M = 4.37), and combined engineered and ecosystem solutions (M = 4.10) did not differ by worldview. The sharpest divide concerned knowledge: anthropocentric residents rejected the idea that local knowledge is as valuable as scientific knowledge (M = 1.85), while hybrid and ecocentric residents endorsed it (M = 4.06 and 4.30; p < .001). Of three management scenarios, residents rated integrated adaptive management highest (M = 4.56; 89.9% agreeing), consistent with scenario discussions and expert interviews favoring a combination of structural protection, ecosystem restoration, and participatory governance. The findings suggest that worldview diversity need not block agreement on flood measures, but that resilience planning in these communities must also address whose knowledge counts in decision-making.

articles_hidden.title: Occupational mobility and developments of inequality along the life course: The German case
articles_hidden.authors: Steffen Hillmert
articles_hidden.abstract: On the basis of inter-cohort comparisons, this paper describes patterns of intra-generational occupational mobility in Germany and their long-term trends since World War II. It also presents conceptual links between individual mobility and developments of inequality along the life course, with a special focus on the question to what extent employment careers are characterised by specific forms of cumulative advantage and disadvantage. Finally, it is asked how intra-generational developments are related to inter-generational social mobility. The paper also discusses how mobility patterns can be linked to specific institutions which – together with labour market conditions – are crucial determinants of the development of inequality within a cohort. In its empirical part, the paper presents evidence from cohort-specific analyses based on life-course data from a broad range of West German birth cohorts.

articles_hidden.title: From Catastrophe to Legislation: The Payatas Dumpsite and the Transition to Ecological Solid Waste Management
articles_hidden.authors: Marloudiza McMillan; Erick Glenn Juanich; Ma. Kresna Mansueto; Anna Rossini Parcero; Maria Theresa Valderama
articles_hidden.abstract:
The 2000 Payatas landfill collapse in Quezon City, Philippines in which hundreds of people were crushed by an avalanche of trash after a landslide at a landfill created by illegal trash disposal was a critical destabilizing event that changed the solid waste governance regime for the Philippines. It led to the passing of Republic Act 9003 (Ecological Solid Waste Management Act). Twenty plus years have passed since this event and while there has been progress towards ecological solid waste management it is still incomplete. Progress occurred at the National Level through legislation, however, local governments continue to struggle implementing the law due to ongoing practices of open dumping, and continued marginalization of community based actors.
This study examines the Payatas transition as a case of sustainability in the Philippines utilizing four theories from transition management literature: (1) governance principles of diversity, dynamics & complexity; (2) The Transition Management Cycle that includes arena-building, visioning, experimentation & monitoring; (3) The X-Curve Framework developed by Hebinck et al. (2022), analyzing the case along the paths of Breakdown/Buildup and evaluating the composite regime strength score for each pathway; and (4) Evaluating government, market & community coordinating mechanisms. Results indicate persistent deficits in co-production among stakeholders, long-standing capacity shortfalls in funding and technical capabilities on the part of LGUs, low utilization of the knowledge and skills provided by informal waste sector workers, and lack of formally established multi-stakeholder transition arenas. Based upon a SWOT Analysis of the Payatas Community, four transitional action plans are suggested: Formalize community enterprises; Establish a community health, housing & human capital program; Develop community-led Zero-Waste Hubs with a digital monitoring system and integrated digital markets platform; create a community political voice/governance platform.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Bürgergeld: Who Can Afford to Say No? Guaranteed Minimum Income, the Refusal of Work, and Control over One's Time
articles_hidden.authors: Klaus-Uwe Gerhardt
articles_hidden.abstract:
Germany’s July 2026 welfare reform strengthened the priority of job placement and the use of benefit sanctions, reinforcing the disciplinary role of means-tested income support. This paper examines whether a guaranteed min-imum income (GMI), independent of work-availability requirements, could weaken these pressures and strengthen workers’ capacity to resist unfavorable employment conditions.
Drawing on Italian operaismo, the paper approaches wage labor and social protection as contested relations of power. Its central premise is that economic dependence and workplace domination can generate resistance and that collective countervailing power can emerge even under adverse conditions.
The analysis distinguishes individual autonomy, bargaining power, and collective organization as related but dis-tinct dimensions of economic security. Evidence from recent cash-transfer experiments is examined alongside the institutional alternative of an adequate, accessible minimum-income scheme with limited work requirements. The findings suggest that material security can expand individual choices, but neither improved working conditions nor collective power follows automatically.
A guaranteed minimum income cannot replace collective struggle. It may, however, change the material conditions under which workers resist, organize, and challenge existing power relations.

articles_hidden.title: Pakistan Is Not Poor, It Is Poorly Managed: An Empirical Investigation of Energy, Water, and Demographics in Pakistan
articles_hidden.authors: Anam Sajjad
articles_hidden.abstract:
Context: Developing economies frequently attribute macroeconomic instability and infrastructure deficits to natural resource scarcity. This study evaluates that claim in Pakistan by comparing physical resource endowments with actual developmental outcomes across three core sectors: energy, water, and human capital.

Interdisciplinary Approach: We combine political economy frameworks—specifically institutional quality, contractual lock-in, and common-pool resources—with practical software and data engineering perspectives, including automated metering, telemetry, and open digital infrastructure. This allows us to pinpoint the governance bottlenecks that prevent effective resource utilization.

Empirical Findings: In the energy sector, although the Thar coalfield holds 175.5 billion tonnes of in-situ lignite, commercially proven measured deposits stand at only 2.70 billion tonnes (with 1.57 billion tonnes mineable in Block II). Meanwhile, rigid take-or-pay sovereign contracts have pushed annual capacity payments past Rs 2.18 trillion, driving total energy circular debt to Rs 5.286 trillion (including Rs 1.835 trillion in power liabilities that breached IMF targets by Rs 221 billion). In the water sector, the 16.2 million hectare Indus Basin Irrigation System delivers over 90% of national food production but maintains live reservoir storage of merely 13.168 million acre-feet (MAF). This represents only a 30-day carryover buffer—compared to 120–220 days in India and 1,000 days in Egypt—worsened by 64% canal conveyance losses and widespread groundwater overdraft (affecting 50.2% of irrigated land). Demographically, the 2023 Digital Census records 241.49 million citizens with 67% under age 30 (160.11 million youth). However, sovereign debt servicing absorbs 81% of net federal tax revenues, heavily crowding out education and public health. Simultaneously, promising IT exports ($4.60 billion in FY2026) face serious infrastructure hurdles, including internet throttling, payment gateway barriers, and unstable power grids.

Policy Model: We formulate a practical, quad-pillar governance model: (1) centralized public project execution dashboards, (2) independent forensic audits of sovereign power generation contracts, (3) real-time smart-meter telemetry for power feeders and canal headworks, and (4) regulatory facilitation for digital service exporters. We conclude that institutional transparency and verifiable data accountability are the essential preconditions for sustainable economic stability in Pakistan.

articles_hidden.title: The Degrees of Freedom Principle of Human Economic Behavior:  From Dissipative Structures to State Spaces
articles_hidden.authors: Qilin Guo
articles_hidden.abstract: For extended periods, the application of entropy theory in economics has been impeded by theoretical bottlenecks such as conceptual generalization, ill-defined states, and the scarcity of rigorous quantitative modeling, frequently casting doubt on its logical isomorphism with thermodynamics and statistical mechanics. To resolve these challenges, this paper formalizes the state space of economic systems from a statistical mechanical perspective and develops a series of entropy models—including Economic Entropy and Consumption Entropy—thereby furnishing mathematical tools for researching the Degrees of Freedom Principle (DFP). The DFP, proposed herein as a foundational postulate for social systems, posits that human agents possess an inherent propensity to expand their behavioral degrees of freedom. Building upon this foundation, this paper establishes a theoretical linkage between utility and negative entropy, investigates the generative mechanisms of human behavioral complexity, and uncovers the intrinsic link between micro-agent behavior and macro-social evolution. Thus, from the evolutionary perspective of open dissipative systems subject to thermodynamic constraints, we construct an entropy dynamics framework for economic behavior. This framework offers a unified analysis of individual actions, resource allocation, and economic state space dynamics, thereby mitigating economic theory's exclusive reliance on subjective psychological preference assumptions and providing a novel theoretical bridge connecting micro-agent agency with macro-system complexity.

articles_hidden.title: Seeds of Change: Black women’s organising, Rosa Parks and the gendered memory of the Montgomery Bus Boycott, 1946–1956
articles_hidden.authors: Olawumi Helen Olalowo
articles_hidden.abstract: The Montgomery Bus Boycott of 1955 to 1956 is remembered as a protest that a single woman’s refusal set in motion. This article argues that the boycott is better understood as the culmination of a decade of organised political work by Black women in Montgomery, and that the compression of that work into the story of one seated woman was itself a gendered process with identifiable causes. Drawing on the memoir of Jo Ann Gibson Robinson, the testimony of boycott participants, the litigation record of Browder v. Gayle and the scholarship on Black women’s activism, the article reconstructs three arenas in which women made the protest possible. The first is the Women’s Political Council, founded in 1946, which proposed a bus boycott eighteen months before Rosa Parks was arrested. The second is the fundraising, catering, driving and walking that sustained a 381-day withdrawal of custom. The third is the federal suit brought by four Black women whose testimony, rather than Parks’s arrest, ended bus segregation in Alabama. The article then asks why the ministerial leadership of the Montgomery Improvement Association and later commemorative practice preserved Parks as a symbol while displacing the organisation around her.

articles_hidden.title: The NGO-ization of Women’s Empowerment in Pakistan: Impacts, Challenges, and the Politics of Inclusion
articles_hidden.authors: Rayan Ehsan
articles_hidden.abstract:
Women’s empowerment has been a key development priority for decades, but Pakistan, which
ranks last out of the 148 countries included in the Global Gender Gap Report 2025, remains
among the world’s most gender unequal societies. This paper argues that the NGO-ization of
women’s empowerment, the shifting of rights-based work from the state to donor-funded NGOs
have depoliticized the struggle for gender equality. By building upon Kabeer’s discussion of
agency in addition to Sen’s capabilities approach and Moser’s distinction between practical and
strategic gender needs, it seeks to demonstrate that the NGO approach of microfinance, skills
training and awareness campaigns address pragmatic needs while leaving the structural causes of
women’s subordination untouched. It then goes on to examine the ways in which donor-driven
design excludes rural and religious-minority women, with a particular reference to the Benazir
Income Support Programme and how the depoliticized logic of charity has made its way into state
policy. This paper concludes by arguing that women’s empowerment is a political responsibility
of the state that cannot be delegated to NGOs

articles_hidden.title: Urban–Rural Gaps in Household Living Conditions in Nepal: Evidence from the 2022 Nepal Demographic and Health Survey
articles_hidden.authors: Porokmi Sambahamphe
articles_hidden.abstract: In 2022, 94 percent of rural Nepali households had electricity, while 21 percent used a clean main cooking fuel. Using 13,786 households from the 2022 Nepal Demographic and Health Survey, I compare nine living conditions across urban and rural municipalities. The largest urban advantages are in clean cooking fuel, finished floors, and finished walls. After adjusting for geography, household assets, and household-head characteristics, the gaps are 18, 15, and 13 percentage points. For housing materials and crowding, the estimated urban gap is 0.357 index points with an asset measure that excludes the outcomes. Adding the three building-material indicators to that measure lowers the estimate to 0.122. Nearly half of the households lacking clean cooking fuel, a finished floor, and finished walls live in urban municipalities. A rural-only rule would reach 51 percent of these households, while a rule based on missing at least one basic service would reach 41 percent.

articles_hidden.title: Measuring Couples' Gender Composition: Evaluating Partner Proxy Reporting on a Two-Step Gender Identity Measure
articles_hidden.authors: Christopher A Julian; Wendy Manning; Alexandra VanBergen; Claire M Kamp Dush
articles_hidden.abstract: Many household surveys rely on proxy reports, in which one respondent answers for other household members. Two-step gender identity measures are well-tested for self-identification. Far less research has tested these measures for partner-proxy reports of couples' gender composition. Using dyadic data from the National Couples' Health and Time Study (NCHAT), we evaluated proxy reporting among partnered adults aged 20–60. Nonresponse to proxy reports of sex assigned at birth and current gender identity was comparable to self-reports, and similar to or lower than proxy nonresponse for other demographic characteristics. Proxy and self-reports on these measures showed high agreement, meeting or exceeding levels observed for other demographic measures. Within the two-step measure, congruence was lower for self-identified transgender or gender-diverse partners than for self-identified cisgender partners. Among discordant reports, proxies were also more likely to report a self-identified transgender or gender-diverse partner as cisgender than to report a self-identified cisgender partner as transgender or gender-diverse. Overall, our findings provide new insights into partner-proxy reporting of gender identity and reveal a directional pattern of discordance that warrants further attention. This study is one step toward better measuring gender diversity within couples and underscores the need to intentionally include couples with an LGBTQ+ partner in data collection.

articles_hidden.title: From Revolutionary Warfare to Humanitarian Internationalism: Cuba, African Liberation, and the Evolution of Revolutionary Legitimacy in the Global South
articles_hidden.authors: Ifoh
articles_hidden.abstract: Comparative scholarship on revolution has largely emphasized insurgency, political rupture, and the seizure of state power, whilst paying less attention to how revolutionary legitimacy is reconstructed internationally after armed struggle recedes. This article examines that problem through Cuba’s evolving engagement with African liberation and Global South humanitarian internationalism. It develops the concept of Humanitarian Revolutionary Legitimacy (HRL) to explain how revolutionary states reconstruct claims to moral authority by translating histories of anti-imperial struggle and sacrifice into humanitarian solidarity and South–South cooperation. Tracing Cuba’s trajectory from guerrilla revolution through military internationalism in Angola and the anti-apartheid struggle to post-Cold War medical diplomacy, the article argues that revolutionary legitimacy can endure through changing practices of solidarity. Yet this legitimacy remains contested: humanitarian commitment coexists with state interests, economic benefits, labour tensions, and domestic racial inequalities. The Cuban case therefore reveals revolutionary legitimacy not as inherited moral authority, but as an evolving and contested historical process.
